pillars.label: Mechanism and Etiology
pillars.text: Hypopituitarism and growth hormone deficiency (GHD) arise from congenital developmental mutations (HESX1, PROP1, POU1F1/PIT1, LHX3, LHX4, OTX2, SOX2, SOX3) affecting pituitary ontogeny, GHRH receptor defects, or acquired insults including craniopharyngiomas, CNS germinomas, histiocytosis, traumatic brain injury, and cranial irradiation (threshold ≥18 Gy, highest risk ≥30 Gy).

pillars.label: Clinical Recognition
pillars.text: Severe neonatal presentation includes recurrent hypoglycemia, prolonged conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and micropenis with cryptorchidism in males. Childhood presentation features progressive deceleration of linear growth velocity (<25th percentile or <4-5 cm/year), delayed bone age, truncal adiposity, midfacial hypoplasia with frontal bossing, and a high-pitched voice.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Workup
pillars.text: Evaluation requires auxology, screening IGF-I and IGFBP-3 (standardized for age, sex, and pubertal stage), and two provocative GH stimulation tests (clonidine, arginine, glucagon, or insulin tolerance test) demonstrating peak GH <7-10 mcg/L. Sex-steroid priming (estrogen or testosterone) is recommended in prepubertal boys ≥11 years and girls ≥10 years with bone age delay to prevent false-positive failures. Brain/pituitary MRI assesses structural integrity, stalk interruption, ectopic neurohypophysis, or intracranial neoplasms.

pillars.label: Treatment and Interventions
pillars.text: Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH/somatropin) is initiated at 22-35 mcg/kg/day (0.16-0.24 mg/kg/week) subcutaneously daily at bedtime. Dose titration is monitored by linear growth velocity, clinical response, and keeping serum IGF-I within the normal reference range (-1 to +1.5 SDS). Concomitant anterior pituitary axes (TSH, ACTH, gonadotropins) must be monitored, as GH replacement accelerates peripheral T4-to-T3 deiodination and may unmask central hypothyroidism.

pillars.label: Outcomes and Safety
pillars.text: Short-term adverse effects include benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri, presenting with headache and papilledema), slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE, presenting with hip/knee pain and limp), scoliosis progression during rapid catch-up growth, and fluid retention. Long-term surveillance indicates no increased risk of primary tumor recurrence in childhood cancer survivors, though secondary solid neoplasm surveillance is maintained.

cards.q: What classic triad in a male neonate strongly suggests congenital anterior pituitary hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Hypoglycemia, prolonged conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and micropenis (with or without undescended testes).

cards.q: Why is sex-steroid priming utilized prior to provocative GH stimulation testing in peripubertal children?
cards.a: Peripubertal children with constitutional growth delay have transient physiological hyposecretion of GH; priming with estrogen or testosterone enhances pituitary somatotroph responsiveness and prevents false-positive failure on provocative tests.

cards.q: What triad of findings on pituitary MRI defines the Pituitary Stalk Interruption Syndrome (PSIS)?
cards.a: An interrupted or absent (thin) pituitary infundibular stalk, an ectopic posterior pituitary bright spot (typically at the median eminence), and severe anterior pituitary hypoplasia.

cards.q: Mutations in which pituitary-specific transcription factor produce combined deficiencies of GH, TSH, and Prolactin while initially sparing ACTH and gonadotropins?
cards.a: POU1F1 (also known as PIT1), whereas PROP1 mutations cause progressive deficiency of GH, TSH, PRL, LH/FSH, and eventually ACTH in adulthood.

cards.q: What is the recommended initial daily starting dose of somatropin for pediatric isolated or combined GHD?
cards.a: 22 to 35 mcg/kg/day (0.16 to 0.24 mg/kg/week) administered as a daily subcutaneous injection at bedtime.

cards.q: A 10-year-old child 2 months into somatropin therapy develops persistent morning headaches and diplopia. What complication must be evaluated by funduscopic examination?
cards.a: Benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri), characterized by papilledema and elevated cerebrospinal fluid opening pressure, requiring temporary cessation or dose reduction.

cards.q: What orthopedic condition should be suspected in a patient on somatropin who develops groin, hip, or referred knee pain with an antalgic limp?
cards.a: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), related to rapid chondrocyte proliferation and structural biomechanical stress at the proximal femoral growth plate.

mcqs.q: A 2-week-old male infant born at term presents with lethargy, a blood glucose of 28 mg/dL, and a total bilirubin of 9.2 mg/dL with a direct fraction of 4.1 mg/dL. Physical examination reveals a stretched penile length of 1.6 cm (reference >2.5 cm) and bilateral descended testes. Thyroid-stimulating hormone is 1.8 mIU/L with free T4 0.6 ng/dL (reference 0.9-2.0 ng/dL). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Immediate critical blood draw for cortisol, GH, and insulin, administration of IV dextrose and hydrocortisone, followed by pituitary MRI
High-dose oral diazoxide therapy for presumed primary congenital hyperinsulinism
Recombinant human growth hormone monotherapy at 50 mcg/kg/day
Observation with frequent feeding intervals and repeat bilirubin in 4 weeks
mcqs.explanation: The infant exhibits the classic presentation of congenital hypopituitarism: neonatal hypoglycemia, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, micropenis, and central hypothyroidism. Prompt evaluation of adrenal status and hydrocortisone replacement are lifesaving before initiating other hormone therapies.

option_notes.text: Critical blood draw during hypoglycemia and immediate hydrocortisone replacement prevent fatal adrenal crisis in congenital hypopituitarism.
Diazoxide treats hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia but does not address central adrenal insufficiency or multiple pituitary deficiencies.
Administering GH before establishing adequate cortisol replacement can precipitate acute adrenal collapse due to increased glucocorticoid clearance.
Observation is contraindicated because untreated neonatal hypoglycemia and central adrenal crisis carry severe mortality and neurodevelopmental morbidity.

mcqs.q: An 11-year-old boy with severe short stature (height SDS -3.2) and growth velocity of 3.2 cm/year undergoes evaluation. Baseline IGF-I is below the 5th percentile. His bone age is 8.5 years and testicular volume is 2 mL bilaterally. Before performing provocative testing with arginine and clonidine, what step should be taken to optimize diagnostic accuracy?
options: Priming with intramuscular testosterone enanthate or oral estrogen 2-3 days prior to testing
Performing an oral glucose tolerance test to rule out reactive hypoglycemia
Withholding evaluation until chronological age 14 years regardless of growth velocity
Administering a trial of oral levothyroxine for 6 months before biochemical testing
mcqs.explanation: In prepubertal boys older than 11 years with bone age delay, sex-steroid priming primes the somatotroph axis, preventing false-positive subnormal GH peaks that occur because of constitutional delay of puberty.

option_notes.text: Sex-steroid priming enhances endogenous somatotroph responsiveness in peripubertal children with delayed maturation, avoiding misdiagnosis of true GHD.
Oral glucose tolerance testing is used to evaluate GH excess/acromegaly through GH suppression, not somatotroph reserve deficiency.
Delaying evaluation until age 14 causes permanent loss of linear height potential during critical prepubertal growing years.
Empiric levothyroxine in a euthyroid child does not correct somatotroph hyposecretion and may cause thyrotoxicosis.

mcqs.q: A 7-year-old girl with confirmed isolated somatotroph deficiency begins subcutaneous somatropin at 30 mcg/kg/day. At her 3-month follow-up, she has grown 3.0 cm, but routine lab testing reveals a drop in free T4 from 1.2 ng/dL to 0.7 ng/dL (reference 0.8-1.8 ng/dL) with an unchanged normal TSH of 2.1 mIU/L. What is the physiological mechanism explaining this finding?
options: Enhanced peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and unmasking of incipient central hypothyroidism
Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells induced by recombinant protein antibodies
Competitive inhibition of thyroid iodine uptake by circulating somatropin molecules
False laboratory assay interference between growth hormone and thyroglobulin
mcqs.explanation: Growth hormone replacement stimulates hepatic and peripheral 5'-deiodinase activity, accelerating conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3). In patients with underlying pituitary pathology, this can unmask central hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine supplementation.

option_notes.text: Growth hormone therapy accelerates peripheral T4-to-T3 deiodination, reducing serum free T4 and revealing central hypothyroidism in patients with subclinical TSH deficiency.
Somatropin does not elicit autoimmune thyroiditis or anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody formation.
Somatropin has no structural or pharmacological mechanism to inhibit the sodium-iodide symporter.
Modern automated chemiluminescent free T4 assays have zero cross-reactivity with somatropin.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old boy who received 24 Gy of prophylactic cranial irradiation for acute lymphoblastic leukemia at age 5 is evaluated for linear growth failure. His height velocity is 2.8 cm/year. What is the pathophysiology of his radiation-induced somatotroph impairment?
options: Hypothalamic radiation injury with loss of pulsatile GHRH secretion and decreased somatotroph reserve
Direct total destruction of pituitary thyrotrophs with sparing of somatotrophs
Primary gonadal failure causing premature epiphyseal closure without pituitary involvement
Peripheral end-organ resistance due to radiation-induced growth hormone receptor mutations
mcqs.explanation: Cranial irradiation at doses ≥18-24 Gy preferentially damages hypothalamic regulatory neurons, causing blunted GHRH secretion and diminished somatotroph pulse amplitude (neurosecretory dysfunction), making somatotroph deficiency the earliest and most frequent post-radiation endocrinopathy.

option_notes.text: Radiation doses ≥18 Gy preferentially damage hypothalamic GHRH-secreting neurons; GHD is the most sensitive and earliest endocrinopathy after cranial irradiation.
Somatotrophs and hypothalamic GHRH neurons are far more radiosensitive than thyrotrophs or corticotrophs.
Prophylactic cranial irradiation does not cause direct gonadal destruction; precocious puberty may occur from hypothalamic disinhibition, but the primary growth failure is somatotroph loss.
Radiation damages CNS neuroendocrine architecture, not the genetic coding sequence of somatic GH receptors.

mcqs.q: A 13-year-old boy with isolated short stature and delayed bone age undergoes genetic evaluation. Sequencing demonstrates a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the POU1F1 (PIT1) gene. Which constellation of anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies is characteristically produced by this defect?
options: Deficiencies of Growth Hormone, Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone, and Prolactin, with normal ACTH and LH/FSH
Panhypopituitarism involving all anterior hormones plus central diabetes insipidus
Isolated adrenocorticotropic hormone deficiency with preserved somatotroph function
Combined LH and FSH deficiency with intact GH, TSH, and ACTH
mcqs.explanation: POU1F1 (PIT1) is a POU-domain homeobox transcription factor required for the differentiation and maintenance of somatotrophs, thyrotrophs, and lactotrophs. Mutations cause combined GH, TSH, and PRL deficiency, while corticotrophs and gonadotrophs remain intact.

option_notes.text: POU1F1/PIT1 specifically directs the lineage differentiation of somatotrophs, thyrotrophs, and lactotrophs, leaving corticotrophs and gonadotrophs unaffected.
Central diabetes insipidus arises from neurohypophyseal or vasopressinergic hypothalamic defects, not POU1F1, which is anterior pituitary-specific.
Isolated ACTH deficiency is caused by TPIT mutations, not POU1F1.
Isolated gonadotropin deficiency is caused by GnRHR, KISS1R, or TACR3 mutations, leaving GH and TSH unaffected.

etiology.text: Etiologies include developmental gene defects (HESX1, PROP1, POU1F1, LHX3, LHX4, OTX2, SOX2, SOX3), GHRH receptor mutations, and acquired lesions including craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, histiocytosis, trauma, and cranial irradiation.

epidemiology.text: Congenital isolated growth hormone deficiency occurs with an incidence of approximately 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 10,000 live births. Acquired causes represent a significant proportion of pediatric endocrinopathy in cancer survivors who received cranial radiotherapy.

diagnostics.text: Diagnostic evaluation integrates auxology, bone age radiography, serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3, two pharmacological GH stimulation tests demonstrating peak GH <7-10 mcg/L, and high-resolution pituitary MRI.

therapies.text: Recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin) is administered subcutaneously daily at bedtime at a dosage of 22–35 mcg/kg/day (0.16–0.24 mg/kg/week). Dosing is adjusted according to growth velocity, weight changes, and serum IGF-I concentrations maintained within the age- and sex-adjusted reference range.

pillars.label: Mechanism and Molecular Etiology
pillars.text: Growth hormone insensitivity (GHI, or Laron syndrome) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous inactivating mutations in the growth hormone receptor (GHR) gene, or downstream defects in STAT5B, PTPN11, IGF1, IGFALS, IGF1R, and PAPP-A2. The classic defect impairs GHR homodimerization or intracellular Jak2-STAT signaling, causing extreme IGF-I deficiency despite normal or markedly elevated circulating GH levels.

pillars.label: Clinical Presentation
pillars.text: Patients exhibit extreme short stature (height SDS -4 to -10), severe midfacial hypoplasia with prominent forehead and depressed nasal bridge ('doll-like' facies), blue sclerae, high-pitched voice, sparse hair, small hands and feet (acromicria), micropenis in males, delayed dentition, marked truncal adiposity, and recurrent fasting hypoglycemia in infancy.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Evaluation
pillars.text: Biochemical hallmarks are elevated basal and stimulated serum GH with severely decreased or undetectable serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3. In extracellular GHR mutations, serum growth hormone-binding protein (GHBP) is low or undetectable. The IGF-I generation test confirms insensitivity: failure of serum IGF-I to rise significantly following 4-7 days of daily rhGH administration (0.1 mg/kg/day).

pillars.label: Treatment and Interventions
pillars.text: Because endogenous GH action is impaired, rhGH is ineffective. Treatment requires recombinant human insulin-like growth factor-1 (rhIGF-I / mecasermin) administered subcutaneously twice daily at an initial dose of 40-80 mcg/kg/dose, titrating to a maximum of 120 mcg/kg/dose twice daily. Mecasermin must be taken shortly before or immediately after a carbohydrate-containing meal or snack to prevent hypoglycemia.

pillars.label: Safety and Outcomes
pillars.text: Primary adverse effects of rhIGF-I include hypoglycemia (mitigated by carbohydrate co-ingestion), lymphoid tissue hypertrophy (tonsillar and adenoidal enlargement causing sleep apnea), coarsening of facial features, and intracranial hypertension. Interestingly, homozygous GHR mutation carriers (such as the Ecuadorian cohort) display near-complete protection from cancer and type 2 diabetes despite severe obesity.

cards.q: What discordant biochemical profile distinguishes classic growth hormone insensitivity from growth hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Elevated or normal circulating GH levels combined with profoundly depressed or undetectable serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3.

cards.q: Why is serum growth hormone-binding protein (GHBP) undetectable in classic Laron syndrome?
cards.a: GHBP is generated by proteolytic cleavage of the extracellular domain of the GHR; mutations affecting the extracellular domain prevent GHBP production and release into the circulation.

cards.q: What approved pharmacological agent is indicated for children with severe primary IGF-I deficiency due to GHR mutations?
cards.a: Recombinant human IGF-I (mecasermin), dosed at 40 to 120 mcg/kg subcutaneously twice daily with meals.

cards.q: What critical administration guideline must be followed with every mecasermin injection to prevent an acute medical emergency?
cards.a: Mecasermin must be injected immediately before or after a meal or carbohydrate snack to prevent severe, life-threatening hypoglycemia.

cards.q: Mutations in STAT5B cause severe growth failure combined with which distinct non-endocrine clinical feature?
cards.a: Severe immune deficiency with eczema, recurrent pulmonary infections, and autoimmune lymphoproliferation, due to impaired regulatory T-cell signaling.

cards.q: What molecular defect causes moderate short stature with markedly low IGF-I and IGFBP-3, but normal free IGF-I and no hypoglycemia?
cards.a: IGFALS (acid-labile subunit) gene mutations, which disrupt formation of the 150-kDa circulating ternary complex but leave binary complexes intact.

cards.q: What unexpected long-term metabolic finding has been documented in Ecuadorian cohorts with homozygous E180splice GHR mutations?
cards.a: Near-total protection from malignant neoplasms (cancer) and clinical type 2 diabetes mellitus despite marked lifelong obesity.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with severe proportional short stature (height SDS -5.4), frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, small hands and feet, and high-pitched voice. Laboratory investigation shows basal serum GH 38 ng/mL (reference <5 ng/mL) and peak stimulated GH 64 ng/mL. Serum IGF-I is <15 ng/mL (reference 50-250 ng/mL) and IGFBP-3 is undetectable. A 4-day IGF-I generation test with high-dose rhGH yields no increase in serum IGF-I. What is the most likely molecular diagnosis?
options: Homozygous inactivating mutation in the Growth Hormone Receptor (GHR) gene
Pituitary adenoma secreting bioinactive growth hormone
Homozygous mutation in the GHRH receptor gene
Isolated neurosecretory growth hormone deficiency
mcqs.explanation: High circulating GH with undetectable IGF-I, unresponsiveness to exogenous rhGH in an IGF-I generation test, and classic craniofacial dysmorphism are diagnostic of severe growth hormone insensitivity (Laron syndrome) due to GHR mutations.

option_notes.text: Inactivating GHR mutations prevent downstream intracellular signaling and IGF-I synthesis despite massive endogenous or exogenous GH.
A bioinactive GH would respond to exogenous wild-type rhGH with a prompt rise in serum IGF-I on the generation test.
GHRH receptor mutations cause profound GH deficiency with low, not elevated, serum GH levels.
Neurosecretory dysfunction exhibits low 24-hour integrated GH secretion and normal responsiveness to rhGH replacement.

mcqs.q: A 6-year-old girl with confirmed severe primary IGF-I deficiency due to GHR exon deletion is prescribed mecasermin. Which instruction is mandatory for her parents to minimize the most frequent serious adverse effect of this therapy?
options: Administer each subcutaneous injection within 20 minutes before or after a meal or carbohydrate snack
Administer the injection strictly while fasting first thing in the morning
Co-administer a sodium polystyrene sulfonate resin to bind potassium
Limit fluid intake to less than 500 mL per day to prevent acute hypernatremia
mcqs.explanation: Because IGF-I possesses approximately 10% of the insulin receptor-activating potency of insulin, rhIGF-I induces rapid hypoglycemia. Injections must be paired with carbohydrate-containing food.

option_notes.text: Co-ingestion of carbohydrates with rhIGF-I prevents severe acute neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.
Fasting administration of rhIGF-I triggers severe hypoglycemic seizures.
rhIGF-I does not cause hyperkalemia; ion-exchange resins are irrelevant.
Fluid restriction is contraindicated and has no role in mecasermin management.

mcqs.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with severe short stature (height SDS -4.8), severe generalized eczema, autoimmune thyroiditis, and recurrent bacterial pneumonia. Endocrine labs show peak GH 42 ng/mL and undetectable IGF-I. Genetic testing is most likely to identify a mutation in which gene?
options: STAT5B
GH1
POU1F1
GHRHR
mcqs.explanation: STAT5B is essential both for growth hormone receptor signal transduction in hepatocytes and for IL-2 receptor signaling in regulatory T cells. Inactivating STAT5B mutations uniquely combine severe growth failure with profound immune dysregulation.

option_notes.text: STAT5B mutations cause a distinct clinical syndrome combining growth hormone insensitivity with severe immunodeficiency and autoimmunity.
GH1 mutations cause isolated growth hormone deficiency without immunological compromise.
POU1F1 mutations cause combined GH, TSH, and Prolactin deficiency without primary immunodeficiency.
GHRHR mutations cause isolated GHD without autoimmune lung disease or eczema.

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old boy with mild short stature (height SDS -2.3) is evaluated. Laboratory testing reveals serum IGF-I SDS -3.4 and IGFBP-3 SDS -3.8. Surprisingly, his serum free IGF-I concentration is within normal limits, and he has never experienced hypoglycemia. What molecular defect accounts for this dissociation?
options: Inactivating mutation in the IGFALS gene encoding the acid-labile subunit
Complete deletion of the extracellular domain of the growth hormone receptor
Homozygous missense mutation in the insulin receptor gene (INSR)
Severe pituitary stalk transection with panhypopituitarism
mcqs.explanation: Acid-labile subunit (ALS) deficiency prevents formation of the 150-kDa ternary complex (IGF-I, IGFBP-3, ALS), accelerating clearance of bound IGF-I and leading to markedly reduced total IGF-I and IGFBP-3. However, free active IGF-I is preserved, resulting in only mild height reduction without hypoglycemia.

option_notes.text: ALS deficiency impairs ternary complex assembly, severely lowering circulating total IGF-I and IGFBP-3 while free IGF-I remains relatively preserved.
Complete GHR deletion produces extreme short stature (SDS -5 to -10) and very low free IGF-I with fasting hypoglycemia.
INSR mutations cause Donohue or Rabson-Mendenhall syndromes with extreme hyperinsulinemia and acanthosis nigricans.
Pituitary stalk transection produces multiple anterior hormone deficiencies and low free IGF-I.

mcqs.q: A 9-year-old boy with severe Laron syndrome has been treated with mecasermin (120 mcg/kg twice daily) for 2 years. His parents note new-onset loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. Examination demonstrates marked enlargement of the palatine tonsils and adenoidal facies. What is the underlying cause of this finding?
options: IGF-I-mediated stimulation of lymphoid tissue proliferation in Waldeyer's ring
Recurrent streptococcal pharyngitis secondary to acquired agammaglobulinemia
Skeletal compression of the nasopharynx by acromegalic bone overgrowth
Allergic reaction to the preservative in the mecasermin formulation
mcqs.explanation: Mecasermin therapy commonly stimulates the growth of lymphoid tissues, particularly the tonsils and adenoids, which express high densities of IGF-I receptors. This can lead to upper airway obstruction and obstructive sleep apnea requiring surgical adenotonsillectomy.

option_notes.text: Tonsillar and adenoidal hypertrophy is a recognized adverse effect of rhIGF-I therapy due to strong mitogenic stimulation of lymphoid tissue.
rhIGF-I does not cause agammaglobulinemia or selective humoral immunodeficiency.
Patients with GHI do not develop acromegalic bony overgrowth; their cranial growth remains delayed.
Lymphoid hypertrophy is a direct pharmacodynamic effect of IGF-I, not an allergic contact reaction.

etiology.text: Etiologies include homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in GHR, STAT5B, PTPN11, IGF1, IGFALS, IGF1R, and PAPP-A2, producing insensitivity to growth hormone or impaired IGF-I generation.

epidemiology.text: Autosomal recessive GHI is rare globally but occurs with high prevalence in consanguineous populations and in specific genetic isolates, notably in southern Ecuador (E180splice GHR mutation) and Mediterranean regions.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis is confirmed by normal to elevated GH with severely low IGF-I/IGFBP-3, low or absent serum GHBP (in extracellular GHR defects), lack of IGF-I response to exogenous rhGH in an IGF-I generation test, and targeted genetic sequencing.

therapies.text: Recombinant human IGF-I (mecasermin) is indicated for severe primary IGF-I deficiency at an initial dose of 40–80 mcg/kg subcutaneously twice daily, titrated up to a maximum of 120 mcg/kg twice daily. Injections must be administered with or immediately after a meal or snack.

pillars.label: Definitions and Categorization
pillars.text: Idiopathic Short Stature (ISS) describes children whose height is >2.25 SD below the population mean (<1.2th percentile) with normal birth weight/length, normal body proportions, no evidence of systemic, endocrine, nutritional, or chromosomal abnormalities, and normal growth hormone sufficiency. Normal variants include Familial Short Stature (FSS) and Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP).

pillars.label: Auxologic Differentiation
pillars.text: In FSS, bone age is consistent with chronological age, growth velocity is normal, and height tracks along or slightly below the target midparental height. In CDGP, bone age is delayed (typically 2-4 years), growth deceleration occurs during infancy and late childhood, onset of puberty is delayed, but growth continues for a longer duration, resulting in an adult height near midparental target.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Evaluation
pillars.text: Evaluation includes serial auxology (height velocity over ≥6-12 months), target midparental height calculation, left hand/wrist bone age radiography, and exclusion of occult pathology (celiac serology, CBC, ESR, renal/hepatic panels, thyroid function, karyotype/microarray in girls to rule out Turner syndrome). GH testing shows normal peak GH (≥10 mcg/L).

pillars.label: Management Options
pillars.text: For CDGP, reassurance and observation are first line; in boys ≥14 years with psychosocial distress, a short course of low-dose testosterone (50-100 mg IM monthly for 3-6 months) accelerates secondary sexual characteristics and linear growth without accelerating bone age disproportionately. For severe ISS (height SDS <-2.25 with predicted adult height <-2 SD), FDA-approved rhGH (somatropin) at 0.30-0.37 mg/kg/week (43-53 mcg/kg/day) produces an average adult height gain of 3.5-7.5 cm.

pillars.label: Outcomes and Prognosis
pillars.text: Height gains with somatropin are variable; early age at initiation, higher dose, greater degree of short stature, and adherence predict superior response. Aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole) can delay epiphyseal fusion in adolescent males, though bone health and long-term vertebral outcomes require cautious monitoring.

cards.q: How does bone age typically differ between Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP) and Familial Short Stature (FSS)?
cards.a: In CDGP, bone age is significantly delayed relative to chronological age; in FSS, bone age is consistent with chronological age.

cards.q: How is midparental target height calculated for a boy and a girl?
cards.a: Boy: [Father's height + (Mother's height + 13 cm)] / 2. Girl: [(Father's height - 13 cm) + Mother's height] / 2.

cards.q: What height threshold defines Idiopathic Short Stature (ISS) for consideration of growth hormone therapy?
cards.a: Height more than 2.25 standard deviations below the mean (height SDS <-2.25 or approximately below the 1.2th percentile) with poor predicted adult height.

cards.q: What regimen of low-dose androgen is used to jumpstart growth in adolescent boys with constitutional delay and severe psychosocial distress?
cards.a: Testosterone enanthate or cypionate 50 to 100 mg intramuscularly once monthly for 3 to 6 months.

cards.q: What is the typical FDA-approved somatropin dose range for idiopathic short stature?
cards.a: 0.30 to 0.37 mg/kg/week (approximately 43 to 53 mcg/kg/day) given by daily subcutaneous injection.

cards.q: What class of medication is sometimes combined with GH in adolescent males with short stature to slow bone age maturation?
cards.a: Aromatase inhibitors (e.g., anastrozole, letrozole), which block the conversion of androgens to estrogens in growth plate chondrocytes.

cards.q: Why is a karyotype or chromosomal microarray indicated in every girl presenting with unexplained short stature, even without dysmorphic features?
cards.a: To rule out Turner syndrome (such as mosaic 45,X/46,XX), where short stature may be the only presenting physical feature in up to 10% of cases.

mcqs.q: A 14.5-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of short stature and lack of pubertal development. His height is at the 1st percentile (height SDS -2.3). His father had a pubertal growth spurt at age 17 and his mother entered menarche at 14. Physical exam shows prepubertal Tanner stage 1 pubic hair and testicular volume of 3 mL bilaterally. Radiograph of the left hand and wrist reveals a bone age of 11.5 years. Provocative GH testing with clonidine yields a peak GH of 14 ng/mL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP)
Familial Short Stature (FSS)
Classical Isolated Growth Hormone Deficiency
Primary Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism with Kallmann Syndrome
mcqs.explanation: A family history of late maturation, delayed bone age (>2 years behind chronological age), prepubertal status at age 14.5, and normal peak GH (>10 ng/mL) characterize constitutional delay of growth and puberty.

option_notes.text: Delayed bone age, paternal history of delayed growth spurt, and intact GH reserve are diagnostic of CDGP.
In familial short stature, bone age is consistent with chronological age and adult height remains short.
The peak GH of 14 ng/mL (>10 ng/mL) excludes classical growth hormone deficiency.
Permanent hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is rare and typically accompanied by microphallus or anosmia; bone age delay and family history point to CDGP.

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. Her height is at the 0.5th percentile (height SDS -2.6). Her midparental target height is at the 25th percentile. Past medical history and systemic review are negative. Laboratory workup reveals normal CBC, ESR, tissue transglutaminase IgA, thyroid panel, and electrolyte panel. Bone age is 8.0 years. What diagnostic step must be completed before categorizing her condition as idiopathic short stature?
options: Karyotype or chromosomal microarray to exclude Turner syndrome
Immediate 24-hour urinary free cortisol measurement
Skeletal survey to look for osteogenesis imperfecta type IV
Diagnostic renal biopsy to evaluate for occult nephritis
mcqs.explanation: Guidelines recommend karyotype or chromosomal microarray in all girls presenting with unexplained short stature, as mosaic Turner syndrome frequently presents without overt classical physical stigmas.

option_notes.text: Chromosomal analysis is mandatory in any short female lacking an overt cause to detect non-dysmorphic Turner syndrome.
Cushing syndrome presents with weight gain crossing percentiles upwards alongside growth cessation, not isolated short stature.
Osteogenesis imperfecta features recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, and skeletal deformity.
Renal biopsy is invasive and unwarranted in a child with normal urinalysis, BUN, creatinine, and electrolytes.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old boy with constitutional delay of growth and puberty is experiencing severe depression and bullying due to short stature (height SDS -2.4, bone age 11.5 years). He has prepubertal genitalia. Which management strategy provides safe, targeted acceleration of linear growth without causing premature epiphyseal fusion?
options: Short-course intramuscular testosterone enanthate 50 mg monthly for 3 to 6 months
Oral ethinyl estradiol 50 mcg daily for 1 year
High-dose recombinant human growth hormone at 0.48 mg/kg/week until adult height
Continuous GnRH agonist therapy for 2 years
mcqs.explanation: Low-dose testosterone (50-100 mg IM monthly for 3-6 months) is a safe, established intervention in adolescent boys ≥14 years with constitutional delay to promote linear growth and virilization without prematurely advancing epiphyseal fusion.

option_notes.text: Low-dose androgen therapy promotes growth velocity and virilization while preserving adult height potential in adolescent constitutional delay.
Estrogen therapy in males causes feminization and accelerates epiphyseal fusion.
Somatropin is not indicated for simple constitutional delay of growth and puberty in a child with normal adult height prediction.
GnRH agonists suppress pubertal development and worsen growth deceleration in delayed puberty.

mcqs.q: A 9-year-old boy has non-familial idiopathic short stature with height SDS -2.7 and a Bayley-Pinneau predicted adult height of 156 cm (SDS -2.8). The family elects to initiate FDA-approved somatropin therapy. Based on clinical trial evidence, what is the expected average adult height gain associated with somatropin therapy in this setting?
options: Approximately 3.5 to 7.5 cm (1.4 to 3 inches) above untreated predicted height
Approximately 15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches) above untreated predicted height
Zero change in adult height compared to untreated controls
A net decrease in adult height due to accelerated skeletal maturation
mcqs.explanation: Meta-analyses and randomized trials of somatropin in idiopathic short stature demonstrate an average adult height gain of 3.5 to 7.5 cm, with significant individual variation depending on starting age, dose, and adherence.

option_notes.text: Published trials demonstrate an average height benefit of 3.5 to 7.5 cm in children with idiopathic short stature treated with somatropin.
Gains of 15 to 20 cm are unrealistic and not supported by pediatric clinical trial data.
Controlled studies demonstrate statistically significant height gains over untreated controls.
Somatropin does not disproportionately advance bone age in ISS; it does not reduce adult height.

mcqs.q: An 11-year-old boy presents for short stature evaluation. His height is at the 3rd percentile, his father is 162 cm (5th percentile), and his mother is 148 cm (3rd percentile). His bone age is 11.0 years, matching his chronological age. His height velocity has been 5.2 cm/year over the past 2 years. Which diagnostic entity best accounts for these findings?
options: Familial Short Stature
Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty
Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
Primary Growth Hormone Insensitivity
mcqs.explanation: Familial short stature is characterized by short parents, child's height tracking near midparental target, normal annual height velocity (5 cm/year), and a bone age that matches chronological age.

option_notes.text: Familial short stature features normal growth velocity, concordant bone age, and height tracking within target midparental expectations.
Constitutional delay is distinguished by delayed bone age (>1.5-2 years behind) and delayed pubertal timing.
Craniopharyngioma typically presents with severe growth deceleration (<4 cm/yr), headaches, or visual field deficits.
Growth hormone insensitivity produces severe growth failure (SDS <-4) and markedly delayed bone age.

etiology.text: Idiopathic short stature encompasses heterogeneous non-pathological variations in growth without identifiable systemic, endocrine, or nutritional defects, including polygenic familial short stature and constitutional delay of growth and puberty.

epidemiology.text: By statistical definition, children with heights more than 2 SD below the mean comprise 2.3% of the pediatric population, the majority of whom have non-pathological short stature.

diagnostics.text: Evaluation requires serial height velocity measurement, midparental target height calculation, bone age radiography, basic metabolic/celiac screening, and exclusion of Turner syndrome in females.

therapies.text: For severe idiopathic short stature (height SDS <-2.25 with projected adult height <-2 SD), somatropin is FDA-approved at doses of 0.30–0.37 mg/kg/week (43–53 mcg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection. For adolescent males with CDGP and psychological distress, testosterone enanthate 50–100 mg IM monthly for 3–6 months can be considered.

pillars.label: Definition and Catch-Up Dynamics
pillars.text: Small for Gestational Age (SGA) is defined as birth weight and/or length ≥2 standard deviations below the mean for gestational age and sex (<2.3rd percentile). Approximately 85-90% of SGA infants demonstrate spontaneous catch-up growth within the first 2 years of life (extended to 4 years in preterm infants). The 10-15% who fail to catch up remain at substantial risk for persistent short adult stature and adult metabolic disease.

pillars.label: Etiology and Pathophysiology
pillars.text: Etiologies include maternal factors (hypertension, preeclampsia, smoking, malnutrition), placental insufficiency, and fetal factors (chromosomal anomalies, genetic syndromes like Silver-Russell, and imprinted gene defects at 11p15 or 7p12). Pathophysiology involves relative growth hormone resistance, altered IGF-I bioactivity, reduced insulin sensitivity, and programmed metabolic adaptations.

pillars.label: Indications and Timing for rhGH
pillars.text: In the United States (FDA), somatropin is approved for children born SGA who fail to manifest catch-up growth by 2 years of age with persistent height SDS <-2.0. In Europe (EMA), the criteria specify age ≥4 years, height SDS <-2.5, and height velocity SDS <0. Early treatment (between ages 2-4 years) optimizes long-term catch-up and final adult height potential.

pillars.label: Dosing and Management
pillars.text: Approved rhGH dosing ranges from 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (35 to 70 mcg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection. Dose titrations are individualized according to initial growth velocity, age at initiation, and serum IGF-I concentrations. Height gains average 1.2 to 2.0 SDS, allowing the majority of treated children to reach adult heights within their target midparental range.

pillars.label: Safety and Metabolic Surveillance
pillars.text: Children born SGA have an intrinsic propensity toward visceral adiposity, hyperinsulinemia, and type 2 diabetes. While rhGH induces physiological insulin resistance during treatment, long-term studies demonstrate that fasting glucose remains stable, beta-cell reserve compensates, and adverse effects (e.g., pseudotumor cerebri, SCFE) occur at rates comparable to other GH-treated cohorts.

cards.q: What statistical criteria define an infant as born Small for Gestational Age (SGA)?
cards.a: Birth weight and/or birth length at least 2 standard deviations below the mean (SDS ≤ -2.0, <2.3rd percentile) for gestational age and sex.

cards.q: What percentage of children born SGA experience spontaneous catch-up growth to normal height by 2 years of age?
cards.a: Approximately 85% to 90%; the remaining 10% to 15% fail to catch up and are candidates for evaluation.

cards.q: What age and height criteria are required by the US FDA for initiating somatropin in a child born SGA?
cards.a: Age ≥ 2 years with height SDS ≤ -2.0 and documented failure to manifest catch-up growth.

cards.q: What is the approved somatropin dosage range for children born SGA without catch-up growth?
cards.a: 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (approximately 35 to 70 mcg/kg/day) given by daily subcutaneous injection.

cards.q: Which specific genetic syndrome presents with severe intrauterine growth restriction, body asymmetry, triangular facies, and fifth finger clinodactyly?
cards.a: Silver-Russell syndrome, associated with loss of methylation at 11p15.5 or maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 7.

cards.q: What long-term adult metabolic risks are increased in individuals born SGA who experience rapid post-infancy weight catch-up?
cards.a: Metabolic syndrome, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus, visceral obesity, and premature cardiovascular disease.

cards.q: What circulating biochemical marker is routinely monitored during somatropin therapy in SGA children to adjust dosage safely?
cards.a: Serum IGF-I concentration, maintaining levels within +1 to +2 SDS for age and pubertal stage.

mcqs.q: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature. She was born at 39 weeks gestation with a birth weight of 2100 g (SDS -2.4) and length of 44 cm (SDS -2.5). Her current height is at the 0.2nd percentile (height SDS -2.8). Extensive evaluation reveals normal systemic, renal, and thyroid function. Which statement regarding her management is correct according to clinical guidelines?
options: She meets FDA criteria for recombinant human growth hormone therapy because she is older than 2 years with persistent height SDS <-2.0
Growth hormone therapy is contraindicated until bone age reaches chronological age 10 years
She should be managed with high-calorie nutritional supplementation alone until pubertal onset
Growth hormone therapy should be withheld until provocative GH stimulation testing confirms peak GH <5 ng/mL
mcqs.explanation: Children born SGA who fail to manifest catch-up growth by age 2 years with persistent height SDS <-2.0 are eligible for FDA-approved somatropin therapy regardless of GH stimulation test results.

option_notes.text: FDA approval specifies age ≥2 years and persistent height SDS <-2.0 without spontaneous catch-up; GH stimulation testing is not required.
Delaying treatment until age 10 misses the critical prepubertal window for optimal catch-up growth.
Excessive high-calorie supplementation in SGA without catch-up induces rapid adiposity and worsens metabolic risk without improving linear height.
SGA children have relative GH resistance and normal or elevated stimulated GH; testing is not required for the SGA indication.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old boy born SGA at 38 weeks with birth weight 1950 g presents with height SDS -3.2. Physical exam reveals a prominent forehead, triangular facies, down-turned mouth, and significant hemihypotrophy of the left lower extremity. What is the most appropriate molecular testing to establish the diagnosis?
options: Methylation-specific multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MS-MLPA) for chromosome 11p15.5 and maternal UPD7
Sequencing of the GHR gene for Laron syndrome
Karyotype to evaluate for Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) for 22q11.2 deletion
mcqs.explanation: Triangular facies, relative macrocephaly, body asymmetry/hemihypotrophy, and severe intrauterine growth failure are the classic features of Silver-Russell syndrome, caused by loss of methylation at 11p15.5 (50%) or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 (10%).

option_notes.text: MS-MLPA detects 11p15.5 epimutations and maternal UPD7, the primary molecular etiologies of Silver-Russell syndrome.
GHR mutations cause Laron syndrome, which presents with symmetrical growth failure, not hemihypotrophy.
Klinefelter syndrome presents with tall stature, eunuchoid proportions, and gynecomastia.
22q11.2 deletion causes DiGeorge syndrome, featuring conotruncal cardiac defects, cleft palate, and hypocalcemia.

mcqs.q: A 5-year-old boy born SGA without catch-up growth begins somatropin at 45 mcg/kg/day. At baseline, his fasting blood glucose is 88 mg/dL and fasting insulin is 8 mcIU/mL. After 12 months, his growth velocity has accelerated from 4.0 to 9.2 cm/year. Repeat fasting labs show glucose 92 mg/dL and fasting insulin 16 mcIU/mL. What is the correct interpretation of these metabolic changes?
options: Physiological compensatory hyperinsulinemia secondary to the known anti-insulin actions of somatropin
Development of overt autoimmune type 1 diabetes requiring insulin initiation
Acute drug-induced ketoacidosis requiring immediate emergency hospitalization
Primary adrenal failure causing secondary reactive insulin hypersecretion
mcqs.explanation: Growth hormone possesses physiological anti-insulin (lipolytic and glycogenolytic) actions that mildly decrease peripheral insulin sensitivity, which is compensated for by an appropriate increase in fasting insulin without overt hyperglycemia.

option_notes.text: Somatropin induces mild peripheral insulin resistance that is normally compensated for by increased pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion.
Type 1 diabetes presents with absolute insulin deficiency, polyuria, weight loss, and marked hyperglycemia.
The patient has a normal glucose of 92 mg/dL with no acidosis or ketonemia.
Adrenal failure causes hypoglycemia and decreased insulin secretion, not compensatory hyperinsulinemia.

mcqs.q: A pediatric endocrinologist plans somatropin therapy for a 3-year-old child born SGA (height SDS -2.8). Which dosing strategy is supported by international consensus guidelines for optimizing adult height outcomes?
options: 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (35 to 70 mcg/kg/day), titrating according to growth response and serum IGF-I
Low-dose pulse therapy at 5 mcg/kg/day administered once weekly
A fixed adult dose of 4.0 mg per day regardless of patient weight
High-dose intramuscular injections of 200 mcg/kg administered every 3 months
mcqs.explanation: Standard consensus guidelines recommend somatropin at 35 to 70 mcg/kg/day (0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week) as daily subcutaneous injections, adjusting the dose to maintain serum IGF-I in the upper normal range (+1 to +2 SDS).

option_notes.text: Standard approved dosing is 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week given daily subcutaneously.
Weekly low-dose pulsing is ineffective for overcoming the relative GH resistance characteristic of SGA.
Fixed adult dosing in a 3-year-old child causes massive drug overdose and severe toxicity.
Infrequent depot bolus dosing is unphysiological and does not stimulate sustained chondrocyte linear proliferation.

mcqs.q: During routine follow-up of a 7-year-old girl born SGA receiving somatropin (40 mcg/kg/day), her serum IGF-I is measured at +3.2 SDS for age and sex. Her linear growth rate is excellent at 8.5 cm/year. What is the most appropriate management decision?
options: Reduce the somatropin dosage by 15-25% and recheck serum IGF-I in 3 to 6 months
Double the dose of somatropin to maximize peak pubertal height velocity
Discontinue therapy permanently and tell the parents no further growth is possible
Initiate high-dose hydrocortisone to suppress circulating IGF-I concentrations
mcqs.explanation: When serum IGF-I exceeds +2.0 to +2.5 SDS during somatropin therapy, consensus guidelines recommend dose reduction (typically 15-25%) to maintain IGF-I within safe physiological bounds while monitoring growth velocity.

option_notes.text: Reducing the dose brings IGF-I back into the target reference range (+1 to +2 SDS) while avoiding supranormal mitogenic exposure.
Doubling the dose is dangerous and will further elevate supranormal IGF-I levels.
Permanent discontinuation is unwarranted when a simple downward titration safely resolves elevated IGF-I.
Glucocorticoids suppress growth plate chondrogenesis and are never used to manage elevated IGF-I levels.

etiology.text: SGA results from heterogeneous maternal, placental, or fetal mechanisms leading to intrauterine growth restriction, including maternal vascular disorders, placental insufficiency, and fetal epigenetic anomalies (e.g., 11p15 loss of methylation in Silver-Russell syndrome).

epidemiology.text: SGA affects 2.3% of newborns by definition. Of these, 10% to 15% fail to exhibit spontaneous catch-up growth by age 2 years, accounting for roughly 20% of all adults with short stature.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis requires accurate gestational age determination, verified birth records (weight/length < -2 SDS), serial auxology documenting failure of catch-up growth, and exclusion of dysmorphic syndromes and systemic disorders.

therapies.text: Somatropin is FDA-approved for children born SGA with failure of catch-up growth by 2 years of age at a dosage of 0.24 to 0.48 mg/kg/week (35 to 70 mcg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection. Titration is based on annual height velocity and keeping serum IGF-I below +2.0 SDS.
therapies.section: Somatropin Regimen in Children Born SGA

pillars.label: Genetics and Pathophysiology
pillars.text: Prader-Willi Syndrome (PWS) is a complex neurogenetic disorder resulting from loss of expression of paternal genes in the 15q11.2-q13 imprinted region, caused by paternal deletion (65-75%), maternal uniparental disomy 15 (20-30%), or imprinting defects (1-3%). Pathophysiology is characterized by hypothalamic dysfunction producing severe neonatal hypotonia, infantile feeding failure, followed by insatiable hyperphagia, morbid obesity, hypogonadism, and growth hormone deficiency.

pillars.label: Body Composition Abnormalities
pillars.text: Individuals with PWS have a distinct body composition phenotype characterized by high fat mass and reduced lean muscle mass, even in infancy prior to the onset of obesity. Decreased spontaneous physical activity, resting energy expenditure, and motor strength are driven by intrinsic somatotroph hyposecretion and central neuromuscular alterations.

pillars.label: Benefits of rhGH Therapy
pillars.text: Somatropin therapy substantially alters the natural history of PWS: it accelerates linear growth, normalizes adult height, increases lean muscle mass, reduces body fat percentage, elevates resting energy expenditure, and improves motor strength, physical agility, and cognitive developmental scores.

pillars.label: Safety and Respiratory Precautions
pillars.text: Reports of sudden death following rhGH initiation in severely obese infants with PWS led to stringent safety guidelines. Potential mechanisms include upper airway lymphoid hypertrophy in children with preexisting hypotonia, sleep-disordered breathing, and undiagnosed respiratory tract infections. Mandatory pre-treatment polysomnography (sleep study) and ENT evaluation are required.

pillars.label: Contraindications and Monitoring
pillars.text: Absolute contraindications to initiating rhGH in PWS include severe untreated obesity, uncontrolled obstructive sleep apnea, severe active respiratory infection, and active psychosis. Recommended starting dose is 0.5 mg/m2/day (approx 0.015-0.020 mg/kg/day), titrating to 1.0 mg/m2/day. Polysomnography should be repeated 6-12 weeks after treatment initiation.

cards.q: What is the primary genetic mechanism causing Prader-Willi Syndrome in 65% to 75% of cases?
cards.a: Paternal microdeletion of the 15q11.2-q13 chromosomal region; maternal uniparental disomy (UPD15) accounts for most remaining cases.

cards.q: What pathognomonic body composition abnormality is present in infants with PWS even prior to the development of obesity?
cards.a: Markedly increased percent body fat and severely reduced lean muscle mass, accompanied by decreased resting energy expenditure.

cards.q: What diagnostic evaluation is mandatory prior to initiating somatropin in a child with PWS to prevent fatal airway complications?
cards.a: Polysomnography (sleep study) and an upper airway ENT examination to evaluate for obstructive sleep apnea and adenotonsillar hypertrophy.

cards.q: Name three absolute contraindications to starting or continuing somatropin therapy in Prader-Willi Syndrome.
cards.a: Severe uncontrolled obesity, severe untreated obstructive sleep apnea, and active systemic respiratory tract infection.

cards.q: What is the standard recommended maintenance dose of somatropin for children with Prader-Willi Syndrome?
cards.a: 1.0 mg/m2/day (approximately 0.035 mg/kg/day), often initiated at 0.5 mg/m2/day and titrated upward.

cards.q: Beyond linear height, what major developmental benefits does early somatropin therapy confer on young children with PWS?
cards.a: Accelerated gross motor milestone achievement, increased physical stamina, and improved expressive language and cognitive developmental quotients.

cards.q: When should repeat polysomnography be performed after initiating somatropin in an infant or child with PWS?
cards.a: Within 6 to 12 weeks after treatment initiation, or promptly if new or worsening snoring or sleep apnea occurs.

mcqs.q: A 9-month-old infant with genetically confirmed Prader-Willi syndrome (paternal 15q11-q13 deletion) is evaluated for somatropin therapy. He has marked hypotonia, poor head control, and short stature (length SDS -2.3). Before prescribing somatropin, which diagnostic investigation is mandatory to establish treatment safety?
options: Overnight polysomnography and ENT evaluation for adenotonsillar hypertrophy
Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry to assess total body calcium
24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
Lumbar puncture to rule out elevated intracranial pressure
mcqs.explanation: Because somatropin can stimulate lymphoid tissue proliferation and potentially exacerbate preexisting upper airway obstruction in hypotonic infants with PWS, baseline polysomnography and ENT assessment are mandatory before initiation.

option_notes.text: Polysomnography identifies occult obstructive sleep apnea, which must be addressed before safe somatropin initiation in PWS.
DXA scans are informative for body composition research but are not safety prerequisites for starting therapy.
Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring is not a standard screening requirement in hypotonic infants with PWS.
Lumbar puncture is an invasive test with no clinical indication prior to somatropin initiation in PWS.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old boy with Prader-Willi syndrome has been treated with somatropin (1.0 mg/m2/day) for 2 years. His parents ask what measurable changes in body composition have been established by long-term clinical trials. What is the most accurate response?
options: Statistically significant increase in lean muscle mass and sustained reduction in body fat percentage
Total cure of hyperphagia with normalization of satiety signaling
Complete conversion of white adipose tissue to functional brown adipose tissue
No measurable change in body composition despite acceleration of linear height
mcqs.explanation: Extensive randomized and longitudinal trials demonstrate that somatropin therapy significantly improves body composition in PWS by increasing lean muscle mass, decreasing fat mass, and boosting resting energy expenditure, though it does not abolish underlying hypothalamic hyperphagia.

option_notes.text: Clinical trials demonstrate consistent increases in lean body mass and decreases in fat mass with somatropin in PWS.
Somatropin does not cure underlying hypothalamic hyperphagia; dietary environmental restriction remains essential.
Somatropin does not convert white fat to brown fat; its lipolytic effect operates through hormone-sensitive lipase.
Body composition benefits are well-established and represent one of the primary indications for GH in PWS.

mcqs.q: A 2-year-old girl with Prader-Willi syndrome is undergoing consideration for somatropin therapy. Pre-treatment polysomnography reveals severe obstructive sleep apnea with an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 22 events/hour and oxygen desaturations to 74%. Examination reveals 4+ kissing tonsils. What is the correct clinical management?
options: Defer somatropin, refer for adenotonsillectomy, and re-evaluate with repeat polysomnography postoperatively
Start somatropin immediately at double dose to strengthen pharyngeal musculature
Initiate continuous mecasermin therapy as an alternative to somatropin
Administer high-dose dexamethasone for 2 weeks followed by immediate somatropin
mcqs.explanation: Severe obstructive sleep apnea is a contraindication to starting somatropin. Airway obstruction must be resolved surgically (adenotonsillectomy) or with positive airway pressure, with post-intervention polysomnography confirming resolution before somatropin can be safely initiated.

option_notes.text: Treating airway obstruction prior to somatropin prevents fatal respiratory compromise in patients with PWS.
Starting somatropin in the presence of severe OSA risks rapid worsening of lymphoid hypertrophy and fatal asphyxia.
Mecasermin has no indication in PWS and carries the same or greater risk of lymphoid proliferation.
High-dose dexamethasone is catabolic to muscle, causes severe metabolic disturbance, and is contraindicated.

mcqs.q: A 14-month-old boy with Prader-Willi syndrome initiates somatropin at 0.5 mg/m2/day. Six weeks into therapy, his mother reports that he has developed new-onset loud snoring and mouth breathing during sleep. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Suspend somatropin therapy and perform urgent ENT examination and polysomnography
Reassure the mother that snoring indicates expanding respiratory vital capacity
Increase the somatropin dose to 1.5 mg/m2/day to accelerate laryngeal maturation
Prescribe over-the-counter diphenhydramine at bedtime
mcqs.explanation: New-onset or worsening sleep-disordered breathing in a child with PWS following somatropin initiation warrants temporary suspension of therapy, clinical ENT evaluation for adenoid/tonsillar enlargement, and repeat polysomnography.

option_notes.text: New snoring suggests treatment-induced lymphoid hypertrophy or worsened OSA; safety requires immediate evaluation.
Snoring is a symptom of upper airway obstruction, not healthy lung expansion.
Increasing the dose increases the risk of acute respiratory obstruction.
Sedating antihistamines can relax pharyngeal muscle tone, worsening upper airway collapse.

mcqs.q: Which genetic mechanism underlying Prader-Willi syndrome carries a higher documented risk of maternal age-related meiotic non-disjunction and a lower risk of hypopigmentation compared to paternal deletions?
options: Maternal uniparental disomy 15 (UPD15)
Paternal 15q11.2-q13 microdeletion
Imprinting center microdeletion
Balanced paternal translocation involving 15q
mcqs.explanation: Maternal uniparental disomy (UPD15) accounts for ~25% of PWS cases and is associated with advanced maternal age. Because both OCA2 genes are retained, these children do not exhibit the marked hypopigmentation seen in large paternal 15q deletions.

option_notes.text: Maternal UPD15 is associated with older maternal age and preserves both maternal copies of OCA2, avoiding hypopigmentation.
Paternal deletions involve hemizygous loss of the OCA2 gene, leading to fair skin and light hair.
Imprinting center mutations are typically familial and not correlated with maternal age.
Paternal translocations are rare structural rearrangements not dependent on maternal age.

etiology.text: PWS is caused by absent expression of paternal active genes in the 15q11.2-q13 chromosomal domain, resulting from paternal microdeletion (65-75%), maternal uniparental disomy (20-30%), or imprinting center defects (1-3%).

epidemiology.text: Estimated prevalence is 1 in 15,000 to 1 in 25,000 live births, affecting males and females equally across all racial and ethnic groups.

diagnostics.text: DNA methylation analysis of the SNRPN locus on 15q11-q13 detects >99% of PWS cases by demonstrating maternal-only methylation, followed by FISH or MS-MLPA to differentiate deletion from UPD or imprinting defect.

therapies.text: Recombinant human growth hormone is administered at an initial dose of 0.5 mg/m2/day, titrating to a target maintenance dose of 1.0 mg/m2/day (approx 0.035 mg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection. Baseline and 6- to 12-week post-initiation polysomnography and ENT evaluations are mandatory.

pillars.label: Genetics and Pathophysiology
pillars.text: Turner Syndrome (TS) results from complete or partial absence of one X chromosome (45,X in 50%, mosaicism or structural X anomalies in 50%). Short stature is largely caused by haploinsufficiency of the SHOX gene in the pseudoautosomal region (PAR1). Noonan Syndrome (NS) is an autosomal dominant RASopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in PTPN11 (50%), SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, or KRAS, altering the MAPK signaling cascade and producing post-receptor GH resistance. Isolated SHOX haploinsufficiency causes Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis or variable idiopathic short stature.

pillars.label: Clinical Recognition
pillars.text: TS features growth failure, gonadal dysgenesis (streak ovaries), webbed neck (pterygium colli), low posterior hairline, cubitus valgus, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, lymphedema, and left-sided congenital cardiac defects (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation). NS features short stature, pectus excavatum/carinatum, hypertelorism, low-set posteriorly rotated ears, bleeding diathesis, and right-sided cardiac defects (pulmonary valve stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy). SHOX deficiency features mesomelia, Madelung wrist deformity, and muscular hypertrophy.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Protocol
pillars.text: Diagnosis of TS requires standard 30-cell karyotype or chromosomal microarray. Cardiovascular evaluation with echocardiogram and cardiac MRI is critical for assessing aortic dilation and coarctation. NS is diagnosed by multigene RASopathy panel. SHOX deficiency is evaluated by MLPA (to detect PAR1 deletions) and Sanger/NGS sequencing of the SHOX coding region.

pillars.label: Somatropin Therapy in TS, NS, and SHOX
pillars.text: Somatropin is FDA-approved for all three conditions: TS dose is 0.35 to 0.375 mg/kg/week (50 mcg/kg/day); SHOX deficiency dose is 0.35 mg/kg/week (50 mcg/kg/day); Noonan syndrome dose is up to 0.46 mg/kg/week (66 mcg/kg/day). Early initiation in TS (by age 4-6 years) optimizes height gain. In TS girls ≥9-10 years with severe height deficit, the non-aromatizable anabolic steroid oxandrolone (0.03-0.05 mg/kg/day) can be added to augment final adult height.

pillars.label: Safety and Multidisciplinary Management
pillars.text: In TS, surveillance includes annual screening for autoimmune thyroiditis (anti-TPO antibodies), celiac disease, sensorineural hearing loss, and serial aortic root dimension monitoring by echocardiogram/cardiac MRI to prevent aortic dissection. In NS, serial echocardiograms monitor pulmonary valve stenosis and progression of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

cards.q: Contrast the classic congenital cardiovascular anomalies characteristic of Turner syndrome versus Noonan syndrome.
cards.a: Turner syndrome features left-sided lesions (bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of the aorta, aortic root dilation); Noonan syndrome features right-sided and myocardial lesions (pulmonary valve stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy).

cards.q: What specific gene located in the pseudoautosomal region (PAR1) of the X and Y chromosomes is responsible for the short stature in Turner syndrome and Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis?
cards.a: SHOX (Short Stature Homeobox gene), whose haploinsufficiency causes disproportionate short stature and mesomelia.

cards.q: Mutations in which pathway cause Noonan syndrome and explain the relative resistance to growth hormone?
cards.a: The RAS-MAPK signal transduction pathway (most commonly PTPN11 gain-of-function mutations encoding SHP2), which impairs post-receptor IGF-I generation.

cards.q: What non-aromatizable androgen can be co-administered with somatropin in Turner syndrome girls older than 9-10 years to augment final adult height?
cards.a: Oxandrolone, typically administered at a low dose of 0.03 to 0.05 mg/kg/day to minimize virilizing side effects.

cards.q: What characteristic wrist abnormality is observed in adolescent females with SHOX mutations and Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis?
cards.a: Madelung deformity, featuring bowing of the distal radius, dorsal subluxation of the distal ulna, and triangular carpal wedging.

cards.q: Which autoimmune conditions occur with increased frequency in girls with Turner syndrome, requiring annual laboratory screening?
cards.a: Autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis (hypothyroidism) and celiac disease.

cards.q: What is the recommended somatropin dosage for girls with Turner syndrome to achieve optimal adult height catch-up?
cards.a: 0.35 to 0.375 mg/kg/week (approximately 50 mcg/kg/day) by daily subcutaneous injection.

mcqs.q: A 5-year-old girl is evaluated for progressive growth deceleration. Her height is at the 1st percentile (height SDS -2.4). Examination reveals a low posterior hairline, high-arched palate, broad chest with widely spaced nipples, and mild cubitus valgus. Cardiovascular exam reveals a grade 2/6 systolic murmur. Echocardiogram demonstrates a bicuspid aortic valve with normal ventricular function. What is the most definitive test to confirm her diagnosis?
options: 30-cell peripheral blood karyotype or chromosomal microarray
Provocative growth hormone stimulation testing with clonidine and arginine
Targeted sequencing of the PTPN11 gene
24-hour ambulatory urinary growth hormone excretion
mcqs.explanation: A karyotype or chromosomal microarray is the gold standard to establish Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaicism), which accounts for her short stature, somatic stigmas, and bicuspid aortic valve.

option_notes.text: Karyotyping detects complete or mosaic absence of the second sex chromosome, confirming Turner syndrome.
Girls with Turner syndrome are generally growth hormone sufficient; provocative testing is not the diagnostic test of choice.
PTPN11 testing evaluates Noonan syndrome, which typically features right-sided heart defects, not bicuspid aortic valve.
Urinary GH excretion is unreliable and has no clinical utility in the diagnosis of Turner syndrome.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old girl with confirmed 45,X Turner syndrome has received somatropin (0.375 mg/kg/week) for 3 years, but her height SDS remains -2.7 despite good adherence. Her bone age is 8.5 years. To augment her final adult height, which adjunctive medication is supported by clinical consensus guidelines?
options: Low-dose oral oxandrolone at 0.03 to 0.05 mg/kg/day
High-dose transdermal estradiol at adult feminizing doses
Continuous subcutaneous GnRH antagonist therapy
Daily oral fludrocortisone acetate
mcqs.explanation: In girls with Turner syndrome aged ≥9-10 years with significant height deficits, adding low-dose oxandrolone (0.03-0.05 mg/kg/day) to somatropin synergistically enhances linear height velocity and adult height without causing unacceptable virilization.

option_notes.text: Low-dose oxandrolone acts as a non-aromatizable anabolic steroid that augments final height when combined with somatropin.
High-dose estrogen therapy prematurely fuses epiphyseal plates and drastically truncates final adult height.
GnRH antagonists are not indicated in prepubertal girls who already have primary hypogonadism.
Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid for adrenal insufficiency and has no growth-promoting efficacy.

mcqs.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with short stature (height SDS -2.6), hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears, a webbed neck, and pectus excavatum. Echocardiogram reveals dysplastic pulmonary valve stenosis with mild right ventricular outflow tract obstruction. Genetic testing is most likely to reveal a pathogenic gain-of-function mutation in which gene?
options: PTPN11
GHR
FGFR3
GH1
mcqs.explanation: Noonan syndrome is most commonly (approx. 50%) caused by gain-of-function mutations in PTPN11, encoding the SHP2 protein tyrosine phosphatase in the RAS-MAPK pathway, classically presenting with pulmonary valve stenosis and dysmorphism.

option_notes.text: PTPN11 mutations account for ~50% of Noonan syndrome cases, classically associated with pulmonary valve stenosis.
GHR mutations cause Laron syndrome without facial dysmorphism or pulmonary valve stenosis.
FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia or hypochondroplasia with marked rhizomelia and macrocephaly.
GH1 mutations cause isolated growth hormone deficiency without congenital heart defects or RASopathy facies.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and bilateral wrist pain. Physical exam reveals forearm shortening (mesomelia), prominent ulnar styloids, and limited wrist extension and supination. Wrist radiographs show bilateral curvature of the distal radius with triangular carpal bones and dorsal dislocation of the distal ulna (Madelung deformity). What is the underlying molecular defect?
options: Haploinsufficiency of the SHOX gene on the pseudoautosomal region of chromosome Xp22.3/Yp11.3
Activating mutation in the PTH1R gene encoding the parathyroid hormone receptor
Inactivating mutation in the CASR gene encoding the calcium-sensing receptor
Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the SOX9 gene
mcqs.explanation: Madelung deformity in association with mesomelic short stature is the hallmark of Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, caused by heterozygous deletion or point mutation of the SHOX gene in the pseudoautosomal region (PAR1).

option_notes.text: SHOX haploinsufficiency causes defective chondrocyte hypertrophy and premature growth plate fusion in the distal radius, producing Madelung deformity.
PTH1R activating mutations cause Jansen-type metaphyseal chondrodysplasia with severe hypercalcemia.
CASR inactivating mutations cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia without skeletal dysostosis.
SOX9 mutations cause campomelic dysplasia with bowed long bones, sex reversal, and neonatal respiratory distress.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old female with Turner syndrome who is completing somatropin therapy presents for transition planning. Her blood pressure is 138/86 mmHg. Transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrates an aortic root diameter index of 2.6 cm/m2 (normal <2.0 cm/m2). What is the primary clinical significance of this finding?
options: High lifetime risk of catastrophic aortic dissection requiring aggressive blood pressure control and cardiac MRI monitoring
Normal physiological adaptation to growth hormone therapy requiring no intervention
Transient post-pubertal remodeling that will spontaneously regress by age 21
Indication for immediate cardiac transplantation within 30 days
mcqs.explanation: Aortic dilation in Turner syndrome carries a catastrophic risk of fatal aortic dissection and rupture. Aortic diameter index ≥2.5 cm/m2 requires tight blood pressure control (typically beta-blockers/ARBs), restriction of competitive isometric exertion, and serial surveillance by cardiac MRI.

option_notes.text: Aortic root enlargement in Turner syndrome is a major cause of premature mortality; surveillance and hemodynamic control are mandatory.
Aortic dilation is not a normal physiological response to somatropin; it represents intrinsic medial vascular degeneration.
Aortic dilation does not resolve spontaneously; it tends to expand progressively over time.
Elective prophylactic surgical aortic root replacement is considered at critical dimensions, not immediate cardiac transplantation.

etiology.text: Turner syndrome is caused by complete or partial loss of the second sex chromosome. Noonan syndrome is caused by heterozygous mutations in RAS-MAPK genes (PTPN11, SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS). SHOX deficiency is caused by microdeletions or point mutations in the pseudoautosomal SHOX locus.

epidemiology.text: Turner syndrome occurs in approximately 1 in 2,500 live female births. Noonan syndrome affects 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 2,500 live births of both sexes. SHOX deficiency accounts for 2-15% of children classified with idiopathic short stature.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype or microarray for Turner syndrome, targeted multi-gene NGS panel for Noonan syndrome, and MLPA or sequencing of the SHOX gene on Xp22.33/Yp11.32.

therapies.text: Somatropin is FDA-approved for Turner syndrome at 0.35–0.375 mg/kg/week (approx 50 mcg/kg/day); for Noonan syndrome up to 0.46 mg/kg/week (66 mcg/kg/day); and for SHOX deficiency at 0.35 mg/kg/week (50 mcg/kg/day). In Turner syndrome girls ≥9–10 years, adjunctive oxandrolone at 0.03–0.05 mg/kg/day can be added.
therapies.section: Somatropin Regimens in TS, NS, and SHOX

pillars.label: The Transition Period
pillars.text: The transition period spans late adolescence to early adulthood (from completion of linear growth through age 25), during which peak bone mass, skeletal muscle mass, cardiac maturation, and adult lipid/body composition profiles are established. Growth hormone plays a vital metabolic role in somatic maturation beyond linear elongation.

pillars.label: Indications for Re-testing
pillars.text: Patients with childhood-onset GHD (CO-GHD) must be categorized at completion of growth: those with high risk of irreversible GHD (multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies ≥3, severe genetic defects, or structural suprasellar lesions) do not require provocative re-testing if IGF-I is <-2 SDS. Conversely, those with isolated idiopathic CO-GHD must undergo formal re-testing after at least 1-3 months off somatropin.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Re-testing Protocols
pillars.text: The insulin tolerance test (ITT) is the diagnostic reference standard, with severe adult GHD defined as peak GH <3 mcg/L (or <5 mcg/L in the transition period). Alternative validated provocative tests include the glucagon stimulation test (peak GH <1-3 mcg/L depending on BMI) and macimorelin (oral ghrelin receptor agonist, cutoff 2.8-5.1 ng/mL).

pillars.label: Adult Dosing Paradigm
pillars.text: Adult GH dosing is not weight-based, but starts low and is titrated against clinical response and serum IGF-I concentrations. Starting dose is typically 0.1 to 0.2 mg/day in adults (0.2 to 0.5 mg/day in transition adolescents). Women taking oral estrogens require significantly higher doses due to hepatic first-pass attenuation of GH-induced IGF-I generation.

pillars.label: Metabolic Benefits and Monitoring
pillars.text: Adult GH replacement reduces visceral adiposity, improves serum lipid profiles (decreasing LDL cholesterol and apolipoprotein B), increases lean muscle mass and exercise capacity, enhances bone mineral density, and improves psychological quality of life. IGF-I must be maintained within the middle of the age-adjusted reference range (0 to +1 SDS).

cards.q: What biological processes define the 'transition period' in growth hormone management after linear growth ceases?
cards.a: The acquisition of peak bone mass, accrual of adult muscle mass, maturation of cardiac ventricular geometry, and stabilization of adult lipid and metabolic homeostasis.

cards.q: Which patients with childhood-onset GHD do NOT require provocative re-testing after epiphyseal closure before adult GH continuation?
cards.a: Patients with ≥3 other pituitary hormone deficiencies, severe proven genetic defects, or severe structural hypothalamic-pituitary lesions with serum IGF-I < -2.0 SDS.

cards.q: What peak growth hormone cutoff on the insulin tolerance test (ITT) confirms persistent severe GHD during the transition period versus older adulthood?
cards.a: Peak GH < 5.0 mcg/L in the transition period, compared to < 3.0 mcg/L in older adult life.

cards.q: How does adult growth hormone replacement dosing fundamentally differ from pediatric growth hormone replacement dosing?
cards.a: Adult dosing is non-weight-based, starting at low fixed doses (0.1-0.3 mg/day) and titrated individually based on serum IGF-I concentrations and tolerance.

cards.q: Why do adult females taking oral estrogen contraceptives or hormone replacement require higher growth hormone doses than males?
cards.a: Oral estrogens undergo first-pass hepatic metabolism, inducing SOCS2 and suppressing hepatic GH-stimulated IGF-I production.

cards.q: What common adverse effects reflect excessive somatropin dosing in adults?
cards.a: Fluid retention, peripheral edema, arthralgias, carpal tunnel syndrome, and worsening insulin resistance.

cards.q: What is the recommended target serum IGF-I concentration during long-term adult growth hormone replacement?
cards.a: Within the age- and sex-adjusted normal range, typically targeted between 0 and +1.0 SDS.

mcqs.q: An 18-year-old male with childhood-onset panhypopituitarism secondary to a large craniopharyngioma resected at age 8 has reached epiphyseal fusion (height velocity <1.5 cm/year). He is on stable replacement with levothyroxine, hydrocortisone, desmopressin, and testosterone. Somatropin is withheld for 6 weeks; his repeat serum IGF-I is 45 ng/mL (SDS -3.6). What is the appropriate next step regarding growth hormone management?
options: Resume somatropin at an adult transition starting dose without requiring provocative stimulation testing
Perform an insulin tolerance test to confirm severe growth hormone deficiency
Discontinue growth hormone permanently because linear growth is completed
Perform an oral glucose tolerance test to evaluate for residual somatotroph hypersecretion
mcqs.explanation: Patients with multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies (≥3) secondary to structural lesions with a low IGF-I (SDS <-2.0) have an extremely high probability of permanent severe GHD; consensus guidelines state they do not require provocative testing.

option_notes.text: Patients with panhypopituitarism and low IGF-I have documented permanent GHD; adult GH therapy should resume without re-testing.
Provocative testing with ITT is redundant and carries unnecessary hypoglycemic risks in patients with multiple documented central deficiencies.
Discontinuing GH leads to loss of bone mineral density, increased visceral adiposity, and unfavorable cardiovascular lipid profiles.
An oral glucose tolerance test evaluates GH excess, which is impossible in complete panhypopituitarism.

mcqs.q: A 19-year-old female with childhood isolated idiopathic growth hormone deficiency reaches final height. She stops somatropin for 2 months. She is healthy, takes an oral combined ethinyl estradiol/levonorgestrel contraceptive, and has a normal BMI. Her IGF-I is at -1.4 SDS. What is the most appropriate next step to evaluate whether she requires adult GH continuation?
options: Perform a validated provocative growth hormone stimulation test such as the insulin tolerance test or glucagon test
Resume pediatric-dose somatropin (30 mcg/kg/day) immediately based on the borderline IGF-I
Switch to oral mecasermin monotherapy for lifelong metabolic support
Perform a cranial MRI scan and prescribe growth hormone only if a microadenoma is seen
mcqs.explanation: In childhood isolated idiopathic GHD, up to 70-80% of patients demonstrate normal somatotroph reserve when re-tested after puberty. A provocative test (ITT or glucagon) is mandatory before diagnosing permanent adult GHD.

option_notes.text: Provocative re-testing is mandatory for isolated idiopathic childhood GHD because most patients test normal in adulthood.
Resuming pediatric weight-based dosing in adults causes severe edema, arthralgias, and carpal tunnel syndrome.
Mecasermin is indicated only for severe primary IGF-I deficiency, not secondary GHD.
Pituitary MRI does not evaluate dynamic somatotroph secretory capacity in idiopathic GHD.

mcqs.q: A 22-year-old female with confirmed persistent adult growth hormone deficiency is on stable somatropin replacement (0.3 mg daily) with an IGF-I of 0.0 SDS. She begins taking an oral combined estrogen-progestin contraceptive. Three months later, she reports fatigue, and her repeat serum IGF-I has dropped to -2.1 SDS despite strict adherence. What is the mechanism explaining this decline?
options: First-pass hepatic metabolism of oral estrogen induces SOCS2, inhibiting hepatic GH-mediated IGF-I generation
Estrogen binds directly to circulating somatropin, causing rapid renal clearance
Oral progestins directly destroy pituitary somatotroph secretory granules
