Estrogen alters laboratory antibody recognition in automated IGF-I immunoassays
mcqs.explanation: Oral estrogens pass directly through the liver via the portal vein, upregulating suppressor of cytokine signaling 2 (SOCS2) and inhibiting Jak2/STAT5 signaling downstream of the hepatic GH receptor, attenuating IGF-I generation. Switching to transdermal estrogen or increasing the somatropin dose overcomes this effect.

option_notes.text: First-pass hepatic exposure to oral estrogen suppresses GHR signaling, requiring higher somatropin doses or transdermal estrogen.
Estrogen does not bind somatropin in circulation.
Progestins do not destroy somatotroph granules; the patient has persistent GHD with exogenous replacement.
Estrogen does not interfere with modern automated IGF-I immunoassay antibodies.

mcqs.q: A 24-year-old male with persistent severe adult GHD starts somatropin at 0.8 mg daily (an inappropriately high starting dose). Within 3 weeks, he develops bilateral wrist paresthesias in the median nerve distribution, finger stiffness, and pitting pedal edema. What is the pathophysiological cause of these symptoms?
options: Growth hormone-induced sodium and water retention causing elevated tissue interstitial turgor and carpal tunnel compression
Autoimmune demyelinating peripheral polyneuropathy triggered by recombinant protein
Acute skeletal overgrowth of the carpal bones causing bony canal stenosis
Development of acute hypokalemic periodic paralysis
mcqs.explanation: Growth hormone stimulates renal tubular sodium reabsorption and extracellular fluid expansion. In adults, excessive starting doses commonly trigger fluid retention, soft tissue swelling, arthralgias, and compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

option_notes.text: GH-mediated renal sodium retention and extracellular fluid expansion cause soft tissue edema and median nerve compression.
Somatropin does not cause autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy.
Bony carpal remodeling takes years in acromegaly and does not occur in 3 weeks of replacement.
Somatropin does not cause acute hypokalemic periodic paralysis.

mcqs.q: Which metabolic parameter has been demonstrated to improve consistently when growth hormone replacement is maintained during adulthood in patients with documented severe persistent GHD?
options: Increase in lean body mass, reduction in visceral fat, and improvement in lumbar spine bone mineral density
Complete reversal of central diabetes insipidus allowing cessation of desmopressin
Permanent cure of primary panhypopituitarism with spontaneous recovery of other axes
Reduction in total blood volume and reduction in left ventricular posterior wall thickness
mcqs.explanation: Adult GH replacement consistently produces favorable somatic and metabolic changes: increased lean body mass, decreased visceral and total body fat, improved bone mineral density accrual, and enhanced quality-of-life scores.

option_notes.text: Prospective trials demonstrate gains in lean mass, reductions in trunk fat, and preservation of bone mineral density.
GH replacement does not restore vasopressin secretion; diabetes insipidus requires lifelong desmopressin.
Underlying pituitary damage is irreversible; other hormone deficiencies persist.
GH normalizes, rather than decreases, left ventricular mass and cardiac output.

etiology.text: Childhood-onset GHD persistent into adulthood arises from congenital pituitary developmental defects (PROP1, POU1F1), congenital CNS malformations, or acquired insults such as craniopharyngiomas, germinomas, histiocytosis, surgery, and radiotherapy.

epidemiology.text: While up to 80% of children with isolated idiopathic GHD re-test as growth hormone sufficient in adulthood, virtually 100% of those with multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies or severe structural lesions have permanent GHD.

diagnostics.text: Diagnostic evaluation requires re-testing after epiphyseal fusion and ≥1-3 months off somatropin using ITT (peak GH <5.0 mcg/L transition, <3.0 mcg/L adult), glucagon test, or macimorelin, unless the patient has ≥3 other pituitary deficiencies and IGF-I <-2.0 SDS.

therapies.text: Adult somatropin dosing is non-weight-based, initiating at 0.2 to 0.5 mg/day in the transition period (0.1 to 0.2 mg/day in older adults) subcutaneously at bedtime, titrating by 0.1 to 0.2 mg/day every 4–8 weeks to achieve an IGF-I within the middle of the age-adjusted reference range (0 to +1.0 SDS).

pillars.label: Molecular Classification
pillars.text: Skeletal dysplasias comprise over 450 distinct genetic disorders of bone and cartilage development. Common categories include FGFR3-related chondrodysplasias (achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia, thanatophoric dysplasia), type II collagenopathies (COL2A1; achondrogenesis, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia), type I collagenopathies (COL1A1, COL1A2; osteogenesis imperfecta), and pseudoautosomal SHOX defects (Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis).

pillars.label: Achondroplasia Pathophysiology
pillars.text: Achondroplasia is the most common disproportionate short stature dysplasia, caused by heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in FGFR3 (most commonly c.1138G>A, p.Gly380Arg). Constitutive activation of the FGFR3 tyrosine kinase hyperactivates the downstream MAPK/ERK pathway, which constitutively inhibits endochondral chondrocyte proliferation and terminal differentiation in the cartilaginous growth plate.

pillars.label: Clinical and Radiographic Presentation
pillars.text: Features include severe rhizomelic limb shortening (proximal segments shortest), macrocephaly with frontal bossing and midface hypoplasia, depressed nasal bridge, trident hand configuration, thoracolumbar kyphosis in infancy, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, and foramen magnum stenosis. Radiographs show narrowed interpedicular distances in the lumbar spine, square iliac wings, horizontal acetabular roofs, and metaphyseal flare.

pillars.label: Targeted Molecular Therapies
pillars.text: Historically, surgical limb lengthening or palliative decompression were the primary options. In 2021, the C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) analog vosoritide was approved for achondroplasia in growing children (open epiphyses). Vosoritide binds the NPR-B receptor, generating intracellular cGMP which inhibits the MAPK/ERK cascade, counteracting constitutive FGFR3 signaling and significantly improving annual growth velocity (mean gain ~1.5 cm/year).

pillars.label: Complications and Surveillance
pillars.text: Major clinical complications include foramen magnum stenosis causing cervical medullary compression, central sleep apnea, and sudden infant death; thoracolumbar kyphosis; spinal canal stenosis in adulthood causing neurogenic claudication; chronic otitis media and conductive hearing loss; and genu varum. Somatropin produces only modest transient gains and does not alter underlying disproportion.

cards.q: What specific genetic mutation accounts for more than 98% of cases of achondroplasia?
cards.a: A heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3, most commonly c.1138G>A (p.Gly380Arg), resulting in constitutive activation of the receptor tyrosine kinase.

cards.q: What pattern of limb shortening is characteristically observed in achondroplasia?
cards.a: Rhizomelic shortening, where proximal segments (femur and humerus) are disproportionately shorter than middle or distal segments.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of vosoritide, the FDA-approved medical therapy for achondroplasia?
cards.a: It is a recombinant C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) analog that binds NPR-B, stimulating cGMP to inhibit the hyperactive MAPK/ERK pathway downstream of mutated FGFR3.

cards.q: What anatomical narrowing in infants with achondroplasia carries a significant risk of cervicomedullary compression and sudden death?
cards.a: Foramen magnum stenosis, requiring baseline polysomnography and high-resolution neuroimaging (CT/MRI) of the craniocervical junction.

cards.q: What pathognomonic finding is seen on anteroposterior lumbar spine radiography in achondroplasia?
cards.a: Progressive caudal narrowing of the interpedicular distance from L1 to L5 (in contrast to normal widening).

cards.q: Mutations in COL1A1 and COL1A2 cause what skeletal disorder characterized by bone fragility and blue sclerae?
cards.a: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), ranging from perinatal lethal type II to mild non-deforming type I.

cards.q: What distinct physical feature of the hands is typical in achondroplasia?
cards.a: A 'trident hand' configuration, characterized by short, broad digits with persistent divergence between the third and fourth fingers.

mcqs.q: A newborn infant is noted to have short limbs, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, and a depressed nasal bridge. Radiographs demonstrate shortened long bones with flared metaphyses, square iliac wings with horizontal acetabular roofs, and narrowing of the lumbar interpedicular distances caudally. What is the fundamental cellular mechanism causing this skeletal dysplasia?
options: Constitutive activation of FGFR3 signaling that hyperactivates MAPK/ERK, inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate
Defective synthesis of type II collagen alpha-1 chains impairing articular cartilage tensile strength
Overexpression of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) leading to chondrocyte hyperproliferation
Failure of osteoclast proton pump vacuolar ATPase causing generalized dense bone accumulation
mcqs.explanation: Achondroplasia is caused by a heterozygous gain-of-function mutation in FGFR3, which constitutively activates MAPK/ERK signaling and suppresses endochondral growth plate chondrogenesis.

option_notes.text: FGFR3 gain-of-function constitutively signals through MAPK/ERK, inhibiting chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.
Type II collagen defects cause spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, not achondroplasia.
PTHrP does not cause achondroplasia; Jansen metaphyseal dysplasia involves the PTH1R receptor.
Osteoclast proton pump failure causes osteopetrosis with dense, marble-like bones, not achondroplasia.

mcqs.q: A 2-month-old infant with achondroplasia undergoes routine health supervision. The infant has hypotonia and head lag. Polysomnography demonstrates recurrent central apneas with desaturations to 82%. What urgent diagnostic test is indicated to guide clinical management?
options: MRI or thin-slice CT scan of the craniocervical junction to evaluate for foramen magnum stenosis
Continuous 24-hour video EEG to rule out infantile epileptic spasms
Echocardiogram to rule out coarctation of the aorta
Barium swallow study to assess for tracheoesophageal fistula
mcqs.explanation: In achondroplasia, endochondral ossification failure severely restricts the growth of the cranial base, causing foramen magnum stenosis. In infants, this can compress the brainstem and cervical spinal cord, causing central apneas and sudden death requiring suboccipital surgical decompression.

option_notes.text: Craniocervical neuroimaging identifies life-threatening foramen magnum stenosis and cervicomedullary compression in achondroplasia.
EEG does not identify the structural brainstem compression that causes central sleep apnea in achondroplasia.
Coarctation of the aorta is a feature of Turner syndrome, not achondroplasia.
Barium swallow is unrelated to the central neurogenic apnea of craniocervical compression.

mcqs.q: A 6-year-old boy with genetically confirmed achondroplasia is started on vosoritide (15 mcg/kg subcutaneously daily). By what mechanism does this therapeutic agent counteract his underlying molecular disease process?
options: Binds to the natriuretic peptide receptor-B (NPR-B), increasing intracellular cGMP and inhibiting the hyperactive MAPK/ERK cascade
Directly cleaves circulating FGFR3 molecules via monoclonal antibody-mediated proteolysis
Stimulates hepatic growth hormone receptors to produce supranormal levels of IGF-I
Selectively binds bone hydroxyapatite crystals to prevent osteoclast-mediated bone resorption
mcqs.explanation: Vosoritide is a recombinant modified C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) analog that binds the NPR-B receptor, triggering intracellular cGMP generation. cGMP-dependent signals antagonize the overactive MAPK/ERK pathway downstream of mutant FGFR3, restoring growth plate chondrogenesis.

option_notes.text: Vosoritide binds NPR-B to stimulate cGMP, which downregulates hyperactive MAPK/ERK signaling and promotes endochondral bone formation.
Vosoritide is a peptide analog, not a proteolytic antibody.
Vosoritide works locally in cartilage growth plates, independent of hepatic GH/IGF-I axis stimulation.
Inhibiting osteoclast bone resorption describes bisphosphonates, not vosoritide.

mcqs.q: A 7-year-old child presents with mild disproportionate short stature (height SDS -2.8). She does not have the classic macrocephaly, frontal bossing, or trident hand configuration seen in achondroplasia, but radiographs demonstrate mild rhizomelic shortening of the long bones and minimal lumbar interpedicular narrowing. Genetic testing reveals a heterozygous p.Asn540Lys mutation in FGFR3. What is the diagnosis?
options: Hypochondroplasia
Thanatophoric dysplasia type I
Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita
Campomelic dysplasia
mcqs.explanation: Hypochondroplasia is a milder skeletal dysplasia caused by heterozygous FGFR3 mutations (most commonly p.Asn540Lys). Children have rhizomelic short stature but typically lack severe craniofacial dysmorphism.

option_notes.text: Hypochondroplasia is classically caused by FGFR3 p.Asn540Lys, presenting with milder rhizomelia and subtle spine changes.
Thanatophoric dysplasia is perinatal lethal with cloverleaf skull and extreme micromelia.
Spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia is caused by COL2A1 mutations and features severe spinal shortening and epiphyseal dysplasia.
Campomelic dysplasia is caused by SOX9 mutations with bowed tibia, sex reversal, and hypoplastic scapulae.

mcqs.q: A 3-year-old girl with recurrent fractures following minor trauma is evaluated. Physical examination reveals blue sclerae, joint hypermobility, and normal teeth (no dentinogenesis imperfecta). Radiographs demonstrate osteopenia, gracile long bones, and healed fractures without wormian bones or metaphyseal flaring. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Osteogenesis imperfecta type I
Achondroplasia
Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis
Hypochondroplasia
mcqs.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta type I (mild non-deforming) is caused by heterozygous null mutations in COL1A1 leading to quantitative reduction of normal type I collagen, presenting with recurrent fractures, blue sclerae, and normal teeth.

option_notes.text: OI type I presents with skeletal fragility, blue sclerae, and normal dentition due to quantitative reduction in type I collagen.
Achondroplasia does not cause bone fragility, recurrent fractures, or blue sclerae.
Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis causes mesomelia and Madelung deformity, not recurrent fractures.
Hypochondroplasia is an FGFR3 chondrodysplasia with short limbs, not a collagen fragility syndrome.

etiology.text: Skeletal dysplasias are heterogeneous monogenic disorders affecting bone and cartilage formation, most frequently caused by mutations in FGFR3 (achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia), COL2A1, COL1A1/COL1A2 (osteogenesis imperfecta), and SHOX.

epidemiology.text: Collectively, skeletal dysplasias occur in approximately 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 5,000 live births, with achondroplasia being the most common non-lethal form (1 in 15,000 to 1 in 40,000).

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis integrates clinical auxology, skeletal radiographic survey (skull, spine, pelvis, long bones, hands), and targeted or exome-based genetic sequencing.

therapies.text: Vosoritide (recombinant human C-type natriuretic peptide analog) is approved for children with achondroplasia aged 5 years and older (and down to younger ages where approved) with open epiphyses, administered at 15 mcg/kg subcutaneously once daily. Somatropin produces only modest transient gains and is not standard of care.

pillars.label: Etiology of Tall Stature and Overgrowth
pillars.text: Overgrowth in children divides into primary cellular/genetic syndromes (Beckwith-Wiedemann, Sotos, Weaver, Marfan, Simpson-Golabi-Behmel, homocystinuria) and secondary endocrine hypersecretion (growth hormone excess, precocious puberty, hyperthyroidism, infant of diabetic mother). Pituitary gigantism is exceedingly rare in childhood and is caused by GH-secreting somatotroph or mammosomatotroph adenomas, McCune-Albright syndrome (GNAS mosaicism), Carney complex (PRKAR1A), MEN1, or X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG / GPR101 microduplication).

pillars.label: Clinical Manifestations
pillars.text: Pituitary gigantism presents with massive linear growth acceleration crossing percentiles upwards, coarse facial features, prognathism, macrodactyly, excessive perspiration, arthralgias, and visual field defects or cranial neuropathies from tumor mass effect. In genetic overgrowth, Sotos syndrome features macrocephaly, pointed chin, and learning disabilities (NSD1); Marfan syndrome features arachnodactyly, pectus deformities, and ectopia lentis (FBN1).

pillars.label: Diagnostic Evaluation
pillars.text: Screening for GH excess requires elevated serum IGF-I and IGFBP-3 matched to pubertal stage. The gold standard diagnostic confirmation is an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT, 1.75 g/kg up to 75 g): failure to suppress serum GH to <1.0 mcg/L (or <0.4 mcg/L on sensitive assays) establishes autonomous hypersecretion. Pituitary high-resolution MRI with contrast evaluates macroadenomas. Genetic panels test for AIP, GNAS, PRKAR1A, MEN1, and GPR101.

pillars.label: Surgical and Medical Management
pillars.text: Transsphenoidal adenomectomy is the primary first-line therapy for resectable somatotroph adenomas. When residual tumor or hypersecretion persists, medical therapy utilizes first-generation somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide, lanreotide), dopamine receptor agonists (cabergoline), or the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant (10-30 mg daily/weekly SC). In non-endocrine constitutional tall stature, high-dose sex steroids were historically used to accelerate epiphyseal fusion, though percutaneous epiphysiodesis is now favored when intervention is requested.

pillars.label: Complications and Surveillance
pillars.text: Complications of untreated pituitary gigantism include severe cardiovascular morbidity (cardiomegaly, biventricular hypertrophy, hypertension, arrhythmias), sleep apnea, insulin resistance and diabetes mellitus, hypopituitarism from tumor mass or surgery, and premature mortality. Long-term surveillance requires serial IGF-I, pituitary MRI, visual field testing, and monitoring of all anterior pituitary axes.

cards.q: What dynamic endocrine test confirms autonomous growth hormone hypersecretion in a child with tall stature?
cards.a: Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT, 1.75 g/kg up to 75 g), demonstrating failure to suppress serum GH to < 1.0 mcg/L (or < 0.4 mcg/L on modern ultrasensitive assays).

cards.q: What infant-onset overgrowth syndrome features duplication of chromosome Xq26.3 involving the GPR101 gene, causing massive gigantism and hyperprolactinemia before age 5?
cards.a: X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG), presenting with extreme early-onset linear acceleration and large pituitary adenomas or hyperplasia.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of pegvisomant in the medical management of refractory growth hormone excess?
cards.a: It is a genetically engineered growth hormone receptor antagonist that prevents GHR functional dimerization and blocks peripheral IGF-I generation.

cards.q: Which overgrowth syndrome is caused by haploinsufficiency of the NSD1 gene, characterized by macrocephaly, prominent forehead, pointed chin, and developmental delay?
cards.a: Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism).

cards.q: What is the primary definitive first-line treatment for pediatric pituitary gigantism caused by a somatotroph adenoma?
cards.a: Transsphenoidal surgical resection of the pituitary adenoma.

cards.q: What class of medications (e.g., octreotide, lanreotide) acts on somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) to inhibit pituitary GH secretion?
cards.a: Somatostatin receptor ligands (somatostatin analogs).

cards.q: What major cardiac pathology is the leading cause of premature mortality in patients with chronic, untreated growth hormone excess?
cards.a: Acromegalic cardiomyopathy, characterized by biventricular concentric hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and heart failure.

mcqs.q: A 13-year-old boy is brought for evaluation of rapid linear growth. Over the past 18 months, his height has jumped from the 75th percentile to well above the 99th percentile (height SDS +3.4), with a height velocity of 12.5 cm/year. Physical exam reveals coarse facial features, mandibular prognathism, large fleshy hands and feet, and hyperhidrosis. Serum IGF-I is markedly elevated at +4.8 SDS. What test is required to confirm autonomous growth hormone hypersecretion?
options: Standard oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) evaluating for failure of serum growth hormone suppression
Arginine plus growth hormone-releasing hormone stimulation test
Random morning serum growth hormone measurement following an overnight fast
24-hour urinary free cortisol excretion
mcqs.explanation: In normal individuals, an oral glucose load suppresses serum GH to <1.0 mcg/L (or <0.4 mcg/L on sensitive assays). Failure to suppress GH during an OGTT confirms autonomous GH hypersecretion (pituitary gigantism/acromegaly).

option_notes.text: Failure to suppress GH to <1.0 mcg/L during an oral glucose challenge is the gold standard diagnostic confirmation of gigantism.
Arginine-GHRH is a provocative stimulation test used to diagnose GH deficiency, not hypersecretion.
Random GH is pulsatile and can be normally elevated in growing adolescents, leading to false-positive or false-negative results.
Urinary cortisol evaluates Cushing syndrome, which causes growth deceleration, not accelerated gigantism.

mcqs.q: A 2-year-old female presents with massive accelerated linear growth (height SDS +4.2), generalized soft tissue overgrowth, voracious appetite, and acromegalic facial features that began at 8 months of age. Laboratory workup reveals GH 68 ng/mL, IGF-I SDS +5.1, and prolactin 88 ng/mL (reference <20 ng/mL). Brain MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing pituitary macroadenoma with suprasellar extension. Microarray analysis is most likely to identify which molecular etiology?
options: Microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3 involving the GPR101 gene (X-linked acrogigantism / X-LAG)
Inactivating mutation in the NSD1 gene causing Sotos syndrome
Heterozygous fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutation causing Marfan syndrome
Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causing Prader-Willi syndrome
mcqs.explanation: X-LAG (X-linked acrogigantism) is caused by microduplication of Xq26.3 encompassing GPR101. It is the classic cause of infancy-onset gigantism (onset <5 years, often <12 months) characterized by extreme growth velocity, high GH and prolactin, and massive pituitary adenomas or hyperplasia.

option_notes.text: Xq26.3 microduplication (GPR101) causes X-LAG, presenting with early infant-onset gigantism and hyperprolactinemia.
NSD1 mutations cause Sotos syndrome, which features overgrowth with macrocephaly, not pituitary macroadenomas.
FBN1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome, presenting with tall stature and arachnodactyly without GH hypersecretion.
Paternal 15q11-q13 deletion causes Prader-Willi syndrome, which features short stature and GHD.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old male undergoes transsphenoidal surgical debulking for an invasive pituitary somatotroph macroadenoma. Postoperatively, his serum IGF-I remains elevated at +3.2 SDS, and MRI demonstrates residual cavernous sinus invasion. He is initiated on long-acting octreotide, but his IGF-I remains elevated after 6 months. What pharmacological agent with a distinct mechanism of action can be added to block peripheral IGF-I generation?
options: Pegvisomant
Mecasermin
Somatropin
Fludrocortisone
mcqs.explanation: Pegvisomant is a genetically engineered growth hormone receptor antagonist that binds to the GHR and prevents functional receptor dimerization, blocking peripheral IGF-I production without requiring pituitary tumor shrinkage.

option_notes.text: Pegvisomant acts as a GHR competitive antagonist, directly reducing serum IGF-I in patients refractory to somatostatin analogs.
Mecasermin is recombinant IGF-I and would dangerously exacerbate hyper-IGF-I toxicity.
Somatropin is recombinant growth hormone and is absolutely contraindicated in gigantism.
Fludrocortisone is a mineralocorticoid with no effect on the growth hormone receptor.

mcqs.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with accelerated growth (height SDS +3.1), macrocephaly (head circumference >98th percentile), prominent high forehead with frontoparietal balding, down-slanting palpebral fissures, a long narrow face, and a pointed chin. He has mild intellectual disability. Endocrine testing demonstrates a normal basal IGF-I and normal suppression of GH on oral glucose testing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sotos syndrome (cerebral gigantism)
Pituitary gigantism secondary to somatotroph adenoma
Precocious puberty secondary to a hypothalamic hamartoma
McCune-Albright syndrome with autonomous somatotroph hyperplasia
mcqs.explanation: Sotos syndrome (caused by NSD1 haploinsufficiency) is a classic genetic overgrowth disorder presenting with macrocephaly, characteristic facial gestalt (high forehead, pointed chin), intellectual disability, and normal growth hormone regulation.

option_notes.text: Sotos syndrome presents with non-endocrine genetic overgrowth, macrocephaly, pointed chin, and learning difficulties.
Pituitary gigantism exhibits autonomous failure of GH suppression on OGTT and elevated IGF-I.
Precocious puberty presents with secondary sexual characteristics, testicular enlargement, and advanced bone age.
McCune-Albright syndrome features fibrous dysplasia, cafe-au-lait macules, and elevated GH/IGF-I.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old girl with Marfan syndrome is evaluated for severe tall stature (height SDS +3.2, current height 184 cm) with projected adult height of 195 cm. She has severe pectus excavatum, arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility, and aortic root dilation (Z-score +2.8). Which management strategy is contraindicated for reducing her linear growth potential?
options: High-dose estrogen therapy, due to the unacceptable risk of accelerating aortic root dilation and thromboembolism
Percutaneous bilateral epiphysiodesis of the distal femur and proximal tibia
Tight blood pressure control with an angiotensin receptor blocker or beta-blocker
Annual surveillance with transthoracic echocardiogram
mcqs.explanation: Historically, high-dose supraphysiological estrogen was used to accelerate epiphyseal fusion in tall girls; however, in Marfan syndrome, high-dose estrogens are contraindicated because they can increase cardiovascular risk, accelerate aortic root enlargement, and increase thromboembolic complications. Percutaneous epiphysiodesis is preferred if height reduction is indicated.

option_notes.text: High-dose estrogen therapy carries significant vascular risks and may worsen connective tissue laxity and aortic dilation in Marfan syndrome.
Percutaneous epiphysiodesis is a safe, targeted orthopedic procedure to arrest long-bone growth without systemic hormonal adverse effects.
Hemodynamic control with ARBs or beta-blockers is the standard of care to retard aortic root enlargement in Marfan syndrome.
Serial echocardiography is mandatory in all Marfan patients to monitor aortic root dimensions.

etiology.text: Etiologies include pituitary somatotroph adenomas, syndromic gigantism (X-LAG / GPR101, McCune-Albright, Carney complex, MEN1, AIP mutations), and primary genetic overgrowth syndromes (Sotos, Marfan, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Weaver).

epidemiology.text: Pituitary gigantism is extremely rare in pediatric practice, with an annual incidence of roughly 1 per million population. Primary genetic overgrowth syndromes occur more frequently.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis requires demonstrating failure to suppress serum GH to <1.0 mcg/L during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), elevated IGF-I/IGFBP-3, contrast-enhanced pituitary MRI, and genetic panel testing.

therapies.text: First-line therapy is transsphenoidal surgical resection. Medical therapy for persistent hypersecretion includes somatostatin analogs (octreotide LAR 10–30 mg IM monthly; lanreotide 60–120 mg SC monthly), dopamine agonists (cabergoline 0.25–2.0 mg/week), or the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant (10–30 mg SC daily).

pillars.label: Etiology and Classification
pillars.text: Adrenal insufficiency (AI) is classified as primary (adrenocortical destruction/dysgenesis; high ACTH, low cortisol, variable mineralocorticoid deficiency) or secondary/central (hypothalamic-pituitary CRH/ACTH deficiency; low/normal ACTH, low cortisol, preserved aldosterone). Primary causes include congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2), autoimmune Addison disease (isolated or APS-1/APS-2), X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1), congenital adrenal hypoplasia (DAX1/NR0B1), Triple A syndrome (AAAS), and infectious or hemorrhagic adrenal destruction (Waterhouse-Friderichsen).

pillars.label: Clinical Recognition
pillars.text: Chronic manifestations include progressive fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, generalized hyperpigmentation (palmar creases, vermilion border, scars, gingiva; primary AI only due to POMC/ACTH elevation), postural dizziness, salt craving, and hypoglycemia. Acute adrenal crisis presents with refractory hypotension, vascular collapse, shock, vomiting, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia (primary AI), and neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Protocols
pillars.text: Morning baseline cortisol (<3-5 mcg/dL highly suggestive; >15-18 mcg/dL reassuring) coupled with plasma ACTH differentiates primary (ACTH >100-2000 pg/mL) from secondary AI. The standard-dose cosyntropin stimulation test (250 mcg IV/IM) is the diagnostic reference: peak cortisol <18 mcg/dL (500 nmol/L) at 30 or 60 minutes confirms AI. In primary AI, plasma renin activity (PRA) is elevated and aldosterone is low.

pillars.label: Emergency Management of Adrenal Crisis
pillars.text: Adrenal crisis is a critical medical emergency. Immediate management requires intravenous bolus of normal saline (20 mL/kg, repeated as needed for shock) with 5-10% dextrose to correct hypoglycemia, followed by immediate IV hydrocortisone bolus (50-100 mg/m2 or age-based: <3 yr: 25 mg; 3-12 yr: 50 mg; >12 yr: 100 mg). Continuous infusion (50-100 mg/m2/day) or divided IV doses every 6 hours are continued until clinical stabilization.

pillars.label: Maintenance and Stress Dosing
pillars.text: Maintenance hydrocortisone is dosed at 8-10 mg/m2/day (up to 12 mg/m2/day) divided into 3 daily doses, honoring circadian rhythm (largest dose upon awakening). Primary AI requires mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone (0.05-0.2 mg daily) and oral sodium chloride in infants (1-2 g/day). Patients and families must receive emergency hydrocortisone injectable kits and instructions for 2-3x stress oral dosing for fever/illness.

cards.q: What two biochemical parameters distinguish primary adrenal insufficiency from central/secondary adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: Markedly elevated plasma ACTH and hyperkalemia (with elevated renin/low aldosterone) are present in primary AI, whereas central AI features low/inappropriately normal ACTH with preserved mineralocorticoid secretion and normal potassium.

cards.q: What peak serum cortisol threshold during a 250 mcg cosyntropin stimulation test is required to define normal adrenocortical reserve?
cards.a: A peak serum cortisol of ≥ 18 mcg/dL (approx 500 nmol/L) at 30 or 60 minutes.

cards.q: What is the initial intravenous hydrocortisone stress dose for an acute adrenal crisis in a school-aged child (ages 3–12 years)?
cards.a: 50 mg IV bolus (or 50 to 100 mg/m2 IV), accompanied by 20 mL/kg isotonic saline with 5–10% dextrose.

cards.q: What is the physiological daily maintenance hydrocortisone dose in pediatric adrenal insufficiency?
cards.a: 8 to 10 mg/m2/day (divided into three doses, with the highest dose taken first thing in the morning).

cards.q: What oral medication and standard starting dose are utilized for mineralocorticoid replacement in primary adrenal failure?
cards.a: Fludrocortisone acetate at 0.05 to 0.2 mg orally once daily, adjusted by blood pressure and plasma renin activity.

cards.q: What X-linked peroxisomal disorder causes progressive primary adrenal insufficiency and neurocognitive regression in boys aged 4 to 10 years?
cards.a: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD), caused by ABCD1 mutations leading to accumulation of very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs).

cards.q: Why does cutaneous hyperpigmentation occur in primary adrenal failure but not in secondary adrenal failure?
cards.a: Lack of cortisol negative feedback drives massive pituitary POMC cleavage into ACTH and alpha-MSH, which bind melanocortin 1 receptors (MC1R) on dermal melanocytes.

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with severe vomiting, lethargy, and dehydration. Blood pressure is 74/42 mmHg and heart rate is 144 bpm. Physical exam reveals marked hyperpigmentation of the gingival mucosa and knuckles. Laboratory analysis shows sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 6.8 mEq/L, and blood glucose 42 mg/dL. What is the immediate life-saving treatment?
options: Intravenous bolus of 0.9% normal saline (20 mL/kg) with 5% dextrose and immediate IV hydrocortisone 50 mg
Continuous intravenous insulin infusion with 50% dextrose to treat hyperkalemia
Immediate oral fludrocortisone 0.1 mg and oral rehydration solution
Intravenous hypertonic 3% sodium chloride bolus without glucocorticoids
mcqs.explanation: This patient is in acute primary adrenal crisis with hypotensive shock, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypoglycemia. Immediate resuscitation with isotonic saline/dextrose boluses and parenteral hydrocortisone is vital.

option_notes.text: Isotonic fluid resuscitation and parenteral hydrocortisone rapidly correct intravascular volume depletion and adrenal collapse.
Insulin will exacerbate the life-threatening hypoglycemia (glucose 42 mg/dL); hydrocortisone and IV fluids correct the hyperkalemia.
Oral administration is contraindicated in an emetic, obtunded child in hypovolemic shock.
Administering hypertonic saline without hydrocortisone fails to treat the underlying vascular collapse and risks pontine myelinolysis.

mcqs.q: A 7-year-old previously healthy boy develops progressive fatigue, declining school performance, and skin bronzing over 6 months. Neurological exam reveals hyperreflexia and mild visual tracking impairment. Plasma ACTH is 840 pg/mL with morning cortisol 2.1 mcg/dL. Plasma renin activity is elevated. What diagnostic test should be prioritized to identify the underlying etiology?
options: Plasma very long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) analysis and brain MRI
Sweat chloride test to rule out cystic fibrosis
Serum anti-streptolysin O titer and complement levels
Gastric emptying scintigraphy and upper endoscopy
mcqs.explanation: In young boys presenting with primary adrenal insufficiency (elevated ACTH, low cortisol) and subtle neurocognitive changes, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1 mutation) must be excluded by measuring plasma very long-chain fatty acids (VLCFA) and brain MRI to detect cerebral demyelination.

option_notes.text: Elevated hexacosanoic acid (C26:0) and VLCFA ratios confirm X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, a leading cause of primary AI in young males.
Cystic fibrosis does not cause primary adrenal failure or cutaneous hyperpigmentation.
Post-streptococcal disease causes glomerulonephritis, not primary adrenal failure.
Gastric scintigraphy does not diagnose adrenal failure or white matter neurodegenerative disease.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old girl with autoimmune Addison disease (primary adrenocortical failure) on maintenance hydrocortisone (9 mg/m2/day) and fludrocortisone (0.1 mg daily) develops acute streptococcal pharyngitis with fever of 39.4°C (103°F). What instruction must be given to her parents regarding steroid dosing?
options: Triple her oral hydrocortisone dose (25–30 mg/m2/day) divided every 8 hours until fever resolves, keeping fludrocortisone unchanged
Discontinue hydrocortisone completely to allow the immune system to fight the bacterial infection
Increase fludrocortisone to 1.0 mg daily and reduce hydrocortisone to half dose
Administer oral dexamethasone 4 mg once daily without taking any fluids
mcqs.explanation: During febrile illness (>38.5°C), endogenous cortisol secretion in healthy individuals triples. Patients with adrenal insufficiency require 'stress dosing' (doubling or tripling the maintenance oral hydrocortisone dose) to prevent adrenal crisis. Fludrocortisone dosing remains unchanged.

option_notes.text: Stress dosing (2-3x maintenance hydrocortisone) replicates normal physiological stress responses during fever and prevents adrenal crisis.
Discontinuing hydrocortisone during febrile illness precipitates fatal adrenal crisis within hours.
Fludrocortisone dose is not increased during routine fever; hydrocortisone at high doses provides cross-reactive mineralocorticoid activity.
High-dose dexamethasone is unmonitored, causes prolonged suppression, and omitting fluids leads to hypovolemia.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old boy with severe Crohn disease has been treated with oral prednisone (40 mg daily) for 6 months. His gastroenterologist abruptly stops the prednisone after achieving mucosal healing. Five days later, the boy presents with severe fatigue, dizziness, nausea, and a blood pressure of 82/48 mmHg. Laboratory testing shows sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, and glucose 64 mg/dL. What is the diagnosis?
options: Tertiary (iatrogenic) adrenal insufficiency due to prolonged hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression
Acute primary autoimmune adrenalitis with destruction of all three adrenocortical zones
Acute primary mineralocorticoid deficiency secondary to renal tubular injury
Cushing disease relapse secondary to an ACTH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma
mcqs.explanation: Prolonged exogenous supraphysiological glucocorticoid therapy suppresses hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH secretion, resulting in adrenocortical atrophy. Abrupt cessation unmasks central/tertiary adrenal insufficiency, characterized by normal potassium (intact mineralocorticoid axis) but symptomatic glucocorticoid deficiency.

option_notes.text: Abrupt withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoids is the most common cause of tertiary adrenal insufficiency, requiring gradual tapering.
Primary autoimmune destruction presents with hyperkalemia, elevated ACTH, and skin hyperpigmentation, which are absent here.
Mineralocorticoid secretion (aldosterone) is regulated by the renin-angiotensin system, not ACTH, and remains preserved.
Cushing disease features hypercortisolemia and hypertension, the opposite of this presentation.

mcqs.q: A 6-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia, fatigue, and alacrima (inability to produce tears). Physical examination also reveals mild difficulty swallowing (achalasia). Laboratory testing confirms primary adrenocortical failure with ACTH 650 pg/mL and cortisol 1.8 mcg/dL. What rare autosomal recessive syndrome is defined by this constellation of findings?
options: Triple A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome, caused by AAAS mutations)
Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome type 1 (APS-1, caused by AIRE mutations)
Werdnig-Hoffmann spinal muscular atrophy
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency
mcqs.explanation: Triple A syndrome (Allgrove syndrome) is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the AAAS gene (encoding the nuclear pore protein aladin), characterized by the triad of Adrenal insufficiency, Achalasia, and Alacrima.

option_notes.text: AAAS mutations cause Triple A syndrome with ACTH-resistant adrenal failure, achalasia, and alacrima.
APS-1 presents with chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease, without achalasia.
Spinal muscular atrophy affects anterior horn cells and does not cause primary adrenal failure.
11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency features virilization and hypertension due to DOC accumulation, without alacrima.

etiology.text: Etiologies include congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2), autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison disease, APS-1, APS-2), X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1), congenital adrenal hypoplasia (DAX1/NR0B1), Triple A syndrome (AAAS), bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, and exogenous steroid withdrawal.

epidemiology.text: Primary adrenal insufficiency occurs in approximately 1 in 10,000 individuals, with congenital adrenal hyperplasia being the most frequent genetic etiology in children and autoimmune adrenalitis predominant in adolescents.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis is confirmed by morning cortisol (<3-5 mcg/dL) and elevated ACTH (>100 pg/mL in primary AI), failure of cortisol to rise to ≥18 mcg/dL on a standard cosyntropin stimulation test, elevated plasma renin activity, and targeted autoantibody or genetic testing.

therapies.text: Maintenance hydrocortisone is dosed at 8–10 mg/m2/day orally in 3 divided doses. Primary AI also requires fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg once daily. For acute adrenal crisis, immediate resuscitation requires IV normal saline bolus (20 mL/kg) with 5–10% dextrose and IV hydrocortisone 50–100 mg/m2 (or age-based: <3 yr: 25 mg, 3–12 yr: 50 mg, >12 yr: 100 mg).

pillars.label: Steroidogenic Pathways and Genetics
pillars.text: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) is a group of autosomal recessive disorders of cortisol biosynthesis. More than 90-95% of cases are caused by mutations in CYP21A2 encoding 21-hydroxylase. Deficiency impairs conversion of 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) to 11-deoxycortisol and progesterone to 11-deoxycorticosterone, shunting steroid precursors into the adrenal androgen pathway.

pillars.label: Clinical Phenotypes
pillars.text: Classic salt-wasting (SW) CAH presents at 1-3 weeks of life with life-threatening salt-wasting crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypovolemia, shock) and prenatal virilization in 46,XX females (clitoromegaly, labial fusion, urogenital sinus; Prader stages I-V). Classic simple-virilizing (SV) CAH retains sufficient aldosterone synthesis (~1-2%) to prevent salt crisis but causes prenatal virilization in females and rapid post-natal somatic growth with premature epiphyseal fusion in both sexes. Non-classic (NC) CAH presents in childhood or adolescence with premature pubarche, hirsutism, severe acne, and menstrual irregularities.

pillars.label: Newborn Screening and Diagnostics
pillars.text: Universal newborn screening measures 17-OHP on dried blood spots via immunoassay, with gestational age- and birthweight-adjusted cutoffs, followed by second-tier LC-MS/MS steroid profiling. Confirmation requires elevated baseline and cosyntropin-stimulated 17-OHP (>1,000 ng/dL in classic CAH; >1,500 ng/dL post-ACTH in NC-CAH), elevated 21-deoxycortisol, high androstenedione, and CYP21A2 gene deletion/mutation analysis.

pillars.label: Medical Replacement Protocols
pillars.text: Classic CAH requires lifelong dual hormone replacement: hydrocortisone (10-15 mg/m2/day in growing children, divided 3 times daily) to suppress excess ACTH-driven androgens while preserving growth, and fludrocortisone (0.05-0.2 mg/day) to restore sodium balance. Infants also require oral sodium chloride supplementation (1-2 g/day, approx 17-34 mEq/day) due to immature renal tubular sodium reabsorption. Stress dosing (2-3x maintenance hydrocortisone) is mandatory during intercurrent illness.

pillars.label: Monitoring and Novel Therapies
pillars.text: Therapeutic monitoring balances androgen suppression against hypercortisolemia (growth suppression, cushingoid weight gain, osteopenia). Parameters monitored include serial linear height velocity, bone age radiographs, and mid-morning/pre-dose 17-OHP and androstenedione. In post-pubertal males, regular testicular ultrasound screens for Testicular Adrenal Rest Tumors (TART). Novel therapies include modified-release hydrocortisone formulations (Chronocort/Efmody) and oral ACTH receptor (MC2R) antagonists (crinecerfont).

cards.q: What enzyme deficiency accounts for more than 90% to 95% of all cases of congenital adrenal hyperplasia?
cards.a: 21-Hydroxylase deficiency, caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the CYP21A2 gene on chromosome 6p21.3.

cards.q: At what age do male infants with undiagnosed classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency typically present with acute crisis?
cards.a: At 7 to 21 days (1 to 3 weeks) of life, presenting with poor feeding, vomiting, failure to thrive, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hypovolemic shock.

cards.q: What primary analyte is measured on newborn dried blood spots to screen for classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency?
cards.a: 17-Hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP), with cutoffs adjusted for gestational age and birth weight to reduce false-positive rates in premature infants.

cards.q: Why is oral sodium chloride supplementation (1 to 2 g/day) specifically required in infants with classic salt-wasting CAH in addition to fludrocortisone?
cards.a: Immature neonatal renal tubules have reduced sensitivity to mineralocorticoids and high fractional sodium excretion, requiring exogenous sodium supplementation until dietary sodium intake increases.

cards.q: What benign tumor occurs in the testes of adolescent and adult males with classic CAH due to poor disease control?
cards.a: Testicular Adrenal Rest Tumors (TART), which can cause testicular pain, obstruction of seminiferous tubules, and irreversible azoospermia.

cards.q: Which rare form of CAH features severe virilization accompanied by low-renin hypertension and hypokalemia?
cards.a: 11-Beta-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP11B1), due to accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone (DOC), a potent mineralocorticoid agonist.

cards.q: What newly characterized pathway accounts for persistent virilization in classic CAH despite suppression of conventional circulating androgens?
cards.a: The alternative 'backdoor pathway' (generating 11-oxygenated androgens like 11-ketotestosterone and 11-hydroxytestosterone from 17-OHP).

mcqs.q: A 12-day-old male infant born at term presents with poor feeding, lethargy, and a 15% weight loss from birth. He has normal male external genitalia with bilateral descended testes and hyperpigmentation of the scrotum. Serum electrolytes demonstrate sodium 116 mEq/L and potassium 8.2 mEq/L. Blood glucose is 48 mg/dL. What diagnostic finding confirms the most likely diagnosis?
options: Markedly elevated serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (>10,000 ng/dL) and high plasma renin activity
Elevated plasma aldosterone with suppressed plasma renin activity
Low ACTH with elevated serum cortisol (>35 mcg/dL)
Elevated 11-deoxycorticosterone with metabolic alkalosis
mcqs.explanation: The male infant exhibits acute salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency presenting in the second week of life with hyperkalemia, severe hyponatremia, and scrotal hyperpigmentation. Massive elevation of 17-OHP and elevated plasma renin confirm classic salt-wasting CAH.

option_notes.text: Massive 17-OHP accumulation due to 21-hydroxylase block coupled with aldosterone deficiency drives high renin and severe salt loss.
Aldosterone is deficient in salt-wasting CAH; high aldosterone with low renin defines primary aldosteronism.
Cortisol is deficient and ACTH is elevated due to loss of negative feedback.
Accumulation of DOC occurs in 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, causing hypertension and hypokalemia, not salt wasting.

mcqs.q: A full-term newborn is noted to have ambiguous genitalia: marked clitoromegaly with a glanular groove, complete labial fusion, and a single perineal urogenital orifice (Prader stage IV). Neither gonad is palpable in the labioscrotal folds. Peripheral blood karyotype reveals 46,XX. What is the underlying hormonal mechanism producing this phenotype?
options: Inability to 21-hydroxylate progesterone precursors, resulting in massive ACTH stimulation and shunting into adrenal androgen biosynthesis in utero
Complete peripheral end-organ resistance to dihydrotestosterone due to an androgen receptor mutation
Autonomous secretion of testosterone from an undifferentiated dysgenetic intra-abdominal ovary
Placental aromatase hyperactivation converting fetal estrogens into testosterone
mcqs.explanation: In 46,XX classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, impaired cortisol synthesis removes negative feedback on the pituitary, causing massive ACTH secretion. Accumulated precursors are shunted into androstenedione and testosterone, virilizing the bipotential external genitalia in utero.

option_notes.text: Prenatal excess adrenal androgens virilize 46,XX external genitalia while internal Müllerian ducts remain intact.
Androgen insensitivity syndrome occurs in 46,XY individuals and presents with female or ambiguous external genitalia, not virilized 46,XX.
Dysgenetic ovaries do not produce massive androgens in utero.
Placental aromatase converts androgens to estrogens; deficiency (not hyperactivation) causes virilization.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old male with classic salt-wasting CAH maintained on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone undergoes routine evaluation. Testicular examination reveals firm, painless, multinodular lobulated masses bilaterally in the medial aspect of the testes adjacent to the mediastinum testis. Serum 17-OHP is 4,200 ng/dL (reference <200 ng/dL) and androstenedione is elevated. Testicular ultrasound confirms bilateral hypoechoic lobulated lesions. What is the diagnosis and correct clinical management?
options: Testicular Adrenal Rest Tumors (TART); optimize compliance and intensify glucocorticoid suppression to regress the lesions
Bilateral malignant testicular seminomas; proceed with immediate bilateral radical orchiectomy
Bilateral epididymal cysts; observe with annual scrotal palpation alone
Leydig cell adenomas; initiate high-dose mitotane chemotherapy
mcqs.explanation: Testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART) are benign ACTH-responsive lesions arising from aberrant adrenal cortical cells in the testes of males with CAH. Poor endocrine control (elevated ACTH/17-OHP) stimulates tumor hypertrophy. Increasing glucocorticoid therapy to suppress ACTH leads to tumor regression and preserves fertility.

option_notes.text: TARTs are benign, ACTH-dependent tumors that regress with intensified glucocorticoid replacement; biopsy or orchiectomy is contraindicated.
TARTs are completely benign and must not be misdiagnosed as malignant seminomas, avoiding tragic unnecessary bilateral orchiectomy.
The lesions reside within the testicular parenchyma at the rete testis, not the epididymis.
Mitotane is adrenolytic chemotherapy for adrenocortical carcinoma and has no role in benign TART management.

mcqs.q: A 17-year-old female presents with severe facial acne, male-pattern terminal hair growth on the chin and lower abdomen (Ferriman-Gallwey score 12), and oligomenorrhea (3 periods per year). Baseline morning 17-OHP is 380 ng/dL (reference <100 ng/dL). An intravenous cosyntropin stimulation test (250 mcg) produces a 60-minute 17-OHP of 2,400 ng/dL. What is the definitive diagnosis?
options: Non-classic (late-onset) Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia
Polycystic Ovary Syndrome with normal adrenal steroidogenesis
Cushing disease secondary to pituitary ACTH macroadenoma
Primary hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (premature ovarian failure)
mcqs.explanation: A cosyntropin-stimulated 17-OHP level >1,500 ng/dL (and typically >1,000-2,000 ng/dL) is diagnostic of non-classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which commonly masquerades as PCOS in adolescent and young adult females.

option_notes.text: Post-ACTH 17-OHP >1,500 ng/dL confirms non-classic CAH, distinguishing it from idiopathic polycystic ovary syndrome.
In classic PCOS without CAH, stimulated 17-OHP remains well below 1,000 ng/dL.
Cushing disease presents with central obesity, moon facies, striae, and elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol.
Premature ovarian failure presents with elevated gonadotropins (FSH >40 IU/L) and hypoestrogenism without 17-OHP hypersecretion.

mcqs.q: A 3-week-old female infant with confirmed classic simple-virilizing CAH (46,XX, Prader III) is prescribed maintenance therapy. Her serum electrolytes and blood pressure are normal. Which medication regimen should be prescribed for ongoing maintenance?
options: Oral hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m2/day divided in three daily doses, with fludrocortisone monitoring
High-dose oral dexamethasone 2 mg daily given as a single nighttime dose
Spironolactone monotherapy at 5 mg/kg/day without glucocorticoid replacement
Continuous subcutaneous infusion of octreotide at 20 mcg/kg/day
mcqs.explanation: In growing infants and children with classic CAH, short-acting hydrocortisone (10-15 mg/m2/day divided three times daily) is the preferred glucocorticoid because longer-acting agents (dexamethasone, prednisone) cause severe linear growth suppression and metabolic toxicity.

option_notes.text: Short-acting oral hydrocortisone suppresses adrenal androgens while minimizing growth plate suppression in young pediatric patients.
Dexamethasone is 30-40 times more potent than hydrocortisone, lacks mineralocorticoid activity, and severely suppresses growth in infants.
Spironolactone does not replace deficient cortisol and will precipitate fatal adrenal crisis.
Octreotide has no role in CAH and inhibits growth hormone secretion.

etiology.text: Autosomal recessive enzymatic block in adrenal steroidogenesis, caused by CYP21A2 mutations (21-hydroxylase deficiency, >95%), CYP11B1 (11-beta-hydroxylase), HSD3B2 (3-beta-HSD), CYP17A1 (17-hydroxylase), StAR (lipoid CAH), or POR (oxidoreductase).

epidemiology.text: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency occurs in approximately 1 in 14,000 to 1 in 18,000 live births globally (higher in Yupik Inuits, 1:280). Non-classic CAH is one of the most common autosomal recessive disorders, affecting 1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000 individuals depending on ethnicity.

diagnostics.text: Universal newborn screening via blood spot 17-OHP immunoassay and LC-MS/MS; confirmation by serum 17-OHP, 21-deoxycortisol, androstenedione, plasma renin activity, and comprehensive CYP21A2 gene deletion/sequencing analysis.

therapies.text: Maintenance glucocorticoid is oral hydrocortisone 10–15 mg/m2/day divided in 3 doses. Salt-wasting forms require fludrocortisone 0.05–0.2 mg once daily, plus oral sodium chloride 1–2 g/day (approx 17–34 mEq/day) in infants. Intercurrent febrile stress requires 2–3x maintenance hydrocortisone.
therapies.section: Standard Medical Regimen in Classic CAH

pillars.label: Etiology and Classification
pillars.text: Cushing syndrome (CS) in childhood is divided into exogenous (iatrogenic glucocorticoid administration, the most common overall) and endogenous causes. Endogenous CS is categorized into ACTH-dependent (Cushing disease secondary to ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma in >75% of children >7 years; ectopic ACTH/CRH secretion) and ACTH-independent (adrenocortical adenoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease [PPNAD/Carney complex], or McCune-Albright syndrome, predominant in infants and toddlers <5 years).

pillars.label: Hallmark Clinical Manifestation
pillars.text: The cardinal clinical hallmark of pediatric Cushing syndrome is the combination of progressive excessive weight gain crossing percentiles upwards alongside concurrent severe deceleration or cessation of linear growth (crossing height percentiles downward). Other signs include facial plethoric mooning, dorsal fat pad ('buffalo hump'), violaceous dermal striae (>1 cm wide), hirsutism, hypertension, osteopenia, and emotional lability.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Screening Protocols
pillars.text: Confirmation of hypercortisolemia requires at least two abnormal first-line screening tests: elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC, >3-fold upper limit of normal), elevated late-night salivary cortisol (>0.15 mcg/dL at 23:00 h on two separate nights), or failure of serum cortisol suppression to <1.8 mcg/dL (50 nmol/L) following an overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test (1 mg oral at 23:00 h, or 30 mcg/kg in children <40 kg).

pillars.label: Differential Localization Protocols
pillars.text: Once hypercortisolemia is established, plasma ACTH distinguishes ACTH-independent (<5-10 pg/mL; indicates adrenal CT/MRI) from ACTH-dependent (>15-20 pg/mL). In ACTH-dependent CS, high-dose dexamethasone suppression (8 mg overnight or 80 mcg/kg) and CRH stimulation test distinguish Cushing disease (cortisol suppresses >50%, ACTH rises >50% with CRH) from ectopic ACTH. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) with CRH stimulation is the gold standard when pituitary MRI fails to show a clear adenoma >6 mm.

pillars.label: Surgical and Medical Management
pillars.text: Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy is the treatment of choice for Cushing disease, offering cure rates >70-90% in experienced pediatric centers. Successful cure produces transient profound central adrenal insufficiency (morning cortisol <1-2 mcg/dL), requiring temporary hydrocortisone replacement for 6-18 months. Adrenal tumors require laparoscopic or open adrenalectomy. Medical steroidogenesis inhibitors (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat) provide bridge therapy before definitive surgery.

cards.q: What pathognomonic growth pattern distinguishes pediatric Cushing syndrome from simple nutritional/exogenous obesity?
cards.a: Excessive weight gain accompanied by severe linear growth deceleration or arrest (in contrast to simple obesity, where height velocity is accelerated and children are tall for age).

cards.q: What is the most frequent cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome in children under 5 years versus children older than 7 years?
cards.a: In children <5 years, primary adrenal tumors (adenomas and carcinomas) predominate; in children >7 years, ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas (Cushing disease) account for >75% to 85% of cases.

cards.q: Name the three approved first-line screening tests used to establish pathological hypercortisolemia in children.
cards.a: 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC), late-night (23:00 h) salivary cortisol (on two separate nights), and the low-dose dexamethasone suppression test.

cards.q: What serum cortisol cutoff following an overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test excludes Cushing syndrome with high sensitivity?
cards.a: Serum cortisol < 1.8 mcg/dL (approx 50 nmol/L) measured at 08:00 h following dexamethasone administration.

cards.q: What invasive procedure is the diagnostic reference standard for distinguishing pituitary Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH secretion when pituitary MRI is equivocal?
cards.a: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) with CRH stimulation, demonstrating an IPS-to-peripheral ACTH ratio ≥2.0 at baseline or ≥3.0 post-CRH.

cards.q: What biochemical finding within 24 to 72 hours following transsphenoidal surgery indicates surgical cure of Cushing disease?
cards.a: Profound transient central adrenal insufficiency with morning serum cortisol < 1.0 to 2.0 mcg/dL.

cards.q: Which syndrome featuring primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD), cardiac myxomas, and spotty skin pigmentation is caused by PRKAR1A mutations?
cards.a: Carney complex, an autosomal dominant disorder causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome with cyclical hypercortisolemia.

mcqs.q: An 11-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of rapid weight gain. Over the past 2 years, her BMI percentile increased from the 60th to the 98th percentile, while her linear height velocity plummeted from 5.5 cm/year to 1.8 cm/year (height dropping from the 50th to the 10th percentile). She has plethoric moon facies, dark purplish abdominal striae measuring 1.5 cm in width, and a blood pressure of 136/88 mmHg. What is the most critical feature differentiating her condition from simple exogenous obesity?
options: Severe deceleration of linear growth velocity in the presence of advancing weight gain
Elevated fasting serum insulin concentrations
Development of mild acanthosis nigricans in skin folds
Presence of increased subcutaneous adipose tissue over the triceps
mcqs.explanation: Simple nutritional obesity stimulates linear growth and bone age maturation, so children are tall for their age. Conversely, Cushing syndrome uniquely combines rapid weight gain with dramatic growth deceleration and bone age delay due to the catabolic effects of glucocorticoids on the growth plate.

option_notes.text: Linear growth arrest paired with weight gain is the hallmark clinical feature that distinguishes Cushing syndrome from simple obesity.
Hyperinsulinemia is universal in simple obesity and does not distinguish Cushing syndrome.
Acanthosis nigricans occurs in both conditions due to hyperinsulinemia and insulin resistance.
Subcutaneous fat accumulation occurs in all forms of generalized obesity.

mcqs.q: A 13-year-old boy has confirmed pathological hypercortisolemia based on elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol (4-fold above normal) and elevated late-night salivary cortisol. His 08:00 h plasma ACTH is measured at 2.4 pg/mL (reference 10–60 pg/mL, with undetectable repeated value <5 pg/mL). What is the appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: High-resolution dedicated contrast-enhanced adrenal CT or MRI scan
Pituitary MRI with dynamic gadolinium enhancement
Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation
High-resolution chest CT scan to evaluate for bronchial carcinoid tumor
mcqs.explanation: A suppressed plasma ACTH (<5 pg/mL) indicates ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome, pointing directly to primary autonomous adrenal pathology (adenoma, carcinoma, PPNAD). Imaging of the adrenal glands is the mandatory next step.

option_notes.text: Suppressed plasma ACTH confirms ACTH-independent hypercortisolemia; adrenal imaging is mandatory to locate the primary adrenal lesion.
Pituitary MRI is indicated for ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, not when ACTH is suppressed.
BIPSS differentiates pituitary from ectopic sources when ACTH is elevated, and is contraindicated in ACTH-independent disease.
Bronchial carcinoids secrete ectopic ACTH, which causes elevated, not suppressed, ACTH.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old boy with severe Cushing syndrome has elevated 24-hour UFC and a plasma ACTH of 65 pg/mL. Pituitary MRI demonstrates no visible focal adenoma. A high-dose dexamethasone suppression test produces a 75% reduction in morning cortisol, and peripheral CRH administration elicits a 95% rise in ACTH. What diagnostic test should be performed before proceeding with neurosurgical exploration?
options: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) with CRH stimulation to confirm central ACTH gradient and lateralization
Total bilateral adrenalectomy as first-line definitive management
Lifelong high-dose metyrapone monotherapy without further testing
Abdominal ultrasound to look for ovarian rest tumors
mcqs.explanation: When ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is diagnosed but pituitary MRI is normal or equivocal (<6 mm lesion), BIPSS with CRH stimulation is the gold standard to prove a pituitary source (central-to-peripheral ACTH ratio ≥2 baseline or ≥3 post-CRH) and aid inter-sinus lateralization.

option_notes.text: BIPSS confirms a pituitary origin over occult ectopic ACTH and guides the neurosurgeon when MRI fails to identify a clear microadenoma.
Bilateral adrenalectomy is a last-resort therapy that causes Nelson syndrome (invasive corticotroph tumor growth) and permanent adrenal insufficiency.
Metyrapone is a temporary medical inhibitor, not definitive diagnostic or curative management.
Ovarian rest tumors occur in CAH, not Cushing disease, and the patient is a male.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old girl undergoes successful transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy for a 4 mm corticotroph microadenoma. On postoperative day 2, she feels weak and nauseated. Laboratory testing reveals morning serum cortisol 0.6 mcg/dL (reference 5–20 mcg/dL) and ACTH 4.2 pg/mL. What is the clinical significance of this finding?
options: Indicates complete surgical resection and cure, requiring temporary hydrocortisone replacement therapy
Represents acute surgical failure and indicates immediate re-exploration of the sella
Reflects permanent panhypopituitarism requiring permanent desmopressin and levothyroxine
Indicates transformation of the corticotroph tumor into an aggressive silent carcinoma
mcqs.explanation: Profound transient hypocortisolemia (morning cortisol <1-2 mcg/dL) following transsphenoidal adenomectomy is the hallmark of surgical cure. It reflects suppression of the normal surrounding hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis by prolonged prior hypercortisolemia. Temporary hydrocortisone replacement is required until the HPA axis recovers.

option_notes.text: Postoperative morning cortisol <1-2 mcg/dL demonstrates complete resection of the autonomous adenoma and confirms surgical cure.
Surgical failure would manifest as persistently elevated or normal unsuppressed cortisol (>5 mcg/dL).
Selective adenomectomy preserves other pituitary cell lines; hypocortisolemia is temporary and usually recovers over 6-18 months.
Low cortisol indicates absence of functional corticotroph tissue, the opposite of carcinoma progression.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for Cushing syndrome. Physical examination reveals pigmented lentigines on her eyelids, lips, and oral mucosa. Echocardiogram demonstrates a benign right atrial myxoma. Endocrine testing reveals ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome. What gene defect is responsible for this condition?
options: Inactivating mutation in PRKAR1A encoding the protein kinase A regulatory subunit type 1A
Activating mutation in the GNAS gene encoding G-alpha-s
Loss-of-function mutation in the MEN1 gene encoding menin
Germline mutation in the RET proto-oncogene
mcqs.explanation: Carney complex is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A, leading to constitutive PKA activation, cardiac myxomas, spotty skin pigmentation (lentigines), and primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD).

option_notes.text: PRKAR1A mutations cause Carney complex with PPNAD, cardiac myxomas, and spotty pigmentation.
GNAS mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome featuring fibrous dysplasia, precocious puberty, and cafe-au-lait macules.
MEN1 causes parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumors, not cardiac myxomas or PPNAD.
RET mutations cause MEN2 with medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

etiology.text: Etiologies include ACTH-dependent Cushing disease (pituitary corticotroph adenoma, >75% of older children), ectopic ACTH secretion, and ACTH-independent adrenal pathology (adrenocortical adenoma/carcinoma, PPNAD in Carney complex [PRKAR1A], and McCune-Albright syndrome [GNAS]).

epidemiology.text: Endogenous Cushing syndrome is rare in pediatrics, with an incidence of approximately 2 to 5 per million per year. Adrenal tumors predominate in early childhood (<5 years), while pituitary microadenomas predominate in adolescents.

diagnostics.text: Diagnosis requires demonstrating hypercortisolemia using 24-hour UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, or overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, followed by plasma ACTH measurement, high-dose dexamethasone suppression, pituitary dynamic MRI, and BIPSS.

therapies.text: Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy is the curative treatment of choice for Cushing disease. Postoperative adrenal insufficiency is managed with hydrocortisone (10–12 mg/m2/day in 2–3 divided doses) until the HPA axis recovers (typically 6–18 months). Medical inhibitors (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat) are used for pre-surgical control.
therapies.section: Curative and Perioperative Management in Cushing Syndrome

pillars.label: Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone Physiology
pillars.text: Aldosterone, synthesized in the adrenal zona glomerulosa by aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), binds the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in the renal collecting duct principal cells. MR activation upregulates the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, promoting sodium and water reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ion excretion. Renin, stimulated by hypovolemia and renal hypoperfusion, drives angiotensin II-mediated aldosterone synthesis.

pillars.label: Hypoaldosteronism and Pseudohypoaldosteronism
pillars.text: Hypoaldosteronism features hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis with normal cortisol. Aldosterone synthase deficiency (CYP11B2) features high renin and low aldosterone. Pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA) represents mineralocorticoid resistance: Renal PHA1 is autosomal dominant (NR3C2/MR mutation), improving with age; Systemic PHA1 is autosomal recessive (SCNN1A, SCNN1B, SCNN1G / ENaC loss of function), severe and lifelong, involving salivary and sweat glands; Secondary PHA (PHA3) is transient, triggered by urinary tract infections or obstructive uropathy in infants.

pillars.label: Endocrine Hypertension Classification
pillars.text: Monogenic and endocrine causes of hypertension feature suppressed plasma renin activity (low-renin hypertension). Primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome, aldosterone-producing adenoma) features high aldosterone and low renin. Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA / Familial Hyperaldosteronism Type I) is caused by a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 fusion gene driven by ACTH. Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) is caused by HSD11B2 mutations, preventing conversion of cortisol to inactive cortisone and allowing cortisol to flood and activate the MR.

pillars.label: Liddle Syndrome and Enzymatic Mimics
pillars.text: Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant pseudoaldosteronism caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCNN1B or SCNN1G encoding ENaC subunits, preventing PY motif ubiquitination and causing constitutive ENaC cell-surface retention, resulting in severe hypertension, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and suppressed levels of BOTH renin AND aldosterone. Licorice ingestion (glycyrrhetinic acid) pharmacologically inhibits 11beta-HSD2, mimicking genetic AME.

pillars.label: Targeted Diagnostic and Treatment Algorithms
pillars.text: Screening for mineralocorticoid hypertension requires paired plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) and plasma renin activity (PRA). PAC/PRA ratio >20-30 with PAC >15 ng/dL indicates primary aldosteronism. GRA is treated with physiological glucocorticoid suppression (dexamethasone 0.125-0.25 mg daily) or amiloride/eplerenone. AME and licorice-induced hypertension respond to MR antagonists (spironolactone) and potassium repletion. Liddle syndrome is completely resistant to spironolactone but responds dramatically to ENaC blockers (amiloride 5-10 mg daily or triamterene).

cards.q: What electrolyte and acid-base triad is classic for states of mineralocorticoid excess?
cards.a: Hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, usually accompanied by suppressed plasma renin activity.

cards.q: What paired screening test establishes the diagnosis of low-renin primary aldosteronism?
cards.a: The plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC) to plasma renin activity (PRA) ratio, where PAC/PRA > 20 to 30 (with PAC > 15 ng/dL) is diagnostic.

cards.q: What unique genetic mechanism causes Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA / Familial Hyperaldosteronism Type I)?
cards.a: An unequal crossing-over event creating a chimeric gene linking the ACTH-responsive CYP11B1 promoter to the aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) coding sequence.

cards.q: What enzyme protects the non-selective mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol activation by rapidly converting cortisol to cortisone?
cards.a: 11-Beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (11beta-HSD2), encoded by the HSD11B2 gene.

cards.q: Why is Liddle syndrome completely unresponsive to spironolactone, and which drug class provides effective treatment?
cards.a: The mutation causes constitutive ENaC channel surface overexpression independent of the mineralocorticoid receptor; treatment requires direct ENaC channel blockers (amiloride or triamterene).

cards.q: What clinical differences distinguish autosomal dominant Renal PHA1 from autosomal recessive Systemic PHA1?
cards.a: Renal PHA1 (MR mutation) is restricted to the kidney and improves spontaneously with age; Systemic PHA1 (ENaC subunit mutations) affects sweat, salivary, and lung epithelia, causing severe lifelong salt wasting.

cards.q: What common pediatric clinical scenario produces transient secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA3) in young infants?
cards.a: Acute pyelonephritis (urinary tract infection) associated with underlying congenital obstructive uropathy (e.g., posterior urethral valves or hydronephrosis).

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for severe hypertension (blood pressure 152/96 mmHg). Laboratory testing reveals sodium 144 mEq/L, potassium 2.7 mEq/L, and serum bicarbonate 32 mEq/L. Plasma renin activity is profoundly suppressed (<0.1 ng/mL/h), and plasma aldosterone concentration is also undetectable (<1.0 ng/dL). Urinary free cortisol-to-cortisone ratio is normal. Treatment with high-dose spironolactone produces no reduction in blood pressure. However, initiating oral amiloride normalizes her blood pressure and potassium within 72 hours. What is the molecular diagnosis?
options: Liddle syndrome, caused by a gain-of-function mutation in an epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) subunit
Primary aldosteronism secondary to a solitary unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma
Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA) secondary to a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene
Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) secondary to an HSD11B2 gene mutation
mcqs.explanation: Liddle syndrome is an autosomal dominant channelopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCNN1B or SCNN1G that disrupt the PY motif, preventing ENaC degradation. The constitutive channel activation reabsorbs sodium independently of aldosterone, suppressing both renin and aldosterone. Because the mineralocorticoid receptor is bypassed, spironolactone fails, while direct ENaC blockers (amiloride) are curative.

option_notes.text: Liddle syndrome uniquely combines low renin, low aldosterone, hypokalemia, and selective responsiveness to amiloride over spironolactone.
Primary aldosteronism features markedly elevated plasma aldosterone concentration (PAC >15 ng/dL).
GRA features elevated aldosterone (driven by ACTH) that suppresses with dexamethasone.
AME exhibits a markedly elevated urinary free cortisol-to-cortisone ratio (>10:1) and responds to spironolactone.

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old boy presents with severe hypertension (148/92 mmHg) and mild hypokalemia (potassium 3.1 mEq/L). His father and paternal grandfather had early-onset hypertension and suffered fatal hemorrhagic strokes in their early 30s. Lab evaluation shows suppressed plasma renin activity (<0.2 ng/mL/h) and elevated plasma aldosterone (38 ng/dL). Administering oral dexamethasone 0.5 mg daily for 4 days results in complete normalization of blood pressure and normalization of plasma aldosterone to <2 ng/dL. What is the genetic basis of this disorder?
options: Unequal crossover fusing the promoter region of 11-beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) with the coding region of aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2)
Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 (HSD11B2) gene
Activating somatic mutation in the KCNJ5 potassium channel gene in the adrenal cortex
Germline loss-of-function mutation in the mineralocorticoid receptor (NR3C2) gene
mcqs.explanation: Glucocorticoid-Remediable Aldosteronism (GRA / Familial Hyperaldosteronism Type I) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 fusion gene. Aldosterone is ectopically synthesized in the zona fasciculata under the regulation of ACTH rather than angiotensin II. Low-dose dexamethasone suppresses ACTH, completely shutting down aldosterone production and curing the hypertension.

option_notes.text: The chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene places aldosterone synthase under ACTH regulation; suppression with dexamethasone is pathognomonic.
HSD11B2 mutations cause AME, which features low, not elevated, aldosterone levels.
KCNJ5 somatic mutations cause sporadic aldosterone-producing adenomas, which do not suppress with dexamethasone.
NR3C2 loss-of-function causes pseudohypoaldosteronism with hypotension and hyperkalemia.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with severe hypertension (142/90 mmHg), growth failure, and recurrent hypokalemic weakness (serum potassium 2.4 mEq/L). Plasma renin activity is <0.1 ng/mL/h and plasma aldosterone is undetectable (<1.0 ng/dL). 24-hour urine steroid metabolite profiling by GC-MS demonstrates a urinary ratio of (tetrahydrocortisol + 5alpha-tetrahydrocortisol) to tetrahydrocortisone of 18:1 (normal reference <1.0). What is the diagnosis?
options: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME)
Liddle syndrome
Primary aldosteronism
Renal artery stenosis
mcqs.explanation: Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess (AME) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in HSD11B2. Cortisol is not inactivated to cortisone in renal tubular cells, flooding the mineralocorticoid receptor (which has equal affinity for cortisol and aldosterone) and producing low-renin, low-aldosterone hypertension with a massively elevated urinary cortisol-to-cortisone metabolite ratio.

option_notes.text: Inactivating HSD11B2 mutations allow cortisol to hyperactivate the MR, marked by low renin, low aldosterone, and a massive urinary cortisol/cortisone ratio.
Liddle syndrome is an ENaC channelopathy with normal urinary cortisol-to-cortisone ratios.
Primary aldosteronism presents with high plasma aldosterone concentrations, not undetectable levels.
Renal artery stenosis causes high-renin, high-aldosterone secondary hypertension.

mcqs.q: A 3-week-old male infant presents with failure to thrive, vomiting, and profound dehydration. Lab testing shows sodium 121 mEq/L, potassium 7.6 mEq/L, and BUN 38 mg/dL. He has normal male genitalia. Urinalysis reveals pyuria, and renal ultrasound shows severe bilateral hydronephrosis with a dilated posterior urethra. Plasma aldosterone is markedly elevated at 280 ng/dL, and plasma renin activity is high. What is the diagnosis?
options: Secondary pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA3) triggered by urinary tract obstruction and infection
Classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Congenital aldosterone synthase deficiency (CYP11B2)
Liddle syndrome
mcqs.explanation: Secondary (type 3) pseudohypoaldosteronism is a transient resistance of the renal tubules to aldosterone, classically triggered in infants by acute urinary tract infection in the setting of congenital obstructive uropathy (posterior urethral valves). High aldosterone and renin in the presence of severe salt wasting and hyperkalemia confirm mineralocorticoid resistance.

option_notes.text: Pyelonephritis with obstructive uropathy impairs tubular responsiveness to aldosterone, causing transient severe salt loss and hyperkalemia.
Classic salt-wasting CAH features aldosterone deficiency, not massive elevation of circulating aldosterone.
Aldosterone synthase deficiency features undetectable or low aldosterone with elevated precursors.
