Liddle syndrome causes hypertension and hypokalemia, the exact opposite of salt-wasting hyperkalemia.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with hypertension (150/94 mmHg) and hypokalemia (potassium 2.8 mEq/L). Laboratory testing shows suppressed plasma renin and suppressed aldosterone. On detailed dietary history, he admits to eating large quantities (200 g daily) of traditional black licorice imported from Europe over the past 3 months. What active substance in the licorice is responsible for his presentation?
options: Glycyrrhetinic acid, which reversibly inhibits the 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 enzyme
Ephedrine alkaloids that directly stimulate alpha-1 adrenergic vascular receptors
Sodium chloride crystals that saturate the proximal tubule sodium-glucose cotransporter
Cyanogenic glycosides that block mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase
mcqs.explanation: Black licorice contains glycyrrhizin, which is metabolized to glycyrrhetinic acid. Glycyrrhetinic acid is a potent competitive inhibitor of 11beta-HSD2 in the renal collecting duct, preventing the normal enzymatic conversion of cortisol to inactive cortisone and producing an acquired form of Apparent Mineralocorticoid Excess.

option_notes.text: Glycyrrhetinic acid inhibits 11beta-HSD2, enabling endogenous cortisol to flood and hyperactivate renal mineralocorticoid receptors.
Ephedrine causes tachycardia and vasoconstriction but does not cause profound hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with suppressed aldosterone.
Sodium loading suppresses renin and aldosterone but does not cause hypokalemia with 11beta-HSD2 inhibition.
Cyanide toxicity causes cellular hypoxia and lactic acidosis, not mineralocorticoid excess.

etiology.text: Mineralocorticoid disorders encompass primary aldosterone excess (Conn adenoma, bilateral hyperplasia), monogenic low-renin hypertension (GRA / CYP11B1-CYP11B2 chimera, AME / HSD11B2, Liddle syndrome / ENaC), and mineralocorticoid resistance (PHA1 / MR or ENaC; PHA3 / UTI and uropathy).

epidemiology.text: Endocrine causes account for approximately 5% to 10% of pediatric secondary hypertension, with monogenic forms carrying high risk of premature cerebrovascular complications if unrecognized.

diagnostics.text: Screening uses paired PAC/PRA ratio, serum electrolytes (hypokalemia), urinary free cortisol/cortisone ratio (AME), and targeted genetic testing for CYP11B1/CYP11B2 chimera, SCNN1B/SCNN1G, and HSD11B2.

therapies.text: Treatment is etiology-specific: GRA is treated with low-dose dexamethasone (0.125–0.25 mg daily) or eplerenone. AME responds to spironolactone (1–3 mg/kg/day) and potassium supplementation. Liddle syndrome requires amiloride (5–10 mg daily) or triamterene; spironolactone is ineffective.
therapies.section: Targeted Medical Therapy in Endocrine Hypertension

pillars.label: Etiology and Molecular Classification
pillars.text: Congenital hypothyroidism (CH) occurs in approximately 1 in 2000 to 1 in 3000 live births and is categorized as primary permanent (85%), primary transient (10-15%), or central/secondary (1 in 25,000 to 1 in 100,000). Primary CH is subdivided into thyroid dysgenesis (80-85%; ectopic thyroid [lingual/sublingual], athyreosis/aplasia, or hypoplasia due to mutations in PAX8, NKX2-1, FOXE1, TSHR) and dyshormonogenesis (10-15%; autosomal recessive defects in hormone biosynthesis including TPO, SLC5A5/NIS, SLC26A4/pendrin, TG, DUOX2, DUOXA2, and IYD). Transient CH results from maternal TSH-receptor-blocking antibodies (TRBAb), maternal antithyroid drug exposure, extreme prematurity, or iodine deficiency/excess.

pillars.label: Newborn Screening and Early Recognition
pillars.text: Because maternal thyroxine (T4) crosses the placenta in modest amounts (~30-50% of fetal levels at delivery), >95% of affected newborns appear clinically normal at birth. Clinical signs emerge subtly over weeks and include prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (>2 weeks), wide posterior fontanel (>0.5 cm), umbilical hernia, macroglossia, abdominal distension, hypothermia, hoarse cry, cold/mottled skin, and delayed passage of meconium. Newborn screening (NBS) utilizing primary TSH or primary T4 with reflex TSH detects infants before neurocognitive injury occurs.

pillars.label: Confirmatory Diagnostics and Imaging
pillars.text: Any abnormal screening result requires an immediate confirmatory venous serum free T4 and TSH. Severe primary CH presents with venous TSH >40-100 mIU/L and markedly depressed free T4. Scintigraphy using technetium-99m pertechnetate (99mTc) or iodine-123 (123I) coupled with high-resolution thyroid ultrasound distinguishes athyreosis (absent uptake/tissue), ectopia (uptake along the thyroglossal duct tract, typically base of tongue), and in situ goitrous dyshormonogenesis (enlarged gland with high or absent uptake). Knee radiographs demonstrating absent distal femoral epiphyses indicate severe prenatal intra-uterine hypothyroidism.

pillars.label: Immediate Levothyroxine Replacement
pillars.text: Treatment must be initiated immediately upon confirmation, ideally within the first 14 days of life, to prevent permanent loss of neurodevelopmental IQ potential. The recommended starting dose of oral levothyroxine (L-T4) is 10-15 mcg/kg/day (typically 37.5 to 50 mcg daily for term infants). Tablets should be crushed in a small volume (a few milliliters) of water or breastmilk and administered orally on an empty stomach; co-administration with soy formulas, concentrated iron, calcium supplements, or fiber binders must be avoided due to significant chelation and impaired gastrointestinal absorption.

pillars.label: Biochemical Goals and Surveillance
pillars.text: The primary biochemical objective is rapid normalization of serum free T4 within 3-7 days into the upper half of the age-specific reference interval (e.g., 1.4-2.3 ng/dL) and normalization of serum TSH within 2-4 weeks (<5 mIU/L). Serum TSH and free T4 should be monitored every 1-2 months during the first 6 months of life, every 2-3 months from 6 to 36 months, and every 3-12 months thereafter until linear growth is completed. If an in situ gland was present and permanent etiology was not established molecularly, a formal trial off therapy is conducted at age 3 years for 30 days to differentiate transient from permanent hypothyroidism.

cards.q: What is the most frequent overall developmental cause of permanent congenital hypothyroidism, and what is its most common anatomical subtype?
cards.a: Thyroid dysgenesis accounts for 80-85% of permanent primary congenital hypothyroidism, with ectopic thyroid (sublingual/lingual gland located along the migratory path) being the most common subtype (responsible for ~60% of dysgenesis cases).

cards.q: What is the recommended initial daily starting dose of oral levothyroxine in neonates with confirmed congenital hypothyroidism?
cards.a: 10-15 mcg/kg/day (equivalent to 37.5 to 50 mcg/day for most term infants), aimed at rapidly restoring serum free T4 into the upper half of the normal reference range within 3-7 days.

cards.q: Why is routine neonatal blood-spot screening for congenital hypothyroidism ideally obtained between 24 and 48 hours of life rather than immediately at birth?
cards.a: A physiological surge in neonatal TSH occurs within 30 minutes of birth, peaking up to 60-80 mIU/L and declining over the subsequent 24-48 hours. Testing during this initial surge produces high rates of false-positive TSH elevations.

cards.q: Which infant dietary components and nutritional supplements significantly impair the gastrointestinal absorption of crushed oral levothyroxine?
cards.a: Soy-based infant formulas, oral iron supplements (ferrous sulfate), oral calcium carbonate/citrate, and aluminum-containing medications chelate levothyroxine in the gut and must not be administered concurrently.

cards.q: What diagnostic radiologic sign on a newborn knee film indicates significant intra-uterine prenatal thyroid hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Absence of the distal femoral epiphysis (which normally ossifies by 36-37 weeks of gestation) reflects severe, long-standing prenatal hypothyroidism in term neonates.

cards.q: What maternal autoimmune factor causes transient primary congenital hypothyroidism in offspring of mothers with autoimmune thyroid disease?
cards.a: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH receptor-blocking antibodies (TRBAb), which inhibit fetal TSH receptor activation and resolve spontaneously over 2-4 months as maternal IgG antibodies clear.

cards.q: At what age and under what conditions should a trial off levothyroxine be performed to establish whether congenital hypothyroidism is permanent?
cards.a: At age 3 years, provided thyroid tissue was identified in situ on neonatal imaging and dysgenesis/permanent genetic mutations have not been confirmed; levothyroxine is discontinued for 30 days to measure serum TSH and free T4.

mcqs.q: A 9-day-old male infant born at 39 weeks of gestation is recalled after newborn screening reveals an elevated TSH of 74 mIU/L. Confirmatory serum testing demonstrates venous TSH >100 mIU/L and free T4 0.3 ng/dL (reference: 1.1-2.2 ng/dL). Examination shows an infant with a 1.5-cm posterior fontanel, mild macroglossia, and an umbilical hernia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy?
options: Levothyroxine oral suspension at 2-5 mcg/kg/day administered with soy formula
Oral levothyroxine tablets crushed in breastmilk at 10-15 mcg/kg/day on an empty stomach
Intravenous liothyronine (triiodothyronine) bolus followed by maintenance L-T3
Observation for 4 weeks with repeat serum TSH before initiating therapy
mcqs.explanation: Guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology (ESPE) mandate immediate treatment of confirmed primary congenital hypothyroidism with oral levothyroxine at 10-15 mcg/kg/day (typically 37.5-50 mcg/day). The tablet should be crushed in a few milliliters of water or breastmilk. Soy formula impairs absorption and should be avoided. Liothyronine is not standard initial therapy and causes erratic peaks.
option_notes: Incorrect. 2-5 mcg/kg/day is inadequate for a neonate (neonatal clearance is high), and soy formula binds levothyroxine, preventing absorption.
Correct. 10-15 mcg/kg/day using crushed commercial tablets rapidly normalizes free T4 within 3-7 days, which is vital for cerebral neurodevelopment.
Incorrect. T3 (liothyronine) is unnecessary, causes abrupt unphysiological fluctuations, and does not provide stable cerebral intracrine T3 generation.
Incorrect. Delaying treatment past 2-3 weeks of life is associated with irreversible loss of cognitive intelligence quotients.

mcqs.q: A 2-week-old female diagnosed with severe primary neonatal hypothyroidism undergoes diagnostic thyroid imaging. Radionuclide scintigraphy using technetium-99m pertechnetate demonstrates intense focal radioisotope uptake at the base of the tongue with complete absence of uptake in the lower anterior neck. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Athyreosis (complete thyroid agenesis)
Lingual thyroid (ectopic thyroid dysgenesis)
Thyroid dyshormonogenesis due to TPO gene mutation
Maternal antithyroid drug-induced goitrous hypothyroidism
mcqs.explanation: Ectopic thyroid occurs when embryonic thyroid tissue fails to migrate normally along the thyroglossal duct tract from the foramen cecum to the normal pretracheal cervical position. Scintigraphy demonstrating focal tracer accumulation at the base of the tongue with no tracer in the lower neck is diagnostic of a lingual or sublingual ectopic thyroid, which represents ~60% of thyroid dysgenesis cases.
option_notes: Incorrect. Athyreosis shows complete absence of tracer accumulation in both the tongue base and the neck.
Correct. Focal radiotracer uptake at the tongue base along the midline thyroglossal tract is pathognomonic for ectopic lingual thyroid tissue.
Incorrect. Dyshormonogenesis features an in situ cervical gland, frequently enlarged (goiter), with variable tracer trapping depending on the defect.
Incorrect. Maternal drug transfer causes an enlarged, normally positioned (cervical) in situ goiter.

mcqs.q: A full-term infant with severe neonatal hypothyroidism is started on levothyroxine 12 mcg/kg/day at day 10 of life. Which of the following monitoring targets reflects optimal early therapy during the first 6 months of life?
options: Serum TSH maintained between 5 and 10 mIU/L with free T4 in the lower quartile of reference range
Serum free T4 rapidly normalized into the upper half of the normal reference range with TSH suppressed <0.01 mIU/L
Serum free T4 in the upper half of the reference range and serum TSH normalized <5 mIU/L within 2-4 weeks
Discontinuation of levothyroxine every 2 months to assess spontaneous endogenous thyroid recovery
mcqs.explanation: Treatment goals in congenital hypothyroidism emphasize restoring serum free T4 into the upper half of the normal age-specific reference interval (e.g., 1.4-2.3 ng/dL) within 1-2 weeks and lowering TSH to <5 mIU/L within 2-4 weeks. Over-suppression (TSH <0.01 mIU/L) carries risks of craniosynostosis and behavior disturbance, while under-treatment compromises brain development.
option_notes: Incorrect. Free T4 in the lower quartile with TSH 5-10 mIU/L represents under-treatment, which degrades cognitive outcomes.
Incorrect. Completely suppressing TSH (<0.01 mIU/L) risks iatrogenic hyperthyroidism, craniosynostosis, and cardiac overdrive.
Correct. Maintaining free T4 in the upper half of the normal range while achieving normal TSH (<5 mIU/L) ensures adequate brain myelination without toxicity.
Incorrect. Intermittent withdrawal during the critical first 3 years of brain development is contraindicated and causes neurocognitive damage.

mcqs.q: An infant with sensorineural deafness and primary neonatal hypothyroidism is found to have an enlarged in situ goitrous thyroid on ultrasound. Scintigraphy demonstrates normal pertechnetate trapping, but rapid discharge of iodide occurs upon administration of sodium perchlorate (positive perchlorate discharge test >30%). What gene mutation is most likely responsible for this condition?
options: SLC26A4 (Pendrin)
PAX8 (Paired box gene 8)
TSHR (Thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor)
NKX2-1 (Thyroid transcription factor 1)
mcqs.explanation: Pendred syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in SLC26A4, which encodes pendrin, an anion exchanger involved in iodide transport at the apical follicular membrane. It is characterized by sensorineural hearing loss (associated with enlarged vestibular aqueducts on temporal bone CT), goitrous dyshormonogenesis, and an abnormal perchlorate discharge test reflecting impaired iodide organification.
option_notes: Correct. SLC26A4 mutations cause Pendred syndrome, combining goitrous dyshormonogenesis, organification defect, and sensorineural deafness.
Incorrect. PAX8 mutations cause thyroid dysgenesis (hypoplasia/ectopia) without sensorineural hearing loss.
Incorrect. TSHR mutations cause resistance to TSH or thyroid hypoplasia with blunted cAMP signaling, not an organification defect with deafness.
Incorrect. NKX2-1 mutations cause brain-lung-thyroid syndrome (choreoathetosis, infant respiratory distress, and CH).

mcqs.q: A female infant born at 39 weeks has an initial newborn screen revealing low total T4 with a normal TSH of 4.2 mIU/L. Repeat venous testing confirms low free T4 (0.6 ng/dL) with persistently normal TSH (3.1 mIU/L). Which of the following evaluations is most urgently indicated?
options: Diagnostic radioiodine uptake and perchlorate discharge test
Evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis for central hypopituitarism and cortisol deficiency
Measurement of maternal antithyroglobulin and anti-TPO antibodies
Observation without treatment until 6 months of age
mcqs.explanation: Low free T4 in the presence of an inappropriately normal or low TSH indicates central (hypothalamic-pituitary) hypothyroidism. Central hypothyroidism is rarely isolated and is frequently associated with congenital hypopituitarism (multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies), including potentially fatal central adrenal insufficiency (ACTH deficiency) and growth hormone deficiency. An urgent pituitary axis evaluation and pituitary MRI are required. If hydrocortisone deficiency is present, glucocorticoid replacement must precede or accompany levothyroxine to prevent acute adrenal crisis.
option_notes: Incorrect. Scintigraphy and perchlorate discharge are used for primary goitrous dyshormonogenesis, not central hypothyroidism.
Correct. Central hypothyroidism demands urgent screening for ACTH/cortisol deficiency and GH deficiency, alongside neuroimaging of the pituitary gland.
Incorrect. Maternal thyroid autoantibodies produce primary hypothyroidism with elevated TSH, not central low-TSH hypothyroidism.
Incorrect. Ignoring low FT4 in an infant risks profound developmental disability and unaddressed adrenal crisis.

atlas.etiology: Primary congenital hypothyroidism is caused by thyroid dysgenesis (80-85%: ectopia ~60%, athyreosis ~30%, hypoplasia ~10%) or thyroid dyshormonogenesis (10-15%: TPO, SLC5A5, SLC26A4, TG, DUOX2, IYD). Central CH occurs in 1:25,000 live births (TSHB, TRHR, PROP1, POU1F1, HESX1).
atlas.epidemiology: Incidence is ~1 in 2000 to 1 in 3000 live births, with a female-to-male ratio of 2:1 in thyroid dysgenesis. Higher prevalence occurs in Hispanic and Native American populations; lower in Black infants.
atlas.diagnostics: Venous TSH and free T4 confirmatory assay; 99mTc pertechnetate or 123I scintigraphy; neck ultrasound; knee radiographs for osseous maturation (distal femoral epiphysis).

therapies.text: Initiate oral levothyroxine tablets (crushed in 3-5 mL of breastmilk or water) at 10-15 mcg/kg/day (typically 37.5 to 50 mcg/day for term infants) within the first 14 days of life. Avoid soy formula, iron, or calcium co-administration. Monitor TSH and FT4 every 1-2 months during the first 6 months, aiming for FT4 in the upper half of normal range and TSH <5 mIU/L.

pillars.label: Pathophysiology and Autoimmunity
pillars.text: Autoimmune thyroid disease (AITD) encompasses Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis) and Graves' disease. Both are characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland, breakdown of self-tolerance, and production of thyroid-specific autoantibodies. Hashimoto thyroiditis features predominant CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell infiltration, follicular cell apoptosis, and autoantibodies directed against thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and thyroglobulin (anti-TG). Graves' disease is driven by stimulating autoantibodies directed against the TSH receptor (thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins, TSI / TRAb), which constitutively activate cAMP signaling, promoting autonomous thyroid hypertrophy, hyperplasia, and excessive thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) synthesis.

pillars.label: Hashimoto Thyroiditis Clinical Spectrum
pillars.text: Hashimoto thyroiditis is the leading cause of acquired hypothyroidism and sporadic goiter in children and adolescents, displaying a 4:1 to 7:1 female predominance with peak incidence in early adolescence. Clinical manifestations include painless, non-tender, firm goiter (with a pebbly or lobulated surface), linear growth deceleration with progressive weight gain (declining height velocity with increasing BMI), fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, and delayed puberty. Severe juvenile primary hypothyroidism can occasionally present paradoxically with pseudoprecocious puberty (Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome: breast development and vaginal bleeding in girls, testicular enlargement without virilization in boys) mediated by TSH cross-activation of FSH receptors.

pillars.label: Management of Hashimoto Hypothyroidism
pillars.text: Overt hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, low free T4) mandates daily oral levothyroxine (L-T4) replacement. Age-adjusted starting dosages are: 1-5 years: 4-6 mcg/kg/day; 6-12 years: 2.5-3.5 mcg/kg/day; adolescents (>12 years): 1.6-1.8 mcg/kg/day (typically 75-125 mcg daily). Levothyroxine should be ingested once daily in the morning 30-60 minutes before breakfast or at bedtime on an empty stomach. The clinical goal is normalization of TSH into the lower half of the normal reference range (0.5-2.5 mIU/L) with normal free T4 and complete restoration of normal linear growth velocity.

pillars.label: Graves' Disease Presentation and Pharmacotherapy
pillars.text: Graves' disease causes >90% of pediatric thyrotoxicosis, presenting with emotional lability, declining school performance, heat intolerance, diaphoresis, resting tachycardia, widened pulse pressure, accelerated linear growth, advanced bone age, and diffuse smooth vascular goiter (often with an audible bruit). First-line medical therapy is methimazole (MMI) dosed at 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day (up to 1.0 mg/kg/day; maximum 30-40 mg daily) divided once or twice daily. Propylthiouracil (PTU) is black-box contraindicated in pediatric patients due to unacceptable risks of fulminant fatal hepatic failure. Beta-adrenergic blockers (atenolol 1-2 mg/kg/day or propranolol 1-2 mg/kg/day) are used acutely to control adrenergic hyperactivation.

pillars.label: Definitive Therapies and Neonatal Graves'
pillars.text: Pediatric Graves' remits medically in only 25-30% of patients after 2 years of methimazole. Definitive modalities include radioactive iodine (131I; targeted dose 200-300 mcg/g of tissue or fixed 10-15 mCi; generally reserved for children >5-10 years) or total/near-total thyroidectomy performed by an experienced pediatric thyroid surgeon. Neonatal Graves' disease occurs in 1-2% of infants born to mothers with active or past Graves' disease due to transplacental transfer of maternal TSI. Symptoms appear within the first 2-7 days of life (irritability, tachycardia, failure to thrive, goiter, craniosynostosis) and require prompt treatment with methimazole, beta-blockers, and occasionally Lugol's iodine until maternal antibodies clear over 2-4 months.

cards.q: Why is propylthiouracil (PTU) strictly contraindicated as first-line medical therapy for hyperthyroidism in children?
cards.a: PTU carries a black-box FDA warning in pediatric patients due to high risks of idiosyncratic fulminant hepatic necrosis, liver failure, and death requiring emergent liver transplantation. Methimazole is the only recommended antithyroid drug.

cards.q: What life-threatening adverse reaction to methimazole requires immediate complete blood count monitoring and drug cessation if fever or severe pharyngitis develops?
cards.a: Agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count <500/mcL), which occurs in ~0.3-0.5% of treated patients and predisposes to rapid, fatal sepsis.

cards.q: What is Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome, and what is its pathophysiological mechanism?
cards.a: A syndrome of severe, long-standing primary juvenile hypothyroidism presenting paradoxically with precocious puberty (isosexual precocity in girls, macrorchidism without virilization in boys) caused by extreme TSH elevation cross-activating gonadal FSH receptors.

cards.q: What causes neonatal Graves' disease, and how long does the clinical condition typically persist in the infant?
cards.a: Transplacental passage of maternal TSH-receptor-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI / TRAb); the hyperthyroidism persists for 2 to 4 months until circulating maternal IgG antibodies are cleared from neonatal circulation.

cards.q: How does childhood Graves' disease affect linear growth and skeletal maturation compared to childhood hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Graves' disease accelerates linear growth velocity and advances skeletal maturation (accelerated bone age), whereas hypothyroidism profoundly decelerates linear growth velocity and delays bone age.

cards.q: Which circulating autoantibodies are most sensitive for confirming the diagnosis of Hashimoto thyroiditis in a child with a goiter?
cards.a: Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies (>90-95% sensitive) and anti-thyroglobulin (anti-TG) antibodies.

cards.q: What is the typical maintenance dosage of levothyroxine in an adolescent with overt Hashimoto hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Approximately 1.6-1.8 mcg/kg/day (typically 75 to 125 mcg once daily orally on an empty stomach).

mcqs.q: A 13-year-old girl is evaluated for declining academic grades, emotional lability, heat intolerance, and resting palpitations. On examination, pulse is 118 bpm, blood pressure is 128/62 mmHg, and she has a smooth, non-tender, diffusely enlarged thyroid gland with an audible continuous bruit. Laboratory testing reveals TSH <0.01 mIU/L, free T4 3.8 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), and highly elevated thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI). What is the most appropriate initial medical therapy?
options: Propylthiouracil 5 mg/kg/day divided every 8 hours
Methimazole 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day once daily plus atenolol for symptom control
Immediate radioactive iodine (131I) ablation at 15 mCi
Lugol's strong iodine solution monotherapy
mcqs.explanation: Methimazole (MMI, 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day, up to 1.0 mg/kg/day) is the only antithyroid drug recommended for pediatric Graves' disease. Propylthiouracil (PTU) is black-box contraindicated due to fulminant hepatic necrosis. Beta-blockers (e.g., atenolol 1-2 mg/kg/day) are added to control adrenergic hyperactivation (tachycardia, tremor). 131I is a definitive modality usually considered if medical therapy fails or causes toxic reactions.
option_notes: Incorrect. PTU has an FDA black-box warning prohibiting its use in pediatric patients due to fatal hepatic failure.
Correct. Methimazole at 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day combined with a beta-blocker is the first-line medical therapy for pediatric Graves' disease.
Incorrect. Radioactive iodine is a definitive second-line option, not standard immediate emergency therapy before medical stabilization.
Incorrect. Lugol's iodine alone results in transient Wolff-Chaikoff effect followed by escape and exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old male with Graves' disease has been taking methimazole 20 mg daily for 4 weeks. He presents to the urgent care clinic with a 2-day history of high fever (39.2°C), severe sore throat, and dysphagia. Examination shows an erythematous pharynx with tonsillar exudate. What is the most critical immediate clinical action?
options: Prescribe oral amoxicillin and continue methimazole unchanged
Immediately discontinue methimazole and obtain an emergent complete blood count with differential
Increase methimazole to 30 mg daily to treat an acute thyrotoxic storm
Switch methimazole immediately to oral propylthiouracil
mcqs.explanation: Agranulocytosis (absolute neutrophil count <500/mcL) is a rare but life-threatening idiosyncratic complication of methimazole occurring in 0.3-0.5% of patients. Any child on antithyroid medication who develops acute fever or severe sore throat must stop the drug immediately and have an urgent CBC with differential to rule out neutropenia. If agranulocytosis is confirmed, the drug is permanently discontinued and broad-spectrum antibiotics/G-CSF are initiated.
option_notes: Incorrect. Continuing methimazole without checking the neutrophil count risks fatal septic shock from drug-induced agranulocytosis.
Correct. Immediate drug cessation and emergent CBC evaluation are mandatory to diagnose or exclude drug-induced agranulocytosis.
Incorrect. Fever and pharyngitis suggest agranulocytosis or severe infection; increasing the drug dose could prove lethal.
Incorrect. PTU shares cross-reactivity for agranulocytosis and is contraindicated in children due to fulminant hepatotoxicity.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old girl is referred for evaluation of declining height velocity. Over the past 2 years, her height percentile has dropped from the 50th to the 10th percentile, while her weight percentile has increased from the 45th to the 75th percentile. On physical exam, she has dry skin, sluggish deep tendon reflexes, and a firm, non-tender, lobulated goiter. Bone age is delayed by 3.5 years. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options: Cushing syndrome due to an ACTH-secreting pituitary microadenoma
Chronic autoimmune (Hashimoto) thyroiditis
Isolated growth hormone neurosecretory dysfunction
Graves' disease with autonomous toxic nodule
mcqs.explanation: The classic growth pattern of juvenile acquired hypothyroidism (most commonly Hashimoto thyroiditis) is marked linear growth deceleration with preserved or increasing weight-for-height (crossing height percentiles downward while BMI increases), accompanied by severe bone age retardation and a firm, lobulated goiter. Cushing syndrome also causes growth failure with obesity, but is not accompanied by a lobulated goiter or marked bone age delay of this degree.
option_notes: Incorrect. Cushing syndrome presents with hypercortisolemia, central obesity, striae, and hypertension, not a firm lobulated goiter.
Correct. Hashimoto thyroiditis classically produces growth arrest with reciprocal weight gain, delayed bone age, and a lobulated goiter.
Incorrect. Isolated GH deficiency does not cause goiter, dry skin, or sluggish relaxation of deep tendon reflexes.
Incorrect. Graves' disease accelerates linear growth velocity and advances bone age rather than delaying it.

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old girl presents with significant bilateral breast enlargement (Tanner stage 3) and an episode of vaginal bleeding. Her height is at the 15th percentile (down from the 50th percentile 2 years ago), and bone age is delayed by 2 years. Pelvic ultrasound reveals enlarged multicystic ovaries. Thyroid panel reveals TSH 480 mIU/L and free T4 0.1 ng/dL. What is the term and physiological mechanism for this clinical condition?
options: McCune-Albright syndrome due to GNAS mutation
Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome due to TSH cross-reactivity at the ovarian FSH receptor
Central precocious puberty due to hypothalamic hamartoma
Autonomous granulosa cell tumor secreting estradiol
mcqs.explanation: Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome is a rare manifestation of long-standing, severe, untreated primary juvenile hypothyroidism characterized by isosexual pseudoprecocious puberty (breast development, vaginal bleeding, multicystic ovaries) occurring paradoxically with delayed linear growth and delayed bone age. The extreme elevation of circulating TSH exhibits weak cross-reactivity and agonism at the G-protein-coupled FSH receptor in the ovaries. Prompt treatment with levothyroxine completely reverses the ovarian cysts, pubertal signs, and elevated TSH.
option_notes: Incorrect. McCune-Albright features café-au-lait macules, fibrous dysplasia, and advanced bone age, whereas bone age is delayed here.
Correct. Van Wyk-Grumbach syndrome results from massive TSH elevations cross-stimulating ovarian FSH receptors, resolving completely with L-T4.
Incorrect. Central precocious puberty features accelerated growth velocity and advanced bone age, not severe growth arrest and delayed bone age.
Incorrect. Granulosa cell tumor does not cause massive TSH elevations or delayed bone age.

mcqs.q: A pregnant woman at 36 weeks of gestation with Graves' disease treated with methimazole delivers a male infant. At day 4 of life, the infant becomes irritable, with a resting heart rate of 190 bpm, poor feeding, diaphoresis, and a small palpable goiter. Serum free T4 is markedly elevated at 4.6 ng/dL with TSH <0.02 mIU/L. What is the primary etiology of this infant's thyrotoxicosis?
options: Autonomous activating mutation in the neonatal TSH receptor gene
Transplacental transfer of maternal thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI / TRAb)
Neonatal thyroid adenoma
Neonatal iodine-induced hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow)
mcqs.explanation: Neonatal Graves' disease is caused by the passive transplacental passage of maternal IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI/TRAb) during pregnancy. Clinical onset is often delayed until day 2-7 of life as transplacentally transferred maternal antithyroid drug (methimazole) clears from the infant's circulation. It is self-limited, typically resolving in 2 to 4 months as maternal IgG antibodies are degraded.
option_notes: Incorrect. TSHR germline activating mutations cause persistent familial non-autoimmune hyperthyroidism, not transient neonatal disease.
Correct. Transplacental transfer of maternal TSI causes transient neonatal Graves' disease that resolves as maternal IgG antibodies clear.
Incorrect. Toxic adenomas are exceptionally rare in neonates and do not resolve spontaneously.
Incorrect. Iodine overload in neonates typically causes transient hypothyroidism (Wolff-Chaikoff effect), not neonatal Graves'.

atlas.etiology: AITD includes Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune lymphocytic destruction; anti-TPO, anti-TG) and Graves' disease (autoimmune stimulation of TSHR via TSI/TRAb). Linked to HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, CTLA4, PTPN22, and syndromes including Turner, Down, Klinefelter, T1D, and APS.
atlas.epidemiology: Hashimoto thyroiditis affects 1-3% of children, 4:1 to 7:1 female predominance. Graves' disease affects ~1 in 10,000 children, peak in adolescence (80% females).
atlas.diagnostics: TSH, free T4, total T3; anti-TPO, anti-TG, TSI/TRAb antibodies; thyroid ultrasound (heterogeneous hypoechogenicity, increased vascularity ['thyroid inferno'] on Doppler).

therapies.text: Methimazole (MMI) 0.2-0.5 mg/kg/day (up to 1.0 mg/kg/day; maximum 30-40 mg daily) orally in 1-2 divided doses. Add atenolol 1-2 mg/kg/day or propranolol 1-2 mg/kg/day for adrenergic symptoms. Propylthiouracil is strictly contraindicated in children. If neutropenia/agranulocytosis occurs, stop immediately.
Levothyroxine (L-T4) orally once daily: 1-5 yr: 4-6 mcg/kg/day; 6-12 yr: 2.5-3.5 mcg/kg/day; >12 yr: 1.6-1.8 mcg/kg/day (75-125 mcg daily). Administer on an empty stomach.

pillars.label: Definition and Conceptual Model
pillars.text: Non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS), formerly known as euthyroid sick syndrome, encompasses alterations in circulating thyroid hormone and TSH concentrations that occur in patients with acute or chronic non-thyroidal systemic illnesses (sepsis, severe trauma, cardiopulmonary bypass, starvation/anorexia, ketoacidosis, burns, and critical illness) in the absence of intrinsic hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid gland pathology. NTIS represents an evolutionary conserved adaptive metabolic response that downregulates basal metabolic rate and cellular energy expenditure to conserve protein and substrates during catabolic stress.

pillars.label: Deiodinase Dysregulation and Alterations
pillars.text: The primary biochemical hallmark of mild-to-moderate NTIS is 'low T3 syndrome': marked reduction in total and free triiodothyronine (T3) accompanied by elevation of reverse T3 (rT3). This shift results from downregulation of hepatic type 1 deiodinase (DIO1) and type 2 deiodinase (DIO2), which impairs the outer-ring deiodination of T4 to active T3, combined with upregulation of type 3 deiodinase (DIO3) in tissues, which rapidly converts T4 to inactive reverse T3 and degrades T3 to diiodothyronine (T2). Elevated circulating inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1-beta, IFN-gamma) and endogenous glucocorticoids directly drive this deiodinase reprogramming.

pillars.label: Severe Illness and Central Downregulation
pillars.text: In severe or prolonged critical illness, the syndrome progresses to 'low T4 / low T3 syndrome', characterized by profound drops in total T4, low or low-normal free T4, and inappropriately normal or suppressed serum TSH (frequently <0.1 mIU/L). Hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) expression is markedly suppressed in the paraventricular nucleus, mediated by cytokine activation, central dopaminergic and somatostatinergic pathways, and exogenous medications (e.g., dopamine infusions, high-dose corticosteroids). The magnitude of free T4 reduction correlates directly with intensive care unit mortality.

pillars.label: Differential Diagnosis and Diagnostic Pitfalls
pillars.text: Differentiating severe NTIS from central (hypopituitary) hypothyroidism or primary hypothyroidism is a frequent pediatric ICU challenge. Unlike primary hypothyroidism (where TSH is markedly elevated >20-100 mIU/L), TSH in NTIS is low or normal. Unlike central hypothyroidism, patients with NTIS typically have elevated reverse T3 (rT3) levels (rT3 is low in central hypothyroidism) and exhibit normal anterior pituitary hormones once recovered. During the clinical recovery phase of NTIS, serum TSH frequently exhibits a transient rebound surge above the upper reference limit (often 5-15 mIU/L) before normalizing, which must not be mistaken for permanent primary hypothyroidism.

pillars.label: Therapeutic Recommendations and Evidence
pillars.text: Randomized controlled trials in pediatric and adult intensive care populations have consistently demonstrated that routine thyroid hormone replacement (administration of intravenous or oral levothyroxine [T4] or liothyronine [T3]) does not improve clinical survival, duration of mechanical ventilation, or inotropic dependence, and can suppress endogenous recovery or increase catabolism. Consequently, consensus guidelines recommend against routine thyroid hormone administration in pediatric NTIS. Clinical management centers exclusively on aggressive treatment of the underlying systemic illness, nutritional support, and watchful waiting.

cards.q: What is the earliest and most common circulating thyroid hormone alteration in non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS)?
cards.a: Low total and free triiodothyronine (T3) accompanied by elevated reverse T3 (rT3) ('low T3 syndrome'), caused by impaired 5'-deiodination of T4 to T3 and increased clearance to rT3.

cards.q: Which deiodinase enzyme is pathologically upregulated in peripheral tissues during severe systemic illness, driving the conversion of T4 into inactive reverse T3?
cards.a: Type 3 iodothyronine deiodinase (DIO3), which mediates inner-ring deiodination of T4 to rT3 and degrades active T3 to inactive 3,3'-T2.

cards.q: How does serum reverse T3 (rT3) distinguish severe non-thyroidal illness syndrome from central (pituitary) hypothyroidism?
cards.a: Reverse T3 is typically elevated or high-normal in NTIS (due to increased DIO3 activity and reduced rT3 clearance), whereas rT3 is low in central hypothyroidism (due to low substrate T4 secretion without peripheral shunting).

cards.q: What transient biochemical phenomenon occurs in serum TSH during clinical recovery from critical non-thyroidal illness?
cards.a: A transient rebound elevation of serum TSH (frequently 5-15 mIU/L) occurs as hypothalamic-pituitary suppression resolves, which normalizes spontaneously and should not be misdiagnosed as permanent primary hypothyroidism.

cards.q: Is routine thyroid hormone replacement (T4 or T3) recommended for critically ill pediatric patients with low T3/T4 in NTIS?
cards.a: No. Randomized controlled trials show no clinical benefit in mortality or ICU length of stay, and guidelines recommend against routine replacement therapy; management focuses on treating the underlying illness.

cards.q: Which common intensive care medications directly suppress pituitary TSH secretion, exacerbating low TSH levels in critically ill children?
cards.a: Dopamine infusions and high-dose exogenous glucocorticoids directly inhibit pituitary thyrotrope TSH release.

cards.q: What is the clinical prognostic significance of a profoundly depressed free T4 level in a child with severe critical illness?
cards.a: Profound reduction in free T4 correlates directly with illness severity, multi-organ failure, and increased risk of intensive care mortality.

mcqs.q: A 6-year-old boy in the pediatric intensive care unit with severe septic shock requiring mechanical ventilation and dopamine infusion undergoes routine thyroid testing. Results show TSH 0.12 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L), total T3 22 ng/dL (reference: 85-170 ng/dL), and free T4 0.6 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL). Serum reverse T3 (rT3) is markedly elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding his thyroid status?
options: Initiate intravenous levothyroxine 2 mcg/kg/day to restore normal cellular metabolism
Initiate oral liothyronine (T3) replacement to normalize circulating T3 levels
Do not administer thyroid hormones; continue intensive management of septic shock and monitor
Perform urgent emergent total thyroidectomy
mcqs.explanation: This patient exhibits classic severe non-thyroidal illness syndrome (NTIS, low T4/low T3 with suppressed TSH and elevated rT3) compounded by dopamine infusion, which suppresses TSH secretion. Randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that treating NTIS with either T4 or T3 does not improve clinical outcomes or survival and may be harmful. Current guidelines advise against thyroid hormone replacement and mandate focus on treating the primary systemic pathology.
option_notes: Incorrect. IV levothyroxine has been shown in clinical trials not to improve survival, extubation rates, or hemodynamics in pediatric critical illness.
Incorrect. Liothyronine therapy does not reduce mortality and may exacerbate tissue catabolism during acute critical illness.
Correct. Guidelines recommend against routine thyroid hormone replacement in NTIS; therapy centers on treating the underlying sepsis.
Incorrect. Thyroidectomy has no therapeutic role in NTIS and would be catastrophic in septic shock.

mcqs.q: Which enzymatic alteration is primarily responsible for the rapid reduction of active triiodothyronine (T3) and simultaneous rise of reverse T3 (rT3) in acute non-thyroidal illness?
options: Upregulation of hepatic type 1 deiodinase (DIO1)
Upregulation of type 3 deiodinase (DIO3) with downregulation of type 1 (DIO1) and type 2 (DIO2) deiodinases
Inactivation of thyroid peroxidase (TPO) by circulating endotoxins
Increased activity of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) degrading proteases
mcqs.explanation: In NTIS, inflammatory cytokines downregulate type 1 (DIO1) and type 2 (DIO2) iodothyronine deiodinases, impairing 5'-deiodination of T4 to T3. Concurrently, type 3 deiodinase (DIO3) is induced in peripheral tissues, which actively deiodinates T4 into reverse T3 and degrades T3 into T2, causing the hallmark low T3 and high rT3 pattern.
option_notes: Incorrect. Hepatic DIO1 is downregulated, not upregulated, during acute critical illness.
Correct. Induction of DIO3 coupled with downregulation of DIO1 and DIO2 shunts thyroid hormone metabolism toward inactive rT3 and degrades active T3.
Incorrect. TPO is an intrathyroidal enzyme involved in hormone synthesis, not the primary driver of peripheral T3/rT3 shunting.
Incorrect. While TBG levels can drop, alterations in TBG do not explain the selective reciprocal changes in free T3 and rT3.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old girl is recovering from severe bacterial pneumonia in the pediatric ward. Three weeks ago in the ICU, her TSH was 0.2 mIU/L with a low free T3. Today, repeat morning labs show TSH 8.4 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L) with normal free T4 1.2 ng/dL and normal free T3. She is clinically asymptomatic and eating well. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Diagnose permanent primary Hashimoto thyroiditis and initiate levothyroxine 50 mcg daily
Recognize this as a transient TSH rebound surge during recovery from non-thyroidal illness and recheck in 4-6 weeks without starting medication
Order emergent radioiodine thyroid scintigraphy and thyroid ultrasound
Obtain pituitary MRI to evaluate for a TSH-secreting pituitary macroadenoma
mcqs.explanation: During recovery from severe non-thyroidal illness, hypothalamic-pituitary suppression resolves, frequently producing a transient rebound elevation of serum TSH (typically 5-15 mIU/L) with normal or recovering peripheral thyroid hormone levels. This transient physiological surge stimulates the thyroid gland to replenish hormone stores and normalizes spontaneously within 4 to 8 weeks. Levothyroxine is not indicated.
option_notes: Incorrect. Initiating levothyroxine is inappropriate for a benign, self-limited post-illness physiological rebound.
Correct. The transient TSH elevation represents expected neuroendocrine recovery from NTIS; re-evaluation in 4-6 weeks will confirm resolution.
Incorrect. Scintigraphy and ultrasound are not indicated for an expected transient biochemical surge post-illness.
Incorrect. TSHoma is an exceedingly rare condition that presents with elevated FT4 and unsuppressed TSH, not post-pneumonia recovery.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old child with severe septic shock is receiving continuous infusions of dopamine, epinephrine, and high-dose hydrocortisone. Thyroid function testing reveals TSH <0.05 mIU/L and free T4 0.5 ng/dL. Which factor is most directly contributing to the profound suppression of TSH in this patient?
options: Direct central inhibition of pituitary thyrotropes by dopamine and pharmacological glucocorticoids
Severe metabolic acidosis accelerating renal excretion of TSH
Activation of pituitary TSH receptor antibodies
Elevated circulating free fatty acids competing for TSH binding sites
mcqs.explanation: Both dopamine and pharmacological doses of glucocorticoids are potent central inhibitors of pituitary thyrotropes, directly suppressing pulsatile and basal TSH secretion. In critically ill children receiving dopamine and hydrocortisone, TSH is almost universally suppressed to undetectable or near-undetectable levels, simulating severe central hypothyroidism.
option_notes: Correct. Dopamine and glucocorticoids directly suppress pituitary thyrotrope secretion of TSH.
Incorrect. Acidosis does not accelerate renal clearance of glycoprotein hormones like TSH.
Incorrect. TSH receptor antibodies do not suppress pituitary TSH directly; they stimulate the thyroid gland.
Incorrect. Free fatty acids interfere with protein binding of T4/T3 in vitro, but do not directly suppress pituitary thyrotrope gene expression.

mcqs.q: When evaluating a critically ill pediatric patient with low free T4 and low-normal TSH, which biochemical test is most useful to help differentiate euthyroid sick syndrome from central (hypopituitary) hypothyroidism?
options: Serum reverse T3 (rT3)
Serum thyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies
Serum thyroglobulin concentration
Urinary iodine concentration
mcqs.explanation: Serum reverse T3 (rT3) is the most valuable differentiator: in non-thyroidal illness syndrome, rT3 is characteristically elevated or high-normal due to DIO3 activation and reduced peripheral clearance. In contrast, in central hypothyroidism, pituitary failure causes a global deficiency of substrate T4 secretion without peripheral shunting, resulting in a low or undetectable serum rT3.
option_notes: Correct. Serum rT3 is elevated in NTIS due to enhanced DIO3 clearance of T4, whereas rT3 is low in central hypothyroidism.
Incorrect. TPO antibodies identify autoimmune thyroiditis (primary hypothyroidism), but do not distinguish NTIS from central hypothyroidism.
Incorrect. Thyroglobulin is a non-specific marker of thyroid tissue integrity and does not reliably distinguish central AI/hypothyroidism from NTIS.
Incorrect. Urinary iodine assesses nutritional iodine sufficiency, which is not the distinguishing feature between NTIS and hypopituitarism.

atlas.etiology: Adaptive neuroendocrine response to acute or chronic severe illness (sepsis, burns, trauma, cardiac surgery, starvation). Driven by proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha), endogenous/exogenous glucocorticoids, and dopamine.
atlas.epidemiology: Present in 40-70% of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) patients; prevalence and depth correlate with APACHE/PRISM illness severity scores.
atlas.diagnostics: Low free T3, elevated reverse T3 (rT3); in severe stages, low free T4 and suppressed TSH. Transient rebound hyperthyrotropinemia (TSH 5-15 mIU/L) occurs during recovery.

therapies.text: Routine thyroid hormone replacement with levothyroxine (T4) or liothyronine (T3) is NOT recommended in pediatric non-thyroidal illness syndrome. Clinical management focuses on aggressive treatment of the underlying systemic illness, hemodynamic support, and nutritional recovery. Repeat thyroid testing 4-6 weeks after resolution of acute illness.

pillars.label: RTH-Beta Etiology and Pathogenesis
pillars.text: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous mutations in the thyroid hormone receptor beta gene (THRB on chromosome 3p24). The mutant TR-beta receptor exhibits impaired triiodothyronine (T3) binding or defective recruitment of coactivators, exerting a dominant-negative effect over the wild-type receptor. Because TR-beta is the predominant receptor isoform in the anterior pituitary thyrotrope and hypothalamic paraventricular nucleus, negative feedback inhibition of TSH by circulating free T4 and T3 is blunted, leading to unsuppressed or elevated TSH despite high serum thyroid hormone levels.

pillars.label: RTH-Beta Clinical Manifestations
pillars.text: Clinical presentation in RTH-beta is highly variable due to differential tissue distribution of TR-beta versus TR-alpha. Most patients are clinically euthyroid because elevated circulating thyroid hormones compensate for impaired receptor sensitivity. However, tissues where TR-alpha predominates—notably cardiac myocytes—are exposed to high circulating thyroid hormone concentrations, resulting in resting sinus tachycardia, palpitations, and systolic hypertension. Other frequent findings include diffuse goiter (due to persistent TSH stimulation), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; 40-60%), sensorineural hearing loss, learning disabilities, and mild short stature with delayed bone age.

pillars.label: RTH-Alpha Phenotypic Spectrum
pillars.text: Resistance to thyroid hormone alpha (RTH-alpha) is caused by heterozygous de novo or dominant mutations in the THRA gene (encoding TR-alpha1 on chromosome 17q21). Because TR-alpha1 is the major isoform expressed in brain, skeletal tissue, and the gastrointestinal tract, while TR-beta mediates pituitary feedback, patients exhibit a distinct hormonal profile: normal or near-normal TSH, low or low-normal free T4, high or high-normal free T3 (markedly low free T4 to free T3 ratio), and very low reverse T3. The clinical phenotype includes severe skeletal dysplasia, delayed bone age, open fontanels, delayed tooth eruption, macrocephaly, constipation, bradycardia, and neurodevelopmental delay.

pillars.label: Transporter Defects and Allan-Herndon-Dudley
pillars.text: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (AHDS) is an X-linked disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC16A2 gene, which encodes the monocarboxylate transporter 8 (MCT8), an essential specific transporter for thyroid hormone entry across the blood-brain barrier and into neuronal cells. Affected hemizygous males present in infancy with severe muscular hypotonia, progressive spastic paraplegia or quadriplegia, dystonia, athetoid movements, and profound intellectual disability. The characteristic biochemical triad is strikingly elevated serum free T3, low free T4, and normal or slightly elevated serum TSH.

pillars.label: Differential Diagnosis and Management
pillars.text: The critical differential diagnosis for RTH-beta is a TSH-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (TSHoma). Key distinguishing features: TSHomas typically exhibit elevated serum alpha-subunit (alpha-subunit/TSH molar ratio >1.0), blunted TSH response to TRH stimulation, failure of TSH suppression with supraphysiological T3, and a visible pituitary adenoma on MRI, whereas RTH-beta displays a normal alpha-subunit ratio, brisk TSH response to TRH, familial inheritance, and normal pituitary MRI. Treatment for RTH-beta: asymptomatic patients require no therapy; tachycardia is treated with beta-blockers (atenolol); TRIAC (tiratricol, an analog with high affinity for TR-beta) can reduce TSH and goiter.

cards.q: What gene is mutated in the classic form of resistance to thyroid hormone (RTH-beta), and what is its mode of inheritance?
cards.a: THRB gene (encoding thyroid hormone receptor beta), inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern with a dominant-negative effect (or occurring as de novo mutations).

cards.q: What is the hallmark circulating thyroid hormone pattern in resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta)?
cards.a: Elevated serum free T4 and free T3 accompanied by an inappropriately normal or mildly elevated serum TSH concentration.

cards.q: What neuroendocrine tumor must be differentiated from RTH-beta, and what biochemical ratio helps confirm the tumor?
cards.a: TSH-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (TSHoma); an elevated glycoprotein alpha-subunit concentration and alpha-subunit/TSH molar ratio (>1.0) strongly favor a TSHoma.

cards.q: Why do patients with RTH-beta frequently suffer from resting tachycardia despite generalized peripheral tissue hormone resistance?
cards.a: Cardiac myocytes predominantly express the TR-alpha isoform (encoded by THRA), which is normal in RTH-beta; high circulating thyroid hormones therefore over-stimulate cardiac TR-alpha, causing tachycardia and palpitations.

cards.q: What is the biochemical and clinical phenotype of Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (MCT8 transporter deficiency)?
cards.a: X-linked severe neurodevelopmental disability, central hypotonia, progressive spastic quadriplegia, and dystonia, with a biochemical profile of markedly elevated free T3, low free T4, and normal/slightly elevated TSH.

cards.q: How does the thyroid hormone profile in RTH-alpha (THRA mutation) differ from classic RTH-beta?
cards.a: RTH-alpha features normal or near-normal TSH, low or low-normal free T4, high or high-normal free T3 (markedly low FT4/FT3 ratio), and very low reverse T3, accompanied by severe skeletal dysplasia and constipation.

cards.q: What thyroid hormone analog with high affinity for TR-beta can be used in symptomatic RTH-beta to suppress elevated TSH and reduce goiter size?
cards.a: Tiratricol (TRIAC / 3,5,3'-triiodothyroacetic acid), which binds TR-beta with higher relative affinity than T3 to inhibit pituitary TSH secretion without aggravating peripheral hyperthyroidism.

mcqs.q: A 9-year-old boy is evaluated for learning difficulties and hyperactivity. Routine screening reveals free T4 2.8 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), free T3 6.4 pg/mL (reference: 2.3-4.2 pg/mL), and TSH 3.8 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L). Examination reveals a resting heart rate of 105 bpm and a mild, diffuse, non-tender goiter without orbitopathy. His mother and maternal uncle are reported to have similar laboratory findings and were erroneously treated with radioactive iodine in the past. What is the most likely molecular defect?
options: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the TSHR gene
Heterozygous dominant-negative mutation in the THRB gene
Hemizygous inactivating mutation in the SLC16A2 (MCT8) gene
Activating mutation in the GNAS gene
mcqs.explanation: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the THRB gene. It is characterized by elevated free T4 and free T3 with an unsuppressed (normal or slightly elevated) TSH. Due to differential receptor expression, TR-alpha in the heart is stimulated by elevated hormones, causing resting sinus tachycardia, while goiter arises from unsuppressed TSH. Autosomal dominant transmission in the mother and uncle confirms RTH-beta.
option_notes: Incorrect. TSHR mutations cause resistance to TSH (elevated TSH with low or normal FT4), not elevated FT4/FT3.
Correct. Heterozygous mutations in THRB cause RTH-beta, displaying elevated FT4/FT3 with unsuppressed TSH and familial autosomal dominant transmission.
Incorrect. SLC16A2 mutations cause Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome with high T3, low T4, and severe neurological spastic quadriplegia.
Incorrect. Activating GNAS mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome with fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait macules, and precocious puberty.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old girl is found to have elevated free T4 (2.6 ng/dL) and free T3 (5.8 pg/mL) with a serum TSH of 4.5 mIU/L. To differentiate between resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta) and a TSH-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (TSHoma), which diagnostic finding would most strongly support a TSHoma?
options: A markedly elevated glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit concentration and alpha-subunit/TSH ratio >1.0
A 3-fold rise in serum TSH in response to an intravenous TRH stimulation test
Presence of a heterozygous mutation in the THRB gene
Complete absence of symptoms of thyrotoxicosis
mcqs.explanation: Both RTH-beta and TSHomas present with high free T4/T3 and unsuppressed TSH. A TSHoma is distinguished by an elevated circulating pituitary glycoprotein hormone alpha-subunit level and an alpha-subunit/TSH molar ratio >1.0 (present in >80% of TSHomas), blunted TSH response to TRH stimulation, and a visible pituitary lesion on contrast MRI. In contrast, RTH-beta typically shows a normal alpha-subunit ratio and a brisk, normal TSH rise to TRH.
option_notes: Correct. Elevated free alpha-subunit and an alpha-subunit/TSH molar ratio >1.0 strongly indicate an autonomous TSH-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor.
Incorrect. A brisk 3-fold TSH rise after TRH stimulation is characteristic of RTH-beta, whereas TSHomas show a blunted or flat response.
Incorrect. A THRB mutation confirms RTH-beta, refuting the diagnosis of TSHoma.
Incorrect. Both conditions can present with minimal or mixed thyrotoxic symptoms.

mcqs.q: A 7-month-old infant boy is evaluated for profound hypotonia, failure to achieve head control, and severe developmental delay. Examination reveals generalized weakness, spasticity in lower extremities, dystonic posturing, and poor weight gain. Laboratory testing demonstrates serum total T3 380 ng/dL (reference: 105-245 ng/dL), free T4 0.5 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), and TSH 3.2 mIU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTH-beta)
Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (MCT8 deficiency)
Congenital hypopituitarism with isolated TSH deficiency
Thyroid dysgenesis with lingual thyroid
mcqs.explanation: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome is an X-linked inherited neurodevelopmental disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in SLC16A2 (encoding MCT8), which mediates thyroid hormone transport into neurons. Affected males exhibit severe cognitive disability, central hypotonia, progressive spasticity, dystonia, and a pathognomonic serum thyroid panel: high total and free T3, low free T4, and normal or slightly elevated TSH.
option_notes: Incorrect. RTH-beta presents with high free T4 and high free T3, not low free T4.
Correct. Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome features severe spastic quadriplegia, profound cognitive impairment, high T3, low T4, and normal TSH.
Incorrect. Isolated TSH deficiency produces low T4 and low TSH without markedly elevated T3.
Incorrect. Thyroid dysgenesis causes primary hypothyroidism with elevated TSH and low T4/T3.

mcqs.q: A 5-year-old child presents with severe skeletal dysplasia, delayed fontanel closure, delayed tooth eruption, marked constipation, and bradycardia. Biochemical evaluation reveals normal TSH (2.1 mIU/L), low-normal free T4 (0.8 ng/dL), high-normal free T3 (4.4 pg/mL), a markedly reduced free T4 to free T3 ratio, and very low reverse T3. What receptor is defective in this child?
options: Thyroid hormone receptor beta (TR-beta)
Thyroid hormone receptor alpha (TR-alpha1)
TSH receptor (TSHR)
Glucocorticoid receptor (GR)
mcqs.explanation: Resistance to thyroid hormone alpha (RTH-alpha) is caused by heterozygous mutations in THRA. Because TR-alpha1 is heavily expressed in bone, brain, and intestine, while TR-beta regulates pituitary feedback, patients exhibit tissue-specific hypothyroid symptoms (skeletal dysplasia, delayed tooth eruption, macrocephaly, constipation, bradycardia) with a distinctive hormonal signature: near-normal TSH, low-normal FT4, high FT3, low FT4/FT3 ratio, and extremely low rT3.
option_notes: Incorrect. TR-beta defects cause RTH-beta with high FT4, high FT3, unsuppressed TSH, and cardiac tachycardia.
Correct. Mutations in THRA (TR-alpha1) cause severe skeletal dysplasia, delayed bone age, constipation, bradycardia, low FT4/FT3 ratio, and very low rT3.
Incorrect. TSHR mutations cause elevated TSH with normal/low thyroid hormones (resistance to TSH).
Incorrect. Glucocorticoid receptor defects cause Chrousos syndrome (adrenal hyperandrogenism, hypertension, fatigue).

mcqs.q: An 11-year-old asymptomatic boy is diagnosed with RTH-beta after genetic testing confirms a heterozygous pathogenic mutation in THRB. His free T4 is 2.5 ng/dL, free T3 is 5.2 pg/mL, and TSH is 3.1 mIU/L. His resting pulse is 80 bpm and height is tracking along the 50th percentile. Which management strategy is most appropriate?
options: Immediate radioactive iodine ablation to normalize circulating thyroid hormones
Observation and clinical monitoring without antithyroid medications or levothyroxine
High-dose methimazole to normalize free T4 and free T3
Subtotal thyroidectomy to treat subclinical thyrotoxicosis
mcqs.explanation: In asymptomatic patients with RTH-beta who have normal growth and no cardiovascular compromise, no pharmacological treatment is required. Elevated circulating thyroid hormone levels are necessary to overcome the end-organ receptor resistance. Attempting to lower thyroid hormone levels with antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or surgery causes pituitary TSH overdrive, massive goiter expansion, and severe tissue hypothyroidism.
option_notes: Incorrect. Radioiodine ablation or surgery leads to massive TSH elevation, pituitary thyrotrope hyperplasia, and severe tissue hypothyroid symptoms.
Correct. Asymptomatic patients with RTH-beta compensate well with elevated endogenous hormones; conservative observation without treatment is standard of care.
Incorrect. Methimazole reduces thyroid hormone levels, which triggers massive TSH surge, rapid goiter growth, and clinical hypothyroidism.
Incorrect. Thyroidectomy is contraindicated and induces severe pituitary hypertrophy.

atlas.etiology: RTH-beta: Autosomal dominant dominant-negative mutations in THRB (3p24). RTH-alpha: Mutations in THRA (17q21). Allan-Herndon-Dudley: X-linked mutations in SLC16A2 (MCT8). Resistance to TSH (RTSH): Inactivating TSHR mutations.
atlas.epidemiology: RTH-beta prevalence is ~1 in 40,000 live births; equal gender distribution. RTH-alpha and AHDS are rare orphan disorders.
atlas.diagnostics: Free T4, free T3, TSH, reverse T3; glycoprotein alpha-subunit/TSH ratio; TRH stimulation testing; pituitary MRI; THRB/THRA/SLC16A2 genetic sequencing.

therapies.text: Asymptomatic patients require no treatment. If resting tachycardia or palpitations are problematic, selective beta-blockers (atenolol 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day) provide symptomatic relief. If massive goiter or elevated TSH persists, tiratricol (TRIAC, 1-3 mg/day in divided doses) can be considered to suppress pituitary TSH secretion.

pillars.label: Pediatric Thyroid Nodule Epidemiology
pillars.text: Thyroid nodules (TN) occur in approximately 1-2% of children and adolescents, which is significantly less frequent than in adults (where prevalence is 20-50%). However, the risk of malignancy in a pediatric thyroid nodule is substantially higher: approximately 22-26% of solitary nodules in children are malignant, compared to only 5-10% in adults. Any thyroid nodule discovered clinically or incidentally on imaging in a pediatric patient warrants systematic, dedicated diagnostic investigation.

pillars.label: Sonographic and Laboratory Stratification
pillars.text: Initial evaluation requires measurement of serum TSH and a high-resolution neck ultrasound evaluating the nodule and all cervical lymph node chains. If TSH is suppressed, radionuclide scintigraphy (123I or 99mTc) is performed; autonomously functioning ('hot') nodules are rarely malignant in children. If TSH is normal or elevated, sonographic risk stratification is performed. High-risk features include hypoechogenicity, irregular or infiltrative margins, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape, absence of an acoustic halo, extrathyroidal extension, and suspicious regional lymphadenopathy (rounded, microcalcified, loss of fatty hilum).

pillars.label: Fine-Needle Aspiration and Cytopathology
pillars.text: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) is the gold-standard diagnostic modality for evaluating pediatric thyroid nodules >=1 cm with suspicious sonographic features, or nodules of any size associated with suspicious cervical lymph nodes. Cytopathology is categorized according to the Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology (Bethesda I-VI). In pediatric patients, indeterminate cytology (Bethesda III [AUS/FLUS] and Bethesda IV [FN/SFN]) carries a substantially higher risk of malignancy (28-40%) than in adults, frequently prompting diagnostic hemithyroidectomy or molecular testing rather than prolonged observation.

pillars.label: Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma (DTC)
pillars.text: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) comprises 80-90% of pediatric thyroid malignancies, with follicular thyroid carcinoma (FTC) accounting for 5-10%. Children with PTC frequently present with advanced, aggressive disease: regional cervical lymph node metastasis occurs in 40-80%, extrathyroidal extension in 20-30%, and distant pulmonary metastasis in 10-20%. Molecular drivers in pediatric PTC include RET/PTC gene fusions (frequent in young children and post-radiation tumors) and NTRK/ALK fusions, with BRAF V600E mutations being less frequent than in adults. Despite advanced presentation, disease-specific survival exceeds 98%.

pillars.label: Surgical Strategy and Postoperative Management
pillars.text: Pediatric Endocrine Society (PES) and American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines recommend total or near-total thyroidectomy with routine central compartment (level VI) lymph node dissection for malignant or high-risk nodules to reduce recurrence risk and optimize radioiodine staging. Surgery should be performed by high-volume pediatric thyroid surgeons (>30 cases/year) to minimize hypoparathyroidism and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. Postoperative radioactive iodine (131I) remnant ablation is indicated for intermediate- and high-risk DTC (extranodal extension, extensive nodal disease, pulmonary metastases). Postoperative levothyroxine is dosed to suppress TSH (<0.1 mIU/L in high-risk; 0.1-0.5 mIU/L in intermediate-risk), monitoring serum thyroglobulin (Tg) as a tumor marker.

cards.q: How does the malignancy risk of a discrete thyroid nodule in a pediatric patient compare with that in an adult?
cards.a: A discrete pediatric thyroid nodule carries a significantly higher malignancy rate: ~22-26% in children compared to only 5-10% in adults.

cards.q: Which ultrasound characteristics of a thyroid nodule are most strongly associated with malignancy?
cards.a: Marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular/infiltrative margins, taller-than-wide geometry, absence of a halo, extrathyroidal extension, and abnormal cervical lymph nodes.

cards.q: When is ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy indicated for a pediatric thyroid nodule?
cards.a: For any solid nodule >=1 cm with suspicious sonographic features, any nodule associated with suspicious cervical lymph nodes, or a growing nodule in high-risk patients (e.g., prior head/neck radiation).

cards.q: What is the most prevalent histological type of differentiated thyroid cancer in pediatric patients, and what is its typical pattern of metastatic spread?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC, 80-90% of cases); it characteristically spreads early to regional cervical lymph nodes (40-80%) and hematogenously to the lungs (10-20%).

cards.q: What germline mutation causes hereditary medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) in MEN2A and MEN2B, and what is the timing for prophylactic thyroidectomy in MEN2B?
cards.a: Gain-of-function RET proto-oncogene mutations; in MEN2B (codon M918T), prophylactic total thyroidectomy is recommended during the first year of life (within the first months of life) due to virulent early metastatic spread.

cards.q: What is the recommended surgical extent for pediatric differentiated thyroid cancer to minimize recurrence and facilitate radioiodine ablation?
cards.a: Total or near-total thyroidectomy coupled with central neck (level VI) lymph node dissection performed by a high-volume pediatric thyroid surgeon.

cards.q: What serum protein serves as the primary tumor marker for surveillance following total thyroidectomy and 131I ablation in differentiated thyroid cancer?
cards.a: Serum thyroglobulin (Tg), monitored alongside anti-thyroglobulin (anti-Tg) antibodies (which can falsely suppress immunoassay measurements of Tg).

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old girl is found to have an asymptomatic 1.4-cm solitary firm nodule in the right thyroid lobe on routine physical examination. Serum TSH is 1.8 mIU/L (normal: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L). Thyroid ultrasound reveals a solid, hypoechoic nodule measuring 1.4 x 1.1 x 1.3 cm with multiple punctate microcalcifications and irregular margins; two ipsilateral jugular lymph nodes show rounded morphology and loss of fatty hila. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Radioiodine (123I) uptake and scan to evaluate nodule functionality
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of the nodule and suspicious lymph nodes
Empirical levothyroxine therapy to suppress TSH and reassess nodule size in 6 months
Immediate core needle biopsy of the right lobe under general anesthesia
mcqs.explanation: In a euthyroid child with a solitary solid thyroid nodule >=1 cm displaying high-risk sonographic features (hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular borders) and suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy, ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) of both the primary nodule and the suspicious lymph nodes is the gold-standard diagnostic step. 123I scan is indicated only if TSH is suppressed. Levothyroxine suppression is ineffective and delays diagnosis. FNA is preferred over core needle biopsy.
option_notes: Incorrect. Scintigraphy is indicated only if TSH is subnormal/suppressed to look for a toxic adenoma.
Correct. Ultrasound-guided FNA of the nodule and suspicious lymph nodes is the primary diagnostic procedure of choice.
Incorrect. Levothyroxine suppression therapy has no role in modern management and dangerously delays oncologic diagnosis.
Incorrect. Core needle biopsy carries higher complication risks in children and is not the standard first-line diagnostic modality.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old male undergoes total thyroidectomy and central neck dissection for a 2.5-cm papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). Final pathology reveals multifocal PTC with extrathyroidal extension and 6 of 11 central lymph nodes positive for metastatic carcinoma. Staging chest CT reveals multiple 2-3 mm bilateral pulmonary nodules with radioiodine avidity. Which postoperative adjuvant therapy is indicated?
options: External beam radiotherapy to the neck and thorax
Radioactive iodine (131I) therapy following recombinant human TSH (rhTSH) or thyroid hormone withdrawal
Systemic multi-agent cytotoxic chemotherapy (doxorubicin and cisplatin)
Observation without levothyroxine suppression
mcqs.explanation: In pediatric differentiated thyroid carcinoma with high-risk features (extrathyroidal extension, multiple lymph node metastases, distant pulmonary metastases), radioactive iodine (131I) ablation and treatment is the established standard adjuvant therapy. Pediatric pulmonary metastases from PTC are overwhelmingly radioiodine-avid and respond favorably to 131I. Chemotherapy and external beam radiation are ineffective and contraindicated.
option_notes: Incorrect. External beam radiotherapy is reserved for rare refractory, non-iodine avid, locally aggressive adult anaplastic tumors.
Correct. Radioactive iodine (131I) is the definitive adjuvant systemic therapy for radioiodine-avid nodal and pulmonary metastatic PTC.
Incorrect. Systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy is ineffective against differentiated papillary thyroid carcinoma.
Incorrect. High-risk PTC requires both radioiodine therapy and aggressive TSH suppression (<0.1 mIU/L) with levothyroxine.

mcqs.q: A newborn infant is found on genetic testing to carry a de novo heterozygous RET proto-oncogene germline mutation (M918T in exon 16), diagnostic of Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B (MEN2B). When is prophylactic total thyroidectomy recommended to prevent metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC)?
options: Within the first year of life (optimally in the first months of life)
At age 5 to 6 years before entering elementary school
At the onset of spontaneous puberty (Tanner stage 2)
Only after serum calcitonin rises above 100 pg/mL
mcqs.explanation: MEN2B caused by the RET M918T mutation confers the highest risk category ('highest risk / ATA-HST') for medullary thyroid carcinoma. MTC in MEN2B develops within the first year of life and exhibits extremely virulent, early metastatic spread to lymph nodes and liver. American Thyroid Association guidelines recommend prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first year of life, preferably in the first months of life.
option_notes: Correct. In MEN2B (RET M918T), prophylactic total thyroidectomy is performed in the first year (first months) of life due to aggressive infancy metastasis.
Incorrect. Age 5 years is the recommended cutoff for MEN2A (e.g., codon 634), which has a less virulent course than MEN2B.
Incorrect. Waiting until puberty in MEN2B guarantees incurable widely disseminated metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma.
Incorrect. Prophylactic thyroidectomy must precede calcitonin elevation or clinical tumor detection to ensure curative resection.

mcqs.q: What is the targeted postoperative serum TSH suppression level for a 13-year-old child who has undergone total thyroidectomy for high-risk papillary thyroid carcinoma with gross extrathyroidal extension and lung metastases?
options: TSH maintained in the upper normal range (2.5-4.5 mIU/L)
TSH suppressed to <0.1 mIU/L
TSH maintained at 1.0-2.0 mIU/L
TSH elevated above 30 mIU/L to stimulate residual tissue differentiation
mcqs.explanation: In high-risk pediatric differentiated thyroid carcinoma (persistent metastatic disease, extensive nodal involvement, gross extrathyroidal invasion), TSH acts as a trophic growth factor for follicular cells. Guidelines recommend aggressive TSH suppression to <0.1 mIU/L using supra-physiological levothyroxine dosing, while monitoring for iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis and maintaining bone density.
option_notes: Incorrect. Upper normal TSH provides trophic stimulus for tumor cell growth and recurrence.
Correct. TSH suppression to <0.1 mIU/L is recommended for high-risk pediatric thyroid cancer to inhibit residual tumor proliferation.
Incorrect. TSH 1.0-2.0 mIU/L is targeted in low-risk patients who have achieved complete clinical and biochemical remission.
Incorrect. TSH >30 mIU/L is used only transiently immediately prior to diagnostic or therapeutic 131I administration.

mcqs.q: During surveillance of a pediatric patient 1 year after total thyroidectomy and 131I ablation for papillary thyroid cancer, serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is reported as undetectable (<0.1 ng/mL). However, anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) are markedly elevated at 450 IU/mL (reference: <20 IU/mL). How should the clinician interpret these laboratory results?
options: The undetectable Tg proves complete cure and absence of any residual thyroid tissue
The undetectable Tg result may be falsely low due to antibody interference in immunometric assays
High TgAb levels prove that the original tumor was an anaplastic carcinoma
Elevated TgAb levels indicate concurrent Graves' disease of the remnant
mcqs.explanation: In immunometric assays (sandwich ICMA), endogenous anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) bind to serum thyroglobulin and sterically hinder assay antibody binding, producing falsely low or undetectable measured Tg values. Whenever TgAb is positive, a low/undetectable Tg cannot be relied upon as evidence of tumor absence; trending serial TgAb titers (rising titers indicate recurrence) and radioiodine/ultrasound surveillance are required.
option_notes: Incorrect. Undetectable Tg is unreliable in the presence of high TgAb because antibodies cause false-negative immunoassay results.
Correct. Anti-Tg antibodies cause steric hindrance in immunometric assays, causing falsely low or undetectable measured thyroglobulin levels.
Incorrect. TgAb elevation reflects thyroid autoimmunity or tumor-associated immune response, not anaplastic transformation.
Incorrect. After total thyroidectomy and radioiodine ablation, Graves' disease does not occur; rising TgAb suggests residual antigen/tumor.

atlas.etiology: Differentiated thyroid carcinoma (PTC 80-90%, FTC 5-10%); medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC 2-5% in MEN2). Genetic drivers: RET/PTC fusions, NTRK/ALK fusions, BRAF V600E, DICER1, RET point mutations (M918T, C634).
atlas.epidemiology: Thyroid nodules occur in 1-2% of children, but have a 22-26% malignancy rate. PTC has a female predominance (3:1 in adolescents). Excellent prognosis (>98% 30-year survival).
atlas.diagnostics: TSH, neck ultrasound (cervical lymph nodes); ultrasound-guided FNA with Bethesda reporting; RET/NTRK molecular panels; postop serum thyroglobulin (Tg) and anti-Tg antibodies; neck US.

therapies.text: Total or near-total thyroidectomy with central compartment (level VI) lymph node dissection by a high-volume surgeon. For intermediate/high-risk differentiated thyroid cancer, administer adjuvant radioactive iodine (131I, 1-2 mCi/kg or dosimetry-based 30-100 mCi). Postoperative levothyroxine suppression: maintain TSH <0.1 mIU/L for high-risk disease, 0.1-0.5 mIU/L for intermediate-risk.

pillars.label: Calcium Regulation and Sensor Physiology
pillars.text: Extracellular ionized calcium (iCa) is maintained within a narrow physiological range (1.15-1.32 mmol/L; total serum calcium 8.8-10.2 mg/dL in older children, higher in neonates) by the integrated feedback loop between parathyroid hormone (PTH), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), and the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR). The CaSR, a G-protein-coupled receptor on parathyroid cells and renal thick ascending limb tubules, detects minute shifts in iCa. Hypocalcemia relieves CaSR tonic inhibition, triggering rapid PTH exocytosis; PTH stimulates renal tubular calcium reabsorption, osteoclastic calcium resorption, and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) synthesis of calcitriol, which enhances enterocyte calcium absorption.

pillars.label: Neonatal and Pediatric Hypocalcemia
pillars.text: Neonatal hypocalcemia is divided chronologically into early-onset (first 72 hours of life; prematurity, maternal diabetes, perinatal asphyxia, delayed feeding) and late-onset (>72 hours of life; high-phosphate cow's milk formulas, hypomagnesemia, congenital hypoparathyroidism including DiGeorge syndrome/22q11.2 deletion, and activating CaSR mutations). In older infants and children, causes include postsurgical hypoparathyroidism, autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APS-1), vitamin D deficiency, and pseudohypoparathyroidism. Neuromuscular irritability manifests as jitteriness, tetany, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, laryngospasm, focal or generalized seizures, and electrocardiographic QTc prolongation.

pillars.label: Acute and Chronic Hypocalcemia Management
