pillars.text: Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia (tetany, seizures, laryngospasm) is a medical emergency treated with intravenous 10% calcium gluconate at 1-2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg, equivalent to 9-18 mg elemental calcium/kg; maximum single dose 10-20 mL or 1-2 g) infused slowly over 10-20 minutes under continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring. Chronic hypoparathyroidism requires active vitamin D (calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day or 0.25-1.0 mcg daily in divided doses) combined with oral elemental calcium (30-50 mg/kg/day). Because PTH is absent, renal calcium wasting occurs; therapy aims to keep serum calcium in the low-normal range (8.5-9.0 mg/dL) and calcium-to-creatinine ratio <0.2 to prevent hypercalciuria, nephrocalcinosis, and renal failure.

pillars.label: Pediatric Hypercalcemia Etiologies
pillars.text: Hypercalcemia (total calcium >10.5 mg/dL, iCa >1.35 mmol/L) presents with anorexia, nausea, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, lethargy, muscle weakness, and shortened QTc interval. Causes are categorized by PTH status: PTH-dependent includes primary hyperparathyroidism (solitary parathyroid adenoma, MEN1, MEN2A), familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH; heterozygous inactivating CaSR mutations), and neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT; homozygous CaSR mutations). PTH-independent etiologies include hypervitaminosis D, Williams-Beuren syndrome (7q11.23 deletion), subcutaneous fat necrosis in newborns, immobilization, granulomatous disease (excessive macrophage CYP27B1), and malignancy.

pillars.label: FHH Differentiation and Hypercalcemia Crisis
pillars.text: Differentiating FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism is critical: FHH is a benign, autosomal dominant condition characterized by lifelong asymptomatic hypercalcemia, inappropriately normal or mildly elevated PTH, and low urinary calcium excretion with a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) <0.01 (whereas primary hyperparathyroidism typically exhibits CCCR >0.02); parathyroidectomy is ineffective and contraindicated in FHH. In acute hypercalcemic crisis (calcium >14 mg/dL), immediate therapy entails vigorous volume expansion with IV 0.9% normal saline at 2-3 times maintenance, followed by loop diuretics (furosemide 1-2 mg/kg), IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid 0.025-0.05 mg/kg or pamidronate 0.5-1.0 mg/kg), and calcitonin for rapid transient reduction.

cards.q: What is the recommended dose and administration protocol for intravenous calcium gluconate in acute symptomatic hypocalcemia with tetany or seizures?
cards.a: Intravenous 10% calcium gluconate at 1-2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg; maximum 1-2 g or 10-20 mL) infused slowly over 10 to 20 minutes under continuous ECG monitoring to avoid bradycardia or cardiac arrest.

cards.q: What is the targeted serum calcium level in children with chronic hypoparathyroidism on calcitriol and oral calcium therapy?
cards.a: Low-normal serum calcium (8.5-9.0 mg/dL), keeping the 24-hour urine calcium excretion <4 mg/kg/day (urine Ca/Cr ratio <0.2) to prevent nephrocalcinosis and renal impairment.

cards.q: What biochemical index distinguishes familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) from primary hyperparathyroidism, and what is its cutoff value?
cards.a: The urinary calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR); a ratio <0.01 strongly indicates FHH, whereas primary hyperparathyroidism typically displays CCCR >0.02.

cards.q: What receptor mutation is responsible for familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) and neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT)?
cards.a: Heterozygous loss-of-function/inactivating mutations in the CaSR gene cause FHH; homozygous or compound heterozygous inactivating mutations cause life-threatening NSHPT.

cards.q: What characteristic electrocardiographic intervals reflect acute hypocalcemia and severe acute hypercalcemia, respectively?
cards.a: Acute hypocalcemia produces prolonged QTc interval (prolonged ST segment), whereas hypercalcemia produces shortened QTc interval.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of hypercalcemia associated with subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn?
cards.a: Unregulated extra-renal production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) by activated macrophages within the inflammatory subcutaneous granulomas.

cards.q: Which classes of medications are utilized in the acute inpatient treatment of severe symptomatic hypercalcemia (calcium >14 mg/dL)?
cards.a: Vigorous IV 0.9% normal saline hyperhydration, loop diuretics (furosemide, only after volume restoration), IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or pamidronate), and calcitonin.

mcqs.q: A 10-day-old male infant presents with generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Laboratory testing demonstrates serum total calcium 5.8 mg/dL (reference: 8.8-10.5 mg/dL), ionized calcium 0.70 mmol/L (reference: 1.15-1.32 mmol/L), serum phosphate 9.8 mg/dL (reference: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL), magnesium 1.8 mg/dL, and intact PTH 4 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). Cardiac evaluation reveals a conotruncal cardiac defect (truncus arteriosus). What is the underlying genetic diagnosis?
options: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome)
Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (GNAS mutation)
Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (CaSR mutation)
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (PHEX mutation)
mcqs.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) results from defective development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to congenital hypoparathyroidism (absent or hypoplastic parathyroid glands presenting with profound hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and inappropriately low PTH), conotruncal cardiac anomalies (truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch, tetralogy of Fallot), thymic hypoplasia (T-cell immunodeficiency), and facial dysmorphisms.
option_notes: Correct. 22q11.2 deletion causes parathyroid hypoplasia, congenital hypocalcemia, truncus arteriosus, and immune defect.
Incorrect. GNAS mutations cause pseudohypoparathyroidism with elevated PTH, not low/absent PTH.
Incorrect. CaSR loss-of-function causes hypercalcemia (FHH), not severe hypocalcemia.
Incorrect. PHEX mutations cause hypophosphatemia and rickets, not hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia and low PTH.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old asymptomatic boy is referred for incidental hypercalcemia found on a sports physical. Serum total calcium is 11.2 mg/dL, ionized calcium 1.42 mmol/L, serum phosphate 3.2 mg/dL, and intact PTH 52 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). A 24-hour urine collection reveals low urinary calcium with a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) of 0.005. His father and paternal grandfather also have mild asymptomatic hypercalcemia. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Urgent four-gland surgical parathyroid exploration and subtotal parathyroidectomy
Reassurance and observation without surgical intervention
Intravenous zoledronic acid infusion every 6 months
High-dose oral furosemide and sodium chloride tablets daily
mcqs.explanation: This patient has classic familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), an autosomal dominant condition caused by a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in the CaSR gene. Diagnostic hallmarks are lifelong mild-to-moderate hypercalcemia, inappropriately normal intact PTH, and marked hypocalciuria with a calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR) <0.01. FHH is entirely benign, does not cause end-organ injury (no nephrolithiasis or bone loss), and parathyroidectomy does not cure the condition. Surgical intervention is contraindicated.
option_notes: Incorrect. Parathyroidectomy does not correct the altered CaSR set-point throughout tissues and is completely ineffective and contraindicated.
Correct. FHH is a benign familial trait requiring no medical or surgical intervention; observation and reassurance are indicated.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates are unnecessary and ineffective for the reset homeostatic set-point in FHH.
Incorrect. Diuretics and sodium loading are indicated for acute hypercalcemic crisis, not benign asymptomatic FHH.

mcqs.q: A 7-year-old girl with postsurgical hypoparathyroidism following total thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer is treated with calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and oral calcium carbonate 500 mg elemental calcium twice daily. On follow-up, serum total calcium is 8.8 mg/dL, phosphate is 5.2 mg/dL, and a spot urine calcium-to-creatinine ratio is 0.38 mg/mg (normal <0.20). Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. What adjustment in medical therapy is indicated?
options: Increase calcitriol to 1.0 mcg daily to bring serum calcium into the high-normal range
Decrease calcitriol and oral calcium to lower urine calcium excretion, targeting serum calcium of 8.0-8.5 mg/dL, and consider adding a thiazide diuretic
Discontinue calcitriol and start daily recombinant human parathyroid hormone injections
Add oral sodium phosphate supplements
mcqs.explanation: In hypoparathyroidism, the absence of PTH removes the primary stimulus for renal tubular calcium reabsorption. Exogenous calcium and calcitriol easily precipitate hypercalciuria (urine Ca/Cr >0.2 mg/mg) and nephrocalcinosis. Management requires reducing calcitriol/calcium to keep serum calcium in the low-normal range (8.0-8.5 mg/dL) and adding a thiazide diuretic (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide), which promotes proximal and distal tubular calcium reabsorption to reduce urinary calcium excretion.
option_notes: Incorrect. Increasing calcitriol will exacerbate hypercalciuria and worsen nephrocalcinosis.
Correct. Reducing calcitriol/calcium to maintain low-normal serum calcium and initiating a thiazide diuretic reduces hypercalciuria.
Incorrect. While rhPTH is an emerging therapy, standard established pediatric management begins with dosing adjustment and thiazide diuretics.
Incorrect. Oral phosphate will cause severe hyperphosphatemia and metastatic tissue calcification.

mcqs.q: A newborn infant presents at 4 days of life with severe hypotonia, failure to thrive, rib fractures, and respiratory distress. Serum calcium is markedly elevated at 17.5 mg/dL, phosphate is 2.8 mg/dL, and intact PTH is 650 pg/mL. Skeletal radiographs show diffuse demineralization and subperiosteal resorption. Genetic testing confirms a homozygous inactivating mutation in the CaSR gene. What is the definitive life-saving therapy?
options: Emergent total parathyroidectomy
Lifelong high-dose intravenous calcium infusions
Oral calcitriol and dietary phosphate restriction
Bilateral adrenalectomy
mcqs.explanation: Neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in CaSR. Without functioning calcium sensors, parathyroid cells do not recognize extreme hypercalcemia, producing massive PTH secretion and torrential skeletal resorption with fractures and respiratory failure. Emergent total parathyroidectomy (with autotransplantation of parathyroid tissue or lifelong hypoparathyroidism management) is life-saving; medical therapy alone is rarely sufficient.
option_notes: Correct. Total parathyroidectomy is the definitive life-saving intervention for neonatal severe primary hyperparathyroidism.
Incorrect. Administering calcium would be fatal in a neonate with calcium of 17.5 mg/dL.
Incorrect. Calcitriol would further elevate serum calcium and worsen hypercalcemic crisis.
Incorrect. Adrenalectomy has no role in parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor disorders.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with carpopedal spasm and facial twitching upon tapping the facial nerve anterior to the ear. What are the clinical names of these two physical signs, and what electrolyte disturbance do they indicate?
options: Trousseau sign and Chvostek sign; acute hypocalcemia
Kernig sign and Brudzinski sign; hypomagnesemia
Gowers sign and Trendelenburg sign; hypercalcemia
Tinels sign and Phalens sign; hyperphosphatemia
mcqs.explanation: Carpopedal spasm induced by inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes is Trousseau sign. Twitching of facial muscles elicited by tapping the facial nerve trunk anterior to the external auditory meatus is Chvostek sign. Both are classical clinical signs of latent neuromuscular excitability (tetany) secondary to acute hypocalcemia (or profound hypomagnesemia).
option_notes: Correct. Trousseau (carpopedal spasm) and Chvostek (facial twitch) signs are pathognomonic physical markers of hypocalcemia.
Incorrect. Kernig and Brudzinski signs indicate meningeal irritation in meningitis.
Incorrect. Gowers and Trendelenburg signs indicate proximal muscle weakness and hip abductor insufficiency.
Incorrect. Tinel and Phalen signs detect median nerve compression in carpal tunnel syndrome.

atlas.etiology: Hypocalcemia: Early/late neonatal; hypoparathyroidism (DiGeorge/22q11.2, CaSR activating mutations, APS-1); pseudohypoparathyroidism; vitamin D deficiency. Hypercalcemia: FHH (heterozygous CaSR), NSHPT (homozygous CaSR), primary hyperparathyroidism, Williams syndrome (7q11.23), subcutaneous fat necrosis, immobilization.
atlas.epidemiology: DiGeorge syndrome occurs in 1:4000 live births. FHH prevalence is ~1:78,000. Primary hyperparathyroidism is rare in children (1-2 per 100,000).
atlas.diagnostics: Ionized and total calcium, phosphate, magnesium, intact PTH, 25-OH-D, 1,25-(OH)2-D; spot urine Ca/Cr and 24-hr urine calcium/creatinine clearance ratio (CCCR); renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis; ECG (QTc interval).

therapies.text: 10% Calcium gluconate IV at 1-2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg; maximum 1-2 g or 10-20 mL) infused slowly over 10-20 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring. If hypomagnesemia is present, administer 50% magnesium sulfate 25-50 mg/kg IV.

Calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day (0.25-1.0 mcg/day) orally divided BID plus oral elemental calcium 30-50 mg/kg/day divided TID. Target low-normal serum calcium (8.5-9.0 mg/dL) and urine Ca/Cr <0.20 to prevent nephrocalcinosis.

pillars.label: Phosphate Physiology and Renal Handling
pillars.text: Inorganic phosphate is vital for skeletal hydroxyapatite mineralization, cellular high-energy ATP synthesis, cell membrane phospholipids, and intracellular signaling cascades. Serum phosphate is maintained within age-specific reference intervals (infants: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL; children: 4.0-5.8 mg/dL; adolescents/adults: 2.7-4.5 mg/dL). Renal proximal tubules regulate systemic phosphate balance via sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporters: NaPi-IIa (SLC34A1) and NaPi-IIc (SLC34A3). Renal phosphate reabsorption is quantified by calculating the tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TRP) and tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate per unit of glomerular filtration rate (TmP/GFR).

pillars.label: FGF23 Biology and Signaling Axis
pillars.text: Fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) is a phosphaturic hormone synthesized primarily by osteocytes and osteoblasts in response to elevated serum phosphate and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Circulating intact FGF23 binds the FGF receptor-1 (FGFR1) and its essential obligate coreceptor alpha-Klotho in renal proximal tubular cells. FGF23 induces endocytic retrieval and degradation of NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc cotransporters, producing marked phosphaturia. Concurrently, FGF23 suppresses renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) and upregulates 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1), causing inappropriately low or normal 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D levels despite profound hypophosphatemia.

pillars.label: FGF23-Dependent Hypophosphatemic Disorders
pillars.text: FGF23-dependent hypophosphatemias feature renal phosphate wasting (low TmP/GFR) driven by elevated or inappropriately normal intact FGF23. X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH) is the most common hereditary form, caused by inactivating mutations in PHEX (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase homolog, X-linked) on chromosome Xp22.1. Other forms include Autosomal Dominant Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ADHR; cleavage-resistant mutations in FGF23 at R176/R179), Autosomal Recessive Hypophosphatemic Rickets (ARHR; DMP1 or ENPP1 mutations), and Tumor-Induced Osteomalacia (TIO; benign mesenchymal phosphaturic tumors producing FGF23).

pillars.label: Clinical Features and Burosumab Therapy in XLH
pillars.text: XLH manifests after weight-bearing begins in toddlers with progressive lower-extremity bowing (genu varum/valgum), waddling gait, rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, cranial synostosis, severe dental abscesses (due to defective dentin mineralization), and marked disproportionate short stature. Traditional therapy with oral phosphate salts (20-40 mg/kg/day divided 4-5 times daily) plus calcitriol (20-30 ng/kg/day) required cumbersome dosing and frequently caused nephrocalcinosis and tertiary hyperparathyroidism. Burosumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody directed against intact FGF23, administered subcutaneously at 0.8-2.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks, directly restores renal phosphate reabsorption, heals rickets, accelerates growth, and eliminates nephrocalcinosis risk.

pillars.label: FGF23-Independent Wasting and Hyperphosphatemia
pillars.text: FGF23-independent hypophosphatemia includes Hereditary Hypophosphatemic Rickets with Hypercalciuria (HHRH; biallelic SLC34A3 mutations encoding NaPi-IIc), characterized by suppressed FGF23, elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, hypercalciuria, and nephrolithiasis; treatment is oral phosphate alone (calcitriol is strictly contraindicated). Fanconi syndrome exhibits generalized proximal tubulopathy (glucosuria, aminoaciduria, proximal RTA). Conversely, hyperphosphatemia arises from renal failure, hypoparathyroidism/PHP, or Hyperphosphatemic Familial Tumoral Calcinosis (HFTC; loss-of-function mutations in FGF23, GALNT3, or KL/Klotho), presenting with severe hyperphosphatemia, high calcitriol, and massive periarticular calcific masses.

cards.q: What gene is mutated in X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH), and what is its mode of inheritance?
cards.a: PHEX gene (phosphate-regulating endopeptidase homolog, X-linked) on chromosome Xp22.1; inherited in an X-linked dominant manner.

cards.q: How does elevated FGF23 affect renal tubular phosphate reabsorption and vitamin D metabolism?
cards.a: FGF23 downregulates NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc cotransporters, causing renal phosphate wasting, and simultaneously inhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) while inducing 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1), lowering 1,25-(OH)2D.

cards.q: What is burosumab, and what is its dosing schedule in pediatric patients with XLH?
cards.a: A fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody targeting intact FGF23; administered subcutaneously at 0.8 mg/kg every 2 weeks (titrated up to 2.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks based on serum phosphate).

cards.q: Why is calcitriol contraindicated in hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH; SLC34A3 mutation)?
cards.a: In HHRH, FGF23 is suppressed, causing endogenous 1,25-(OH)2D to be markedly elevated; exogenous calcitriol would cause severe hypercalcemia, torrential hypercalciuria, and nephrolithiasis.

cards.q: What distinctive dental pathology frequently leads to the initial diagnosis of XLH in early childhood?
cards.a: Spontaneous non-traumatic periapical dental abscesses occurring in caries-free primary teeth, caused by defective dentin mineralization with enlarged pulp chambers allowing bacterial tracking.

cards.q: What diagnostic calculation establishes renal phosphate wasting in a hypophosphatemic child?
cards.a: Reduced tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate per unit GFR (TmP/GFR), calculated from fasting simultaneous serum and urine phosphate and creatinine concentrations.

cards.q: What molecular defects cause Hyperphosphatemic Familial Tumoral Calcinosis (HFTC)?
cards.a: Inactivating biallelic mutations in FGF23, GALNT3 (polypeptide N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase 3), or KL (Klotho), resulting in FGF23 deficiency/resistance, severe hyperphosphatemia, and ectopic periarticular calcifications.

mcqs.q: An 18-month-old toddler boy presents with marked progressive bowing of both legs (genu varum) and waddling gait since starting to walk at 14 months. Serum testing reveals: calcium 9.4 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 2.1 mg/dL (normal: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 950 U/L (normal: 150-400 U/L), intact PTH 55 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38 ng/mL, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D 28 pg/mL (inappropriately normal), and TmP/GFR 1.8 mg/dL (severely reduced). His mother has short stature and bowlegs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets
X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH)
Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A (CYP27B1 mutation)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A
mcqs.explanation: This toddler exhibits classic X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (XLH), an X-linked dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations in PHEX. Hallmarks are normal serum calcium, severe hypophosphatemia due to renal phosphate wasting (reduced TmP/GFR), elevated alkaline phosphatase, normal PTH, and inappropriately normal (rather than elevated) 1,25-(OH)2D driven by elevated intact FGF23. The maternal family history of short stature and bowed legs supports X-linked dominant inheritance.
option_notes: Incorrect. Nutritional rickets presents with low 25-OH-D, elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), and low/normal calcium.
Correct. Normal calcium, low phosphate, reduced TmP/GFR, inappropriately normal 1,25-(OH)2D, and maternal history define XLH.
Incorrect. VDDR1A presents with severe hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D.
Incorrect. PHP1A features hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and markedly elevated PTH, the exact opposite of this patient's profile.

mcqs.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of burosumab in the treatment of pediatric X-linked hypophosphatemia?
mcqs.a: Direct inhibition of intact FGF23 signaling by binding circulating FGF23, thereby restoring renal tubular NaPi-IIa/c expression and normalizing 1,25-(OH)2D synthesis
options: Direct inhibition of intact FGF23 signaling by binding circulating FGF23, thereby restoring renal tubular NaPi-IIa/c expression and normalizing 1,25-(OH)2D synthesis
Allosteric activation of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in parathyroid tissue
Competitive antagonism of parathyroid hormone at the PTH-1 receptor in the proximal tubule
Stimulation of renal 24-hydroxylase (CYP24A1) to promote phosphate reabsorption
mcqs.explanation: Burosumab is a recombinant human IgG1 monoclonal antibody that binds to and neutralizes circulating intact FGF23. By blocking excess FGF23 action at the FGFR1/Klotho complex in the renal proximal tubule, burosumab increases tubular expression of NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc cotransporters, enhancing renal phosphate reabsorption, and relieves suppression of CYP27B1, boosting endogenous 1,25-(OH)2D production.
option_notes: Correct. Burosumab binds circulating intact FGF23, normalizing renal phosphate reabsorption and 1,25-(OH)2D generation.
Incorrect. CaSR activation is the mechanism of calcimimetics like cinacalcet, not burosumab.
Incorrect. Burosumab does not antagonize the PTH receptor; PTH remains in the normal range during treatment.
Incorrect. FGF23 induces CYP24A1; burosumab suppresses CYP24A1 while restoring CYP27B1 activity.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with rickets, genu valgum, and severe recurrent kidney stones. Serum phosphate is low at 2.2 mg/dL with low TmP/GFR. Serum calcium is normal (9.8 mg/dL), but 24-hour urine calcium is markedly elevated at 7.5 mg/kg/day (hypercalciuria). Intact FGF23 is suppressed (<10 pg/mL) and serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is markedly elevated at 145 pg/mL. What is the diagnosis and appropriate therapy?
options: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets; treat with burosumab
Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH); treat with oral phosphate salts alone
Vitamin D deficiency rickets; treat with high-dose ergocalciferol
Primary hyperparathyroidism; perform parathyroidectomy
mcqs.explanation: Hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria (HHRH) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic mutations in SLC34A3 (encoding NaPi-IIc). Defective renal phosphate reabsorption leads to hypophosphatemia, which appropriately suppresses FGF23. Low FGF23 disinhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase, causing massive 1,25-(OH)2D production, hyperabsorption of intestinal calcium, and severe hypercalciuria with nephrolithiasis. Treatment is oral phosphate salts alone to replenish phosphate, which suppresses 1,25-(OH)2D and cures hypercalciuria. Exogenous calcitriol is strictly contraindicated.
option_notes: Incorrect. XLH features high/normal FGF23, low/normal 1,25-(OH)2D, and hypocalciuria, the opposite of this profile.
Correct. HHRH exhibits low phosphate, suppressed FGF23, high 1,25-(OH)2D, and hypercalciuria; oral phosphate alone is the curative therapy.
Incorrect. High-dose vitamin D would aggravate the already dangerous hypercalciuria and nephrolithiasis.
Incorrect. PTH is normal or suppressed in HHRH; parathyroidectomy is not indicated.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old child with XLH has been treated for 5 years with conventional therapy consisting of high-dose oral phosphate supplements and calcitriol. Routine surveillance reveals serum calcium 9.6 mg/dL, phosphate 3.0 mg/dL, but intact PTH has risen progressively to 450 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). Renal ultrasound demonstrates bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis. What complication of conventional therapy has developed?
options: Tertiary (autonomous) hyperparathyroidism secondary to chronic phosphate administration
Transformation of XLH into osteogenesis imperfecta
Development of a parathyroid carcinoma
Acute renal cortical necrosis
mcqs.explanation: Conventional therapy for XLH with oral phosphate salts causes repeated transient spikes in serum phosphate, which bind ionized calcium and stimulate parathyroid gland hyperplasia. Over years, this chronic stimulation can induce secondary and ultimately tertiary (autonomous) hyperparathyroidism with profound PTH elevation, compounded by calcitriol-induced hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. This severe complication is a primary reason why burosumab has superseded conventional therapy.
option_notes: Correct. Chronic oral phosphate loading triggers parathyroid hyperplasia, driving secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
Incorrect. Genetic disorders of mineralization do not transform into collagen mutations like osteogenesis imperfecta.
Incorrect. Parathyroid carcinoma is extraordinarily rare in children and not the typical consequence of XLH therapy.
Incorrect. The findings reflect chronic medullary nephrocalcinosis and parathyroid hyperplasia, not acute cortical necrosis.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with progressive bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, fatigue, and multiple metatarsal insufficiency fractures. Labs show serum phosphate 1.6 mg/dL, normal calcium, normal PTH, normal 25-OH-D, low 1,25-(OH)2D, and marked renal phosphate wasting (TmP/GFR 1.2 mg/dL). Serum intact FGF23 is markedly elevated. There is no family history of bone disease. Full-body 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT reveals an intensely avid 1.2-cm soft-tissue lesion in the distal femur. What is the diagnosis?
options: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) caused by a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor
Osteosarcoma with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia
Fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright syndrome
Ewing sarcoma with ectopic ACTH production
mcqs.explanation: Tumor-induced osteomalacia (TIO) is a paraneoplastic syndrome caused by benign, slow-growing phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors (PMTs) that oversecrete FGF23. This results in severe hypophosphatemia, renal phosphate wasting, inappropriately low 1,25-(OH)2D, and severe osteomalacia/fractures. PMTs overexpress somatostatin receptors (SSTR2), making 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT the most sensitive localization modality. Complete surgical resection of the tumor cures the condition.
option_notes: Correct. Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors secrete excess FGF23 causing TIO, localized by 68Ga-DOTATATE and cured by surgical excision.
Incorrect. Osteosarcoma produces osteolytic or blastic lesions, not isolated hypophosphatemic TIO with high FGF23.
Incorrect. McCune-Albright fibrous dysplasia can occasionally secrete FGF23, but DOTATATE uptake in an isolated soft tissue tumor indicates PMT.
Incorrect. Ewing sarcoma does not present with isolated high-FGF23 hypophosphatemic rickets.

atlas.etiology: FGF23-dependent: XLH (PHEX, Xp22.1, X-linked dominant); ADHR (FGF23 R176/R179); ARHR (DMP1, ENPP1); TIO (phosphaturic mesenchymal tumors). FGF23-independent: HHRH (SLC34A3), Fanconi syndrome. Hyperphosphatemia: HFTC (FGF23, GALNT3, KL mutations).
atlas.epidemiology: XLH incidence is ~1 in 20,000 live births; most common form of heritable rickets. ADHR, ARHR, HHRH, and HFTC are rare orphan diseases.
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting serum phosphate, calcium, intact PTH, 25-OH-D, 1,25-(OH)2-D; tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TRP) and TmP/GFR; intact serum FGF23; 24-hr urine calcium; renal ultrasound; PHEX/SLC34A3 genetic panel.

therapies.text: Burosumab-twza subcutaneous injection: initiate at 0.8 mg/kg every 2 weeks (rounded to nearest 10 mg; maximum 90 mg). Measure fasting serum phosphate every 4 weeks initially; titrate step-wise to 1.2 mg/kg, then up to 2.0 mg/kg every 2 weeks to maintain serum phosphate in the lower normal range.

therapies.section: Conventional Oral Phosphate and Calcitriol Therapy
therapies.text: Oral elemental phosphate (Joulie solution or tablets) 20-40 mg/kg/day divided 4-5 times daily plus calcitriol 20-30 ng/kg/day divided BID. Monitor serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and urine Ca/Cr every 3 months; monitor renal US annually for nephrocalcinosis.

pillars.label: Pathophysiological Definition and Physis
pillars.text: Rickets is defined as a disorder of defective chondrocyte maturation and mineralization failure at the growth plate (physis), which occurs exclusively in growing children prior to epiphyseal fusion. Osteomalacia represents defective mineralization of newly synthesized osteoid matrix at trabecular and cortical bone surfaces throughout life. Rickets arises from inadequate extracellular availability or cellular utilization of either calcium or phosphate, categorizing the condition into calcipenic rickets (calcium deficiency, vitamin D deficiency/resistance) and phosphopenic rickets (renal phosphate wasting, XLH).

pillars.label: Biochemical Stages of Calcipenic Rickets
pillars.text: Calcipenic rickets progresses through three defined biochemical stages. Stage 1 (early deficiency): serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls (<12-20 ng/mL), intestinal calcium absorption drops, and transient hypocalcemia triggers compensatory parathyroid hormone (PTH) release. Stage 2 (established secondary hyperparathyroidism): elevated PTH mobilizes skeletal calcium and enhances renal calcium conservation, normalizing serum calcium; however, PTH induces renal phosphate wasting, leading to hypophosphatemia, elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and active rachitic skeletal deformities. Stage 3 (severe rickets): bone buffering capacity fails, resulting in severe hypocalcemia, profound hypophosphatemia, marked ALP elevation, and life-threatening hypocalcemic seizures or cardiomyopathy.

pillars.label: Clinical Manifestations and Deformities
pillars.text: Clinical signs vary by developmental age. In neonates and young infants: craniotabes (soft, ping-pong ball-like compressibility of parietal/occipital bones), delayed closure of the anterior fontanel (>2 years), frontal bossing, delayed tooth eruption with enamel hypoplasia, and hypocalcemic tetany/stridor. In older infants: enlargement of costochondral junctions ('rachitic rosary'), Harrison groove (depression along the lower chest border at the diaphragmatic insertion), and widening of wrists and ankles. Once weight-bearing begins: progressive varus (bowleg) or valgus (knock-knee) lower-extremity deformities, waddling gait, hypotonia, motor developmental delay, and pathognomonic greenstick fractures.

pillars.label: Radiographic Hallmarks of Active Rickets
pillars.text: Diagnostic radiographs (best visualized at high-growth sites: wrists [distal radius/ulna] and knees [distal femur/proximal tibia]) demonstrate pathognomonic abnormalities: widening and thickening of the radiolucent physis (failure of hypertrophic chondrocyte apoptosis), loss of the sharp provisional zone of calcification, cupping (concavity of the metaphysis facing the epiphysis), fraying/flaring (ragged brush-like metaphyseal margins), splaying (widened transverse diameter of metaphysis), and generalized cortical osteopenia with coarse trabecular patterning and pseudofractures (Looser zones). Healing is evidenced radiographically by appearance of a dense line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis within 2-4 weeks of therapy.

pillars.label: Nutritional and Genetic Treatment Protocols
pillars.text: Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets is treated with oral ergocalciferol (D2) or cholecalciferol (D3) at 2000 IU/day (or age-based: <12 months: 2000 IU/day; >12 months: 3000-6000 IU/day) for 8-12 weeks, or single-day high-dose 'stoss' therapy (100,000-300,000 IU orally) under medical supervision, followed by daily maintenance (400-600 IU/day). Concurrent oral elemental calcium supplementation (30-50 mg/kg/day, typically 500 mg daily) is mandatory to prevent hungry bone syndrome-induced hypocalcemia during rapid remineralization. Genetic calcipenic rickets includes Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets type 1A (VDDR1A; CYP27B1 inactivating mutations; treated with calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day) and VDDR2A (VDR mutations; requires massive oral or IV calcium infusions).

cards.q: Why is serum calcium characteristically normal in Stage 2 calcipenic nutritional rickets?
cards.a: Secondary hyperparathyroidism mobilizes calcium from bone and increases renal tubular reabsorption to normalize serum calcium, at the expense of PTH-induced renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphatemia.

cards.q: What are the cardinal radiographic signs of active rickets seen at the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses?
cards.a: Widening of the physis, fraying (ragged margins), cupping (concave metaphyseal contour), and splaying (transverse expansion) of the metaphysis, with loss of the provisional zone of calcification.

cards.q: What is the recommended daily dosage and duration of oral vitamin D for treating nutritional rickets in children over 12 months of age?
cards.a: 3000 to 6000 IU daily of oral cholecalciferol (D3) or ergocalciferol (D2) for 8 to 12 weeks, combined with 500 mg daily of elemental calcium, followed by 400-600 IU daily maintenance.

cards.q: Why must oral elemental calcium supplementation always accompany vitamin D therapy when initiating treatment for nutritional rickets?
cards.a: Rapid skeletal remineralization ('hungry bone syndrome') drives circulating calcium into healing osteoid, which can precipitate severe, symptomatic hypocalcemia and tetany if calcium is not co-administered.

cards.q: What enzymatic defect causes Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets Type 1A (VDDR1A), and what is its specific pharmacotherapy?
cards.a: Inactivating biallelic mutations in CYP27B1 (renal 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase); treated with physiological doses of active calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D, 20-40 ng/kg/day).

cards.q: What is craniotabes, and in what pediatric age group is it the earliest physical manifestation of rickets?
cards.a: Softening and ping-pong ball-like indentability of the cranial vault bones (parietal/occipital); it is the earliest clinical sign in young infants under 3-6 months of age.

cards.q: What is the earliest radiographic indicator of therapeutic response during medical treatment of rickets?
cards.a: Appearance of a dense radiopaque line of provisional calcification across the metaphyseal growth plate margin, typically visible within 2 to 4 weeks.

mcqs.q: A 14-month-old dark-skinned boy who has been exclusively breastfed without vitamin D supplementation presents with delayed walking, frontal bossing, prominent costochondral enlargement ('rachitic rosary'), and marked widening of both wrists. Serum labs show: calcium 8.9 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 2.8 mg/dL (normal: 4.5-6.5 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 1250 U/L (normal: 150-400 U/L), intact PTH 185 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), and 25-hydroxyvitamin D 7 ng/mL (deficiency <12 ng/mL). What biochemical stage of calcipenic nutritional rickets is present?
options: Stage 1 (early rickets with transient hypocalcemia)
Stage 2 (secondary hyperparathyroidism with normal calcium and hypophosphatemia)
Stage 3 (severe decompensated rickets with hypocalcemia and bone buffering failure)
Adynamic bone disease
mcqs.explanation: This child is in Stage 2 calcipenic rickets. In Stage 2, secondary hyperparathyroidism (PTH 185 pg/mL) successfully normalizes serum calcium (8.9 mg/dL) by mobilizing bone mineral and increasing renal calcium reabsorption. However, excess PTH causes renal phosphate wasting, leading to hypophosphatemia (2.8 mg/dL) and marked alkaline phosphatase elevation with classic rachitic skeletal lesions.
option_notes: Incorrect. Stage 1 presents with hypocalcemia before significant PTH-induced renal phosphaturia develops.
Correct. Stage 2 features robust secondary hyperparathyroidism that normalizes calcium while causing hypophosphatemia and high ALP.
Incorrect. Stage 3 presents with severe, decompensated hypocalcemia alongside profound hypophosphatemia.
Incorrect. Adynamic bone disease is a low-turnover state with suppressed PTH and normal/low ALP.

mcqs.q: A 2-year-old child with severe nutritional rickets is prescribed high-dose ergocalciferol 50,000 IU weekly. The physician also prescribes oral elemental calcium 500 mg daily. What adverse complication does concurrent calcium supplementation specifically prevent during the initial weeks of therapy?
options: Hungry bone syndrome with precipitous hypocalcemia and tetany
Acute renal tubular acidosis
Hypercalcemic crisis and nephrocalcinosis
Hyperphosphatemic tumoral calcinosis
mcqs.explanation: When active mineralization is restored by vitamin D administration, large amounts of extracellular calcium and phosphate are rapidly incorporated into the unmineralized osteoid ('hungry bone syndrome'). Without adequate oral calcium supplementation, circulating serum calcium drops precipitously, triggering acute hypocalcemic tetany, seizures, or laryngospasm.
option_notes: Correct. Co-administering elemental calcium prevents hungry bone syndrome-induced hypocalcemia during rapid remineralization.
Incorrect. Calcium supplementation does not prevent proximal or distal renal tubular acidosis.
Incorrect. At recommended doses with rickets, calcium prevents hypocalcemia; hypercalcemic crisis does not occur unless gross overdose occurs.
Incorrect. Tumoral calcinosis is caused by FGF23 deficiency, not nutritional rickets treatment.

mcqs.q: An 8-month-old infant presents with severe rickets, hypocalcemia (6.8 mg/dL), elevated PTH (320 pg/mL), and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal (45 ng/mL), but serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is undetectable (<5 pg/mL). High-dose parent vitamin D3 produces no clinical or biochemical improvement. What gene mutation is responsible for this autosomal recessive disorder?
options: CYP27B1 (encoding 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase)
CYP2R1 (encoding hepatic 25-hydroxylase)
VDR (encoding vitamin D receptor)
PHEX (encoding phosphate-regulating endopeptidase)
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets type 1A (VDDR1A) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in CYP27B1, which encodes renal 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1-alpha-hydroxylase. Patients cannot convert 25-OH-D into active 1,25-(OH)2D, resulting in early severe rickets with normal 25-OH-D and undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D. The condition responds completely to physiological doses of calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D).
option_notes: Correct. CYP27B1 mutations cause VDDR1A with undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D despite normal 25-OH-D, treated with calcitriol.
Incorrect. CYP2R1 mutations cause VDDR1B, which features low 25-OH-D.
Incorrect. VDR mutations cause VDDR2A, which features markedly elevated 1,25-(OH)2D levels (hormone resistance) and total alopecia.
Incorrect. PHEX mutations cause X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets, with normal calcium and normal 25-OH-D.

mcqs.q: A 10-month-old infant with severe rickets is found to have total alopecia (complete absence of scalp hair, eyebrows, and eyelashes). Laboratory testing shows severe hypocalcemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and strikingly elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (>250 pg/mL). What is the underlying disease mechanism?
options: Inactivating mutation in the vitamin D receptor (VDR) causing end-organ hormone resistance (VDDR2A)
CYP27B1 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency
Subcutaneous fat necrosis with hypercalcemia
Nutritional zinc deficiency
mcqs.explanation: Vitamin D-Dependent Rickets type 2A (VDDR2A) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the vitamin D receptor (VDR). Because target tissues cannot respond to 1,25-(OH)2D, serum 1,25-(OH)2D levels rise massively due to loss of negative feedback. Alopecia totalis is a unique phenotypic marker of severe VDR disruption because VDR is essential for hair follicle cycling.
option_notes: Correct. VDR mutations cause end-organ 1,25-(OH)2D resistance, marked 1,25-(OH)2D elevation, and pathognomonic total alopecia.
Incorrect. CYP27B1 deficiency (VDDR1A) has undetectable 1,25-(OH)2D and normal hair development.
Incorrect. Fat necrosis causes hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemic rickets with alopecia.
Incorrect. Zinc deficiency causes periorificial dermatitis, not rickets with massive calcitriol elevation and total alopecia.

mcqs.q: What classic radiographic finding on wrist radiographs confirms healing of rickets following 3 weeks of vitamin D and calcium therapy?
mcqs.a: Appearance of a well-defined, dense radiopaque line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis
options: Appearance of a well-defined, dense radiopaque line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis
Complete disappearance of the distal radial epiphysis
Development of diffuse subperiosteal cortical thinning
Formation of Looser zones along the ulnar diaphysis
mcqs.explanation: The earliest objective radiographic evidence of rachitic healing is the deposition of calcium in the newly mineralizing hypertrophic zone, forming a crisp, linear radiodense band—the line of provisional calcification—across the metaphyseal margin, typically visible within 2 to 4 weeks of starting therapy.
option_notes: Correct. A dense line of provisional calcification across the metaphysis confirms active mineral deposition and rachitic healing.
Incorrect. Epiphyses become more visible and dense during healing, not disappear.
Incorrect. Subperiosteal cortical thinning reflects hyperparathyroidism or demineralization, not healing.
Incorrect. Looser zones are pseudofractures reflecting active osteomalacia, not healing.

atlas.etiology: Calcipenic: Nutritional vitamin D/calcium deficiency; malabsorption (celiac, cystic fibrosis); VDDR1A (CYP27B1), VDDR1B (CYP2R1), VDDR2A (VDR with alopecia). Phosphopenic: XLH (PHEX), ADHR (FGF23), ARHR, HHRH (SLC34A3), Fanconi.
atlas.epidemiology: Nutritional rickets remains prevalent globally in exclusively breastfed infants without supplementation, dark-skinned infants in high latitudes, and restricted diets.
atlas.diagnostics: Serum calcium, phosphate, ALP, intact PTH, 25-OH-D, 1,25-(OH)2-D; wrist/knee plain radiographs (widening, cupping, fraying); urine Ca/Cr and TmP/GFR.

therapies.text: Cholecalciferol (D3) or ergocalciferol (D2) 2000-6000 IU/day orally for 8-12 weeks (or single stoss dose 100,000-300,000 IU) PLUS oral elemental calcium 30-50 mg/kg/day (typically 500 mg daily) to prevent hungry bone syndrome. Transition to 400-600 IU/day maintenance once healed.
Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)2D) 20-40 ng/kg/day orally divided BID. Monitor serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and urine Ca/Cr monthly until healed.

pillars.label: GNAS Locus and Genomic Imprinting
pillars.text: Pseudohypoparathyroidism (PHP) and related disorders are caused by molecular and epigenetic defects at the complex GNAS locus on chromosome 20q13.3, which encodes the alpha-subunit of the stimulatory G-protein (Gs-alpha). Gs-alpha couples G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) to adenylyl cyclase, generating intracellular cyclic AMP. GNAS undergoes tissue-specific parent-of-origin genomic imprinting: in most tissues, Gs-alpha is expressed biallelically; however, in renal proximal tubules, thyroid thyrotropes, pituitary somatotropes, and gonads, Gs-alpha is expressed predominantly or exclusively from the maternal allele, while the paternal allele is silenced.

pillars.label: PHP-1A and Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy
pillars.text: Heterozygous maternally inherited inactivating mutations in GNAS cause Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A). Because the maternal allele is silenced in imprinted target tissues, patients develop multihormone resistance to hormones that signal through Gs-alpha: parathyroid hormone (PTH resistance causing hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia with elevated PTH), TSH (elevated TSH with normal/low free T4), growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH resistance causing GH deficiency), and gonadotropins (LH/FSH resistance causing delayed puberty or oligomenorrhea). Patients also exhibit the Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (AHO) physical phenotype: short adult stature, rounded facies, early-onset obesity, brachydactyly (shortening of 4th and 5th metacarpals/metatarsals), subcutaneous ossifications, and variable cognitive impairment.

pillars.label: Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP)
pillars.text: When identical GNAS inactivating mutations are inherited on the paternal allele, the offspring develops Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP). Because renal tubular Gs-alpha is transcribed from the intact, unmethylated maternal allele, end-organ hormone resistance does NOT develop: serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and TSH levels remain completely normal. However, because skeletal growth plates and subcutaneous tissues lack GNAS imprinting (expressing Gs-alpha biallelically), haploinsufficiency of Gs-alpha causes the complete physical AHO phenotype: brachydactyly, subcutaneous ossifications, and short stature without biochemical endocrinopathy.

pillars.label: PHP-1B, POH, and Inactivating PTH/PTHrP Spectrum
pillars.text: PHP type 1B (PHP-1B) is caused by maternal methylation defects at GNAS differentially methylated regions (DMRs; loss of methylation at exon A/B), resulting in tissue-specific silencing of maternal Gs-alpha. PHP-1B features isolated renal PTH resistance (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH) and mild TSH resistance, characteristically lacking classic AHO physical features. Progressive Osseous Heteroplasia (POH) is caused by paternally inherited GNAS mutations, presenting in infancy with severe, invasive heterotopic ossification extending through dermis into deep skeletal muscle and fascia. In 2016, an international consensus established the umbrella term 'inactivating PTH/PTHrP signaling disorders' (iPPSD) to classify PHP, PPHP, POH, and acrodysostosis.

pillars.label: Medical Management and Long-Term Surveillance
pillars.text: Management of PHP-1A and PHP-1B requires active vitamin D analogs (calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day or 0.25-1.0 mcg daily) combined with oral elemental calcium (30-50 mg/kg/day) to maintain serum calcium in the normal range (8.8-9.5 mg/dL) and lower intact PTH toward the normal reference interval (preventing hyperparathyroid bone disease). TSH resistance is treated promptly with levothyroxine. Annual surveillance includes evaluating linear growth velocity and GH status (treating with rhGH if deficient), monitoring pubertal progression, screening for carpal tunnel syndrome, and measuring urinary calcium excretion and renal ultrasound to prevent nephrocalcinosis.

cards.q: Why does maternal transmission of a GNAS mutation produce multihormone resistance in PHP-1A, whereas paternal transmission produces PPHP without hormone resistance?
cards.a: GNAS undergoes tissue-specific maternal expression in the renal proximal tubule, thyroid, and pituitary; maternal mutations ablate Gs-alpha in these tissues, whereas paternal mutations leave the active maternal allele intact.

cards.q: What physical features define the Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (AHO) phenotype?
cards.a: Short adult stature, rounded facies, early-onset centripetal obesity, brachydactyly (shortening of 4th and 5th metacarpals/metatarsals, dimple sign), subcutaneous heterotopic ossifications, and variable cognitive impairment.

cards.q: What circulating biochemical profile defines untreated pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)?
cards.a: Hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and markedly elevated intact parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels, reflecting end-organ renal proximal tubular resistance to PTH.

cards.q: What clinical feature distinguishes Progressive Osseous Heteroplasia (POH) from the subcutaneous ossifications seen in classic PHP-1A?
cards.a: POH features aggressive, progressive heterotopic ossification that penetrates deeply through the dermis into subcutaneous fat, skeletal muscle, tendons, and deep fascia, severely restricting joint mobility.

cards.q: Which endocrine hormone axes besides PTH frequently exhibit hormone resistance in children with PHP-1A?
cards.a: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (elevated TSH), growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH resistance with GH deficiency), and gonadotropins (LH/FSH resistance with delayed puberty/amenorrhea).

cards.q: What active vitamin D medication is essential to treat PTH resistance in PHP-1A and PHP-1B, and what is its starting dosage?
cards.a: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) at 20-40 ng/kg/day (typically 0.25 to 1.0 mcg daily in divided doses) combined with oral elemental calcium.

cards.q: What consensus classification term established in 2016 unifies PHP, PPHP, POH, and acrodysostosis into a single diagnostic continuum?
cards.a: Inactivating PTH/PTHrP signaling disorders (iPPSD).

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature, rounded facies, and obesity. Physical exam reveals shortening of the 4th and 5th digits of both hands; when she makes a fist, dimples appear in place of the 4th and 5th knuckles (Archibald sign). Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: serum calcium 7.2 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 6.8 mg/dL (normal: 4.0-5.8 mg/dL), intact PTH 380 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), TSH 9.2 mIU/L (normal: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L), and normal free T4. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)
Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP)
Primary hypoparathyroidism
Nutritional vitamin D deficiency rickets
mcqs.explanation: This patient exhibits the classic triad of Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A): Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy physical phenotype (short stature, obesity, round facies, brachydactyly with Archibald sign), renal PTH resistance (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, markedly elevated PTH), and subclinical TSH resistance (elevated TSH). PHP-1A is caused by maternal inheritance of an inactivating GNAS mutation.
option_notes: Correct. AHO features combined with hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH, and high TSH define PHP-1A.
Incorrect. PPHP exhibits the identical physical AHO phenotype but has completely normal calcium, phosphate, PTH, and TSH.
Incorrect. Primary hypoparathyroidism features low or undetectable PTH and lacks AHO skeletal features.
Incorrect. Nutritional rickets presents with hypophosphatemia, not hyperphosphatemia, and lacks AHO brachydactyly.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with short stature, round face, and shortened 4th and 5th metacarpals identical to his sister who has PHP-1A. However, his laboratory evaluation reveals: serum calcium 9.4 mg/dL (normal: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), phosphate 4.2 mg/dL (normal: 4.0-5.8 mg/dL), intact PTH 32 pg/mL (normal: 15-65 pg/mL), and TSH 2.1 mIU/L. From whom did this boy inherit the GNAS mutation?
options: From his father (paternal inheritance)
From his mother (maternal inheritance)
A de novo somatic postzygotic mutation in bone progenitor cells
Mitochondrial maternal transmission
mcqs.explanation: Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP) is caused by paternal inheritance of an inactivating GNAS mutation. Because Gs-alpha expression in the renal proximal tubule and thyroid thyrotrope is derived almost exclusively from the maternal allele, paternal mutations leave the functioning maternal allele intact, preserving normal renal and thyroid hormone signaling (normal calcium, phosphate, PTH, TSH). However, because growth plates express Gs-alpha biallelically, Gs-alpha haploinsufficiency causes AHO physical features.
option_notes: Correct. Paternal inheritance of a GNAS mutation causes PPHP (AHO phenotype with normal serum biochemistry).
Incorrect. Maternal inheritance causes PHP-1A (AHO phenotype WITH severe PTH and TSH resistance).
Incorrect. Postzygotic activating GNAS mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome, not PPHP.
Incorrect. GNAS is an imprinted nuclear gene on chromosome 20q13.3, not a mitochondrial gene.

mcqs.q: What active metabolite must be prescribed to correct hypocalcemia and lower parathyroid hormone levels in a child with PHP type 1A (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy with hormone resistance)?
options: Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D)
Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2)
Cholecalciferol (vitamin D3)
Recombinant human PTH (teriparatide)
mcqs.explanation: In PHP-1A, proximal tubular resistance to PTH impairs PTH-stimulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) activity, resulting in deficient synthesis of active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). Unhydroxylated native vitamin D (D2 or D3) is ineffective. Calcitriol bypasses the enzymatic block, directly restoring intestinal calcium absorption, normalizing serum calcium, and suppressing parathyroid PTH overdrive.
option_notes: Correct. Calcitriol is required because renal PTH resistance impairs endogenous 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-OH-D.
Incorrect. Native ergocalciferol requires intact renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation, which is impaired due to PTH resistance.
Incorrect. Native cholecalciferol cannot bypass the proximal tubular PTH signaling defect.
Incorrect. Teriparatide (PTH 1-34) is ineffective because the end-organ PTH-1 receptor signaling pathway is defective.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old girl with PHP-1A has well-controlled calcium and phosphate on calcitriol and calcium carbonate. However, her height has plateaued at the 1st percentile with growth velocity <2 cm/year. Detailed endocrine testing demonstrates impaired GH peak on clonidine/arginine stimulation tests with low IGF-1. What is the mechanism of growth hormone deficiency in PHP-1A?
options: Pituitary somatotrope resistance to growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) due to maternal Gs-alpha deficiency
Structural destruction of the anterior pituitary gland by ectopic ossifications
Autoimmune lymphocytic hypophysitis
Accelerated hepatic clearance of circulating growth hormone
mcqs.explanation: Pituitary somatotropes express Gs-alpha predominantly from the maternal allele. In PHP-1A, maternally inherited GNAS mutations cause end-organ resistance to GHRH, which signals through Gs-alpha to stimulate GH synthesis and secretion. GHRH resistance causes secondary growth hormone deficiency, contributing significantly to short stature. Recombinant human GH therapy improves linear growth in these patients.
option_notes: Correct. Maternal Gs-alpha deficiency in somatotropes causes resistance to GHRH, leading to growth hormone deficiency.
Incorrect. Pituitary tissue is not destroyed by heterotopic ossifications; the pituitary gland is structurally intact.
Incorrect. Hypophysitis is an autoimmune disorder unrelated to GNAS mutations.
Incorrect. GH clearance is normal; the primary defect is impaired GHRH-stimulated GH synthesis.

mcqs.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with hypocalcemia (7.4 mg/dL), hyperphosphatemia (6.2 mg/dL), and markedly elevated PTH (290 pg/mL). Thyroid function tests show mildly elevated TSH (6.5 mIU/L). On physical examination, he has normal height (50th percentile), normal body weight, no brachydactyly, and no subcutaneous ossifications. Genetic analysis reveals loss of methylation at the GNAS exon A/B differentially methylated region on the maternal allele. What is the diagnosis?
options: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP-1B)
Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP-1A)
Pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP)
Progressive osseous heteroplasia (POH)
mcqs.explanation: Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B (PHP-1B) is characterized by isolated renal PTH resistance (hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, elevated PTH) and mild TSH resistance, without the physical features of Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy (normal stature, no brachydactyly or subcutaneous ossifications). It is caused by epigenetic loss of methylation at maternal GNAS DMRs (specifically exon A/B), leading to tissue-specific suppression of Gs-alpha in renal proximal tubules.
option_notes: Correct. Epigenetic GNAS methylation defect causing PTH/TSH resistance without AHO physical features defines PHP-1B.
Incorrect. PHP-1A is caused by GNAS coding mutations and characteristically features the full AHO physical phenotype.
Incorrect. PPHP exhibits AHO physical features with completely normal serum biochemistry.
Incorrect. POH features deep, invasive heterotopic ossification without endocrine resistance.

atlas.etiology: GNAS locus (20q13.3) encoding Gs-alpha; tissue-specific maternal imprinting in renal proximal tubules, thyroid, pituitary, and gonads. PHP-1A: maternal coding mutations. PPHP: paternal coding mutations. PHP-1B: maternal methylation defects at DMRs. POH: paternal GNAS null mutations.
atlas.epidemiology: PHP prevalence is estimated at 0.3-1.1 per 100,000 live births; equal gender distribution.
atlas.diagnostics: Serum calcium, phosphate, intact PTH, TSH, free T4, IGF-1, LH/FSH; hand radiographs (short 4th/5th metacarpals); GNAS genetic and epigenetic methylation analysis.

therapies.section: Management of PTH Resistance in PHP
therapies.text: Calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day (0.25-1.0 mcg/day) orally divided BID combined with oral elemental calcium 30-50 mg/kg/day divided TID. Titrate to maintain serum calcium in the normal range (8.8-9.5 mg/dL) and bring PTH toward the upper normal range to avoid hyperparathyroid osteopenia. Supplement with levothyroxine for TSH resistance and rhGH if GH deficient.

pillars.label: Pediatric Diagnostic Definition (ISCD Criteria)
pillars.text: According to the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD), the diagnosis of osteoporosis in children and adolescents requires: (1) The presence of one or more low-trauma / fragility vertebral compression fractures, regardless of dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) bone mineral density; OR (2) A clinically significant fracture history defined as >=2 long-bone fractures by age 10 years, or >=3 long-bone fractures by age 19 years, COMBINED with a low bone mineral content (BMC) or areal bone mineral density (aBMD) DXA Z-score <= -2.0, adjusted for age, sex, and height/growth status. A low DXA Z-score alone does not constitute osteoporosis in children.

pillars.label: Primary vs Secondary Pediatric Osteoporosis
pillars.text: Primary osteoporosis arises from intrinsic genetic defects in bone-forming cells or matrix, most commonly Osteogenesis Imperfecta (OI; autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 [types I-IV], or autosomal recessive defects in CRTAP, LEPRE1, PPIB, IFITM5, SERPINF1, WNT1, LRP5, PLS3), characterized by bone fragility, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and wormian bones. Secondary osteoporosis is far more common in pediatric practice, triggered by chronic systemic illnesses: prolonged glucocorticoid therapy (leukemia, nephrotic syndrome, IBD, juvenile idiopathic arthritis), non-ambulatory neuromuscular disorders (cerebral palsy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy), hypogonadism, and chronic malabsorption.

pillars.label: Vertebral Compression Fracture Identification
pillars.text: Vertebral compression fractures (VCFs) are underdiagnosed in pediatric osteoporosis because >50% of affected children are clinically asymptomatic or present with non-specific back pain. Lateral thoracolumbar spine radiographs or lateral DXA vertebral fracture assessment (VFA) using the modified Genant semi-quantitative visual scale (measuring anterior, middle, and posterior vertebral heights: mild 20-25% reduction, moderate 25-40%, severe >40%) are mandatory for routine screening in children initiating high-dose oral glucocorticoids (>3 months) or experiencing localized back pain.

pillars.label: Intravenous Bisphosphonate Therapy Protocols
pillars.text: Intravenous bisphosphonates are the pharmacological mainstay for treating pediatric osteoporosis. By binding hydroxyapatite crystals and inhibiting osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, bisphosphonates arrest osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, allowing osteoblastic bone formation to increase cortical thickness, trabecular volume, and vertebral height. Standard agents include intravenous pamidronate (cyclical infusions: 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day over 3 consecutive days every 3-4 months; annual dose 9 mg/kg/year in infants <2 years, 6 mg/kg/year in older children) and intravenous zoledronic acid (0.025-0.05 mg/kg/dose infused over 30-45 minutes every 6 months; maximum single dose 4 mg).

pillars.label: Acute Phase Reaction, Safety, and Monitoring
pillars.text: The first intravenous bisphosphonate infusion triggers an acute phase reaction in 60-80% of children, characterized by transient high fever, flu-like symptoms, myalgias, bone pain, vomiting, and asymptomatic hypocalcemia occurring within 24-48 hours (mediated by aminobisphosphonate activation of gamma-delta T cells releasing TNF-alpha and IL-6). Pre-treatment optimization of 25-hydroxyvitamin D (>20-30 ng/mL) and prophylactic oral calcium/acetaminophen are mandatory. Unlike adults, growing pediatric vertebrae possess extraordinary remodeling potential under bisphosphonate therapy, with partial or complete restoration of collapsed vertebral heights.

cards.q: What two clinical scenarios satisfy the ISCD pediatric diagnostic definition of osteoporosis?
cards.a: (1) One or more low-trauma vertebral compression fractures alone; OR (2) A clinically significant fracture history (>=2 long-bone fractures by 10 yr, or >=3 by 19 yr) PLUS a DXA Z-score <= -2.0 adjusted for size.

cards.q: Can a low DXA bone mineral density Z-score (<= -2.0) alone be used to diagnose osteoporosis in a child?
cards.a: No. The diagnosis requires a documented low-trauma fracture history alongside the low DXA score (or a vertebral fracture regardless of DXA); a low Z-score alone represents 'low bone mineral mass for chronological age'.

cards.q: What is the typical dose and administration schedule for intravenous zoledronic acid in pediatric osteoporosis?
cards.a: 0.025 to 0.05 mg/kg per dose (maximum 4 mg) administered as an intravenous infusion over 30-45 minutes once every 6 months.

cards.q: What is the acute phase reaction associated with the first dose of intravenous bisphosphonates in children?
cards.a: Transient high fever, influenza-like myalgias, nausea, and mild hypocalcemia within 24-48 hours of infusion, mediated by inflammatory cytokine release from gamma-delta T cells.

cards.q: What collagen genes are mutated in over 85-90% of individuals with classic osteogenesis imperfecta?
cards.a: COL1A1 and COL1A2, which encode the pro-alpha1(I) and pro-alpha2(I) chains of type I collagen, inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.

cards.q: Why do growing children with vertebral compression fractures respond more favorably to bisphosphonate therapy than adults?
cards.a: Growing vertebrae undergo endochondral ossification at the superior and inferior growth plates; bisphosphonate-stabilized trabeculae allow newly formed bone to reshape and rebuild vertebral height.

cards.q: What grading system is standardly used on lateral spine imaging to evaluate pediatric vertebral compression fractures?
cards.a: The modified Genant semi-quantitative visual scale, assessing anterior, middle, and posterior vertebral height reductions (grade 1: 20-25%; grade 2: 25-40%; grade 3: >40%).

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old boy with steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome who has received oral prednisone (1-2 mg/kg/day) for 14 months complains of mild mid-back ache. Lateral thoracolumbar spine radiograph demonstrates a 30% anterior height loss (wedge deformity) of the L1 vertebral body after jumping from a curb. Lumbar spine DXA reveals a bone mineral density Z-score of -1.4. Which statement is correct regarding his bone status?
options: He meets criteria for pediatric osteoporosis based on the presence of a low-trauma vertebral fracture, regardless of the DXA Z-score
He cannot be diagnosed with osteoporosis because his DXA Z-score is greater than -2.0
He has osteopenia, but osteoporosis cannot be diagnosed until he sustains three additional peripheral fractures
His vertebral collapse represents Scheuermann disease rather than osteoporosis
mcqs.explanation: According to the official pediatric positions of the International Society for Clinical Densitometry (ISCD), the finding of one or more low-trauma vertebral compression fractures is sufficient on its own to establish the diagnosis of osteoporosis in children and adolescents, regardless of the measured bone mineral density Z-score. A DXA Z-score <= -2.0 is not required when a fragility vertebral fracture is documented.
option_notes: Correct. A fragility vertebral fracture alone establishes the diagnosis of pediatric osteoporosis regardless of DXA Z-score.
Incorrect. A DXA Z-score <= -2.0 is only required when the fracture history consists exclusively of long-bone fractures, not vertebral fractures.
Incorrect. The term 'osteopenia' is officially obsolete in pediatric densitometry, and additional fractures are not required.
Incorrect. Acute post-steroid height loss following minimal trauma is a steroid-induced vertebral compression fracture, not Scheuermann disease.

mcqs.q: A 9-year-old girl with severe osteogenesis imperfecta type III is admitted to receive her first planned intravenous infusion of pamidronate (1 mg/kg/dose). Which of the following prophylactic clinical measures is most essential prior to initiating the infusion?
options: Verification and repletion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to >20-30 ng/mL and provision of oral calcium and antipyretics
Administration of high-dose intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg/m2
Placement of a permanent tunneled central venous line
Restriction of oral fluids to prevent hypervolemia
mcqs.explanation: The first intravenous bisphosphonate infusion universally triggers an acute phase reaction (fever, flu-like symptoms, myalgias) and rapid influx of extracellular calcium into skeleton. If a patient is vitamin D deficient or hypocalcemic prior to infusion, severe life-threatening hypocalcemia and tetany can occur. Pre-infusion repletion of 25-OH-D (>20-30 ng/mL), normal ionized calcium, oral calcium supplementation, and antipyretic prophylaxis (acetaminophen/ibuprofen) are mandatory standard of care.
option_notes: Correct. Ensuring vitamin D sufficiency (>20-30 ng/mL), adequate oral calcium, and antipyretic preparation prevents acute hypocalcemic crisis.
Incorrect. Glucocorticoids further impair bone metabolism and are not standard prophylaxis for bisphosphonate infusions.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates can be infused safely through a peripheral IV catheter; central venous lines are not required.
Incorrect. Patients should be well hydrated, not fluid restricted, to facilitate renal excretion.

mcqs.q: What is the primary cellular and molecular mechanism by which intravenous bisphosphonates (such as pamidronate and zoledronic acid) increase bone mass and vertebral height in children with osteoporosis?
options: Inhibition of osteoclast farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, inducing osteoclast apoptosis and suppressing bone resorption while growing physis adds new bone
Direct stimulation of osteoblast proliferation and collagen synthesis through the parathyroid hormone receptor
Activation of osteocytic sclerostin secretion to promote Wnt signaling
Inhibition of renal tubular calcium and phosphate excretion
mcqs.explanation: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (pamidronate, zoledronate) are taken up selectively by active osteoclasts during bone resorption and inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) synthase in the mevalonate pathway. This prevents prenylation of small GTPases essential for osteoclast cytoskeletal function and survival, inducing osteoclast apoptosis. By arresting resorption, ongoing endochondral bone formation at growing physeal growth plates continuously deposits new bone, progressively thickening cortical and trabecular architecture and reshaping collapsed vertebral bodies.
option_notes: Correct. Nitrogenous bisphosphonates inhibit osteoclast FPP synthase, suppressing resorption while growing physis reshapes bone.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates do not bind the PTH receptor; they are antiresorptive agents, not direct osteoblast stimulants.
Incorrect. Sclerostin inhibits Wnt signaling; bisphosphonates do not activate sclerostin.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates act directly on skeleton, not primarily on renal tubular mineral transport.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old non-ambulatory adolescent male with Duchenne muscular dystrophy on deflazacort therapy sustains his third low-trauma femur fracture. His lumbar spine DXA Z-score adjusted for height is -3.2. He is initiated on intravenous zoledronic acid 0.05 mg/kg every 6 months. What is the expected physiological impact of bisphosphonate therapy on his vertebral and long-bone health?
options: Reduction in bone pain, prevention of future vertebral compression fractures, and partial or complete vertebral body remodeling
Accelerated progression of scoliosis requiring immediate spinal fusion
Permanent arrest of longitudinal growth at epiphyseal growth plates
Spontaneous cure of Duchenne muscular dystrophy muscle weakness
mcqs.explanation: In glucocorticoid-treated children with secondary osteoporosis (such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy), intravenous zoledronic acid markedly reduces bone pain, prevents new vertebral and long-bone fractures, increases areal and volumetric bone density, and allows growing vertebral bodies to remodel and restore height. It does not arrest growth plate growth and has no curative effect on underlying dystrophin deficiency.
option_notes: Correct. IV bisphosphonates relieve bone pain, prevent fractures, and permit robust vertebral reshaping in growing children.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates stabilize vertebral architecture, which helps protect against progressive kyphoscoliotic deformity.
Incorrect. Standard doses of bisphosphonates do not impair linear growth plate elongation or cause premature epiphyseal fusion.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates treat bone fragility, not the primary muscle dystrophin deficiency.

mcqs.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple recurrent fractures following minimal falls, blue-tinted sclerae, triangular facies, and opalescent amber-brown teeth that chip easily (dentinogenesis imperfecta). Hearing screening shows conductive hearing loss. What is the most likely mode of inheritance and underlying molecular defect?
options: Autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 (Osteogenesis Imperfecta)
Autosomal recessive mutations in the VDR gene
X-linked recessive mutation in the DMD gene
Autosomal dominant activating mutation in the FGFR3 gene
mcqs.explanation: The clinical constellation of recurrent fragility fractures, blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and hearing impairment is pathognomonic for Osteogenesis Imperfecta (types I-IV), caused in over 85-90% of cases by heterozygous autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2, which encode the alpha chains of type I collagen.
option_notes: Correct. Classic OI with blue sclerae and dentinogenesis imperfecta is caused by autosomal dominant COL1A1/COL1A2 mutations.
Incorrect. VDR mutations cause vitamin D-dependent rickets with alopecia, not blue sclerae and dentinogenesis imperfecta.
Incorrect. DMD mutations cause Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which presents with proximal weakness and pseudohypertrophy.
Incorrect. FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia with rhizomelic dwarfism, not fragile bones with dentinogenesis imperfecta.

atlas.etiology: Primary: Osteogenesis Imperfecta (COL1A1, COL1A2, CRTAP, LEPRE1, PPIB, WNT1, LRP5, PLS3); idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis. Secondary: Chronic glucocorticoid exposure, immobilization/neuromuscular (cerebral palsy, DMD), acute lymphoblastic leukemia, IBD, hypogonadism.
atlas.epidemiology: Osteogenesis imperfecta affects ~1 in 15,000 to 20,000 births. Secondary osteoporosis affects up to 30-50% of children on long-term systemic glucocorticoids.
atlas.diagnostics: Lateral thoracolumbar spine radiographs / DXA VFA (modified Genant scale); DXA lumbar spine and total body less head (TBLH) Z-scores adjusted for height/age; serum 25-OH-D, calcium, phosphate, PTH; urine Ca/Cr; COL1A1/COL1A2 genetic sequencing.

therapies.text: Zoledronic acid: 0.025-0.05 mg/kg/dose (max 4 mg) IV infused over 30-45 minutes once every 6 months. Alternatively, intravenous pamidronate: 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day over 3 consecutive days every 3-4 months (annual dose: 9 mg/kg/year in infants <2 yr; 6 mg/kg/year in older children). Pre-treat to ensure 25-OH-D >20-30 ng/mL, provide oral calcium and acetaminophen for acute phase reaction.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Definitions and Chronology
pillars.text: Delayed puberty is clinically defined as the failure to initiate secondary sexual development by >=2 to 2.5 standard deviations above the population mean: in girls, the absence of breast bud development (Tanner stage 2 thelarche) by age 13.0 years, or failure to achieve menarche within 3 years of thelarche or by age 15.0 years (primary amenorrhea); in boys, the absence of testicular enlargement (testicular volume <4 mL or long axis <2.5 cm) by age 14.0 years. Arrested puberty is defined as the failure to complete pubertal progression over a 4-to-5-year span.

pillars.label: Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty
pillars.text: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) is the most common cause of delayed puberty, accounting for >60-65% of cases in boys and ~30% in girls. CDGP represents a benign, non-pathological extreme of normal pubertal timing, characterized by a family history of delayed pubertal maturation ('late bloomers'), delayed skeletal maturation (bone age delayed by 2-4 years, matching height age), normal prepubertal growth velocity for bone age, and predicted adult height consistent with midparental target height. Endogenous activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis occurs spontaneously once skeletal maturation reaches ~11-12 years in girls and ~12-13 years in boys.

pillars.label: Hypergonadotropic Hypogonadism (Primary Failure)
pillars.text: Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism results from intrinsic gonadal destruction or dysgenesis, marked biochemically by elevated serum LH and FSH with low sex steroid levels. In girls, the leading cause is Turner syndrome (45,X and mosaic variants; presenting with short stature, streak gonads, webbed neck, bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation of aorta, and renal anomalies; FSH is markedly elevated in infancy and rises again after age 9-10 years). In boys, the most common etiology is Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY; presenting with tall eunuchoid stature, micro-orchidism with firm small testes [<4 mL], gynecomastia, hypergonadotropic azoospermia, and elevated gonadotropins emerging during mid-puberty). Other causes include Swyer syndrome (46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis), vanishing testes syndrome (anorchia), and gonadotoxic chemotherapy/radiation.

pillars.label: Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (Central Failure)
pillars.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism features low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins (LH/FSH) in the setting of low sex steroids. Etiologies include functional hypogonadotropic hypogonadism secondary to chronic illness (celiac disease, Crohn disease, anorexia nervosa, intensive athletic training) and congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH). CHH is categorized as Kallmann syndrome (CHH associated with anosmia or hyposmia due to defective embryonic migration of olfactory and GnRH neurons; caused by mutations in ANOS1/KAL1, FGFR1, PROKR2, PROK2, CHD7) or normosmic CHH (GNRHR, TAC3, TACR3, KISS1, KISS1R). Olfactory testing (UPSIT) and cranial MRI evaluating olfactory bulbs/sulci are essential.

pillars.label: Pubertal Induction and Testosterone/Estrogen Regimens
pillars.text: In boys with severe psychological distress from CDGP or confirmed hypogonadism, low-dose intramuscular depot testosterone (enanthate or cypionate) is initiated at 25-50 mg once monthly for 3-6 months; in CDGP, this brief course jump-starts the hypothalamic axis without accelerating epiphyseal fusion. In permanent hypogonadism, testosterone is titrated upwards every 6-12 months (50, 100, 150, to adult maintenance 200 mg every 2 weeks). In girls, pubertal induction begins with very low-dose 17-beta estradiol (transdermal matrix patch 6.25-12.5 mcg/day, or micronized oral estradiol 0.25-0.5 mg/day) escalated gradually over 2-3 years to optimize breast contour and uterine growth; cyclic oral progesterone (100-200 mg micronized progesterone daily for 10-12 days/month) is added only after >=18-24 months of estrogen or upon spontaneous breakthrough bleeding to prevent endometrial hyperplasia.

cards.q: What chronological age cutoffs define delayed puberty in girls and boys, respectively?
cards.a: Lack of breast development (Tanner 2 thelarche) by age 13.0 years in girls; lack of testicular enlargement (volume <4 mL) by age 14.0 years in boys.

cards.q: What clinical and radiographic findings characterize constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)?
cards.a: Family history of delayed puberty, delayed bone age matching height age, prepubertal growth velocity appropriate for bone age, normal predicted adult height, and eventual spontaneous pubertal completion.

cards.q: What clinical feature uniquely differentiates Kallmann syndrome from normosmic congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism?
cards.a: Anosmia or hyposmia (loss of smell), caused by embryonic failure of GnRH neurons and olfactory axons to migrate together from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus.

cards.q: What are the classic karyotypes and gonadal features of Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome?
cards.a: Turner syndrome is 45,X with streak gonads and ovarian failure; Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY with small, firm testes (<4 mL) and hypergonadotropic azoospermia.

cards.q: Why must progesterone therapy be delayed for at least 18-24 months when inducing puberty with estrogen in girls with primary hypogonadism?
cards.a: Premature progesterone exposure antagonizes estrogen-stimulated ductile branching, resulting in abnormal, tubular breast morphology, and interrupts maximal uterine growth.

cards.q: What is the initial low-dose depot testosterone regimen used to promote pubertal onset in adolescent boys with constitutional delay?
cards.a: Intramuscular testosterone enanthate or cypionate 25 to 50 mg once monthly for 3 to 6 months, which accelerates linear growth and secondary sex characteristics without premature epiphyseal fusion.

cards.q: How does serum gonadotropin (LH/FSH) measurement differentiate primary from secondary hypogonadism?
