cards.a: Elevated LH and FSH indicate primary (hypergonadotropic) gonadal failure, whereas low or inappropriately normal LH and FSH indicate central (hypogonadotropic) failure.

mcqs.q: A 14.5-year-old boy is brought to the endocrine clinic by his parents because he has not shown any signs of puberty. On examination, he is prepubertal (Tanner stage 1: no pubic hair, bilateral testicular volume 2.5 mL). His height is at the 5th percentile, but his calculated midparental target height is at the 50th percentile. His father underwent a late growth spurt at age 16. Left hand radiograph reveals a bone age of 11.5 years (delayed by 3 years). Serum LH is 0.4 IU/L, FSH is 0.8 IU/L, and morning total testosterone is 15 ng/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP)
Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY)
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
mcqs.explanation: This boy exhibits the classic hallmark profile of constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP): male sex, lack of pubertal onset by age 14 (testicular volume <4 mL), positive paternal history of delayed pubertal timing ('late bloomer'), delayed bone age (11.5 years) that matches his height age, and normal prepubertal gonadotropins and testosterone. When his bone age advances to 12-13 years, spontaneous puberty will occur.
option_notes: Correct. CDGP is characterized by delayed bone age matching height age, familial late pubertal timing, and low prepubertal gonadotropins.
Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome presents with elevated gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism) in mid-puberty, tall stature, and small firm testes.
Incorrect. Complete androgen insensitivity occurs in 46,XY phenotypic females with female external genitalia, not boys presenting with delayed male puberty.
Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma causes severe growth arrest, headaches, visual field defects, and multiple anterior pituitary deficiencies.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old phenotypic female presents for evaluation of primary amenorrhea and lack of pubertal development. Physical examination reveals Tanner stage 1 breasts, Tanner stage 1 pubic hair, a high-arched palate, low posterior hairline, and wide-spaced nipples. Her height is well below the 3rd percentile. Serum FSH is markedly elevated at 88 IU/L and LH is 34 IU/L. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a small prepubertal uterus and bilateral streak ovaries. What diagnostic test should be ordered next?
options: Peripheral blood karyotype analysis
Intravenous GnRH stimulation test
Head MRI with dedicated pituitary cuts
24-hour urinary free cortisol
mcqs.explanation: The clinical constellation of short stature, primary amenorrhea, absent breast development, webbed neck/low hairline, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (elevated FSH/LH with streak ovaries) is pathognomonic for Turner syndrome. A peripheral blood karyotype analysis (with count of at least 30-50 metaphase cells to rule out mosaicism and Y-chromosome material) is the mandatory next diagnostic test.
option_notes: Correct. Blood karyotype confirms Turner syndrome (45,X or mosaicism) in a girl with short stature and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.
Incorrect. GnRH stimulation is redundant because baseline gonadotropins are already strikingly elevated due to absence of ovarian feedback.
Incorrect. Pituitary MRI is indicated for hypogonadotropic (central) hypogonadism, not primary ovarian dysgenesis.
Incorrect. Urinary free cortisol evaluates Cushing syndrome, which does not cause streak ovaries with elevated FSH.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with complete absence of pubertal development (testicular volume 2 mL bilaterally). On detailed review of systems, he reports that he has never been able to smell coffee, smoke, or perfume. Serum LH and FSH are low-normal, and morning testosterone is <10 ng/dL. Cranial MRI reveals aplasia of the olfactory bulbs and absent olfactory sulci. What is the diagnosis?
options: Kallmann syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome
Vanishing testes syndrome
mcqs.explanation: Kallmann syndrome is congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism paired with anosmia or hyposmia. It is caused by mutations in genes such as ANOS1 (KAL1), FGFR1, or PROKR2 that disrupt the embryonic co-migration of GnRH neuroendocrine cells and olfactory axons from the olfactory placode into the forebrain. Absent olfactory bulbs/sulci on MRI confirms the diagnosis.
option_notes: Correct. Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia and absent olfactory bulbs on MRI defines Kallmann syndrome.
Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome presents with elevated gonadotropins (hypergonadotropic), normal olfaction, and small firm testes.
Incorrect. Prader-Willi presents with infantile hypotonia, childhood hyperphagia, morbid obesity, and normal olfaction.
Incorrect. Vanishing testes syndrome produces hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (elevated LH/FSH) with impalpable gonads and normal olfaction.

mcqs.q: A 13-year-old girl with confirmed Turner syndrome (45,X) and complete ovarian failure is ready to begin pubertal induction. What is the recommended strategy for introducing estrogen and progesterone?
options: Initiate very low-dose transdermal 17-beta estradiol monotherapy, gradually escalating over 2-3 years, and delay adding cyclic progesterone for at least 18-24 months
Initiate combination oral contraceptive pills containing 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol and norgestimate immediately
Administer high-dose oral conjugated estrogens with daily medroxyprogesterone from day 1
Withhold estrogen therapy until chronological age 18 years to maximize final adult height
mcqs.explanation: Consensus guidelines for Turner syndrome recommend initiating pubertal induction at age 11-12 years with very low-dose 17-beta estradiol (preferably transdermal patches at 6.25-12.5 mcg/day) to mimic normal physiological puberty. Estrogen is escalated gradually over 2 to 3 years to optimize breast contour, alveolar development, and uterine dimensions. Cyclic progesterone is delayed for 18-24 months (or until breakthrough bleeding occurs) to avoid tubular breast deformity and premature cessation of ductal proliferation.
option_notes: Correct. Gradual low-dose transdermal estradiol monotherapy with progesterone delayed for 18-24 months optimizes breast and uterine maturation.
Incorrect. Adult combination birth control pills provide supraphysiological ethinyl estradiol that causes premature epiphyseal closure and abnormal tubular breasts.
Incorrect. Conjugated estrogens are non-physiological mixtures, and adding progesterone from day 1 halts normal ductile breast budding.
Incorrect. Delaying estrogen to age 18 causes severe osteoporosis, psychological distress, and uterine hypoplasia.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old male with constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP) is experiencing severe anxiety, social withdrawal, and school bullying due to his short stature and lack of sexual development. His bone age is 12 years and testicular volume is 3 mL bilaterally. What is the most appropriate medical management?
options: Reassurance alone with strict refusal of any pharmacological intervention
A short 3- to 6-month course of low-dose depot testosterone enanthate (25-50 mg IM once monthly)
Full adult replacement testosterone enanthate (200 mg IM every 2 weeks)
Subcutaneous recombinant growth hormone therapy at supraphysiological doses
mcqs.explanation: In adolescent boys with CDGP >=14 years of age with significant psychological distress, a short course of low-dose depot testosterone (25-50 mg IM monthly for 3-6 months) is the standard of care. This regimen accelerates linear growth, induces virilization (pubic hair, phallic enlargement), and promotes psychological well-being without causing excessive bone age advancement or compromising adult height. It frequently stimulates the endogenous hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator.
option_notes: Incorrect. Dismissing significant psychological distress when a safe, proven, low-dose regimen exists is suboptimal medical care.
Correct. A 3-6 month course of low-dose depot testosterone (25-50 mg IM monthly) safely promotes growth and virilization without compromising height.
Incorrect. Full adult replacement (200 mg every 2 weeks) causes rapid skeletal maturation and premature epiphyseal closure, compromising adult height.
Incorrect. Growth hormone is not indicated for CDGP in the absence of documented GH deficiency.

atlas.etiology: Hypergonadotropic (primary): Turner (45,X), Klinefelter (47,XXY), 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis, anorchia, radiation/chemotherapy. Hypogonadotropic (central): CDGP (>60% in boys), Kallmann syndrome (ANOS1/KAL1, FGFR1, PROKR2), normosmic CHH, chronic illness, anorexia.
atlas.epidemiology: CDGP is the most common etiology of delayed puberty in boys (65%) and girls (30%). Turner syndrome affects 1:2000 live female births; Klinefelter affects 1:600 male births.
atlas.diagnostics: Bone age radiograph; basal and GnRH-stimulated LH/FSH; early morning total testosterone (LC-MS/MS) or estradiol; pelvic ultrasound; karyotype; smell test (UPSIT) and olfactory MRI.

therapies.text: For CDGP: Testosterone enanthate or cypionate 25-50 mg IM once monthly for 3-6 months. For permanent hypogonadism: escalate slowly: 50 mg/month for 6-12 months, then 100 mg/month, then 150 mg/month, up to adult replacement 200 mg IM every 2 weeks.

Transdermal 17-beta estradiol patch 6.25-12.5 mcg/day changed weekly, or oral micronized estradiol 0.25-0.5 mg/day. Escalate annually over 2-3 years. Delay progesterone for 18-24 months; then add oral micronized progesterone 100-200 mg daily for days 1-12 of each calendar month.

pillars.label: Definitions and Diagnostic Thresholds
pillars.text: Precocious puberty is traditionally defined as the development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8.0 years in girls (thelarche or pubarche) or before age 9.0 years in boys (testicular enlargement >=4 mL). Precocious puberty is categorized pathophysiologically into: (1) Central Precocious Puberty (CPP; GnRH-dependent), driven by premature hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis activation; (2) Peripheral Precocious Puberty (PPP; GnRH-independent), resulting from autonomous gonadal or adrenal sex steroid production independent of pituitary gonadotropins; and (3) Benign pubertal variants (premature thelarche, premature adrenarche).

pillars.label: Central Precocious Puberty (GnRH-Dependent)
pillars.text: In CPP, pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH secretion triggers pituitary LH and FSH release, stimulating gonadal maturation, sex steroid production, linear growth acceleration, and skeletal maturation. In girls, >85-90% of CPP is idiopathic; however, in boys, 40-75% of CPP is secondary to an identifiable underlying central nervous system (CNS) lesion. CNS etiologies include hypothalamic hamartomas (non-neoplastic heterotopias composed of GnRH-secreting neurons and glial tissue, frequently presenting in infancy with gelastic [laughing] seizures), optic pathway gliomas (frequently linked to Neurofibromatosis type 1), astrocytomas, hydrocephalus, and prior cranial irradiation. Genetic causes include loss-of-function mutations in MKRN3 (the most frequent cause of familial CPP; maternally imprinted, paternally inherited) and DLK1.

pillars.label: Peripheral Precocious Puberty (GnRH-Independent)
pillars.text: Peripheral precocious puberty features elevated circulating sex steroids with suppressed basal and GnRH-stimulated gonadotropins (LH <0.1-0.2 IU/L, flat response). In boys, etiologies include testotoxicosis (familial male-limited precocious puberty; activating LHCGR mutations causing autonomous Leydig cell testosterone secretion), congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2; adrenal androgens producing virilization with prepubertal testes <4 mL), Leydig cell tumors (asymmetric testicular enlargement), and hCG-secreting tumors (hepatoblastoma, intracranial germ cell tumors cross-activating LH receptors). In girls, causes include McCune-Albright syndrome (somatic mosaic activating GNAS mutations; recurrent autonomous large ovarian cysts, café-au-lait macules with jagged 'coast of Maine' borders, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia) and granulosa cell tumors.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Differentiation and GnRH Testing
pillars.text: Evaluation begins with a bone age radiograph (advanced skeletal age is common to both progressive CPP and PPP), pelvic ultrasound in girls (uterine length >3.5-4.0 cm, endometrial stripe, ovarian volume >1-2 mL with multiple follicles favor CPP), and testicular ultrasound in boys. The gold standard for confirming CPP is the GnRH (or GnRH agonist) stimulation test: a peak LH >5.0 IU/L (or ultrasensitive basal morning LH >0.2-0.3 IU/L) confirms HPG axis activation. In contrast, PPP exhibits a suppressed peak LH (<0.1-0.2 IU/L). Every boy with CPP and every girl under 6 years (or with rapid progression/neurological signs) must undergo contrast-enhanced brain MRI with thin pituitary/hypothalamic cuts.

pillars.label: GnRH Agonist Pharmacotherapy
pillars.text: The primary clinical objectives of therapy in progressive CPP are preserving final adult height potential (by halting premature epiphyseal fusion) and relieving psychosocial distress. First-line therapy consists of long-acting GnRH agonists (GnRHa), which continuously stimulate and saturate pituitary GnRH receptors, causing receptor downregulation, desensitization, and profound suppression of gonadotropin release. Standard regimens include depot leuprolide acetate (7.5-15 mg IM every 4 weeks or 11.25-30 mg IM every 12 weeks) or subcutaneous histrelin acetate implant (50 mg implant releasing ~65 mcg/day, replaced annually). Therapy is monitored by assessing growth velocity, regression of secondary sexual characteristics, bone age progression, and suppressed stimulated LH (<2-3 IU/L). GnRHa is typically discontinued at normal pubertal age (11.0-11.5 years in girls, 12.0-12.5 years in boys).

cards.q: What chronological age cutoffs define precocious puberty in girls and boys, respectively?
cards.a: Onset of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8.0 years in girls (thelarche or pubarche) or before age 9.0 years in boys (testicular volume >=4 mL).

cards.q: How does the likelihood of an identifiable central nervous system etiology in central precocious puberty differ between boys and girls?
cards.a: In girls, >85-90% of CPP is idiopathic; in boys, 40-75% of CPP is secondary to an identifiable intracranial lesion, mandating routine brain MRI in all affected males.

cards.q: What biochemical result on a GnRH stimulation test confirms the diagnosis of central precocious puberty?
cards.a: A post-stimulation peak LH concentration >5.0 IU/L (or an ultrasensitive basal morning LH >0.2-0.3 IU/L), demonstrating activation of the pituitary gonadotropes.

cards.q: What classic neurological seizure type is uniquely associated with hypothalamic hamartomas in young children with central precocious puberty?
cards.a: Gelastic seizures, characterized by involuntary, paroxysmal, unprovoked bouts of hollow laughter or smirking, often emerging in infancy.

cards.q: What gene mutation is the most frequent cause of familial central precocious puberty, and what is its mode of transmission?
cards.a: Loss-of-function mutations in MKRN3 (makorin ring finger protein 3), a maternally imprinted gene that causes CPP only when inherited from the father (paternal transmission).

cards.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of long-acting GnRH agonists (e.g., leuprolide, histrelin) in treating central precocious puberty?
cards.a: Continuous, non-pulsatile stimulation of pituitary GnRH receptors, causing receptor downregulation, uncoupling, and profound suppression of LH and FSH secretion.

cards.q: What triad of clinical features defines McCune-Albright syndrome presenting with peripheral precocious puberty?
cards.a: Autonomous recurrent estrogen-secreting ovarian follicular cysts, large café-au-lait macules with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders, and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia of bone.

mcqs.q: A 6-year-old girl is evaluated for bilateral breast development (Tanner stage 3) and a growth spurt over the past 8 months. Height is at the 97th percentile (previously 50th percentile). Left hand radiograph reveals a bone age of 8.5 years. A GnRH stimulation test is performed: baseline LH is 0.8 IU/L, and peak stimulated LH at 30 minutes is 9.4 IU/L with peak FSH 7.2 IU/L. Contrast-enhanced brain MRI of the hypothalamic-pituitary region is normal. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Initiate long-acting GnRH agonist therapy (e.g., depot leuprolide or histrelin implant)
Perform bilateral laparoscopic oophorectomy
Prescribe oral spironolactone and anastrozole
Observation without treatment until menarche occurs
mcqs.explanation: This patient has idiopathic central precocious puberty (CPP), documented by early thelarche (<8 years), accelerated growth velocity, advanced bone age, and a robust pubertal peak LH >5.0 IU/L on GnRH stimulation test with a normal brain MRI. In girls under 7-8 years with rapidly progressive CPP and compromised predicted adult height, long-acting GnRH agonists (e.g., depot leuprolide 11.25 mg every 3 months or histrelin implant) are the first-line treatment to preserve final adult height and arrest sexual maturation.
option_notes: Correct. GnRH agonist therapy is the established standard of care for progressive central precocious puberty.
Incorrect. Oophorectomy is mutilating and contraindicated; ovarian activity in CPP is secondary to pituitary drive.
Incorrect. Spironolactone and anastrozole are used in peripheral precocious puberty (e.g., testotoxicosis or McCune-Albright), not CPP.
Incorrect. Withholding treatment will lead to premature epiphyseal fusion, severe compromise of adult height, and early menarche.

mcqs.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with pubic hair development, penile enlargement, and linear growth acceleration. On physical examination, his phallus is 8.5 cm in length, pubic hair is Tanner stage 3, and his testes are symmetric with a volume of 2.0 mL bilaterally (prepubertal). Morning laboratory evaluation reveals serum total testosterone 180 ng/dL (elevated for age), and basal and GnRH-stimulated LH levels are <0.1 IU/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Non-salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency)
Idiopathic central precocious puberty
Hypothalamic hamartoma
Leydig cell testicular adenoma
mcqs.explanation: This boy exhibits peripheral precocious puberty (isosexual pseudoprecocity), characterized by marked virilization (phallic growth, pubic hair, high testosterone) with completely prepubertal testes (<4 mL bilaterally) and suppressed gonadotropins (LH <0.1 IU/L). In boys, the most common cause of peripheral precocity with small prepubertal testes is congenital adrenal hyperplasia (simple virilizing 21-hydroxylase deficiency), where adrenal androgens virilize the external genitalia while suppressing the pituitary HPG axis.
option_notes: Correct. CAH produces adrenal hyperandrogenism, virilizing the phallus while keeping the testes prepubertal (<4 mL) and LH suppressed.
Incorrect. Central precocious puberty features testicular enlargement (>=4 mL) and a robust LH response on GnRH testing.
Incorrect. Hypothalamic hamartomas cause central precocious puberty with enlarged testes and pubertal LH secretion.
Incorrect. Leydig cell tumors produce asymmetric testicular enlargement, with one testis palpably enlarged and firm.

mcqs.q: A 3-year-old male presents with aggressive behavior, accelerated linear growth, phallic enlargement, and bilateral symmetric testicular enlargement (testicular volume 6-8 mL bilaterally). Total testosterone is 350 ng/dL. A GnRH stimulation test shows baseline and peak LH <0.1 IU/L. Cranial MRI is completely normal. Genetic testing reveals an activating heterozygous missense mutation in the LHCGR gene. What is the diagnosis?
options: Testotoxicosis (familial male-limited precocious puberty)
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome
McCune-Albright syndrome
Hypothalamic hamartoma
mcqs.explanation: Testotoxicosis (familial male-limited precocious puberty) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by activating mutations in LHCGR (luteinizing hormone / choriogonadotropin receptor). The constitutively active LH receptor autonomously stimulates Leydig cell cAMP production, causing bilateral testicular enlargement (6-8 mL) and adult-level testosterone secretion in early childhood despite prepubertal/suppressed pituitary LH. Females carrying the mutation are unaffected because ovarian steroidogenesis requires both LH and FSH.
option_notes: Correct. Activating LHCGR mutations cause testotoxicosis, with bilateral testicular enlargement, high testosterone, and suppressed LH.
Incorrect. Complete AIS involves loss of androgen receptor function in 46,XY females, causing lack of virilization.
Incorrect. McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by GNAS somatic mutations and classically causes precocity in girls, not testotoxicosis in boys.
Incorrect. Hypothalamic hamartoma causes GnRH-dependent central precocious puberty with elevated LH levels.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with recurrent episodes of vaginal bleeding without breast enlargement or pubic hair. Physical examination reveals two large light-brown macules on her lower back and buttocks with jagged, irregular borders that do not cross the midline. Skeletal radiographs demonstrate expansile radiolucent lesions with ground-glass appearance in the left femur and pelvis. What is the diagnosis and molecular etiology?
options: McCune-Albright syndrome due to postzygotic activating somatic mutation in GNAS
Neurofibromatosis type 1 due to NF1 germline mutation
Central precocious puberty due to MKRN3 mutation
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome due to STK11 mutation
mcqs.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS) is defined by the classical triad of: (1) peripheral precocious puberty with recurrent large autonomous ovarian cysts and vaginal bleeding; (2) large café-au-lait pigmentation with jagged, irregular 'coast of Maine' borders that typically respect the midline; and (3) polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (ground-glass bone lesions). MAS is caused by a postzygotic mosaic activating somatic mutation in GNAS (encoding Gs-alpha, typically at Arg201), constitutively activating adenylyl cyclase.
option_notes: Correct. Postzygotic GNAS activating mutations cause McCune-Albright syndrome with fibrous dysplasia, jagged café-au-lait macules, and autonomous cysts.
Incorrect. NF1 features smooth-bordered 'coast of California' café-au-lait macules, neurofibromas, and optic gliomas, not fibrous dysplasia with MAS cysts.
Incorrect. MKRN3 mutations cause central precocious puberty with pubertal LH levels and no fibrous dysplasia or jagged macules.
Incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers presents with mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation of lips and hamartomatous intestinal polyps.

mcqs.q: A 15-month-old healthy, thriving girl is noted to have bilateral palpable breast tissue (Tanner stage 2) on routine examination. There is no pubic or axillary hair. Her growth velocity is tracking steadily along the 50th percentile, and left hand radiograph confirms that her bone age is identical to chronological age (15 months). Pelvic ultrasound shows prepubertal uterine length (2.2 cm) without endometrial thickening and normal infantile ovaries. What is the recommended management?
options: Observation and reassurance without pharmacological intervention (benign premature thelarche)
Initiate depot leuprolide 7.5 mg IM monthly
Order emergent head MRI to rule out a hypothalamic tumor
Perform bilateral breast needle aspiration biopsy
mcqs.explanation: This infant has isolated premature thelarche, a common benign pubertal variant that occurs in girls under 2 years of age. It represents transient sensitivity of breast tissue to maternal/neonatal estrogens or transient incomplete activation of the HPG axis with isolated FSH secretion. It is characterized by normal growth velocity, normal bone age, prepubertal pelvic ultrasound, and spontaneous regression or stabilization over 1-2 years. No medical intervention or brain MRI is indicated.
option_notes: Correct. Isolated premature thelarche in a child <2 years with normal growth and bone age is benign and requires only observation.
Incorrect. GnRH agonists are contraindicated in benign pubertal variants.
Incorrect. Brain MRI is unnecessary because there are no signs of progressive central precocious puberty.
Incorrect. Breast biopsy in an infant will damage the developing breast bud and cause permanent amastia.

atlas.etiology: Central (GnRH-dependent): Idiopathic (>85% in girls); CNS lesions (40-75% in boys: hypothalamic hamartoma, optic glioma/NF1, hydrocephalus, radiation); Genetic (MKRN3 [paternal transmission], DLK1, KISS1). Peripheral (GnRH-independent): CAH (CYP21A2), testotoxicosis (LHCGR), McCune-Albright (GNAS), Leydig/granulosa tumors.
atlas.epidemiology: Precocious puberty affects ~1 in 5000 to 1 in 10,000 children; 5:1 to 10:1 female predominance for central precocious puberty.
atlas.diagnostics: Bone age radiograph; basal and GnRH-stimulated LH and FSH (peak LH >5.0 IU/L confirms CPP); estradiol, total testosterone, 17-OHP, DHEAS; pelvic ultrasound (uterine length >3.5 cm, ovarian volume >1-2 mL); brain MRI with thin hypothalamic cuts.

therapies.text: Depot leuprolide acetate: 7.5-15 mg IM every 4 weeks or 11.25-30 mg IM every 12 weeks. Alternatively, histrelin acetate 50 mg subcutaneous implant replaced annually. Monitor growth velocity, bone age, Tanner stage, and stimulated LH (<2-3 IU/L) every 3-6 months. Discontinue around age 11-12 years.

For testotoxicosis: combination therapy with an aromatase inhibitor (anastrozole 1 mg daily or letrozole 2.5 mg daily) plus an antiandrogen (spironolactone 50-100 mg BID or bicalutamide 12.5-25 mg daily). For McCune-Albright: letrozole 2.5 mg daily or fulvestrant/tamoxifen.

pillars.label: Consensus Nomenclature and Classification
pillars.text: Disorders or Differences of Sex Development (DSD) are congenital conditions in which the development of chromosomal, gonadal, or anatomical sex is atypical. The 2006 Chicago Consensus classification categorizes DSD based on karyotype: (1) 46,XX DSD (disorders of gonadal development [ovotesticular DSD] or androgen excess [congenital adrenal hyperplasia, aromatase deficiency, maternal androgen exposure]); (2) 46,XY DSD (disorders of testicular development [complete/partial gonadal dysgenesis: SRY, SOX9, NR5A1/SF1, WT1] or disorders of androgen synthesis/action [androgen insensitivity syndrome, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, 17-beta-HSD-3 deficiency]); and (3) Sex chromosome DSD (45,X Turner, 47,XXY Klinefelter, 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis, 46,XX/46,XY chimerism).

pillars.label: Emergency Neonatal Presentation and CAH
pillars.text: The discovery of atypical genitalia at birth represents a medical and psychological urgency. In a newborn with atypical genitalia and bilateral non-palpable gonads, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2 21-hydroxylase deficiency) must be presumed until proven otherwise. 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for >90% of all 46,XX DSD cases; without urgent diagnosis, affected infants face catastrophic salt-wasting adrenal crisis (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, vascular collapse, death) typically manifesting between days 7 and 14 of life. Immediate stat evaluations include serum electrolytes, 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP), pelvic ultrasound (evaluating for uterus/Müllerian structures), and rapid cytogenetic analysis (FISH for SRY and X/Y chromosomes).

pillars.label: Embryology of Gonads and Internal Ducts
pillars.text: Sex determination requires expression of SRY (sex-determining region Y) on the short arm of the Y chromosome, which upregulates SOX9 and downstream pathways to differentiate bipotential gonads into testes. Sertoli cells in fetal testes synthesize Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH / MIS), inducing regression of ipsilateral paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts (uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina) by 8-10 weeks. Leydig cells synthesize testosterone, which stabilizes mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts (epididymides, vasa deferentia, seminal vesicles). In external genital target tissues, type 2 5-alpha-reductase (SRD5A2) converts testosterone into dihydrotestosterone (DHT), driving phallic elongation, labioscrotal fusion, and urethral groove tubularization.

pillars.label: 46,XY DSD: AIS vs 5-Alpha-Reductase Deficiency
pillars.text: Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the androgen receptor (AR). 46,XY individuals present with completely normal female external genitalia, a short blind-ending vagina, absent uterus/fallopian tubes (intact AMH), and normal intra-abdominal or inguinal testes; at puberty, they develop normal female breast contour (due to aromatization of high testosterone to estrogen) but have absent or sparse pubic/axillary hair. 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency (SRD5A2) presents with variable genital ambiguity at birth, normal Wolffian structures, and absent Müllerian structures; at puberty, high circulating testosterone produces marked virilization (phallic growth, muscle mass, voice deepening) without gynecomastia, displaying an elevated testosterone-to-DHT ratio (>20-30:1) on hCG stimulation.

pillars.label: Multidisciplinary Care and Gonadal Tumor Risk
pillars.text: Comprehensive DSD care requires an integrated multidisciplinary team (pediatric endocrinologist, pediatric urologist, geneticist, neonatologist, child psychologist, and social worker). Gender assignment is withheld until diagnostic evaluations (karyotype, imaging, steroid profiles) are fully synthesized and discussed openly with parents. In patients with dysgenetic gonads containing Y chromosome material (specifically the TSPY region in 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis and 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis), the risk of malignant transformation (gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma/seminoma) is high (15-40%), warranting early prophylactic gonadectomy. In contrast, in CAIS, tumor risk before adulthood is exceptionally low (<1-2%), allowing gonadectomy to be deferred until after spontaneous pubertal feminization.

cards.q: What is the most urgent medical emergency to exclude in a newborn infant presenting with atypical genitalia and bilateral non-palpable gonads?
cards.a: Salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) in a virilized 46,XX infant, which can precipitate fatal salt-wasting shock within 1-2 weeks of life.

cards.q: Which testicular hormone is responsible for the regression of Müllerian ducts (uterus, fallopian tubes, upper vagina) in male fetal development?
cards.a: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH / Müllerian-inhibiting substance), synthesized and secreted by fetal Sertoli cells.

cards.q: What biochemical test and ratio confirm the diagnosis of 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency in an infant with 46,XY DSD?
cards.a: An hCG stimulation test demonstrating an abnormally elevated plasma testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (T:DHT) ratio (>20-30:1).

cards.q: What internal and external anatomical findings characterize an adolescent with Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS)?
cards.a: Phenotypic female external genitalia with a blind-ending vagina, absent uterus and fallopian tubes, absent pubic/axillary hair, normal female breast development, and testes located in the abdomen or labia.

cards.q: Why is prophylactic gonadectomy recommended in individuals with 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis who have intra-abdominal dysgenetic gonads?
cards.a: Dysgenetic gonadal tissue containing Y-chromosomal material (TSPY) carries a 15-40% lifetime risk of developing malignant germ cell tumors (gonadoblastoma and dysgerminoma).

cards.q: What clinical staging scale is standardly utilized to quantify the degree of genital virilization in female infants with CAH?
cards.a: The Prader staging scale (Prader stages 1 to 5, ranging from mild clitoromegaly [stage 1] to a completely virilized penile urethra with fused scrotum and absent palpable gonads [stage 5]).

cards.q: What enzyme mediates the peripheral conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) required for external male genital virilization?
cards.a: Type 2 5-alpha-reductase, encoded by the SRD5A2 gene.

mcqs.q: A full-term newborn is found to have ambiguous external genitalia with a 2.5-cm phallus, severe chordee, a single perineal urogenital orifice, and completely fused labioscrotal folds with no palpable gonads in the folds or inguinal canals. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a distinct uterus and normal upper vaginal cavity. Blood pressure is 68/42 mmHg. Which laboratory test is most critical to obtain immediately?
options: Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP) and serum electrolytes
Serum dihydrotestosterone (DHT) concentration
Urinary gonadotropin peptides
Serum Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH)
mcqs.explanation: A newborn presenting with atypical genitalia, bilateral impalpable gonads, and a documented uterus on ultrasound is a virilized 46,XX infant with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency) until proven otherwise. Immediate measurement of 17-OHP and serum electrolytes (sodium, potassium) is mandatory because life-threatening adrenal salt-wasting crisis can develop rapidly.
option_notes: Correct. 17-OHP and electrolytes urgently diagnose or exclude salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH.
Incorrect. DHT evaluates 5-alpha-reductase deficiency in 46,XY infants (who lack a uterus), not 46,XX infants with a uterus.
Incorrect. Urinary gonadotropins have no role in acute neonatal DSD crisis management.
Incorrect. AMH is absent in 46,XX infants without testes; it does not replace urgent adrenal steroid evaluation.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old phenotypic female presents for evaluation of primary amenorrhea. Physical examination shows excellent Tanner stage 5 breast development, but completely absent pubic and axillary hair (Tanner stage 1). Pelvic examination reveals a blind-ending vagina measuring 2.5 cm in depth. Pelvic ultrasound confirms the absence of a uterus and ovaries. Bilateral masses are palpated in the inguinal canals. Karyotype is 46,XY. Serum testosterone is in the normal adult male range. What is the diagnosis?
options: Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS)
Müllerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome)
5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency
Turner syndrome (45,X)
mcqs.explanation: Complete Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome (CAIS) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the androgen receptor (AR). In 46,XY individuals, testes produce AMH (causing complete Müllerian regression: absent uterus/upper vagina) and testosterone. Because all androgen receptors are completely non-functional, external genitalia develop as phenotypic female, and pubic/axillary hair does not develop. At puberty, high testosterone is peripherally aromatized to estrogen, inducing normal female breast development.
option_notes: Correct. 46,XY karyotype, absent uterus, normal breast development, absent pubic hair, and male testosterone levels define CAIS.
Incorrect. MRKH syndrome occurs in 46,XX females with normal ovaries, normal pubic hair, and female testosterone levels.
Incorrect. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency presents with significant virilization (phallic enlargement, hirsutism) at puberty, not breast development.
Incorrect. Turner syndrome is 45,X with a normal uterus, streak ovaries, short stature, and absent breast development.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old individual raised as a female in a rural community presents with rapid virilization at puberty: deepening of the voice, marked enlargement of the clitoral phallus into an 8-cm penis, development of facial and body hair, and progressive muscular development. There is no breast development. Karyotype is 46,XY. Physical exam reveals a bifid scrotum containing palpable 12-mL testes and a perineal hypospadias. Baseline testosterone is 650 ng/dL, but serum dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is 14 ng/dL (testosterone-to-DHT ratio >40). What enzyme is deficient?
options: Steroid 5-alpha-reductase type 2 (SRD5A2)
Aromatase (CYP19A1)
17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 (HSD17B3)
P450 oxidoreductase (POR)
mcqs.explanation: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in SRD5A2. Impaired conversion of testosterone to DHT in utero impairs external genital virilization, so 46,XY infants are often assigned female at birth. At puberty, massive LH-driven testosterone production virilizes tissues directly through the androgen receptor, causing penile growth, muscle development, and voice deepening without gynecomastia. A markedly elevated testosterone-to-DHT ratio (>20-30:1) is diagnostic.
option_notes: Correct. 5-alpha-reductase deficiency characteristically causes marked pubertal virilization in 46,XY individuals with high T:DHT ratio.
Incorrect. Aromatase deficiency causes virilization in 46,XX females at birth and prevents breast development, but does not occur in 46,XY males.
Incorrect. 17-beta-HSD-3 deficiency impairs conversion of androstenedione to testosterone, presenting with an elevated androstenedione-to-testosterone ratio.
Incorrect. POR deficiency features skeletal malformations (Antley-Bixler phenotype) and combined steroid enzyme blocks.

mcqs.q: A newborn infant presents with asymmetric genitalia: a fully descended normal testis in the right hemiscrotum, and an empty left labioscrotal fold. Laparoscopy reveals a dysgenetic streak gonad and a rudimentary fallopian tube and hemi-uterus on the left side, and a normal testis and vas deferens on the right side. Karyotype is 45,X/46,XY. What is the diagnosis and the most critical oncological recommendation?
options: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis; surgical excision of the dysgenetic streak gonad due to high gonadoblastoma risk
Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome; retain gonads indefinitely
Klinefelter syndrome; initiation of testosterone at birth
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia; high-dose hydrocortisone monotherapy
mcqs.explanation: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis (MGD) is typically associated with a 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype. It features asymmetric internal and external genitalia: a dysgenetic testis on one side with Wolffian structures, and a streak gonad on the contralateral side with persistent Müllerian structures (hemi-uterus). Intra-abdominal dysgenetic gonads containing Y-chromosomal material carry a 15-40% lifetime risk of malignant transformation into gonadoblastoma or dysgerminoma. Immediate surgical removal of the dysgenetic streak gonad is strongly recommended.
option_notes: Correct. 45,X/46,XY mosaicism with asymmetric streak/testis is mixed gonadal dysgenesis; the streak gonad must be removed due to high cancer risk.
Incorrect. CAIS has bilateral normal testes without streak gonads or Müllerian structures.
Incorrect. Klinefelter is 47,XXY without asymmetric internal genitalia, and testosterone is not given at birth.
Incorrect. CAH does not present with a 45,X/46,XY karyotype or asymmetric streak gonads.

mcqs.q: What is the recommended modern management approach regarding immediate sex assignment and irreversible genitoplasty in a newborn with ambiguous genitalia?
options: Perform immediate emergency feminizing genitoplasty within the first 48 hours to relieve parental anxiety
Withhold definitive gender assignment until multidisciplinary diagnostic evaluation is complete, and defer non-emergency cosmetic genitoplasty until the child can participate in decision-making
Assign male sex automatically to all infants with a phallus >1.5 cm
Perform mandatory bilateral gonadectomy in all infants with 46,XX DSD
mcqs.explanation: Modern international consensus guidelines on DSD emphasize: (1) withholding definitive gender assignment until rapid comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation (karyotype, imaging, steroid profiles) is synthesized; (2) fully engaging parents with specialized psychological counseling; and (3) deferring non-urgent, irreversible cosmetic genitoplasty until the patient is old enough to provide informed assent or consent, except for surgeries required to establish unobstructed urinary drainage.
option_notes: Incorrect. Immediate irreversible surgery without full evaluation violates modern clinical guidelines and human rights standards.
Correct. Multi-specialty diagnostic evaluation must precede assignment, and cosmetic surgery should be deferred when feasible.
Incorrect. Sex assignment is never based purely on phallic length; underlying etiology, fertility potential, and brain exposure guide decisions.
Incorrect. In 46,XX CAH, ovaries are completely normal and must be preserved for future endogenous fertility.

atlas.etiology: 46,XX DSD: CAH (CYP21A2 >90%), aromatase deficiency (CYP19A1), ovotesticular DSD. 46,XY DSD: Testicular dysgenesis (SRY, SOX9, NR5A1, WT1); androgen resistance (AR / CAIS/PAIS); 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (SRD5A2); 17-beta-HSD-3. Sex Chromosome DSD: 45,X/46,XY mixed gonadal dysgenesis.
atlas.epidemiology: Atypical genitalia at birth occurs in ~1 in 4500 to 1 in 5000 births. 21-hydroxylase CAH affects ~1 in 14,000 to 18,000 live births.
atlas.diagnostics: Urgent pelvic ultrasound (Müllerian structures); karyotype / SRY FISH; 17-OHP, electrolytes, testosterone, DHT, androstenedione, AMH; hCG stimulation test; gonadal biopsy/laparoscopy.

therapies.text: Intravenous normal saline bolus (20 mL/kg) for salt-wasting crisis; IV hydrocortisone 50-100 mg/m2 (or 25 mg for infants) bolus, followed by 50-100 mg/m2/day. Chronic maintenance: oral hydrocortisone 10-15 mg/m2/day divided TID, fludrocortisone 0.05-0.2 mg/day, and sodium chloride supplements 1-2 g/day.

pillars.label: Adolescent Menstrual Milestones and Norms
pillars.text: Menarche is a late pubertal milestone, typically occurring 2 to 2.5 years after thelarche (average age 12.5 years, Tanner stage 4). In the first 2-3 post-menarchal years, physiological immaturity of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis leads to frequent anovulatory cycles. However, normal menstrual parameters in adolescents are defined as: cycle length between 21 and 45 days; bleeding duration <=7 days; requiring <=3-6 pads or tampons per day without soaking; and cycle regularity establishing within 24-36 months. Any cycle length <21 days or >45 days (or >90 days at any time) represents abnormal uterine bleeding requiring clinical investigation.

pillars.label: Primary and Secondary Amenorrhea Workup
pillars.text: Primary amenorrhea is defined as the absence of menses by age 15 years with normal secondary sexual characteristics, or absence of menses by age 13 years without secondary sex characteristics, or >3 years post-thelarche. Secondary amenorrhea is the cessation of menses for >=90 days (3 consecutive months) in a previously regular adolescent, or >=6 months in an oligomenorrheic girl. Initial evaluation requires excluding pregnancy (urine/serum beta-hCG), measuring serum FSH, LH, TSH, prolactin, and total/free testosterone, and performing pelvic ultrasound to confirm the presence of a normal uterus and exclude outflow tract obstruction (imperforate hymen, transverse vaginal septum).

pillars.label: PCOS Diagnostic Criteria in Adolescence
pillars.text: Pediatric international consensus guidelines mandate stricter criteria for diagnosing Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) in adolescents than in adults. In adolescents, BOTH of the following MUST be present: (1) Menstrual irregularity abnormal for gynecological age (cycles >45 days or <8 cycles/year after the first post-menarchal year; or amenorrhea >90 days); AND (2) Evidence of hyperandrogenism (clinical: moderate-to-severe hirsutism with modified Ferriman-Gallwey score >=6-8, or persistent severe inflammatory acne; and/or biochemical: elevated serum total or free testosterone measured by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry [LC-MS/MS]). Pelvic ultrasound demonstrating polycystic ovarian morphology is NOT recommended as a diagnostic criterion in adolescents within 8 years of menarche due to the high frequency of physiological multifollicular ovaries in healthy teenagers.

pillars.label: Differential Diagnosis of Hyperandrogenism
pillars.text: Before confirming adolescent PCOS, other causes of hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction must be excluded: Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (NCAH; CYP21A2 mutation; excluded by early morning follicular 17-hydroxyprogesterone <200 ng/dL; ACTH stimulation test confirms if 17-OHP >1000 ng/dL); hyperprolactinemia; primary thyroid disease; Cushing syndrome; and androgen-secreting ovarian (Sertoli-Leydig) or adrenal tumors (heralded by rapid progressive virilization, clitoromegaly, voice deepening, and total testosterone >150-200 ng/dL or DHEAS >700-800 mcg/dL). Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA) must also be differentiated, featuring low/normal gonadotropins, low estradiol, and hypoandrogenism driven by energy deficit.

pillars.label: Comprehensive Management of Adolescent PCOS
pillars.text: First-line intervention for overweight or obese adolescents with PCOS is lifestyle modification (dietary optimization and regular physical activity). First-line pharmacological therapy is a combined oral contraceptive pill (COC; containing low-dose ethinyl estradiol [20-30 mcg] plus a progestin with low androgenicity, such as drospirenone or desogestrel). COCs suppress LH secretion (lowering ovarian androgen synthesis), stimulate hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG; lowering circulating free testosterone), regularize menstrual cycles, and prevent endometrial hyperplasia. If hirsutism persists after >=6 months of COC therapy, the antiandrogen spironolactone (50-100 mg twice daily) is added. Metformin (500-2000 mg daily) is added if impaired glucose tolerance, metabolic syndrome, or insulin resistance is present.

cards.q: What two mandatory criteria are required to establish the diagnosis of PCOS in an adolescent?
cards.a: Both (1) Ovulatory dysfunction / menstrual irregularity abnormal for gynecological age AND (2) Clinical and/or biochemical hyperandrogenism; ultrasound morphology is excluded.

cards.q: Why is polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound excluded from the diagnostic criteria for PCOS in adolescents?
cards.a: Multifollicular ovarian morphology is a normal, physiological finding in up to 30-40% of healthy, ovulating post-menarchal teenagers and has high false-positive rates.

cards.q: What is the first-line medical therapy for menstrual irregularity and hyperandrogenism in adolescent PCOS?
cards.a: Combined oral contraceptives (COCs) containing low-dose ethinyl estradiol and a non-androgenic progestin, which restore regular bleeding, raise SHBG, and lower free testosterone.

cards.q: What baseline test is used to rule out non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia (NCAH) in an adolescent with hyperandrogenism?
cards.a: Early morning (8 AM) follicular-phase serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone (17-OHP); a value <200 ng/dL reliably excludes 21-hydroxylase deficiency NCAH.

cards.q: What antiandrogenic medication is added to COCs if moderate-to-severe hirsutism does not improve after 6 months, and what is its dosage?
cards.a: Spironolactone at 50 to 100 mg orally twice daily (must be paired with contraception due to the risk of feminization of a male fetus).

cards.q: What are the acceptable lower and upper limits of menstrual cycle length in adolescents during the first 3 years after menarche?
cards.a: 21 to 45 days; any cycle shorter than 21 days or longer than 45 days (or an interval >90 days) is clinically abnormal.

cards.q: What clinical and biochemical 'red flags' suggest an androgen-secreting neoplasm rather than adolescent PCOS?
cards.a: Rapid virilization (clitoromegaly, voice deepening, temporal balding) accompanied by serum total testosterone >150-200 ng/dL or DHEAS >700-800 mcg/dL.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for irregular menses. Menarche occurred at age 12, but over the past 2 years she has had only 3 menstrual periods per year (cycle intervals 60-90 days). On examination, BMI is 28.5 kg/m2 (96th percentile), she has moderate inflammatory facial acne, and terminal hair growth on the upper lip, chin, and lower abdomen (modified Ferriman-Gallwey score 9). Serum total testosterone is elevated at 68 ng/dL (reference: 15-45 ng/dL). Pelvic ultrasound reveals multifollicular ovaries bilaterally. 17-OHP is 110 ng/dL, TSH is 2.1 mIU/L, and prolactin is normal. What is the diagnosis?
options: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Cushing syndrome
Normal physiological adolescent anovulation
mcqs.explanation: This adolescent meets consensus pediatric criteria for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS): (1) ovulatory dysfunction (oligomenorrhea with cycles >45 days >2 years post-menarche); and (2) both clinical hyperandrogenism (mFG score 9, severe acne) and biochemical hyperandrogenism (elevated testosterone), with exclusion of NCAH (17-OHP <200 ng/dL), thyroid disease, and hyperprolactinemia.
option_notes: Correct. Documented ovulatory dysfunction plus clinical and biochemical hyperandrogenism establishes adolescent PCOS.
Incorrect. NCAH is excluded by a normal morning baseline 17-OHP of 110 ng/dL (<200 ng/dL).
Incorrect. Cushing syndrome presents with rapid central weight gain, purple striae, muscle weakness, and hypertension.
Incorrect. Cycle lengths >45 days and hirsutism with elevated testosterone >2 years post-menarche exceed normal anovulatory variation.

mcqs.q: Why do international pediatric endocrinology consensus guidelines specifically exclude polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound from the diagnostic criteria for PCOS in adolescents?
options: Multifollicular ovarian morphology is a normal physiological finding in up to 30-40% of healthy ovulating teenagers
Pelvic ultrasound cannot visualize ovaries in adolescent females
Ovarian cysts in adolescents always represent malignant teratomas
Transvaginal ultrasound is mandatory and cannot be performed in adolescents
mcqs.explanation: During normal adolescent pubertal development, developing follicles frequently impart a multifollicular or polycystic appearance to ovaries in 30-40% of completely healthy, regularly cycling teenagers. Using ultrasound morphology as a diagnostic criterion in adolescents creates high rates of false-positive overdiagnosis. Thus, guidelines require both ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenism, omitting ultrasound morphology.
option_notes: Correct. High rates of physiological multifollicular ovaries in healthy teenagers invalidate ultrasound as a reliable diagnostic criterion.
Incorrect. Transabdominal pelvic ultrasound readily visualizes ovaries in adolescents.
Incorrect. Simple functional follicular cysts in adolescents are benign, not malignant teratomas.
Incorrect. Transabdominal ultrasound with a full bladder is the standard non-invasive modality.

mcqs.q: What is the primary mechanism by which combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) improve hirsutism and hyperandrogenemia in adolescents with PCOS?
options: Suppression of pituitary LH secretion and stimulation of hepatic sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) synthesis
Direct irreversible inhibition of ovarian 17-alpha-hydroxylase
Selective destruction of the adrenal zona reticularis
Degradation of circulating dihydrotestosterone by renal tubular filtration
mcqs.explanation: Combined oral contraceptives improve hyperandrogenism through a dual mechanism: (1) the progestin component suppresses pituitary LH pulse frequency, decreasing LH-stimulated ovarian theca cell androgen production; and (2) the estrogen component stimulates hepatic synthesis of SHBG, which binds circulating testosterone and sharply lowers the biologically active free testosterone fraction.
option_notes: Correct. COCs suppress pituitary LH-driven theca androgen synthesis and elevate hepatic SHBG, lowering free testosterone.
Incorrect. COCs do not destroy or irreversibly inhibit steroidogenic enzymes.
Incorrect. COCs do not destroy the adrenal zona reticularis.
Incorrect. COCs do not enhance renal clearance of DHT.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with severe, rapidly progressive hirsutism, temporal hair thinning, and deepening of her voice over the past 4 months. Physical examination reveals a 2.5-cm clitoromegaly. Serum total testosterone is markedly elevated at 280 ng/dL (reference: 15-45 ng/dL). DHEAS is normal. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a 4.5-cm solid vascular mass within the right ovary. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Severe polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor of the ovary
Non-classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Adrenal adenoma secreting DHEAS
mcqs.explanation: Rapid onset of virilization (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, male-pattern alopecia), massive elevation of serum total testosterone (>150-200 ng/dL), and a solid unilateral ovarian mass is pathognomonic for an ovarian androgen-secreting neoplasm, most commonly a Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor. PCOS does not cause rapid virilization, clitoromegaly, or a solid unilateral ovarian mass.
option_notes: Incorrect. PCOS causes gradual hirsutism, not rapid virilization, clitoromegaly, testosterone >200 ng/dL, or solid ovarian masses.
Correct. Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor presents with rapid virilization, extreme testosterone elevation, and a solid ovarian tumor.
Incorrect. NCAH does not cause an isolated solid ovarian tumor.
Incorrect. Adrenal androgen tumors are characterized by massive elevations of DHEAS (>700-800 mcg/dL), which is normal here.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old female high school distance runner presents with secondary amenorrhea for 8 months. She runs 50 miles per week and has restricted her caloric intake. BMI is 17.2 kg/m2. Examination shows Tanner 5 breasts and pubic hair without hirsutism or acne. Pregnancy test is negative. Serum LH is 0.8 IU/L, FSH is 2.4 IU/L, estradiol is 18 pg/mL (low), and total testosterone is 12 ng/dL (low-normal). What is the underlying pathophysiology?
options: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA) due to relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S)
Polycystic ovary syndrome with atypical presentation
Premature ovarian insufficiency (POF)
Androgen insensitivity syndrome
mcqs.explanation: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea (FHA) in athletes is caused by chronic low energy availability (energy expenditure exceeding dietary intake, known as Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport [RED-S]). This suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, leading to low/suppressed LH and FSH, hypoestrogenemia (estradiol <20-30 pg/mL), and secondary amenorrhea. In contrast to PCOS, patients with FHA are typically underweight/lean and have low (not high) androgens without hirsutism.
option_notes: Correct. Low energy availability suppresses GnRH pulsatility, causing hypogonadotropic hypoestrogenemic amenorrhea (FHA).
Incorrect. PCOS features hyperandrogenism, elevated LH/FSH ratio, and oligomenorrhea, not low androgens and low LH.
Incorrect. Premature ovarian insufficiency presents with elevated gonadotropins (high FSH >40 IU/L), not low LH/FSH.
Incorrect. Androgen insensitivity syndrome causes primary amenorrhea in 46,XY individuals, not secondary amenorrhea after normal menarche.

atlas.etiology: Amenorrhea: Outflow obstruction (imperforate hymen), gonadal dysgenesis (Turner), FHA (exercise, anorexia), hyperprolactinemia, thyroid disease. Hyperandrogenism: PCOS, NCAH (CYP21A2), Cushing syndrome, androgen-secreting ovarian/adrenal tumors.
atlas.epidemiology: PCOS affects 6-10% of adolescent girls; leading cause of anovulatory infertility and adolescent hirsutism.
atlas.diagnostics: Urine beta-hCG; total/free testosterone (LC-MS/MS), DHEAS, androstenedione; 17-OHP (morning follicular); TSH, prolactin, LH, FSH; transabdominal pelvic ultrasound; fasting lipid panel and 2-hr OGTT.

therapies.text: Combined oral contraceptives (ethinyl estradiol 20-30 mcg + non-androgenic progestin like drospirenone or desogestrel) once daily. If hirsutism persists after 6 months, add spironolactone 50-100 mg orally BID. For impaired glucose tolerance/insulin resistance, add metformin 500-1000 mg BID.

pillars.label: Prolactin Physiology and Dopaminergic Tone
pillars.text: Prolactin is a 198-amino acid polypeptide hormone synthesized and secreted by lactotrope cells in the anterior pituitary gland. Unlike all other anterior pituitary hormones which are predominantly regulated by hypothalamic releasing factors, prolactin secretion is under tonic inhibitory control by hypothalamic dopamine. Dopamine secreted from tuberoinfundibular dopaminergic (TIDA) neurons in the arcuate nucleus travels via the hypophyseal portal system to bind lactotrope D2 dopamine receptors, activating Gi proteins that suppress adenylyl cyclase, hyperpolarize lactotrope membranes, and inhibit prolactin synthesis and exocytosis.

pillars.label: Etiology: Prolactinomas and Stalk Effect
pillars.text: Etiologies of hyperprolactinemia (fasting prolactin >20-25 mcg/L or ng/mL) are categorized as: (1) Prolactinomas (lactotrope neuroendocrine tumors): microprolactinomas (<10 mm) or macroprolactinomas (>=10 mm); prolactin levels typically correlate with tumor volume (>100-200 mcg/L in macroprolactinomas, >1000 mcg/L in giant tumors); (2) Pituitary stalk compression / interruption ('stalk effect'): any mass in the sellar/suprasellar region (craniopharyngioma, germinoma, Rathke cleft cyst, meningioma) that compresses the pituitary stalk, blocking dopamine transport to normal lactotropes; this causes mild-to-moderate hyperprolactinemia (almost universally <100-150 mcg/L); (3) Medications: dopamine D2 receptor antagonists (risperidone, haloperidol, metoclopramide); (4) Primary hypothyroidism: elevated TRH stimulates lactotrope prolactin release.

pillars.label: Pediatric Clinical Presentation
pillars.text: The clinical presentation of hyperprolactinemia varies by sex and tumor size. Pediatric macroprolactinomas are more common in males and adolescent boys, who frequently present with mass effect symptoms: persistent headaches, visual field defects (bitemporal hemianopsia from optic chiasm compression), growth deceleration, delayed puberty, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (hyperprolactinemia directly suppresses hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility). In adolescent girls, microprolactinomas are more frequent, presenting with primary or secondary amenorrhea, oligomenorrhea, galactorrhea (present in 30-50%), and mild hirsutism.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Pearls: Hook Effect and Macroprolactin
pillars.text: Two major laboratory pitfalls must be recognized. The 'hook effect' (high-dose hook effect) occurs in immunometric sandwich assays when immense prolactin concentrations (e.g., >10,000 mcg/L in giant prolactinomas) saturate both capture and detection antibodies simultaneously, producing falsely low measured prolactin (e.g., 50 mcg/L), misleading the clinician to diagnose a non-functioning adenoma with stalk effect; serial 1:100 serum dilution unmasks the true massive concentration. 'Macroprolactinemia' occurs when prolactin complexes with IgG autoantibodies (big-big prolactin, >150 kDa); it is biologically inactive but causes marked in vitro immunoassay elevation; polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation confirms whether monomeric prolactin is truly elevated.

pillars.label: Dopamine Agonist Pharmacotherapy
pillars.text: Medical therapy with dopamine receptor agonists is the first-line treatment for both microprolactinomas and macroprolactinomas. Cabergoline, a high-affinity, selective D2 receptor agonist with a long elimination half-life, is the preferred agent, dosed orally at 0.25 to 0.5 mg once or twice weekly (titrated up to 1.0-2.0 mg weekly as needed). Cabergoline normalizes prolactin in >80-90% of pediatric patients, shrinks tumor volume by >50% in >75% of macroprolactinomas, and rapidly restores visual fields and gonadal function. Bromocriptine (1.25-7.5 mg daily) is a second-line option. Transsphenoidal surgery is reserved for tumors refractory to maximal dopamine agonist therapy, acute apoplexy, or progressive visual loss despite medical therapy.

cards.q: What is the first-line pharmacological treatment for pediatric macroprolactinomas, and what is its dosing schedule?
cards.a: Cabergoline, a selective D2 dopamine receptor agonist, administered orally at 0.25 to 0.5 mg once or twice weekly.

cards.q: What is the 'hook effect' in prolactin immunoassays, and how is it resolved in patients with large pituitary macroadenomas?
cards.a: Extremely high prolactin levels (>10,000 mcg/L) saturate assay antibodies, causing falsely low measured prolactin; it is resolved by performing assay testing on a 1:100 diluted serum sample.

cards.q: What is the typical upper limit of serum prolactin elevation caused by the 'stalk effect' (pituitary stalk compression by non-prolactinoma tumors)?
cards.a: Serum prolactin is almost universally less than 100 to 150 mcg/L (ng/mL); prolactin concentrations >200-250 mcg/L indicate a true prolactinoma.

cards.q: What is macroprolactinemia, and what chemical laboratory method is used to diagnose it?
cards.a: Circulating biologically inactive prolactin-IgG autoantibody complexes; diagnosed by polyethylene glycol (PEG) serum precipitation to measure free monomeric prolactin.

cards.q: Why does severe untreated primary hypothyroidism frequently cause hyperprolactinemia?
cards.a: Elevated hypothalamic thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) acts as a prolactin-releasing factor, directly stimulating pituitary lactotropes to synthesize and release prolactin.

cards.q: What are the most frequent presenting manifestations of macroprolactinomas in adolescent males?
cards.a: Headaches, bitemporal visual field loss, delayed puberty, arrested linear growth, and hypogonadism; galactorrhea is uncommon in males.

cards.q: When is transsphenoidal neurosurgery indicated in pediatric prolactinomas instead of dopamine agonist therapy?
cards.a: When tumors are completely refractory or intolerant to maximal dopamine agonist therapy, or in cases of acute pituitary apoplexy with sudden severe visual failure.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old male presents with persistent frontal headaches and bitemporal hemianopsia on visual field testing. Brain MRI reveals a 2.8-cm sellar and suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Initial serum prolactin is reported as 62 mcg/L (reference: <20 mcg/L). The neurosurgeon suspects a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma with stalk compression and schedules emergent surgical resection. However, the pediatric endocrinologist requests that the laboratory re-assay the sample with a 1:100 dilution, which returns a true prolactin concentration of 4800 mcg/L. What phenomenon explains the initial low reading, and what is the proper therapy?
options: Hook effect; initiate medical therapy with cabergoline immediately
Macroprolactinemia; proceed with transsphenoidal surgical resection
Assay cross-reactivity with GH; administer pegvisomant
Secondary adrenal insufficiency; give high-dose dexamethasone
mcqs.explanation: This patient has a giant macroprolactinoma displaying the 'hook effect' (high-dose hook effect). Immense antigen (prolactin) concentrations saturate both capture and signal antibodies in two-site immunometric assays, causing falsely low readings that mimic stalk compression. A 1:100 dilution reveals the true massive elevation (4800 mcg/L). Macroprolactinomas respond dramatically to medical therapy with dopamine agonists (cabergoline), which rapidly shrinks the tumor and decompresses the optic chiasm, making cabergoline the treatment of choice over immediate surgery.
option_notes: Correct. The hook effect falsely lowers measured prolactin; true macroprolactinomas are treated primarily with cabergoline, not surgery.
Incorrect. Macroprolactinemia is a benign artifact of inactive antibody complexes, not giant invasive macroadenomas.
Incorrect. Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist for acromegaly, not the primary treatment for prolactinomas.
Incorrect. Dexamethasone does not shrink prolactinomas or cure prolactin-mediated chiasmal compression.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old girl presents with secondary amenorrhea and spontaneous bilateral milky breast discharge (galactorrhea). Serum prolactin is 145 mcg/L. Sellar MRI reveals a 6-mm well-circumscribed microadenoma in the left pituitary wing. What is the most effective initial management?
options: Oral cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly
Immediate stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife)
Transsphenoidal microdissection of the left pituitary wing
High-dose combined oral contraceptives
mcqs.explanation: Cabergoline (0.25 to 0.5 mg once or twice weekly) is the established first-line therapy for microprolactinomas in adolescents. Cabergoline normalizes prolactin, resolves galactorrhea, restores regular ovulatory menses, and shrinks or stabilizes tumor size in >90% of patients with minimal adverse effects. Surgery and radiation are reserved for rare refractory cases.
option_notes: Correct. Cabergoline twice weekly is the first-line treatment of choice for microprolactinomas.
Incorrect. Radiosurgery carries significant long-term risks of hypopituitarism and secondary neoplasms and is not first-line.
Incorrect. Surgery is second-line, reserved only for medical therapy failures or intolerance.
Incorrect. Combined oral contraceptives can provide estrogen but do not treat the underlying microprolactinoma and may stimulate tumor growth.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old adolescent with schizophrenia treated with risperidone 3 mg daily for 6 months presents with bilateral breast enlargement and galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is 85 mcg/L. Pituitary MRI is completely normal. What is the pharmacological mechanism causing pathologically elevated prolactin levels in this patient?
options: Antagonism of dopamine D2 receptors on anterior pituitary lactotropes
Direct stimulation of hypothalamic TRH secretion
Inhibition of hepatic prolactin degradation
Downregulation of peripheral estrogen receptors
mcqs.explanation: Risperidone and other first- and second-generation antipsychotics are potent dopamine D2 receptor antagonists. By blocking D2 receptors on anterior pituitary lactotrope cell membranes, they relieve tonic hypothalamic dopaminergic inhibition, resulting in autonomous prolactin synthesis and secretion with hyperprolactinemia (typically 40-150 mcg/L) and galactorrhea.
option_notes: Correct. Risperidone blocks pituitary lactotrope D2 receptors, abolishing tonic dopamine inhibition.
Incorrect. Risperidone acts via dopamine receptor antagonism, not by stimulating TRH.
Incorrect. Prolactin clearance is renal and hepatic; antipsychotics do not block degradative enzymes.
Incorrect. Antipsychotics do not directly downregulate peripheral estrogen receptors.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with severe fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, growth arrest, and mild galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is 58 mcg/L. Pituitary MRI reveals diffuse, symmetric pituitary enlargement ('pituitary hyperplasia'). Thyroid function testing demonstrates TSH 420 mIU/L and free T4 0.1 ng/dL. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Initiate oral levothyroxine replacement and repeat prolactin and MRI after achieving euthyroidism
Initiate high-dose cabergoline and schedule transsphenoidal pituitary resection
Perform urgent biopsy of the pituitary mass to rule out craniopharyngioma
Order whole-brain external beam radiation therapy
mcqs.explanation: Severe primary hypothyroidism causes extreme compensatory hypersecretion of hypothalamic TRH. TRH acts as a potent prolactin secretagogue, causing secondary hyperprolactinemia. Concurrently, chronic lack of thyroid hormone negative feedback causes profound hypertrophy and hyperplasia of pituitary thyrotropes and lactotropes, mimicking a pituitary macroadenoma on MRI. Treatment with levothyroxine restores euthyroidism, normalizes prolactin, and completely resolves pituitary enlargement, avoiding unnecessary pituitary surgery.
option_notes: Correct. Levothyroxine replacement corrects the primary hypothyroidism, resolves hyperprolactinemia, and reverses pituitary hyperplasia.
Incorrect. Cabergoline and surgery are unnecessary and inappropriate for reactive pituitary thyrotrope hyperplasia secondary to hypothyroidism.
Incorrect. Biopsy is contraindicated and carries risks of hypopituitarism for a benign reversible hyperplasia.
Incorrect. Radiation therapy has no role in benign thyrotrope hyperplasia.

mcqs.q: An asymptomatic 17-year-old girl has an incidental serum prolactin of 92 mcg/L measured during a dermatology workup for mild acne. She has completely regular monthly menses and no galactorrhea. Sellar MRI is normal. Serum treatment with polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation reveals that 88% of circulating prolactin precipitates as macroprolactin, with normal free monomeric prolactin. What is the appropriate clinical approach?
options: Reassurance and observation without dopamine agonist therapy
Initiate cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly to prevent future tumor development
Repeat pituitary MRI with dynamic contrast every 6 months
Perform bilateral prophylactic mastectomy
mcqs.explanation: Macroprolactinemia is a benign condition where circulating prolactin forms complexes with immunoglobulin G (IgG) autoantibodies. These high-molecular-weight complexes (>150 kDa) cannot cross capillary walls to bind target tissue prolactin receptors, rendering them biologically inactive (hence the patient has regular menses and no galactorrhea). However, standard immunoassays detect macroprolactin, causing elevated reported levels. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) precipitation precipitates the immune complexes, confirming normal monomeric prolactin. No treatment or imaging surveillance is required.
option_notes: Correct. Macroprolactinemia is a benign laboratory artifact requiring reassurance and no dopamine agonist treatment.
Incorrect. Cabergoline is unnecessary and causes unnecessary side effects for biologically inactive macroprolactin.
Incorrect. Surveillance MRIs are not indicated when sellar imaging is normal and free monomeric prolactin is normal.
Incorrect. Mastectomy is completely inappropriate and mutilating.

atlas.etiology: Prolactinoma (microprolactinoma <10 mm, macroprolactinoma >=10 mm); Stalk compression (craniopharyngioma, germinoma); Drugs (D2 antagonists: risperidone, haloperidol, metoclopramide); Severe primary hypothyroidism (TRH stimulation); Macroprolactinemia (prolactin-IgG).
atlas.epidemiology: Prolactinomas represent ~50% of all pediatric pituitary neuroendocrine tumors. Microadenomas predominate in adolescent females (amenorrhea/galactorrhea); macroadenomas predominate in males (mass effect).
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting serum prolactin (repeat to confirm); 1:100 dilution to exclude hook effect; PEG precipitation for macroprolactin; TSH, free T4, IGF-1, cortisol; visual field perimetry; high-resolution sellar MRI with contrast.

therapies.text: Cabergoline: initiate at 0.25 mg orally once or twice weekly; titrate every 4-8 weeks to 0.5-1.0 mg twice weekly (maximum 2-3 mg/week) until serum prolactin normalizes and tumor shrinkage is confirmed on MRI. Second-line: bromocriptine 1.25-2.5 mg daily with food.

pillars.label: Definition and Whipple Triad
pillars.text: Hypoglycemia in infants and children is defined clinically by Whipple's triad: (1) Symptoms and neuroglycopenic signs consistent with low blood glucose; (2) Concomitantly documented subnormal plasma glucose concentration (<50-55 mg/dL [2.8-3.1 mmol/L]; <60 mg/dL in neonates with suspected congenital hyperinsulinism); and (3) Rapid relief of clinical symptoms upon glucose administration. In neonates, transitional physiological glucose nadirs occur in the first 24-48 hours of life, after which plasma glucose must be maintained >60 mg/dL in infants and >70 mg/dL in older children to prevent irreversible neurocognitive injury.

pillars.label: Critical Sample Collection Protocol
pillars.text: The diagnostic cornerstone of pediatric hypoglycemia is obtaining a 'critical blood sample' at the exact moment of documented spontaneous or fasting-induced hypoglycemia (plasma glucose <50 mg/dL) BEFORE administering rescue dextrose. Essential critical analytes include: plasma glucose, insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB), free fatty acids (FFA), lactate, total and free carnitine, acylcarnitine profile, cortisol, and growth hormone, accompanied by the first post-hypoglycemic urine sample for organic acids and ketones. A glucagon challenge (1 mg IV or IM at the time of hypoglycemia) is performed: a glycemic rise >30 mg/dL confirms inappropriate hepatic glycogen retention driven by hyperinsulinism.

pillars.label: Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI)
pillars.text: Congenital Hyperinsulinism (CHI) is the leading cause of persistent, severe hypoglycemia in neonates and infants. Insulin inhibits glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, and ketogenesis, causing severe hypoketotic, hypo-fatty acidemic hypoglycemia with brain fuel starvation. The most common and severe forms result from inactivating mutations in ABCC8 and KCNJ11 (encoding SUR1 and Kir6.2 subunits of the beta-cell K-ATP channel). Recessive mutations cause diffuse CHI throughout the pancreas, whereas paternal mutations combined with somatic maternal loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at 11p15 cause focal CHI (adenomatous hyperplasia localized preoperatively with 18F-DOPA PET/CT and cured by partial pancreatectomy).

pillars.label: Fatty Acid Oxidation and Glycogen Storage Disorders
pillars.text: Fatty acid oxidation disorders (FAOD, e.g., Medium-Chain Acyl-CoA Dehydrogenase [MCAD] deficiency) present during fasting or intercurrent illness with hypoketotic hypoglycemia, elevated FFA-to-BOHB ratio, hepatomegaly, hyperammonemia, and abnormal acylcarnitine profiles (elevated octanoylcarnitine C8 in MCAD). Ketotic hypoglycemia (elevated BOHB >2.5-3.0 mmol/L and FFA with suppressed insulin <2 mcU/mL) occurs in idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia (accelerated starvation in lean toddlers aged 18 months to 5 years) and counter-regulatory hormone deficiencies (GH and cortisol deficiency). Glycogen storage diseases (GSD-I, G6Pase deficiency) feature severe fasting hypoglycemia with massive hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hypertriglyceridemia, and hyperuricemia.

pillars.label: Acute and Chronic Pharmacotherapy
pillars.text: Acute symptomatic hypoglycemia requires immediate IV bolus of 10% dextrose (D10W) at 2 mL/kg (200 mg/kg), followed by a continuous glucose infusion rate (GIR) of 6-8 mg/kg/min (titrated up to 15-25 mg/kg/min in severe hyperinsulinism). For CHI, first-line medical therapy is diazoxide (K-ATP channel opener; 5-15 mg/kg/day orally divided TID); diazoxide MUST be co-administered with a thiazide diuretic (chlorothiazide 7-10 mg/kg/day) to prevent severe fluid retention, congestive heart failure, and pulmonary hypertension. Second-line medical therapy for diazoxide-unresponsive CHI is octreotide (somatostatin analog; 5-25 mcg/kg/day SC divided Q6-8H or continuous infusion).

cards.q: What diagnostic critical blood analytes must be drawn at the moment of documented hypoglycemia (glucose <50 mg/dL) before giving dextrose?
cards.a: Plasma glucose, insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate (BOHB), free fatty acids (FFA), lactate, cortisol, growth hormone, acylcarnitine profile, and carnitine, plus urine for organic acids and ketones.

cards.q: What glycemic response during a glucagon stimulation test at the time of hypoglycemia confirms hyperinsulinism?
cards.a: An increase in plasma glucose >30 mg/dL within 40 minutes of glucagon administration (1 mg IV/IM), reflecting inappropriate hepatic glycogen retention mediated by insulin.

cards.q: What is the mechanism of action of diazoxide in congenital hyperinsulinism, and what diuretic must be co-prescribed?
cards.a: Diazoxide opens beta-cell K-ATP channels to hyperpolarize the membrane and inhibit insulin exocytosis; chlorothiazide must be co-administered to prevent fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension.

cards.q: What genes encode the beta-cell K-ATP channel implicated in the most common forms of congenital hyperinsulinism?
cards.a: ABCC8 (encoding the SUR1 regulatory subunit) and KCNJ11 (encoding the Kir6.2 pore-forming subunit) on chromosome 11p15.1.

cards.q: What imaging modality specifically localizes a resectable focal pancreatic lesion in congenital hyperinsulinism?
cards.a: 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA positron emission tomography / computed tomography (18F-DOPA PET/CT).

cards.q: How does fatty acid oxidation disorder (e.g., MCAD deficiency) present during fasting compared to ketotic hypoglycemia?
cards.a: FAOD presents with hypoketotic hypoglycemia (low ketones despite fasting) with elevated free fatty acids and dicarboxylic aciduria, whereas ketotic hypoglycemia displays high ketones (BOHB >2.5-3.0 mmol/L).

cards.q: What is the initial intravenous dextrose bolus dose and fluid choice for acute pediatric hypoglycemia?
cards.a: Intravenous 10% dextrose (D10W) at 2 mL/kg (equivalent to 200 mg/kg elemental dextrose) infused over 2-3 minutes.

mcqs.q: A 2-day-old macrosomic male infant (birth weight 4.4 kg) born to a non-diabetic mother presents with lethargy, poor feeding, and jitteriness. Point-of-care blood glucose is 28 mg/dL. A critical blood sample drawn prior to IV dextrose administration reveals: glucose 30 mg/dL, insulin 14 mcU/mL (inappropriately elevated), C-peptide 2.8 ng/mL, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.2 mmol/L (suppressed), and free fatty acids 0.3 mmol/L (suppressed). Glucagon 1 mg IV is given, and blood glucose rises to 78 mg/dL at 30 minutes. What is the diagnosis?
options: Congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI)
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
Growth hormone deficiency
Glycogen storage disease type I
mcqs.explanation: This neonate exhibits the classic biochemical signature of congenital hyperinsulinism: hypoglycemia (30 mg/dL) accompanied by detectable/elevated insulin (14 mcU/mL), elevated C-peptide, suppressed ketones (BOHB 0.2 mmol/L), suppressed free fatty acids, and a robust glycemic rise >30 mg/dL following glucagon challenge. Insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis while locking glycogen in the liver.
option_notes: Correct. Measurable insulin/C-peptide with hypoketotic hypoglycemia and positive glucagon challenge is diagnostic of hyperinsulinism.
Incorrect. MCAD deficiency features suppressed insulin and elevated free fatty acids with abnormal acylcarnitine profile.
Incorrect. GH deficiency causes ketotic hypoglycemia with elevated BOHB and low/undetectable insulin.
Incorrect. GSD type I features massive hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and poor response to glucagon.

mcqs.q: A 1-week-old full-term neonate is diagnosed with diffuse congenital hyperinsulinism due to a homozygous ABCC8 mutation. Diazoxide therapy is initiated at 10 mg/kg/day. Which additional medication must be routinely co-prescribed with diazoxide to prevent a well-documented, life-threatening adverse complication?
options: Chlorothiazide (thiazide diuretic) to prevent fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension
Levothyroxine to prevent acute hypothyroidism
Potassium chloride to prevent severe hypokalemia
Sodium bicarbonate to treat proximal renal tubular acidosis
mcqs.explanation: Diazoxide stimulates renal tubular sodium and water retention through antidiuretic mechanisms. In neonates and young infants, this can precipitate massive fluid overload, congestive heart failure, and life-threatening pulmonary hypertension.
