Co-administration of a thiazide diuretic (such as chlorothiazide 7-10 mg/kg/day) is mandatory to promote natriuresis, prevent edema, and exert a synergistic hyperglycemic effect.
option_notes: Correct. Chlorothiazide is routinely co-prescribed to counteract diazoxide-induced fluid retention and pulmonary hypertension.
Incorrect. Diazoxide does not cause acute hypothyroidism.
Incorrect. Diazoxide does not typically cause severe hypokalemia requiring routine prophylactic KCl.
Incorrect. Diazoxide does not cause proximal RTA requiring bicarbonate.

mcqs.q: A 14-month-old girl with a mild viral gastroenteritis and 14 hours of poor oral intake presents with lethargy, vomiting, and stupor. Serum glucose is 32 mg/dL. Critical labs show: beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.1 mmol/L (suppressed), free fatty acids 3.2 mmol/L (markedly elevated), insulin <1.0 mcU/mL (undetectable), and serum ammonia 120 mcmol/L. Plasma acylcarnitine analysis reveals a marked elevation of octanoylcarnitine (C8). What is the underlying disorder?
options: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency
Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia
Insulinoma
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
mcqs.explanation: MCAD deficiency is the most common fatty acid oxidation defect. During prolonged fasting or catabolic stress, impaired mitochondrial beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids prevents generation of acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies, resulting in hypoketotic hypoglycemia (low BOHB despite elevated FFA) and hyperammonemia. The diagnostic hallmark is marked accumulation of medium-chain acylcarnitines, specifically octanoylcarnitine (C8).
option_notes: Correct. Hypoketotic hypoglycemia with elevated free fatty acids, hyperammonemia, and high C8 acylcarnitine confirms MCAD deficiency.
Incorrect. Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia features robust ketosis (BOHB >3.0 mmol/L), not hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. Insulinomas produce elevated insulin and suppress both ketones and free fatty acids.
Incorrect. CAH produces salt-wasting, hyperkalemia, and elevated 17-OHP, not isolated C8 acylcarnitine elevation.

mcqs.q: A 3-year-old slender boy presents with morning drowsiness and difficulty waking after having an early dinner and missing breakfast. Point-of-care glucose is 42 mg/dL. Blood drawn at that time reveals: insulin <1 mcU/mL, beta-hydroxybutyrate 4.2 mmol/L, free fatty acids 2.8 mmol/L, cortisol 22 mcg/dL, and growth hormone 12 ng/mL. Following a glass of orange juice, he rapidly returns to his normal playful self. What is the diagnosis?
options: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia of childhood
Nesidioblastosis (congenital hyperinsulinism)
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1) deficiency
Primary adrenal insufficiency
mcqs.explanation: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia is the most common cause of hypoglycemia in children between 18 months and 5 years. It represents an exaggerated physiological response to fasting (accelerated starvation) in young, lean children who have limited hepatic glycogen stores and small muscle mass (limiting alanine for gluconeogenesis). The biochemical profile shows robust ketosis (BOHB >3-4 mmol/L), suppressed insulin (<1 mcU/mL), and appropriate counter-regulatory hormone surges (cortisol >18 mcg/dL, GH >10 ng/mL). It resolves spontaneously by age 6-8 years as muscle mass increases.
option_notes: Correct. Fasting hypoglycemia with brisk ketosis, suppressed insulin, and robust cortisol/GH response in a toddler is idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. Hyperinsulinism is hypoketotic (BOHB <1.5-2.0 mmol/L) with measurable insulin.
Incorrect. CPT-1 deficiency is a fatty acid oxidation disorder causing hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
Incorrect. Adrenal insufficiency is excluded by the robust cortisol peak of 22 mcg/dL.

mcqs.q: A newborn male with recurrent persistent neuroglycopenia and low plasma glucose unresponsive to diazoxide undergoes genetic sequencing revealing a single paternally inherited ABCC8 mutation. What diagnostic imaging modality should be performed next to guide surgical planning?
options: 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA PET/CT of the pancreas
Abdominal ultrasound with color Doppler
Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)
mcqs.explanation: Paternal inheritance of a monoallelic K-ATP channel mutation (ABCC8 or KCNJ11) combined with somatic maternal loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at 11p15 causes focal congenital hyperinsulinism. Because beta cells take up L-DOPA and convert it to dopamine via DOPA decarboxylase, 18F-fluoro-L-DOPA PET/CT specifically visualizes and localizes the adenomatous focal lesion, allowing a curative, organ-sparing partial pancreatectomy rather than near-total pancreatectomy.
option_notes: Correct. 18F-DOPA PET/CT is the gold standard for localizing focal adenomatous lesions in congenital hyperinsulinism.
Incorrect. Abdominal ultrasound lacks the spatial and biochemical sensitivity to distinguish focal beta-cell hyperplasia.
Incorrect. Contrast CT cannot distinguish microscopic adenomatous hyperplasia from surrounding normal parenchyma.
Incorrect. MRCP visualizes ductal anatomy, not functional neuroendocrine beta-cell hyperfunction.

atlas.etiology: Hyperinsulinism: CHI (ABCC8, KCNJ11, GLUD1, GCK, HADH, HNF4A); insulinoma; Beckwith-Wiedemann (11p15); infant of diabetic mother. FAOD: MCAD, VLCAD, LCHAD, CPT. Ketotic: Idiopathic ketotic hypoglycemia; hypopituitarism (GH, ACTH). GSD: GSD-I (G6Pase), GSD-III.
atlas.epidemiology: CHI incidence is 1:30,000 to 1:50,000 live births (up to 1:2500 in founder populations). MCAD affects ~1 in 15,000 births.
atlas.diagnostics: Critical sample at glucose <50 mg/dL (insulin, C-peptide, BOHB, FFA, cortisol, GH, acylcarnitine, lactate, total/free carnitine); glucagon challenge test; 18F-DOPA PET/CT; genetic testing panel.

therapies.text: 10% Dextrose (D10W) IV bolus at 2 mL/kg (200 mg/kg) over 2-3 minutes. Follow immediately with continuous IV glucose infusion rate (GIR) at 6-8 mg/kg/min, titrating to maintain blood glucose >70 mg/dL.

Diazoxide: 5-15 mg/kg/day orally divided TID. Co-administer chlorothiazide 7-10 mg/kg/day divided BID to prevent pulmonary hypertension and heart failure. Second-line: Octreotide 5-25 mcg/kg/day SC divided Q6-8H.

pillars.label: Pathophysiology and Autoantibodies
pillars.text: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by immune-mediated destruction of pancreatic beta cells within the islets of Langerhans, leading to absolute insulin deficiency. Genetic susceptibility is strongly linked to human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class II alleles on chromosome 6p21, specifically HLA-DR3-DQ2 and HLA-DR4-DQ8 haplotypes. Progressive lymphocytic insulitis is driven by autoreactive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Circulating islet autoantibodies serve as essential diagnostic markers: glutamic acid decarboxylase-65 (GAD65), insulinoma-associated protein-2 (IA-2), insulin autoantibodies (IAA; prominent in young children), and zinc transporter 8 (ZnT8). The presence of >=2 persistent autoantibodies marks preclinical stage 1/2 T1D.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Criteria and Honeymoon Phase
pillars.text: Diagnostic criteria (ADA and ISPAD) require meeting any of the following: (1) Fasting plasma glucose >=126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L); (2) 2-hour plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) during 75g oral glucose tolerance test; (3) HbA1c >=6.5% (48 mmol/mol); OR (4) Classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss, fatigue) plus a random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L). Following initial insulin stabilization, up to 60-80% of children enter a 'honeymoon' (partial remission) phase, where surviving beta cells temporarily recover endogenous secretory capacity, reducing insulin requirements to <0.5 units/kg/day with HbA1c <7.0%.

pillars.label: Intensive Insulin Regimens and AID Systems
pillars.text: All pediatric patients require intensive physiological insulin therapy matching basal requirements and mealtime carbohydrate excursions. Total daily dose (TDD) ranges from 0.5 to 1.0 units/kg/day (0.2-0.5 U/kg/day during honeymoon; 1.0-1.5 U/kg/day in pubertal adolescents). Regimens include multiple daily injections (MDI) utilizing long-acting basal analogs (glargine, detemir, degludec; 40-50% of TDD) plus rapid-acting mealtime analogs (aspart, lispro, glulisine; 50-60% of TDD) dosed according to Insulin-to-Carbohydrate Ratios (ICR; 500/TDD rule) and Insulin Sensitivity Factors (ISF; 1800/TDD rule). Automated Insulin Delivery (AID / closed-loop) systems combining continuous glucose monitors (CGM) with smart insulin pumps significantly optimize Time in Range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL >70%) and reduce severe hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL <4%).

pillars.label: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) Resuscitation Protocol
pillars.text: DKA is diagnosed by the biochemical triad: hyperglycemia (blood glucose >200 mg/dL), venous pH <7.30 or serum bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L, and ketonemia (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate >=3.0 mmol/L) or ketonuria. Severity is categorized as mild (pH 7.20-7.29, bicarb 10-14), moderate (pH 7.10-7.19, bicarb 5-9), or severe (pH <7.10, bicarb <5). Resuscitation begins with 0.9% normal saline at 10-20 mL/kg over 1 hour. Continuous regular insulin infusion is started at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour 1-2 hours AFTER initiating IV hydration; IV insulin boluses are strictly contraindicated. Replace fluid deficit and maintenance evenly over 24-48 hours. Add 40 mEq/L potassium (KCl + K-phosphate) once urine output is verified and serum potassium <5.5 mEq/L. Add 5% dextrose when glucose drops <250-300 mg/dL to maintain glucose 150-200 mg/dL until ketoacidosis resolves.

pillars.label: DKA Cerebral Edema and Long-Term Surveillance
pillars.text: Cerebral injury / edema is the leading cause of mortality in pediatric DKA, occurring in 0.5-1.0% of episodes. Warning signs include headache, bradycardia, hypertension (Cushing triad), lethargy, irritability, cranial nerve palsies, and sudden neurological deterioration. Emergent treatment requires hyperosmolar therapy with 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg IV over 10-15 minutes) or 20% mannitol (0.5-1.0 g/kg IV over 20 minutes) without waiting for cranial imaging. Long-term surveillance mandates annual screening beginning at age 10 years (or 2-5 years after diagnosis) for diabetic nephropathy (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio), retinopathy (dilated eye exam), neuropathy, and coexisting autoimmune disorders (celiac disease [tTG-IgA] and Hashimoto thyroiditis [TSH, anti-TPO]).

cards.q: What three biochemical criteria define diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) in a pediatric patient?
cards.a: Hyperglycemia (blood glucose >200 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (venous pH <7.30 or bicarbonate <15-18 mmol/L), and ketosis (blood BOHB >=3.0 mmol/L or moderate/large ketonuria).

cards.q: Why is an intravenous bolus of regular insulin strictly contraindicated when initiating DKA therapy?
cards.a: An IV insulin bolus precipitates rapid osmotic fluid shifts and acute hypokalemia, significantly increasing the risk of fatal cerebral edema; continuous infusion without a bolus is mandatory.

cards.q: What is the emergency medical therapy for acute cerebral edema complicating pediatric DKA?
cards.a: Intravenous 3% hypertonic saline (3 to 5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes) or intravenous 20% mannitol (0.5 to 1.0 g/kg over 20 minutes), administered immediately without awaiting head CT.

cards.q: Which islet autoantibodies are standardly evaluated to confirm the autoimmune etiology of type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: GAD65 (glutamic acid decarboxylase-65), IA-2 (insulinoma-associated protein-2), IAA (insulin autoantibodies), and ZnT8 (zinc transporter 8).

cards.q: At what circulating blood glucose threshold should dextrose (5-10%) be added to intravenous fluids during DKA management?
cards.a: When blood glucose decreases to 250 to 300 mg/dL, in order to maintain glucose between 150-200 mg/dL while continuing insulin to clear acidosis and ketosis.

cards.q: What are the internationally recommended Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) targets for youth with type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: Time in Range (TIR 70-180 mg/dL) >70%, Time Below Range (<70 mg/dL) <4%, and Time Below 54 mg/dL <1%.

cards.q: Which two autoimmune conditions require regular routine screening in all children with type 1 diabetes?
cards.a: Autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis, screening with TSH and anti-TPO) and Celiac disease (screening with tissue transglutaminase IgA [tTG-IgA] and total IgA).

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old girl presents to the emergency department with a 3-day history of polydipsia, polyuria, abdominal pain, and Kussmaul respirations. Point-of-care glucose is 480 mg/dL. Venous blood gas reveals pH 7.12, pCO2 18 mmHg, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, sodium 132 mEq/L, potassium 4.8 mEq/L, and blood beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.8 mmol/L. She is alert but tachypneic. After administering an initial 10 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% normal saline over 1 hour, what is the most appropriate next step in her medical management?
options: Administer an IV bolus of regular insulin at 0.1 units/kg followed by continuous infusion
Initiate continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour without an insulin bolus, and plan fluid replacement over 24-48 hours
Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg to correct severe acidosis
Add 10% dextrose to IV fluids immediately
mcqs.explanation: International consensus guidelines (ISPAD/PEDS) dictate that in pediatric moderate-to-severe DKA: (1) Insulin should be administered as a continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour started 1-2 hours after beginning IV fluid resuscitation; (2) An IV insulin bolus is strictly contraindicated because it causes sudden osmotic shifts and triggers hypokalemia, increasing cerebral edema risk; (3) Fluid replacement must be distributed evenly over 24-48 hours; (4) Bicarbonate is contraindicated due to paradoxical CSF acidosis and hypokalemia.
option_notes: Incorrect. IV insulin boluses are strictly contraindicated in pediatric DKA due to increased risk of fatal cerebral edema.
Correct. Continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr without a bolus, coupled with 24-48 hour fluid deficit replacement, is standard.
Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate is contraindicated; it worsens cerebral acidosis and precipitates life-threatening hypokalemia.
Incorrect. Dextrose is added only after blood glucose declines to 250-300 mg/dL, not at 480 mg/dL.

mcqs.q: During management of severe DKA in a 10-year-old boy, blood glucose drops from 480 mg/dL to 260 mg/dL after 4 hours of IV fluids and continuous regular insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour. Venous blood gas shows persistent acidosis: pH 7.18, bicarbonate 11 mmol/L, and urine ketones remain large. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Stop the insulin infusion because the blood glucose is approaching normal
Reduce insulin infusion to 0.01 units/kg/hour and administer subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin
Add 5% dextrose to the IV hydration fluids and continue the insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour to clear the ketoacidosis
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to accelerate acidosis resolution
mcqs.explanation: In DKA, insulin is required not merely to lower blood glucose, but fundamentally to suppress lipolysis, suppress ketogenesis, and stimulate peripheral ketone clearance. When blood glucose approaches 250-300 mg/dL, 5% dextrose (and later 10% dextrose if needed) must be added to the IV fluids while maintaining the insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr. This prevents hypoglycemia while allowing insulin to completely resolve the ketoacidosis.
option_notes: Incorrect. Stopping insulin allows ketoacidosis to worsen, even if glucose is temporarily lower.
Incorrect. Inadequately reducing insulin halts the suppression of ketogenesis and prolongs DKA.
Correct. Adding 5% dextrose while maintaining insulin infusion keeps glucose 150-200 mg/dL while clearing ketoacidosis.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate is contraindicated in pediatric DKA.

mcqs.q: Six hours into treatment for severe DKA, an 11-year-old girl complains of a severe, worsening headache. On exam, her heart rate has dropped from 110 bpm to 58 bpm, blood pressure has risen from 104/65 to 138/88 mmHg, and she is difficult to arouse. What is the most critical immediate intervention?
options: Transport the patient immediately to the radiology suite for an emergent unenhanced head CT
Administer intravenous 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg over 10-15 minutes) or 20% mannitol immediately at the bedside
Increase the rate of 0.9% normal saline infusion to treat hypovolemia
Administer intravenous lorazepam for suspected subclinical status epilepticus
mcqs.explanation: The sudden onset of severe headache, bradycardia, and hypertension (Cushing triad) with neurological deterioration represents impending cerebral herniation from DKA-related cerebral edema. Cerebral edema is a medical emergency with high mortality. Treatment with hyperosmolar therapy (3% hypertonic saline 3-5 mL/kg or 20% mannitol 0.5-1.0 g/kg) must be administered immediately at the bedside; diagnostic imaging must NEVER delay treatment.
option_notes: Incorrect. Delaying hyperosmolar therapy to obtain a CT scan can result in brainstem herniation and fatal arrest.
Correct. Immediate bedside administration of 3% hypertonic saline or mannitol is life-saving and must precede neuroimaging.
Incorrect. Increasing fluid infusion rate will worsen cerebral edema and accelerate herniation.
Incorrect. The findings reflect acute intracranial hypertension (Cushing triad), not primary status epilepticus.

mcqs.q: A 13-year-old male with established type 1 diabetes weighs 50 kg and takes a total daily dose of 40 units of insulin. Using the 500 Rule and 1800 Rule, calculate his estimated Insulin-to-Carbohydrate Ratio (ICR) and Insulin Sensitivity Factor (ISF):
options: ICR: 1 unit per 12.5 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 45 mg/dL
ICR: 1 unit per 5 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 20 mg/dL
ICR: 1 unit per 25 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 70 mg/dL
ICR: 1 unit per 15 g carbohydrate; ISF: 1 unit lowers blood glucose by 90 mg/dL
mcqs.explanation: The standard clinical formulas for estimating starting pump and MDI parameters based on Total Daily Dose (TDD = 40 units) are: (1) 500 Rule for ICR = 500 / TDD = 500 / 40 = 12.5 grams of carbohydrate per 1 unit of rapid-acting insulin; (2) 1800 Rule for ISF = 1800 / TDD = 1800 / 40 = 45 mg/dL reduction in blood glucose per 1 unit of rapid-acting insulin.
option_notes: Correct. ICR = 500/40 = 12.5 g/unit; ISF = 1800/40 = 45 mg/dL/unit.
Incorrect. 1:5 and 20 mg/dL reflect a massively high TDD of ~90-100 units.
Incorrect. 1:25 and 70 mg/dL reflect a low TDD of ~20-25 units.
Incorrect. Mathematical calculation error.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes diagnosed 6 months ago has an HbA1c of 6.2% on a total daily insulin dose of 0.25 units/kg/day. His parents ask if he has been cured of diabetes. What is the explanation for his current low insulin requirement?
options: He is experiencing the 'honeymoon' (partial remission) phase due to temporary recovery of surviving beta cells
He was misdiagnosed and actually has maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY)
He has developed complete insulin sensitivity due to low carbohydrate intake
His islet autoantibodies have permanently disappeared
mcqs.explanation: The 'honeymoon' or partial clinical remission phase occurs in up to 60-80% of children shortly after diagnosis and initial glycemic stabilization. Relief of glucotoxicity allows surviving beta cells to temporarily produce sufficient endogenous insulin to maintain near-normal glycemic control with very low exogenous insulin requirements (<0.5 units/kg/day). This phase typically lasts several months to a year before autoimmune destruction inevitably progresses to absolute insulin deficiency.
option_notes: Correct. The honeymoon phase represents transient endogenous beta-cell recovery with low insulin requirements.
Incorrect. MODY is a monogenic defect; high initial presentation with subsequent partial remission is classic for T1D.
Incorrect. Insulin sensitivity does not account for low insulin requirements in the setting of beta-cell rest.
Incorrect. Autoantibodies persist throughout the disease course and do not permanently disappear during remission.

atlas.etiology: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells mediated by CD4+/CD8+ T-cell insulitis; HLA-DR3-DQ2 and DR4-DQ8 susceptibility. Biomarkers: GAD65, IA-2, IAA, ZnT8 autoantibodies.
atlas.epidemiology: Incidence is rising globally by 2-3% per year; peak incidence occurs in two age cohorts: 4-6 years and 10-14 years (early puberty).
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting glucose >=126 mg/dL, 2-hr OGTT >=200 mg/dL, HbA1c >=6.5%, or random glucose >=200 mg/dL with symptoms; islet autoantibody panel; DKA evaluation (venous blood gas, BOHB, electrolytes, BUN/Cr); CGM metrics.

therapies.text: Initial fluid: 0.9% normal saline 10-20 mL/kg over 1 hour. Continuous regular insulin infusion at 0.05-0.1 units/kg/hour started 1-2 hours AFTER fluid initiation (NEVER give an IV insulin bolus). Replace remaining fluid deficit over 24-48 hours. Add 40 mEq/L potassium once urine output confirmed. Add 5-10% dextrose when glucose <250-300 mg/dL. Treat cerebral edema immediately with 3% hypertonic saline (3-5 mL/kg) or 20% mannitol (0.5-1.0 g/kg).

Total Daily Dose (TDD): 0.5-1.0 units/kg/day (prepabertal: 0.5-0.8 U/kg/day; pubertal: 1.0-1.5 U/kg/day). Basal analog (glargine, detemir, degludec) comprises 40-50% of TDD. Rapid-acting analog (aspart, lispro) comprises 50-60% of TDD, divided by meals using ICR (500/TDD) and correction ISF (1800/TDD). Target HbA1c <7.0%, TIR 70-180 mg/dL >70%.

pillars.label: Epidemiology and Aggressive Pathobiology
pillars.text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) in youth has emerged as a major public health challenge, driven by the global epidemic of pediatric obesity. Unlike adult T2D, youth-onset T2D is characterized by a significantly more aggressive disease biology: accelerated decline in pancreatic beta-cell function (loss of 20-35% of beta-cell capacity per year, ~4 times faster than in adults), early development of insulin dependence, and rapid accrual of microvascular and macrovascular complications. It disproportionately affects adolescents aged 10-19 years during pubertal insulin resistance peaks, with strong predilection for racial and ethnic minorities (Black, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian/Pacific Islander youth).

pillars.label: Pathophysiology and Autoantibody Exclusion
pillars.text: The pathophysiology of youth T2D results from the interplay between severe peripheral insulin resistance (primarily in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, exacerbated by visceral adiposity) and progressive beta-cell failure unable to sustain hyperinsulinemic compensation. Clinical hallmarks include BMI >=85th or >=95th percentile, acanthosis nigricans (present in 85-90% of affected youth, reflecting hyperinsulinemic epidermal stimulation), hypertension, dyslipidemia, and a first- or second-degree family history of T2D. Testing for pancreatic islet autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) is mandatory in all youth diagnosed with diabetes to differentiate T2D from antibody-positive autoimmune type 1 diabetes.

pillars.label: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS) Emergency
pillars.text: Youth with T2D are at high risk of presenting with Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS), a catastrophic medical emergency associated with 10-30% mortality. Diagnostic criteria include: extreme hyperglycemia (plasma glucose >600 mg/dL [33.3 mmol/L]), marked serum hyperosmolality (effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg), profound dehydration, altered mental status or coma, in the absence of significant ketoacidosis (venous pH >7.25-7.30, serum bicarbonate >15 mmol/L, minimal/absent ketones). Management requires cautious, massive isotonic fluid replacement (0.9% saline 20 mL/kg boluses up to 40-60 mL/kg to restore organ perfusion) followed by slow correction of hyperosmolality over 48-72 hours, with low-dose insulin infusion (0.025-0.05 U/kg/hr) delayed until rehydration is underway.

pillars.label: Stratified Pharmacotherapy Algorithm
pillars.text: Initial pharmacological management is stratified by clinical severity: (1) Asymptomatic or metabolically stable youth (HbA1c <8.5%, blood glucose <250 mg/dL, no ketosis): Metformin monotherapy (initiated at 500 mg daily, titrated weekly to 1000 mg twice daily [2000 mg/day]) combined with comprehensive lifestyle intervention; (2) Marked hyperglycemia (HbA1c >=8.5%, blood glucose >=250 mg/dL) without acidosis: Basal insulin (0.25-0.5 units/kg/day) co-administered with Metformin; (3) Ketosis or DKA present: Intravenous insulin according to DKA protocol, transitioning to subcutaneous basal-bolus insulin, adding metformin once acidosis resolves.

pillars.label: Expanded Therapies and Comorbidity Surveillance
pillars.text: For youth >=10 years who fail to achieve glycemic targets (HbA1c <6.5-7.0%) on metformin and basal insulin, FDA-approved second-line agents include Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (liraglutide 0.6-1.8 mg SC daily, dulaglutide 0.75-1.5 mg SC weekly, or exenatide extended-release) and SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin). Because youth-onset T2D develops rapid microvascular complications, baseline and annual surveillance starting at diagnosis includes: diabetic nephropathy (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio), retinopathy (dilated retinal exam), peripheral neuropathy, lipid panel, and screening for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MAFLD; ALT/AST) and obstructive sleep apnea.

cards.q: How does the annual rate of pancreatic beta-cell decline in youth-onset type 2 diabetes compare to adult-onset type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: Youth-onset T2D exhibits a 20-35% annual loss of beta-cell function (~4 times faster than adults), leading to rapid treatment failure and early insulin dependence.

cards.q: What laboratory findings define Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS) in pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: Severe hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, and absence of significant ketoacidosis (venous pH >7.25-7.30, bicarbonate >15 mmol/L).

cards.q: What is the initial medical therapy for an asymptomatic adolescent diagnosed with T2D, HbA1c 7.6%, and no ketosis?
cards.a: Oral metformin (initiated at 500 mg daily, titrated to 2000 mg/day divided twice daily) combined with diet and lifestyle modifications.

cards.q: When is initial basal insulin therapy mandated at the time of diagnosis in pediatric type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: When blood glucose is >=250 mg/dL or HbA1c is >=8.5% at presentation, or whenever ketosis or acidosis is present.

cards.q: Which GLP-1 receptor agonists are FDA-approved for glycemic control and weight reduction in youth aged >=10 years with T2D?
cards.a: Liraglutide (once daily SC), dulaglutide (once weekly SC), and exenatide extended-release (once weekly SC).

cards.q: Why must pancreatic islet autoantibodies be checked in all overweight youth presenting with clinical features of T2D?
cards.a: To exclude autoimmune type 1 diabetes (or latent autoimmune diabetes), which occurs in ~10-15% of obese youth and requires lifelong intensive insulin therapy.

cards.q: At what point should screening for diabetic nephropathy and retinopathy begin in youth with type 2 diabetes?
cards.a: At the time of initial diagnosis (and annually thereafter), because microvascular complications frequently develop prior to clinical detection in youth.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old Hispanic male with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 (98th percentile) presents for a routine sports physical. Examination reveals prominent velvety hyperpigmented plaques on the back of his neck and axillae (acanthosis nigricans). Random blood glucose is 215 mg/dL. Confirmatory testing demonstrates fasting blood glucose 152 mg/dL and HbA1c 7.8%. Urinalysis shows glucosuria without ketones. Islet autoantibodies (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8) are negative. What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?
options: Oral metformin initiated at 500 mg once daily, titrated up to 2000 mg daily in divided doses, plus lifestyle intervention
Immediate initiation of basal-bolus insulin at 1.0 units/kg/day
Sulfonylurea monotherapy with glipizide 10 mg daily
Lifestyle modification alone with no medication for 12 months
mcqs.explanation: In youth diagnosed with antibody-negative type 2 diabetes who are metabolically stable (HbA1c <8.5%, blood glucose <250 mg/dL, no ketosis/acidosis), oral metformin monotherapy (titrated from 500 mg daily up to 1000 mg twice daily) combined with diabetes self-management education and lifestyle modification is the recommended first-line therapy according to ADA and ISPAD guidelines.
option_notes: Correct. Metformin 500-2000 mg/day plus lifestyle intervention is the established first-line regimen for stable youth-onset T2D.
Incorrect. Basal-bolus insulin is reserved for patients presenting with ketoacidosis or marked decompensation (HbA1c >=8.5%).
Incorrect. Sulfonylureas are second-line and accelerate beta-cell exhaustion in youth-onset T2D.
Incorrect. Lifestyle therapy alone has a very high failure rate in youth; guidelines mandate starting metformin at diagnosis.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old obese female presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and fatigue. Serum glucose is 340 mg/dL and HbA1c is 10.4%. Serum electrolytes: sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, bicarbonate 22 mEq/L, and venous pH 7.36. Urinalysis shows 4+ glucose and trace ketones. What is the recommended initial medical management?
options: Initiation of once-daily subcutaneous basal insulin (0.25-0.5 units/kg/day) combined with oral metformin
Intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour according to DKA protocol
Metformin monotherapy 500 mg daily without insulin
Immediate bariatric Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery
mcqs.explanation: In youth with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes presenting with marked hyperglycemia (blood glucose >=250 mg/dL and/or HbA1c >=8.5%) WITHOUT ketoacidosis (normal pH and bicarbonate), the recommended management is initiation of once-daily subcutaneous basal insulin (0.25-0.5 units/kg/day) combined with oral metformin. Once glucotoxicity is relieved and glycemic stability is attained, insulin can frequently be tapered.
option_notes: Correct. Basal insulin combined with metformin is the guideline-directed therapy for marked hyperglycemia (HbA1c >=8.5%) without acidosis.
Incorrect. IV insulin DKA protocol is indicated only when systemic ketoacidosis (pH <7.30, bicarb <15) is present.
Incorrect. Metformin monotherapy is inadequate to rapidly relieve glucotoxicity in a patient with HbA1c of 10.4%.
Incorrect. Metabolic bariatric surgery is an elective option for severe obesity after glycemic stabilization and multidisciplinary review.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old African American male with newly discovered T2D presents in a somnolent, severely dehydrated state. Laboratory findings demonstrate: serum glucose 1050 mg/dL, venous pH 7.32, serum bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, serum sodium 152 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 54 mg/dL. Effective serum osmolality is calculated at 345 mOsm/kg. Urine dipstick shows trace ketones. What is the diagnosis, and what is the primary initial resuscitation priority?
options: Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS); vigorous isotonic fluid resuscitation with 0.9% normal saline
Severe diabetic ketoacidosis; immediate IV insulin bolus followed by high-dose infusion
Central diabetes insipidus; intravenous desmopressin administration
Lactic acidosis secondary to metformin toxicity; emergent hemodialysis
mcqs.explanation: This patient has Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS), characterized by extreme hyperglycemia (>600 mg/dL), severe hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), and altered sensorium in the absence of significant ketoacidosis (pH >7.30, bicarb >15). HHS carries a 10-30% mortality in youth. The primary resuscitation priority is urgent, aggressive expansion of the intravascular volume using isotonic fluids (0.9% saline 20 mL/kg boluses) to restore tissue perfusion before starting low-dose insulin.
option_notes: Correct. Extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality >320 mOsm/kg, and mild acidosis define HHS; isotonic fluid resuscitation is priority one.
Incorrect. DKA features severe acidosis (pH <7.30, bicarb <15) with high ketones; IV insulin boluses are contraindicated.
Incorrect. Diabetes insipidus features dilute polyuria with normal/high sodium, not glucose >1000 mg/dL.
Incorrect. Lactic acidosis presents with a profound high anion gap metabolic acidosis with low pH, not isolated hyperosmolar hyperglycemia.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old female with youth-onset T2D on metformin 2000 mg daily has a repeat HbA1c of 8.2% after 6 months. She has a BMI of 35 kg/m2. She expresses desire to improve glycemic control and lose weight without daily fingerstick insulin adjustments. Which class of medication is FDA-approved for youth aged >=10 years and addresses both glycemic control and weight reduction?
options: GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g., once-weekly subcutaneous dulaglutide or once-daily liraglutide)
Sulfonylurea (e.g., glimepiride)
Thiazolidinedione (e.g., pioglitazone)
Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor (e.g., acarbose)
mcqs.explanation: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (e.g., once-daily liraglutide or once-weekly dulaglutide/exenatide) are FDA-approved as add-on therapy for youth aged >=10 years with type 2 diabetes. GLP-1 receptor agonists stimulate glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppress inappropriate glucagon release, delay gastric emptying, and promote central satiety, leading to significant HbA1c reductions and clinically meaningful weight loss.
option_notes: Correct. GLP-1 receptor agonists are FDA-approved in youth >=10 years to improve glycemic control and promote weight loss.
Incorrect. Sulfonylureas cause significant weight gain and hypoglycemia and accelerate beta-cell exhaustion.
Incorrect. Thiazolidinediones are not approved in youth and cause fluid retention and weight gain.
Incorrect. Acarbose has poor efficacy, frequent gastrointestinal side effects, and does not promote weight loss.

mcqs.q: Unlike children with type 1 diabetes where microvascular screening begins after 2 to 5 years, why must screening for diabetic kidney disease (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) and retinopathy begin at the time of initial diagnosis in youth with type 2 diabetes?
options: Youth with type 2 diabetes frequently have subclinical disease for months to years prior to diagnosis, and microvascular complications progress far more rapidly
Screening tests are only valid during the first month of diabetes diagnosis
Type 2 diabetes damages renal glomeruli through immune-complex glomerulonephritis
Retinal examination is required to rule out retinitis pigmentosa
mcqs.explanation: In youth-onset type 2 diabetes, the preceding asymptomatic period of insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance often persists for years before clinical diagnosis. Studies (such as the TODAY study) have shown that up to 10-20% of youth already have microalbuminuria or early diabetic retinopathy at the time of initial diagnosis, and microvascular complications progress at an accelerated rate compared to type 1 diabetes. Therefore, immediate baseline screening is mandatory.
option_notes: Correct. Pre-existing subclinical hyperglycemia and aggressive complication progression mandate immediate baseline screening.
Incorrect. Screening tests remain valid throughout life; the timing reflects clinical disease risk.
Incorrect. Diabetic kidney disease results from hemodynamic and metabolic microvascular injury, not immune complexes.
Incorrect. Screening detects diabetic microvascular retinopathy, not retinitis pigmentosa.

atlas.etiology: Insulin resistance coupled with rapid beta-cell failure; driven by visceral adiposity, pubertal hormones, genetics (TCF7L2), and ethnicity. Autoantibody negative (GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8 negative).
atlas.epidemiology: Incidence has risen markedly over the past two decades; peak age 12-16 years; female-to-male ratio ~1.5:1; high prevalence in Black, Hispanic, Native American, and South Asian youth.
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting glucose, 2-hr OGTT, HbA1c; islet autoantibody panel (exclude T1D); baseline urine microalbumin/Cr, lipid profile, ALT/AST, dilated eye exam; in HHS: effective osmolality, BUN/Cr.

therapies.text: Metformin: initiate at 500 mg orally once daily with meals; titrate weekly by 500 mg up to 1000 mg BID (max 2000 mg/day). If HbA1c >=8.5% or glucose >=250 mg/dL, add basal insulin (glargine/degludec) 0.25-0.5 units/kg/day SC. Second-line: Liraglutide 0.6 mg SC daily titrated to 1.8 mg daily, or Dulaglutide 0.75-1.5 mg SC weekly for youth >=10 years.

pillars.label: Pediatric Lipid Screening Guidelines
pillars.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) recommend a two-tiered screening strategy for pediatric dyslipidemia: (1) Universal lipid screening for all children once between ages 9 and 11 years, and once between ages 17 and 21 years (using non-fasting non-HDL cholesterol or a fasting lipid profile); and (2) Targeted screening starting at age 2 years (fasting lipid profile) for children with a family history of premature cardiovascular disease (men <55 years, women <65 years) or parent with total cholesterol >=240 mg/dL, or children with high-risk personal conditions (type 1/2 diabetes, hypertension, BMI >=95th percentile, CKD, post-cardiac transplant, Kawasaki disease with aneurysms).

pillars.label: Pediatric Lipid Thresholds and Classification
pillars.text: Pediatric cutoffs define: Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (LDL-C): Acceptable <110 mg/dL (<2.8 mmol/L), Borderline 110-129 mg/dL, Elevated >=130 mg/dL (>=3.4 mmol/L); High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (HDL-C): Acceptable >45 mg/dL, Borderline 40-45 mg/dL, Low <40 mg/dL; Triglycerides (TG): in children 0-9 years, Acceptable <75 mg/dL, Elevated >=100 mg/dL; in youth 10-19 years, Acceptable <90 mg/dL, Elevated >=130 mg/dL. Primary dyslipidemias represent monogenic defects, whereas secondary dyslipidemias stem from obesity/insulin resistance (mild-moderate hypertriglyceridemia with low HDL), nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, or medications.

pillars.label: Familial Hypercholesterolemia (FH)
pillars.text: Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) occurs in ~1 in 250 individuals, caused by autosomal dominant mutations in LDLR (encoding LDL receptor; >85-90%), APOB, or gain-of-function PCSK9 mutations. HeFH is characterized by severe LDL-C elevation (typically 160-400 mg/dL in children), normal triglycerides, tendon xanthomas (pathognomonic nodular thickening of Achilles and extensor digitorum tendons), and premature CAD. Homozygous FH (HoFH; 1 in 300,000) features LDL-C >400-1000 mg/dL, cutaneous planar and tuberous xanthomas in infancy/toddlerhood, aortic root/valvular stenosis, and fatal myocardial infarction before age 20-30 years if untreated.

pillars.label: Severe Hypertriglyceridemia and Chylomicronemia
pillars.text: Severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG >1000 mg/dL [11.3 mmol/L]) carries an acute risk of life-threatening acute necrotizing pancreatitis. Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome (FCS) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in LPL (lipoprotein lipase), APOC2, GPIHBP1, APOA5, or LMF1. In FCS, circulating chylomicrons cannot be cleared, producing lactescent 'milky' plasma, eruptive xanthomas (yellowish papules with erythematous bases on buttocks/extensors), lipemia retinalis (salmon-pink retinal vessels), hepatosplenomegaly, and recurrent pancreatitis. The cornerstone of FCS therapy is strict dietary fat restriction to <10-15% of total caloric intake (typically <15-20 g fat/day).

pillars.label: Statin Pharmacotherapy Protocols
pillars.text: HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins: pravastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin) are the first-line pharmacotherapy for pediatric hypercholesterolemia, approved for youth >=10 years (or >=8-10 years in severe FH). Indications after a 6-month trial of Cardiovascular Health Integrated Lifestyle Diet (CHILD-2): (1) LDL-C persistently >=190 mg/dL; OR (2) LDL-C persistently >=160 mg/dL with a family history of premature CVD or >=2 moderate cardiovascular risk factors; OR (3) LDL-C >=130 mg/dL in children with high-risk conditions (diabetes, CKD, cardiac transplant). Treatment targets LDL-C <130 mg/dL (<100 mg/dL in high-risk). Ezetimibe (10 mg daily) and PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab) are adjunctive options.

cards.q: At what two specific pediatric age intervals is universal lipid screening officially recommended by the AAP and NHLBI?
cards.a: Once between ages 9 and 11 years, and once between ages 17 and 21 years.

cards.q: What is the defined threshold for an 'elevated' LDL cholesterol level in children and adolescents?
cards.a: LDL-C >=130 mg/dL (>=3.4 mmol/L); acceptable is <110 mg/dL, and borderline is 110-129 mg/dL.

cards.q: At what persistent LDL-C level is statin pharmacotherapy indicated in a 12-year-old child without other cardiovascular risk factors?
cards.a: LDL-C persistently >=190 mg/dL despite a 6-month trial of dietary and lifestyle modification.

cards.q: What circulating triglyceride threshold indicates high risk for acute pancreatitis requiring immediate medical and dietary intervention?
cards.a: Serum triglycerides >=1000 mg/dL (and especially >2000 mg/dL), representing massive chylomicronemia.

cards.q: What is the most common gene mutated in autosomal dominant heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH)?
cards.a: The LDLR gene (encoding the low-density lipoprotein receptor), accounting for >85-90% of identified mutations.

cards.q: What physical examination finding is pathognomonic for severe heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in older children?
cards.a: Tendon xanthomas, particularly nodular thickening of the Achilles tendons and extensor tendons of the hands.

cards.q: What is the foundational dietary therapy for children with familial chylomicronemia syndrome (LPL deficiency)?
cards.a: Extreme restriction of dietary fat to less than 10-15% of total daily caloric intake (typically <15-20 grams of fat per day).

mcqs.q: An 11-year-old boy undergoes routine universal lipid screening. Fasting lipid profile reveals: total cholesterol 284 mg/dL, triglycerides 95 mg/dL, HDL-C 48 mg/dL, and LDL-C 217 mg/dL. His father suffered a fatal myocardial infarction at age 38. Physical examination reveals nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons. After 6 months of strict dietary modification (CHILD-2 diet), his repeat fasting LDL-C remains 208 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Initiate HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) therapy, such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, targeting LDL-C <130 mg/dL
Continue dietary modification alone without medications until age 18
Initiate fibrate therapy with fenofibrate
Perform emergency coronary artery bypass grafting
mcqs.explanation: This patient has heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HeFH), documented by severe LDL elevation (>190 mg/dL), tendon xanthomas, and a strong family history of premature CAD. NHLBI and AAP guidelines recommend initiating statin pharmacotherapy (e.g., atorvastatin 10 mg or rosuvastatin 5-10 mg daily) in children >=10 years whose LDL-C remains persistently >=190 mg/dL (or >=160 mg/dL with premature CVD family history) after lifestyle intervention. The therapeutic target is LDL-C <130 mg/dL.
option_notes: Correct. Statin therapy is the guideline-directed first-line therapy for children >=10 years with persistent LDL-C >=190 mg/dL.
Incorrect. Delaying pharmacotherapy until age 18 allows extensive coronary atheroma accumulation and early cardiovascular death.
Incorrect. Fibrates are indicated for hypertriglyceridemia, not isolated familial hypercholesterolemia.
Incorrect. Coronary bypass is an operative intervention for active severe ischemic disease, not initial medical management.

mcqs.q: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the clinic for yellow-orange papules with erythematous bases on her buttocks, elbows, and knees (eruptive xanthomas). Her blood sample drawn in the laboratory separates into a supernatant that resembles heavy cream over clear infranatant. Fasting triglycerides are 2450 mg/dL, while total cholesterol is 210 mg/dL. Genetic testing confirms biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the LPL gene. What acute medical emergency is she at highest risk for developing?
options: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis
Acute myocardial infarction
Hepatic encephalopathy
Rhabdomyolysis
mcqs.explanation: Familial Chylomicronemia Syndrome (FCS) caused by LPL deficiency results in massive accumulation of circulating chylomicrons, eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, and triglyceride concentrations exceeding 1000-2000 mg/dL. The most dangerous acute complication of severe hypertriglyceridemia is acute necrotizing pancreatitis, triggered when pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes massive chylomicron triglycerides, generating toxic free fatty acids that cause capillary thrombosis and acinar necrosis.
option_notes: Correct. Severe hypertriglyceridemia (>1000-2000 mg/dL) precipitates acute, life-threatening pancreatitis.
Incorrect. Myocardial infarction is a long-term risk of hypercholesterolemia (high LDL), not acute chylomicronemia in a 4-year-old.
Incorrect. FCS does not primarily cause acute hepatic encephalopathy.
Incorrect. Rhabdomyolysis is an adverse drug reaction or metabolic myopathy, not the hallmark complication of FCS.

mcqs.q: What is the mechanism of action of ezetimibe, an adjunctive medication used in children with refractory familial hypercholesterolemia who do not meet LDL targets on statins alone?
options: Selective inhibition of the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) transporter in the jejunal brush border, blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption
Inhibition of hepatic HMG-CoA reductase
Binding and sequestration of intestinal bile acids
Monoclonal inhibition of proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9)
mcqs.explanation: Ezetimibe localizes to the brush border of the small intestine and selectively inhibits the Niemann-Pick C1-Like 1 (NPC1L1) sterol transporter. This inhibits the absorption of biliary and dietary cholesterol into enterocytes, reducing intestinal cholesterol delivery to the liver, upregulating hepatic LDL receptors, and lowering circulating LDL-C by an additional 15-20% when added to a statin.
option_notes: Correct. Ezetimibe inhibits NPC1L1 in enterocytes, blocking intestinal cholesterol absorption.
Incorrect. HMG-CoA reductase inhibition is the mechanism of statins.
Incorrect. Bile acid sequestration is the mechanism of colesevelam and cholestyramine.
Incorrect. PCSK9 monoclonal antibody inhibition is the mechanism of evolocumab and alirocumab.

mcqs.q: An 18-month-old child presents with extensive planar xanthomas in the interdigital webs of the hands, popliteal fossae, and buttocks. Fasting lipid panel reveals total cholesterol 840 mg/dL, LDL-C 780 mg/dL, and normal triglycerides. Echocardiogram reveals supravalvular aortic stenosis and aortic root thickening. Both parents have mild hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C ~175 mg/dL). What is the diagnosis?
options: Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HoFH)
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (Type III hyperlipidemia)
Niemann-Pick disease type C
Familial combined hyperlipidemia
mcqs.explanation: Homozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia (HoFH) is a rare, severe condition (1:300,000) caused by biallelic LDLR (or APOB/PCSK9) mutations inherited from both heterozygous parents. Hallmark features include extreme LDL-C elevations (>400-1000 mg/dL), early planar cutaneous xanthomas in infancy/toddlerhood, and rapid development of aortic root atheroma/supravalvular aortic stenosis and fatal myocardial infarction in early childhood without aggressive treatment (such as LDL apheresis and lomitapide/evinacumab).
option_notes: Correct. LDL-C >700 mg/dL, planar xanthomas in infancy, and aortic root stenosis confirm Homozygous FH.
Incorrect. Type III hyperlipidemia features equal elevation of cholesterol and triglycerides (remnant removal disease), presenting in adulthood.
Incorrect. Niemann-Pick type C is a lysosomal storage disease presenting with neurodegeneration and hepatosplenomegaly.
Incorrect. Familial combined hyperlipidemia presents with moderate elevations of both LDL and triglycerides in adults.

mcqs.q: A 13-year-old obese male with BMI at the 98th percentile has a fasting lipid profile showing: total cholesterol 195 mg/dL, triglycerides 280 mg/dL, HDL-C 32 mg/dL, and calculated LDL-C 107 mg/dL. Fasting ALT is 55 U/L. What is the most likely etiology of this lipid abnormality?
options: Obesity-associated dyslipidemia secondary to insulin resistance and increased hepatic VLDL production
Lipoprotein lipase deficiency
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
Abetalipoproteinemia
mcqs.explanation: The most common lipid abnormality in pediatric practice is secondary dyslipidemia related to obesity and insulin resistance. The characteristic atherogenic lipid triad consists of: (1) elevated fasting triglycerides (typically 150-400 mg/dL) driven by excessive hepatic VLDL synthesis and impaired LPL clearance; (2) low HDL cholesterol (<40 mg/dL); and (3) normal or borderline LDL-C with an increased proportion of atherogenic small dense LDL particles. It is frequently accompanied by metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (elevated ALT).
option_notes: Correct. Obesity and insulin resistance characteristically cause high triglycerides, low HDL-C, and normal/borderline LDL-C.
Incorrect. LPL deficiency causes extreme hypertriglyceridemia (>1000-2000 mg/dL) with chylomicronemia, not mild TG elevation of 280 mg/dL.
Incorrect. Heterozygous FH features marked isolated elevation of LDL-C with normal triglycerides.
Incorrect. Abetalipoproteinemia causes complete absence of apoB-containing lipoproteins with undetectable LDL and triglycerides.

atlas.etiology: Primary: HeFH / HoFH (LDLR, APOB, PCSK9); FCS (LPL, APOC2, GPIHBP1); familial combined hyperlipidemia. Secondary: Obesity-associated insulin resistance (hypertriglyceridemia + low HDL), nephrotic syndrome, hypothyroidism, CKD, diabetes.
atlas.epidemiology: HeFH prevalence is 1:250; most common monogenic cardiovascular disorder. Obesity-associated dyslipidemia affects >20-30% of obese adolescents.
atlas.diagnostics: Universal screening at 9-11 yr and 17-21 yr; fasting lipid panel (total chol, TG, HDL-C, direct LDL-C, non-HDL-C); liver enzymes (ALT/AST), TSH, urinalysis; LDLR/APOB/PCSK9 genetic sequencing.

therapies.text: Atorvastatin: initiate at 10 mg orally once daily in children >=10 years; titrate up to 20-40 mg daily to achieve LDL-C <130 mg/dL (or <100 mg/dL in high-risk). Rosuvastatin: 5-20 mg daily. Pravastatin: 10-40 mg daily. If target not met, add Ezetimibe 10 mg daily.

Extreme fat restriction: restrict total dietary fat to <10-15% of total caloric intake (typically <15-20 g/day of fat) to keep triglycerides <1000 mg/dL and prevent acute pancreatitis. Supplement with fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K).

pillars.label: Anorexia Nervosa Neuroendocrine Adaptation
pillars.text: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a serious psychiatric disorder characterized by pathological restriction of energy intake, distorted body image, and intense fear of weight gain, resulting in severe state of chronic undernutrition and negative energy balance. The endocrine alterations in AN represent an evolutionary conserved adaptive survival mechanism designed to downregulate metabolic rate, shut down non-essential reproductive and skeletal functions, and mobilize energy substrates to preserve vital cerebral and cardiac homeostasis.

pillars.label: Endocrine Axes in Under-Nutrition (AN)
pillars.text: Starvation profoundly reprograms all major neuroendocrine axes: (1) HPG axis: hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (leptin deficiency leads to loss of pulsatile hypothalamic GnRH release, prepubertal LH/FSH suppression, low estradiol/testosterone, and functional hypothalamic amenorrhea); (2) GH / IGF-1 axis: acquired growth hormone resistance (elevated circulating GH levels due to absence of negative feedback, combined with low serum IGF-1 due to downregulation of hepatic GH receptors); (3) HPT axis: non-thyroidal illness / 'low T3 syndrome' (low total and free T3, elevated reverse T3, normal/low-normal T4 and TSH; exogenous thyroid hormone is contraindicated); (4) HPA axis: hypercortisolemia (elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol and loss of diurnal rhythm due to enhanced hypothalamic CRH drive and impaired cortisol clearance).

pillars.label: Bone Mineral Loss in Anorexia Nervosa
pillars.text: Severe bone loss occurs rapidly in adolescents with AN, with >80-90% displaying osteopenia and up to 40-50% meeting criteria for osteoporosis. The pathophysiology is multifactorial, driven by severe hypoestrogenemia (accelerating osteoclastic resorption), hypercortisolemia (inhibiting osteoblast differentiation), low IGF-1 (reducing bone formation), and leptin/calcium deficiency. Weight recovery and nutritional rehabilitation are the primary therapies. In adolescents with persistent amenorrhea (>6 months) and low bone density, physiological transdermal 17-beta estradiol (100 mcg matrix patch with cyclic oral micronized progesterone) significantly increases spinal and hip bone mineral density; standard oral contraceptive pills are INEFFECTIVE for bone protection because oral ethinyl estradiol undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism, suppressing IGF-1.

pillars.label: Endocrine Alterations in Pediatric Obesity
pillars.text: Childhood obesity is characterized by hyperinsulinemia and peripheral insulin resistance, driving several endocrine adaptations: (1) Adipokine dysregulation: hyperleptinemia (reflecting central leptin resistance) and hypoadiponectinemia; (2) Linear growth and pubertal timing: accelerated linear growth in prepubertal years despite low or blunted growth hormone peaks on provocative testing ('pseudo-GH deficiency', distinguished from true GH deficiency by normal serum IGF-1 concentrations); bone age is frequently mildly advanced, but final adult height is normal; (3) Female reproductive axis: downregulation of hepatic SHBG elevates free testosterone, promoting hyperandrogenism, hirsutism, and adolescent PCOS; earlier onset of breast thelarche is common.

pillars.label: Metabolic Complications and Management
pillars.text: Cardiometabolic sequelae of pediatric obesity include Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatotic Liver Disease (MAFLD; formerly NAFLD; elevated ALT >22-26 U/L in girls, >26 U/L in boys), dyslipidemia, hypertension, and impaired glucose tolerance / T2D. Comprehensive family-based lifestyle modification (dietary caloric reduction, >=60 minutes of daily moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, screen time reduction) is the foundation of management. Pharmacological adjuncts for youth >=12 years with severe obesity include GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide 2.4 mg SC weekly, liraglutide 3.0 mg SC daily) which act centrally on POMC/CART neurons to reduce appetite and produce substantial weight loss.

cards.q: What characteristic discordance occurs in the growth hormone axis in patients with anorexia nervosa?
cards.a: Elevated circulating growth hormone (GH) levels paired with low serum IGF-1 concentrations, reflecting starvation-induced hepatic growth hormone resistance.

cards.q: What thyroid hormone pattern defines the non-thyroidal illness syndrome seen in anorexia nervosa, and should it be treated?
cards.a: Low total and free T3, elevated reverse T3, and normal/low-normal T4 and TSH ('low T3 syndrome'); it is an adaptive conservation state and thyroid hormone replacement is contraindicated.

cards.q: Why is transdermal 17-beta estradiol superior to combined oral contraceptive pills for restoring bone density in adolescents with anorexia nervosa?
cards.a: Transdermal estradiol bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism, preserving liver IGF-1 synthesis, whereas oral ethinyl estradiol suppresses hepatic IGF-1, preventing bone accretion.

cards.q: How does 'pseudo-GH deficiency' in childhood obesity differ biochemically from true organic growth hormone deficiency?
cards.a: Obese children show blunted GH peaks on provocative stimulation testing, but have normal serum IGF-1 levels and normal or accelerated linear growth velocity.

cards.q: What circulating alterations in leptin and adiponectin characterize obesity-associated metabolic dysfunction?
cards.a: Elevated serum leptin (reflecting adipocyte expansion and central leptin resistance) and decreased serum adiponectin.

cards.q: How does the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis respond to chronic starvation in anorexia nervosa?
cards.a: Hypercortisolemia develops with elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol and loss of diurnal rhythm, driven by increased hypothalamic CRH drive and impaired hepatic cortisol breakdown.

cards.q: Which GLP-1 receptor agonist is FDA-approved for chronic weight management in pediatric patients aged >=12 years with obesity?
cards.a: Semaglutide 2.4 mg administered subcutaneously once weekly (and liraglutide 3.0 mg daily).

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old girl with severe anorexia nervosa has lost 18 kg over the past 8 months. Her current BMI is 14.8 kg/m2. She has been amenorrheic for 7 months. Endocrine laboratory evaluation reveals: serum LH 0.4 IU/L, FSH 1.2 IU/L, estradiol <10 pg/mL, basal growth hormone 18 ng/mL (elevated), IGF-1 92 ng/mL (severely low), total T3 45 ng/dL (low), free T4 0.8 ng/dL (low-normal), and TSH 1.4 mIU/L. What is the physiological mechanism underlying her elevated growth hormone and low IGF-1?
options: Starvation-induced hepatic growth hormone resistance secondary to downregulation of cell-surface GH receptors
A growth hormone-secreting pituitary somatotrope adenoma
Ectopic production of GHRH by retroperitoneal adipose tissue
Excessive renal tubular reabsorption of pituitary growth hormone
mcqs.explanation: In anorexia nervosa and severe under-nutrition, starvation triggers acquired peripheral growth hormone resistance. Nutrient and insulin deprivation causes marked downregulation of hepatic growth hormone receptors and post-receptor signaling pathways (JAK2/STAT5b). Consequently, hepatic synthesis of IGF-1 falls precipitously. The absence of negative feedback inhibition by circulating IGF-1 on the pituitary somatotropes leads to compensatory hypersecretion of growth hormone.
option_notes: Correct. Starvation causes hepatic GH receptor downregulation, causing profound IGF-1 deficiency and high compensatory GH.
Incorrect. A GH-secreting somatotrope adenoma (acromegaly/gigantism) produces high IGF-1 and accelerated growth, not starvation with low IGF-1.
Incorrect. Adipose tissue does not secrete ectopic GHRH in anorexia nervosa.
Incorrect. Elevated GH is due to increased pituitary pulsatile secretion, not altered renal handling.

mcqs.q: A 17-year-old female with anorexia nervosa who has been amenorrheic for 14 months undergoes dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Her lumbar spine bone mineral density Z-score is -2.8. In addition to nutritional rehabilitation and calcium/vitamin D repletion, what pharmacological intervention has been shown in randomized controlled trials to effectively increase bone mineral density in this setting?
options: Physiological replacement with transdermal 17-beta estradiol patches combined with cyclic oral micronized progesterone
Combined oral contraceptive pills containing 35 mcg ethinyl estradiol
Intravenous zoledronic acid infusion every 6 months
Subcutaneous teriparatide (PTH 1-34) monotherapy
mcqs.explanation: Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that physiological transdermal 17-beta estradiol (100 mcg patches applied twice weekly) combined with cyclic oral micronized progesterone (200 mg/day for 12 days/month) significantly increases lumbar spine and femoral bone mineral density in adolescents with anorexia nervosa. In contrast, standard oral contraceptive pills (ethinyl estradiol) do not improve bone density because hepatic first-pass metabolism suppresses hepatic IGF-1 synthesis.
option_notes: Correct. Transdermal estradiol with cyclic progesterone bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism and increases bone density in AN.
Incorrect. Oral contraceptive pills suppress hepatic IGF-1 production through first-pass metabolism and fail to increase bone mass in AN.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates are not first-line in adolescents with anorexia nervosa due to long-term skeletal retention and teratogenicity concerns.
Incorrect. Teriparatide is an anabolic agent approved for postmenopausal osteoporosis, not standard for adolescent anorexia nervosa.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old girl with anorexia nervosa is found on routine screening to have total T3 42 ng/dL (reference: 85-170 ng/dL), free T4 0.9 ng/dL (reference: 0.9-1.8 ng/dL), and TSH 1.6 mIU/L (reference: 0.5-4.5 mIU/L). Reverse T3 is elevated. She complains of cold intolerance and has bradycardia (pulse 48 bpm). What is the appropriate clinical approach to her thyroid status?
options: Withhold thyroid hormone replacement; this represents an adaptive non-thyroidal illness syndrome that will resolve with nutritional refeeding
Initiate oral levothyroxine 50 mcg daily to restore normal metabolic rate
Initiate oral liothyronine (T3) 25 mcg daily to normalize circulating T3
Perform radioiodine uptake scan to rule out toxic adenoma
mcqs.explanation: The thyroid hormone pattern in anorexia nervosa represents non-thyroidal illness syndrome ('low T3 syndrome'), an adaptive hypometabolic state mediated by down-regulation of 5'-deiodinase (reducing T4 to T3 conversion) and upregulation of DIO3 (increasing reverse T3). This adaptation minimizes energy expenditure and tissue catabolism during severe energy deficit. Administering exogenous thyroid hormone (T4 or T3) is strictly contraindicated because it accelerates protein breakdown, induces cardiac arrhythmias, and worsens cachexia.
option_notes: Correct. Low T3 in anorexia is an adaptive conservation mechanism; exogenous thyroid hormone is harmful and contraindicated.
Incorrect. Levothyroxine increases basal metabolic rate and tissue catabolism in a starving patient.
Incorrect. Liothyronine administration worsens cardiac strain and accelerates wasting.
Incorrect. Scintigraphy is not indicated for non-thyroidal illness syndrome without a nodule.

mcqs.q: A 9-year-old boy with severe generalized obesity (BMI 29 kg/m2, >99th percentile) undergoes endocrine evaluation. His linear growth velocity is 7.2 cm/year (accelerated, 85th percentile for age), and his bone age is 10.5 years. Provocative growth hormone testing with clonidine reveals a peak GH of 4.2 ng/mL (subnormal; cut-off <7-10 ng/mL). Serum IGF-1 is normal (240 ng/mL). How should these findings be interpreted?
options: Pseudo-GH deficiency secondary to obesity-induced blunted somatotrope responsiveness, with normal tissue IGF-1 action and accelerated growth
Isolated organic pituitary growth hormone deficiency requiring daily rhGH therapy
Craniopharyngioma with panhypopituitarism
Growth hormone receptor insensitivity (Laron syndrome)
mcqs.explanation: Children with simple obesity characteristically demonstrate blunted stimulated growth hormone secretion on provocative testing ('pseudo-GH deficiency'). Despite low GH peaks, these children maintain normal or elevated serum IGF-1 concentrations, accelerated prepubertal linear growth velocity, and normal or mildly advanced skeletal maturation. This is mediated by hyperinsulinemia and altered neuroendocrine feedback. Daily rhGH therapy is not indicated.
option_notes: Correct. Pseudo-GH deficiency in obesity features blunted GH peaks but normal IGF-1 and accelerated linear growth.
Incorrect. True GH deficiency causes profound linear growth deceleration and delayed bone age, not accelerated growth.
Incorrect. Craniopharyngioma causes severe growth failure, low IGF-1, and visual field deficits.
Incorrect. Laron syndrome features extreme short stature, elevated GH, and undetectable/low IGF-1.

mcqs.q: What is the primary mechanism by which visceral obesity and hyperinsulinemia contribute to clinical hyperandrogenism and hirsutism in adolescent girls?
options: Hyperinsulinemia directly suppresses hepatic production of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), markedly elevating the circulating free, unbound testosterone fraction
Visceral adipocytes directly synthesize testosterone from cholesterol via CYP17A1
Insulin blocks adrenal 21-hydroxylase activity
Leptin stimulates pituitary LH secretion to adult male levels
mcqs.explanation: Hyperinsulinemia resulting from obesity-induced insulin resistance acts directly on hepatocytes to suppress the gene expression and synthesis of sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). Reduced circulating SHBG lowers the binding capacity of serum, resulting in a marked increase in the biologically active free, unbound testosterone fraction. Concurrently, hyperinsulinemia synergizes with LH in ovarian theca cells to augment androgen production.
option_notes: Correct. Insulin suppresses hepatic SHBG synthesis, increasing the biologically active free testosterone fraction.
Incorrect. Adipocytes express aromatase (converting androgens to estrogens), but do not synthesize de novo testosterone from cholesterol.
Incorrect. Insulin does not block 21-hydroxylase; 21-hydroxylase deficiency is a genetic enzyme defect (CAH).
Incorrect. Leptin does not drive LH to adult male levels.

atlas.etiology: Anorexia Nervosa: Psychiatric starvation; adaptive neuroendocrine down-regulation (low T3, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, high GH/low IGF-1, hypercortisolemia). Obesity: Adiposity, insulin resistance, hyperleptinemia, blunted GH peaks (pseudo-GH deficiency), low SHBG.
atlas.epidemiology: Anorexia nervosa affects 0.5-1.0% of adolescent females (10:1 female predominance). Pediatric obesity affects ~20% of children in developed nations.
atlas.diagnostics: AN: LH, FSH, estradiol, total/free T3, rT3, TSH, GH, IGF-1, 24-hr urinary free cortisol; DXA bone mineral density; ECG (QTc, bradycardia). Obesity: Fasting lipid panel, ALT/AST (MAFLD), fasting glucose/HbA1c or OGTT, total/free testosterone, SHBG.

therapies.section: Bone Protection in Adolescent Anorexia Nervosa
therapies.text: Transdermal 17-beta estradiol 100 mcg patch applied twice weekly plus oral micronized progesterone 200 mg daily on days 1-12 of each calendar month for adolescents with amenorrhea >6 months and DXA Z-score <-2.0. Avoid oral contraceptive pills for bone health. Calcium 1000-1300 mg/day and vitamin D 600-1000 IU/day.

Semaglutide: initiate at 0.25 mg SC once weekly for 4 weeks; escalate monthly (0.5 mg, 1.0 mg, 1.7 mg) to target maintenance dose of 2.4 mg SC once weekly for youth >=12 years with BMI >=95th percentile, combined with lifestyle intervention. Alternatively, Liraglutide 3.0 mg SC daily.

pillars.label: Consensus Nomenclature and Physiology
pillars.text: In 2022, an international endocrine consensus updated the nomenclature of diabetes insipidus to eliminate confusion with diabetes mellitus: 'central diabetes insipidus' is designated Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D), and 'nephrogenic diabetes insipidus' is designated Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R). Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is synthesized by hypothalamic magnocellular neurons in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and transported down the infundibulum to the posterior pituitary. In response to hyperosmolality (>280-285 mOsm/kg) or hypovolemia, AVP binds basolateral V2 receptors (AVPR2) on renal collecting duct principal cells, triggering cAMP-mediated exocytic insertion of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels to concentrate urine.

pillars.label: Etiology of AVP Deficiency (AVP-D)
pillars.text: AVP-D results from deficient synthesis, processing, or secretion of AVP. Etiologies include: (1) Sellar/suprasellar neoplasms: craniopharyngioma, dysgerminoma/germinoma, pituitary adenoma; (2) Infiltrative and inflammatory diseases: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH; classic triad of bone lesions, exophthalmos, and AVP-D), neurosarcoidosis, autoimmune lymphocytic infundibuloneurohypophysitis; (3) Neurosurgical trauma (triphasic response: phase 1 acute polyuria [days 1-2]; phase 2 transient SIADH with hyponatremia due to uncontrolled AVP leak [days 3-7]; phase 3 permanent AVP-D [days 8+]); (4) Congenital/midline structural malformations (septo-optic dysplasia, holoprosencephaly); and (5) Genetic: autosomal dominant AVP-neurophysin II (AVP) mutations and Wolfram syndrome (WFS1; DIDMOAD).

pillars.label: Etiology of AVP Resistance (AVP-R)
pillars.text: AVP-R is characterized by normal or elevated circulating AVP but renal collecting duct unresponsiveness. Congenital forms include X-linked recessive mutations in AVPR2 (accounting for >90% of congenital cases; hemizygous males present in infancy with severe hypernatremic dehydration, fever, vomiting, and failure to thrive) and autosomal recessive or dominant mutations in AQP2 (encoding aquaporin-2). Acquired causes include medications (lithium, amphotericin B), chronic severe hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, obstructive uropathy, and sickle cell nephropathy.

pillars.label: Diagnostic Protocols and Copeptin
pillars.text: Clinical presentation features polyuria (urine output >4-5 mL/kg/hour in infants or >2-3 L/m2/day in children), polydipsia, nocturia, enuresis, and hypernatremic dehydration if fluid access is restricted. Standard diagnosis historically relied on the water deprivation test: fluid restriction until serum osmolality >300 mOsm/kg or sodium >145 mEq/L, followed by desmopressin challenge (rise in urine osmolality >50-100% confirms AVP-D, whereas failure to concentrate <300 mOsm/kg confirms AVP-R). Modern diagnostics utilize plasma copeptin (the stable C-terminal cleavage peptide of pre-pro-AVP): basal unstimulated copeptin >21.4 pmol/L confirms AVP-R without water deprivation; hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin <4.9 pmol/L confirms AVP-D. Sellar MRI demonstrates loss of the normal T1-hyperintense posterior pituitary bright spot in AVP-D.

pillars.label: Medical Management and Safety Precautions
pillars.text: AVP-D is treated with desmopressin (DDAVP), a synthetic analog with selective V2 antidiuretic activity and negligible V1 vasopressor action. Formulations include oral melt tablets (60-120 mcg TID), oral tablets (0.1-0.2 mg TID), and intranasal spray (2.5-10 mcg once or twice daily). Crucial safety rule: each subsequent dose must be delayed until a clear breakthrough period of polyuria occurs to prevent water intoxication and fatal hyponatremic seizures! In infants, DDAVP carries extreme risk of water overload; infants are managed primarily with high-volume free water or low-solute formula. AVP-R is treated with low-solute/low-sodium diet, free access to water, and a thiazide diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide 2-4 mg/kg/day) paired with amiloride or indomethacin (1.5-3.0 mg/kg/day).

cards.q: What are the updated international consensus terms for central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus?
cards.a: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D) for central DI, and Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R) for nephrogenic DI.

cards.q: What are the three distinct chronological phases of the triphasic response following pituitary neurosurgery?
cards.a: Phase 1 (days 1-2): acute polyuria (axonal shock); Phase 2 (days 3-7): transient SIADH with hyponatremia (uncontrolled AVP leak from dying axons); Phase 3 (day 8+): permanent AVP-D.

cards.q: What is the most frequent genetic defect in congenital AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI), and what is its inheritance?
cards.a: Inactivating mutations in the AVPR2 gene (encoding the V2 vasopressin receptor), inherited in an X-linked recessive manner (>90% of congenital cases).

cards.q: What circulating peptide biomarker has emerged as the gold standard to differentiate AVP deficiency from AVP resistance without prolonged water deprivation?
cards.a: Plasma copeptin (the C-terminal fragment of the AVP precursor); basal levels >21.4 pmol/L diagnose AVP-R, while stimulated levels <4.9 pmol/L confirm AVP-D.

cards.q: What critical administration rule must be observed when dosing desmopressin (DDAVP) to avoid severe water intoxication?
cards.a: Each dose must be withheld until a distinct breakthrough period of polyuria occurs, verifying water excretion and preventing life-threatening hyponatremia.

cards.q: What characteristic finding on T1-weighted cranial MRI is typically absent in patients with AVP deficiency?
cards.a: The hyperintense 'posterior pituitary bright spot' (which represents stored phospholipid-vesicle bound vasopressin) is absent in AVP-D.

cards.q: What pharmacological combination is used to treat congenital AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)?
cards.a: A low-sodium diet combined with a thiazide diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide) and either amiloride or indomethacin.

mcqs.q: A 9-year-old boy presents with intense polydipsia, drinking 6 liters of ice water daily, and waking 4 to 5 times per night to urinate. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L, serum osmolality is 304 mOsm/kg, and random urine osmolality is 95 mOsm/kg. Subcutaneous desmopressin (DDAVP 1 mcg) is administered. Two hours later, repeat urine osmolality rises to 680 mOsm/kg with a sharp decline in urine output. Sellar MRI demonstrates complete absence of the normal T1 posterior pituitary bright spot and thickening of the pituitary stalk. What is the diagnosis?
options: Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D / central DI)
Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R / nephrogenic DI)
Primary psychogenic polydipsia
Solute diuresis secondary to type 1 diabetes
mcqs.explanation: This patient has classic Arginine Vasopressin Deficiency (AVP-D; central DI): hypertonic polyuria with low baseline urine osmolality (<100 mOsm/kg) in the presence of hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm/kg), followed by a >100% surge in urine osmolality (>600 mOsm/kg) after desmopressin administration. Absence of the T1 posterior pituitary bright spot and stalk thickening on MRI confirm hypothalamic-neurohypophyseal pathology (such as germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis).
option_notes: Correct. Hypertonic polyuria, dramatic >100% response to desmopressin, and absent MRI bright spot confirm AVP-D.
Incorrect. AVP-R is completely unresponsive to desmopressin, with urine osmolality remaining <300 mOsm/kg.
Incorrect. Primary polydipsia presents with hyponatremia/low serum osmolality and concentrates urine spontaneously with fluid restriction.
Incorrect. Solute diuresis in T1D features heavy glucosuria and high urine specific gravity/osmolality, not dilute urine.

mcqs.q: A 12-year-old girl undergoes gross total resection of a suprasellar craniopharyngioma. On postoperative day 1, her urine output surges to 6 mL/kg/hour, urine specific gravity is 1.002, and serum sodium is 149 mEq/L. She is started on IV desmopressin. On postoperative day 4, while still receiving desmopressin, her urine output abruptly plummets, and serum sodium drops sharply to 121 mEq/L. What physiological phase of the post-hypophysectomy triphasic response has occurred?
options: Phase 2: Transient SIADH secondary to uncontrolled AVP release from degenerating hypothalamic neurons
Phase 1: Acute vasopressin deficiency due to surgical axon shock
Phase 3: Permanent neurohypophyseal fibrosis and AVP deficiency
Acute postoperative adrenal crisis
mcqs.explanation: The triphasic response occurs following pituitary stalk or hypothalamic neurosurgery. Phase 1 (days 1-2) is acute DI due to mechanical axon shock. Phase 2 (days 3-7) is transient SIADH: dying, degenerating magnocellular axons unregulatedly release their entire remaining stores of AVP into the circulation, precipitous oliguria and severe dilutional hyponatremia if desmopressin or fluid intake is not halted. Phase 3 (day 8 onward) is permanent AVP-D after all stores are exhausted.
option_notes: Correct. Phase 2 represents transient SIADH from dying axon AVP leakage, causing dilutional hyponatremia.
Incorrect. Phase 1 is the initial transient polyuric DI phase seen on days 1-2.
Incorrect. Phase 3 is the permanent AVP deficiency phase occurring after day 7-8.
Incorrect. Adrenal crisis causes hyponatremia and hyperkalemia with hypotension, not the expected isolated AVP release surge.

mcqs.q: A 3-month-old infant boy presents with recurrent unexplained fevers, vomiting, severe dehydration, and failure to thrive. Laboratory evaluation shows serum sodium 168 mEq/L, serum osmolality 342 mOsm/kg, and simultaneous urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. Subcutaneous desmopressin 2 mcg is administered; two hours later, urine osmolality is unchanged at 115 mOsm/kg, and baseline plasma copeptin is markedly elevated at 48 pmol/L. What is the most likely genetic diagnosis?
options: X-linked Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVPR2 mutation)
Autosomal dominant AVP deficiency (AVP-neurophysin II mutation)
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CYP21A2 mutation)
Bartter syndrome type 1 (SLC12A1 mutation)
mcqs.explanation: This infant has congenital Arginine Vasopressin Resistance (AVP-R; nephrogenic DI), which is X-linked recessive in >90% of cases due to loss-of-function AVPR2 mutations. Hallmark features are extreme hypernatremic dehydration with dilute urine that fails to concentrate following desmopressin, accompanied by high baseline copeptin (>21.4 pmol/L) reflecting appropriate endogenous hypothalamic AVP hypersecretion acting on a completely resistant collecting duct.
option_notes: Correct. Complete lack of response to desmopressin with high copeptin in an infant male confirms X-linked AVPR2 deficiency.
Incorrect. Central AVP deficiency responds briskly to desmopressin and exhibits low copeptin.
Incorrect. CAH causes severe hyponatremia and hyperkalemia (salt-wasting shock), not extreme hypernatremic dehydration.
Incorrect. Bartter syndrome features hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis, not isolated AVP resistance with copeptin >40.

mcqs.q: What is the paradoxical mechanism by which thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) reduce urine volume in patients with AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)?
options: Inhibition of the distal tubule NaCl cotransporter induces mild volume contraction, triggering compensatory proximal tubular reabsorption of sodium and water
Direct binding and activation of renal collecting duct V2 receptors
Inhibition of renal medullary aquaporin-2 degradation
Direct stimulation of hypothalamic vasopressin synthesis
mcqs.explanation: Thiazide diuretics inhibit the Na+-Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule, producing mild natriuresis and extracellular volume depletion. In response to hypovolemia, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and glomerulotubular balance markedly increase sodium and water reabsorption in the proximal tubule. This reduces the total volume of fluid delivered to the collecting ducts, reducing 24-hour urine output by 30-50% in patients with nephrogenic DI.
option_notes: Correct. Thiazides induce mild volume depletion, promoting proximal fluid reabsorption and reducing distal fluid delivery.
Incorrect. Thiazides do not bind or stimulate V2 vasopressin receptors.
Incorrect. Thiazides do not inhibit aquaporin-2 degradation.
Incorrect. Thiazides act on the kidney, not hypothalamic AVP synthesis.

mcqs.q: A 7-year-old child with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) and confirmed AVP deficiency is maintained on oral desmopressin 0.1 mg twice daily.
