The mother is instructed to administer the evening dose only after observing an episode of breakthrough urination. Why is this breakthrough period mandatory?
options: To ensure that water intoxication and life-threatening dilutional hyponatremia do not occur from chronic antidiuresis
To prevent rapid development of tachyphylaxis and drug tolerance
To avoid medication accumulation in the biliary tract
To stimulate endogenous posterior pituitary vasopressin regeneration
mcqs.explanation: Desmopressin produces potent antidiuresis. If consecutive doses are given on a rigid schedule without allowing the drug to wear off, free water intake will exceed urinary excretion, leading to progressive water retention, expansion of intravascular volume, and severe dilutional hyponatremia with brain edema and fatal seizures. Allowing a period of breakthrough polyuria prior to redosing ensures that the patient clears excess free water.
option_notes: Correct. Allowing breakthrough urination prevents water retention and fatal dilutional hyponatremic seizures.
Incorrect. Desmopressin does not undergo significant tachyphylaxis.
Incorrect. Desmopressin is excreted renally, not via biliary accumulation.
Incorrect. Desmopressin is replacement therapy; breakthrough urination does not regenerate destroyed hypothalamic neurons.

atlas.etiology: AVP-D: Craniopharyngioma, germinoma, LCH, pituitary surgery (triphasic response), septo-optic dysplasia, AVP mutations, Wolfram syndrome (WFS1). AVP-R: X-linked AVPR2 mutations (>90%), AQP2 mutations, lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia.
atlas.epidemiology: AVP-D prevalence is 1:25,000; equal sex distribution. Congenital AVP-R is rare (1:100,000 live male births).
atlas.diagnostics: Fasting serum sodium, serum osmolality, urine osmolality; plasma copeptin (basal >21.4 pmol/L confirms AVP-R; stimulated <4.9 confirms AVP-D); water deprivation test with DDAVP challenge; high-resolution sellar MRI.

therapies.text: Desmopressin (DDAVP): Oral melt 60-120 mcg TID, oral tablets 0.1-0.2 mg TID, or intranasal 2.5-10 mcg once or twice daily. Titrate to control polyuria and nocturia while strictly enforcing a breakthrough period of polyuria prior to redosing. In infants, avoid DDAVP; use low-solute formula and free water.

Hydrochlorothiazide 2-4 mg/kg/day orally divided BID combined with amiloride 0.3 mg/kg/day or indomethacin 1.5-3.0 mg/kg/day divided TID, plus low-sodium diet (<1-2 mEq/kg/day) and unrestricted free water access.

pillars.label: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Classification
pillars.text: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndromes (APS) are classified into three major inherited forms: (1) APS-1 (APECED: Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy), an autosomal recessive monogenic disorder caused by mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3; (2) APS-2 (Schmidt syndrome), a polygenic, HLA-DR3/DR4-associated complex disorder characterized by the mandatory presence of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) combined with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes; and (3) IPEX syndrome (Immunodysregulation Polyendocrinopathy Enteropathy X-linked), a fatal infantile disorder caused by FOXP3 mutations.

pillars.label: APS-1 / APECED Triad and Genetics
pillars.text: The autoimmune regulator (AIRE) protein functions in medullary thymic epithelial cells as a master transcription factor driving promiscuous expression of thousands of peripheral tissue-restricted antigens, facilitating central negative selection and apoptosis of autoreactive T cells. AIRE mutations abrogate central tolerance, unleashing multi-organ autoimmunity. The classic diagnostic triad of APS-1 requires >=2 of the following 3 cardinal features (or 1 in siblings of an affected index case): (1) Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC; typically appears before age 5 in oral mucosa, nails, esophagus); (2) Chronic hypoparathyroidism (typically emerges ages 5-10; causes severe hypocalcemia and seizures); and (3) Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease; typically manifests ages 10-15).

pillars.label: Non-Endocrine Manifestations and Type I Interferon Antibodies
pillars.text: APS-1 displays prominent ectodermal and visceral manifestations: dental enamel hypoplasia (pitted/grooved permanent teeth, present in >80%), nail dystrophy, alopecia areata/totalis, vitiligo, keratoconjunctivitis, autoimmune hepatitis, malabsorption, and functional asplenia (conferring lethal risk of encapsulated bacterial sepsis). Highly specific neutralizing autoantibodies against type I interferons (anti-interferon-omega and anti-interferon-alpha2) are present in >95-100% of APS-1 patients from early childhood, preceding clinical endocrinopathies and serving as the definitive screening biomarker.

pillars.label: APS-2 (Schmidt Syndrome)
pillars.text: APS-2 is far more common than APS-1 (prevalence ~1:20,000 vs 1:100,000 for APS-1), exhibiting a 3:1 female predominance with peak presentation in young adulthood and late adolescence. Unlike APS-1, APS-2 is polygenic, linked to HLA-DR3, HLA-DR4, CTLA4, and PTPN22. Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) is the mandatory core component, diagnosed in conjunction with autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis or Graves' disease; Carpenter syndrome) and/or type 1 diabetes. Chronic candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and ectodermal dystrophy do NOT occur in APS-2.

pillars.label: IPEX Syndrome and Therapeutic Principles
pillars.text: IPEX syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by hemizygous mutations in FOXP3 (Xp11.23), the lineage-specification transcription factor required for the development and suppressive function of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells (Tregs). Affected male infants present in the first weeks of life with the lethal triad of: intractable watery secretory diarrhea (autoimmune enteropathy with villous atrophy), early-onset neonatal type 1 diabetes mellitus, and severe eczematous dermatitis. Definitive curative therapy is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) performed early before irreversible organ damage occurs. In APS-1 and APS-2, hormone replacement must be instituted carefully: glucocorticoids MUST precede levothyroxine in combined Addison/hypothyroidism to prevent precipitating acute adrenal crisis.

cards.q: What three cardinal clinical features comprise the diagnostic triad of Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1 / APECED)?
cards.a: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC), chronic hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease); diagnosis requires >=2 of 3 (or 1 in a sibling).

cards.q: What gene is mutated in APS-1, and what is its physiological role in the immune system?
cards.a: The AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3; it mediates ectopic expression of peripheral self-antigens in medullary thymic epithelial cells for negative selection of autoreactive T cells.

cards.q: What neutralizing circulating autoantibodies are present in >95-100% of APS-1 patients from early childhood, serving as a first-line diagnostic biomarker?
cards.a: Autoantibodies against type I interferons, specifically anti-interferon-omega (IFN-omega) and anti-interferon-alpha2 (IFN-alpha2).

cards.q: What endocrine components distinguish APS-2 (Schmidt syndrome) from APS-1?
cards.a: APS-2 requires primary adrenal insufficiency plus autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes, but characteristically lacks chronic candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and ectodermal dystrophy.

cards.q: What classic triad of symptoms characterizes IPEX syndrome in male infants, and what gene is mutated?
cards.a: Intractable secretory enteropathy (diarrhea), neonatal type 1 diabetes, and severe eczematous dermatitis, caused by hemizygous mutations in the FOXP3 gene.

cards.q: What dental enamel abnormality is present in over 80% of children with APS-1?
cards.a: Enamel hypoplasia, characterized by horizontal pitting, grooving, and thinning of the enamel of the permanent dentition.

cards.q: When a patient presents with concurrent untreated primary adrenal insufficiency and severe hypothyroidism, which hormone must be replaced first?
cards.a: Hydrocortisone MUST be initiated before or concurrently with levothyroxine; starting levothyroxine alone accelerates hepatic cortisol metabolism and precipitates fatal adrenal crisis.

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old boy presents with tetany and generalized seizures. Serum calcium is 6.1 mg/dL, phosphate is 8.4 mg/dL, and intact PTH is 4 pg/mL (inappropriately low). His medical history is notable for recurrent, treatment-resistant oral and esophageal thrush since age 18 months, as well as pitted transverse grooves across his permanent incisors. What is the underlying genetic defect?
options: Autosomal recessive mutation in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3
Hemizygous mutation in the FOXP3 gene on chromosome Xp11.23
Heterozygous activating mutation in the CaSR gene
Autosomal dominant mutation in the MEN1 gene
mcqs.explanation: This patient meets criteria for Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1 / APECED), having chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMC), autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, and dental enamel hypoplasia. APS-1 is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the AIRE (autoimmune regulator) gene on chromosome 21q22.3, which disrupts thymic negative selection of autoreactive T-cell clones.
option_notes: Correct. AIRE mutations cause APS-1, presenting with candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and ectodermal dystrophy.
Incorrect. FOXP3 mutations cause IPEX syndrome with infantile diarrhea, neonatal diabetes, and eczema.
Incorrect. CaSR activating mutations cause autosomal dominant hypocalcemia, not candidiasis or enamel hypoplasia.
Incorrect. MEN1 causes primary hyperparathyroidism (hypercalcemia), not hypoparathyroidism.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old girl with established type 1 diabetes presents with progressive fatigue, postural dizziness, weight loss, and darkening of her skin across her palmar creases and gums. Laboratory testing demonstrates serum sodium 128 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, TSH 18.4 mIU/L, free T4 0.6 ng/dL, and morning baseline cortisol 2.2 mcg/dL with plasma ACTH 850 pg/mL. Thyroid antibodies (anti-TPO) and 21-hydroxylase antibodies are strongly positive. What autoimmune syndrome is present?
options: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 2 (APS-2 / Schmidt syndrome)
Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APECED)
McCune-Albright syndrome
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1
mcqs.explanation: Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 2 (APS-2 / Schmidt syndrome) is characterized by the mandatory presence of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease; elevated ACTH, low cortisol, hyperkalemia, hyperpigmentation) in combination with autoimmune thyroid disease (elevated TSH, low FT4) and/or type 1 diabetes. Chronic candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism are absent, distinguishing it from APS-1.
option_notes: Correct. The triad of primary adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune thyroiditis, and type 1 diabetes defines APS-2.
Incorrect. APS-1 features chronic candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and ectodermal dystrophy in early childhood.
Incorrect. McCune-Albright is a mosaic GNAS disorder with fibrous dysplasia and precocious puberty.
Incorrect. MEN1 features parathyroid hyperplasia, pituitary adenomas, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.

mcqs.q: A 3-week-old male infant presents with failure to thrive, severe exfoliative eczematous dermatitis, intractable voluminous watery diarrhea, and a random blood glucose of 480 mg/dL with glucosuria. Flow cytometry demonstrates complete absence of CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ regulatory T cells. What is the diagnosis and definitive curative treatment?
options: IPEX syndrome; allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)
APS-1; high-dose oral fluconazole and calcium carbonate
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID); enzyme replacement therapy with pegademase
Cystic fibrosis; pancreatic enzyme replacement
mcqs.explanation: IPEX (Immunodysregulation Polyendocrinopathy Enteropathy X-linked) syndrome is caused by mutations in FOXP3 on chromosome Xp11.23, leading to absence or functional failure of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells. Male infants present in the first weeks of life with the lethal triad of intractable autoimmune enteropathy (secretory diarrhea), neonatal type 1 diabetes, and severe dermatitis/eczema. Without allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), IPEX is fatal in early childhood.
option_notes: Correct. FOXP3 deficiency causing neonatal diabetes, enteropathy, and eczema is IPEX syndrome, cured by HSCT.
Incorrect. APS-1 presents later in childhood with candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism, not neonatal diabetes and secretory diarrhea.
Incorrect. SCID causes absent T/B cells with opportunistic infections, not the specific triad of neonatal T1D, enteropathy, and eczema.
Incorrect. Cystic fibrosis causes malabsorption, not neonatal autoimmune diabetes with absent Tregs.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old girl with confirmed Autoimmune Polyglandular Syndrome Type 1 (APS-1) has hypoparathyroidism controlled on calcitriol. She is being monitored for development of additional autoimmune endocrinopathies. What is the most common subsequent endocrine component that typically develops between ages 10 and 15 years?
options: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)
Central diabetes insipidus
Primary hyperparathyroidism
Medullary thyroid carcinoma
mcqs.explanation: In APS-1, primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) is the third cardinal component of the diagnostic triad, typically developing between 10 and 15 years of age (following candidiasis in infancy and hypoparathyroidism in early childhood). Annual surveillance with plasma renin activity, morning ACTH, and electrolytes, or testing for 21-hydroxylase antibodies, is mandatory to detect subclinical adrenal insufficiency before fatal crisis occurs.
option_notes: Correct. Addison disease is the third cardinal feature of APS-1, typically developing in late childhood/adolescence.
Incorrect. Central DI is not a component of APS-1.
Incorrect. APS-1 causes autoimmune hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia), not hyperparathyroidism.
Incorrect. Medullary thyroid carcinoma is part of MEN2, not APS-1.

mcqs.q: Why must oral hydrocortisone always be initiated prior to or concurrently with levothyroxine in a patient diagnosed with concurrent Addison disease and autoimmune hypothyroidism?
options: Levothyroxine accelerates hepatic clearance and metabolic turnover of cortisol, which will precipitate acute adrenal crisis in a cortisol-deficient patient
Hydrocortisone prevents thyroid hormone binding to plasma albumin
Levothyroxine causes severe hyperkalemia if given alone
Hydrocortisone inhibits renal excretion of levothyroxine
mcqs.explanation: Thyroid hormone stimulates the hepatic expression of corticosteroid-metabolizing enzymes (such as 11-beta-HSD and 5-alpha/beta-reductases), markedly accelerating the clearance and degradation of endogenous cortisol. In a patient with underlying, untreated adrenal insufficiency, administering levothyroxine alone rapidly depletes residual circulating cortisol, precipitating an acute, life-threatening adrenal crisis with shock and vascular collapse.
option_notes: Correct. Levothyroxine accelerates hepatic cortisol clearance, which triggers acute adrenal crisis if cortisol is not replaced first.
Incorrect. Hydrocortisone does not alter thyroid hormone binding to albumin.
Incorrect. Levothyroxine does not directly cause hyperkalemia; adrenal insufficiency causes hyperkalemia.
Incorrect. Hydrocortisone does not inhibit renal elimination of thyroid hormone.

atlas.etiology: APS-1: Autosomal recessive AIRE mutations (21q22.3); failure of thymic central tolerance. APS-2: Polygenic; HLA-DR3/DR4, CTLA4, PTPN22. IPEX: X-linked recessive FOXP3 mutations (Xp11.23); regulatory T cell deficiency.
atlas.epidemiology: APS-1 prevalence is 1:100,000 (higher in Finns, Sardinians, Iranian Jews). APS-2 prevalence is ~1:20,000 (female predominance 3:1). IPEX is a very rare infantile lethal disorder.
atlas.diagnostics: APS-1: Anti-IFN-omega / anti-IFN-alpha2 antibodies; AIRE genetic sequencing; calcium, phosphate, PTH, ACTH, 21-OH antibodies. APS-2: 21-OH antibodies, TSH, anti-TPO, islet antibodies. IPEX: FOXP3 sequencing, Treg flow cytometry.

therapies.text: Hypoparathyroidism: Calcitriol 20-40 ng/kg/day orally plus oral calcium carbonate 30-50 mg/kg/day. Addison disease: Hydrocortisone 8-10 mg/m2/day orally divided TID plus fludrocortisone 0.05-0.2 mg once daily. Chronic candidiasis: Oral fluconazole 3-6 mg/kg/day. Crucial rule: Always start hydrocortisone before levothyroxine.

pillars.label: MEN1 (Wermer Syndrome) Pathobiology
pillars.text: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by inactivating germline mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13, which encodes menin, a nuclear scaffold protein regulating gene transcription, cell cycle progression, and genome integrity. Following Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, somatic loss of the remaining wild-type allele leads to tumor development in classic endocrine target organs ('the 3 Ps'): parathyroid glands (>95% penetrance), enteropancreatic neuroendocrine tissues (pNETs; 30-70%), and the anterior pituitary gland (30-40%).

pillars.label: MEN1 Pediatric Manifestations and Surveillance
pillars.text: Primary hyperparathyroidism secondary to multiglandular parathyroid hyperplasia is the earliest and most frequent manifestation of MEN1, developing in up to 75% of carriers by age 20 (and detectable from age 8-10 years). Functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNETs) include gastrinomas (causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome; most common overall) and insulinomas (most common functioning pNET presenting in children and adolescents <20 years). Pituitary adenomas occur in 10-20% of children with MEN1 (predominantly prolactinomas, followed by GH-secreting somatotropinomas). Consensus surveillance starting at age 5-8 years includes: annual serum ionized calcium and PTH; annual fasting gastrin, chromogranin A, and abdominal MRI (starting at age 8-10); and pituitary MRI every 3 years.

pillars.label: MEN2A, MEN2B, and RET Proto-Oncogene
pillars.text: MEN2 is caused by autosomal dominant gain-of-function activating germline mutations in the RET proto-oncogene on chromosome 10q11.2, which encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase. MEN2A (95% of MEN2) encompasses Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma (MTC; 100%), Pheochromocytoma (50%), and Primary Hyperparathyroidism (20-30%), most frequently linked to codon 634 mutations in exon 11. MEN2B (5%) features aggressive MTC developing in infancy, Pheochromocytoma (50%), Marfanoid habitus, mucosal neuromas (lips, tongue, conjunctiva), and intestinal ganglioneuromatosis (chronic severe constipation/megacolon), driven in >95% by the RET M918T mutation in exon 16.

pillars.label: Prophylactic Thyroidectomy and Pheochromocytoma Rule
pillars.text: American Thyroid Association (ATA) risk stratification dictates the timing of prophylactic total thyroidectomy: ATA Highest Risk (MEN2B / M918T) mandates prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first year of life (optimally in the first months of life); ATA High Risk (MEN2A / codon 634) mandates total thyroidectomy at or before age 5 years. Annual screening for pheochromocytoma (plasma free fractionated metanephrines) begins at age 5 in MEN2B and age 11 in MEN2A. Cardinal surgical rule: In any patient with MEN2, pheochromocytoma must ALWAYS be excluded or surgically removed BEFORE performing thyroidectomy to prevent fatal intraoperative catecholamine storm.

pillars.label: Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) and X-LAG
pillars.text: Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) is characterized by hereditary pituitary adenomas in the absence of other MEN features. Inactivating germline mutations in AIP (aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein on chromosome 11q13.3) account for ~15-20% of FIPA families. AIP-mutated tumors typically present in childhood or adolescence (median age 15-18 years) as large, aggressive somatotropinomas causing pituitary gigantism or prolactinomas that exhibit resistance to first-generation somatostatin analogs. X-LAG syndrome (X-linked acrogigantism) is caused by microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3 containing GPR101, presenting in infancy (<12-24 months) with rapid, massive linear overgrowth and severe gigantism.

cards.q: What three major endocrine organ systems are characteristically affected in Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1)?
cards.a: Parathyroid glands (multigland hyperplasia), Pancreatic enteroneuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma), and Pituitary adenomas (prolactinoma, somatotropinoma).

cards.q: What genes are mutated in MEN1 and MEN2, and what are their respective molecular mechanisms?
cards.a: MEN1 is caused by inactivating mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (encoding menin); MEN2 is caused by activating gain-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene.

cards.q: Why must screening for pheochromocytoma always precede thyroid surgery in patients with MEN2A or MEN2B?
cards.a: Induction of general anesthesia or neck surgery in a patient with an unmanaged pheochromocytoma triggers massive catecholamine release, precipitating lethal hypertensive crisis and cardiac arrest.

cards.q: When should prophylactic total thyroidectomy be performed in an infant diagnosed with MEN2B carrying the RET M918T mutation?
cards.a: Within the first year of life (optimally in the first months of life) due to the virulent, early metastatic spread of medullary thyroid carcinoma.

cards.q: What is the most common functioning pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor (pNET) presenting in pediatric patients under 20 years with MEN1?
cards.a: Insulinoma, presenting with neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia, fasting hyperinsulinism, and positive critical blood sample.

cards.q: What tumor suppressor gene is mutated in 15-20% of Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) cases, predisposing to aggressive pediatric gigantism?
cards.a: AIP (aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein) on chromosome 11q13.3.

cards.q: What genetic duplication causes X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG syndrome) presenting with extreme linear overgrowth in infants <2 years?
cards.a: Microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3 encompassing the GPR101 gene.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old boy whose mother has MEN1 is brought for routine screening. Serum calcium is elevated at 10.8 mg/dL (reference: 8.8-10.2 mg/dL), ionized calcium is 1.42 mmol/L, and intact PTH is 95 pg/mL (reference: 15-65 pg/mL). 24-hour urine calcium is 340 mg (elevated). Neck ultrasound reveals four enlarged, hypoechoic parathyroid glands. What is the most appropriate surgical management for primary hyperparathyroidism in MEN1?
options: Subtotal parathyroidectomy (resecting 3.5 glands) or total parathyroidectomy with heterotopic forearm autotransplantation
Resection of a single parathyroid adenoma alone
Conservative observation with oral cinacalcet until age 25
Total thyroidectomy without parathyroid exploration
mcqs.explanation: Primary hyperparathyroidism in MEN1 is characterized by asymmetric multiglandular parathyroid hyperplasia involving all four glands, rather than a solitary adenoma. Resection of a single enlarged gland results in virtually 100% recurrence. Consensus guidelines recommend subtotal parathyroidectomy (resection of 3.5 glands with marking of the remnant) or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation of parathyroid tissue into the forearm musculature to treat hypercalcemia while minimizing permanent hypoparathyroidism.
option_notes: Correct. Subtotal parathyroidectomy or total parathyroidectomy with autotransplantation treats multiglandular MEN1 disease.
Incorrect. Resecting a single gland leads to rapid recurrence because all remaining glands harbor the germline MEN1 mutation.
Incorrect. Parathyroidectomy is the definitive therapy to prevent nephrolithiasis and bone mineral loss in young patients.
Incorrect. Thyroidectomy has no therapeutic effect on parathyroid hyperplasia in MEN1.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old girl with a documented germline RET codon 634 mutation (MEN2A) is scheduled to undergo total thyroidectomy for an elevated basal calcitonin. Before proceeding to the operating room, which diagnostic evaluation is mandatory to prevent an intraoperative mortality?
options: Measurement of plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines to rule out pheochromocytoma
Evaluation of serum gastrin and chromogranin A
Brain MRI to rule out a prolactinoma
Technetium-99m sestamibi parathyroid scan
mcqs.explanation: In patients with MEN2A or MEN2B, pheochromocytoma occurs in up to 50% of cases. It is a cardinal rule of endocrine surgery that pheochromocytoma must ALWAYS be excluded (using plasma or urinary free fractionated metanephrines) or surgically resected prior to any planned thyroid or neck surgery. Anesthesia or intraoperative manipulation in a patient with an occult pheochromocytoma can trigger a massive catecholamine surge, fatal hypertensive crisis, and malignant arrhythmia.
option_notes: Correct. Screening for pheochromocytoma with metanephrines is mandatory before thyroidectomy to prevent intraoperative death.
Incorrect. Gastrinomas are part of MEN1, not MEN2.
Incorrect. Pituitary adenomas occur in MEN1, not MEN2.
Incorrect. While hyperparathyroidism occurs in MEN2A, unrecognized pheochromocytoma poses the acute life-threatening operative risk.

mcqs.q: A 2-month-old infant is evaluated for chronic severe constipation, abdominal distension, and poor weight gain. Physical examination reveals prominent fleshy bumps along the mucosal margins of the tongue and inner lips, thickened eyelids with everted margins, and long, slender limbs. Genetic testing reveals a de novo heterozygous RET M918T mutation in exon 16. What is the diagnosis and the most urgent surgical recommendation?
options: Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2B (MEN2B); prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first months of life
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 1 (MEN1); subtotal pancreatectomy
Neurofibromatosis Type 1; optic pathway glioma resection
Cowden syndrome; prophylactic bilateral mastectomy
mcqs.explanation: This infant has classic Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2B (MEN2B), characterized by mucosal neuromas of the tongue/lips, intestinal ganglioneuromatosis (causing chronic megacolon/constipation), marfanoid habitus, and the pathognomonic RET M918T mutation. Medullary thyroid carcinoma in MEN2B develops in early infancy and metastasizes aggressively. ATA guidelines recommend prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first year of life, preferably in the first months of life.
option_notes: Correct. RET M918T confirms MEN2B; prophylactic total thyroidectomy in early infancy is life-saving.
Incorrect. Pancreatectomy is not indicated for MEN2B, which affects C-cells, adrenal medulla, and autonomic nerves.
Incorrect. NF1 does not feature mucosal neuromas of the tongue or the RET M918T mutation.
Incorrect. Cowden syndrome is caused by PTEN mutations and features hamartomas, not infant MTC in MEN2B.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old male presents with extreme tall stature (height 204 cm, >99.9th percentile, +4.2 SD), coarse facial features, prognathism, and massive hands and feet. Sellar MRI reveals a 3.2-cm invasive pituitary macroadenoma invading both cavernous sinuses. Serum IGF-1 is markedly elevated. Genetic analysis reveals a heterozygous germline mutation in the AIP gene. Which family condition is this patient suffering from?
options: Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) with pituitary gigantism
Carney complex due to PRKAR1A mutation
McCune-Albright syndrome due to GNAS mutation
Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2A
mcqs.explanation: Inactivating germline mutations in AIP (aryl hydrocarbon receptor-interacting protein) account for ~15-20% of Familial Isolated Pituitary Adenoma (FIPA) kindreds. AIP-associated pituitary neuroendocrine tumors characteristically manifest in children and adolescents as aggressive, macroadenomatous GH-secreting tumors (somatotropinomas) that cause severe pituitary gigantism, invade parasellar structures, and respond poorly to somatostatin analog medical therapy.
option_notes: Correct. AIP mutation presenting with young-onset aggressive somatotropinoma and gigantism is classic FIPA.
Incorrect. Carney complex is caused by PRKAR1A mutations and features spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas, and PPNAD.
Incorrect. McCune-Albright syndrome is caused by somatic mosaic GNAS mutations, not germline AIP mutations.
Incorrect. MEN2A causes medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism, not pituitary macroadenomas.

mcqs.q: A 14-month-old female infant is evaluated for rapid, dramatic linear overgrowth. Her height velocity has exceeded 20 cm/year, and her height is +5.5 SD above the mean. Laboratory testing demonstrates elevated serum growth hormone, unsuppressed GH on oral glucose testing, and high serum prolactin. Pituitary MRI demonstrates diffuse pituitary enlargement with macroadenoma. Chromosomal microarray reveals a microduplication of chromosome Xq26.3. What is the diagnosis?
options: X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG syndrome) involving GPR101 duplication
Sotos syndrome due to NSD1 mutation
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome due to 11p15 imprinting defect
Marfan syndrome due to FBN1 mutation
mcqs.explanation: X-linked acrogigantism (X-LAG) syndrome is caused by germline or somatic mosaic microduplications on chromosome Xq26.3 encompassing the GPR101 gene. Affected children present in early infancy (<12-24 months of age) with the earliest onset and most severe form of pituitary gigantism known, characterized by marked hypersecretion of both growth hormone and prolactin due to diffuse pituitary hyperplasia or mixed somato-lactotrope macroadenomas.
option_notes: Correct. Microduplication of Xq26.3 containing GPR101 causes X-LAG syndrome with severe infantile gigantism.
Incorrect. Sotos syndrome is an overgrowth disorder with macrocephaly and distinctive facies, without high GH/prolactin or sellar mass.
Incorrect. Beckwith-Wiedemann features macrosomia, omphalocele, and hemihypertrophy, not pituitary GH-secreting adenomas.
Incorrect. Marfan syndrome causes tall stature with arachnodactyly and aortic root dilation, with normal GH and normal sella.

atlas.etiology: MEN1: Inactivating MEN1 tumor suppressor mutations (11q13); 3 Ps (parathyroid, pNET, pituitary). MEN2A: Activating RET mutations (codon 634; MTC, pheo, hyperparathyroid). MEN2B: RET M918T (infant MTC, pheo, mucosal neuromas, ganglioneuromatosis). FIPA: Inactivating AIP mutations (11q13.3). X-LAG: Xq26.3 GPR101 microduplication.
atlas.epidemiology: MEN1 prevalence is 1:30,000. MEN2 prevalence is 1:35,000 (MEN2A 95%, MEN2B 5%). AIP mutations found in 15-20% of FIPA.
atlas.diagnostics: MEN1: Calcium, PTH, gastrin, chromogranin A, prolactin, IGF-1, abdominal and pituitary MRI. MEN2: Calcitonin, plasma free metanephrines, neck US, RET genetic testing. FIPA/X-LAG: GH, IGF-1, prolactin, pituitary MRI, AIP/GPR101 genetic testing.

therapies.text: MEN2B (RET M918T): Prophylactic total thyroidectomy within the first year of life (first months of life). MEN2A (codon 634): Prophylactic total thyroidectomy at or before age 5 years. MANDATORY: Screen for and surgically resect pheochromocytoma (plasma metanephrines) BEFORE performing neck surgery.

Subtotal parathyroidectomy (resecting 3.5 glands) or total parathyroidectomy with forearm autotransplantation for multiglandular parathyroid hyperplasia. Pancreatic NETs: surgical enucleation or partial pancreatectomy for insulinomas and tumors >1-2 cm.

pillars.label: Postzygotic Mosaic Genetics
pillars.text: McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS) is a rare, non-inherited, multi-system disorder caused by postzygotic somatic activating missense mutations in the GNAS gene on chromosome 20q13.3. The mutations almost exclusively replace arginine at codon 201 (R201H or R201C) in the alpha-subunit of the stimulatory G-protein (Gs-alpha). The mutation eliminates the intrinsic GTPase activity of Gs-alpha, trapping the G-protein in a constitutively active GTP-bound conformation that continuously stimulates adenylyl cyclase, driving autonomous cyclic AMP production independent of ligand-receptor activation in affected tissue mosaics.

pillars.label: Classic Clinical Triad
pillars.text: The classic clinical triad of MAS comprises: (1) Polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (FD) of bone; (2) Café-au-lait skin hyperpigmentation; and (3) Hyperfunctioning autonomous endocrinopathies. Because the mutation occurs postzygotically during embryogenesis, the clinical phenotype is remarkably heterogeneous, depending entirely on the timing of the mutation and the anatomical distribution and percentage of mutated cells within tissue mosaics. Diagnosis is established clinically by the presence of >=2 classic triad features (or 1 classic feature plus confirmed GNAS mutation in tissue).

pillars.label: Fibrous Dysplasia and FGF23 Wasting
pillars.text: Fibrous dysplasia (FD) results from constitutive Gs-alpha activation in bone marrow stromal cells, impairing osteoblast differentiation and replacing normal marrow and lamellar bone with expansile fibro-osseous tissue and abnormal woven bone ('Chinese character' trabeculae). Skeletal lesions feature a ground-glass appearance on radiographs, predisposing to chronic bone pain, deformities (shepherd's crook deformity of proximal femur, facial asymmetry), and pathological fractures. Dysplastic stromal cells oversecrete intact FGF23; in extensive polyostotic FD, circulating FGF23 produces renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemia, and severe osteomalacia, aggravating bone fragility.

pillars.label: Endocrinopathies: Precocity, Thyroid, GH, Adrenal
pillars.text: Endocrine manifestations represent ligand-independent autonomous hyperactivity: (1) Precocious puberty: most common in girls, featuring autonomous recurrent estrogen-secreting ovarian follicular cysts with abrupt vaginal bleeding and breast budding (suppressed LH/FSH); in boys, autonomous macro-orchidism; (2) Hyperthyroidism: autonomous multinodular toxic goiter with low TSH; (3) Growth hormone excess: somatotrope hyperplasia/adenoma producing acromegaly or gigantism (present in 20-30%; accelerates craniofacial FD expansion and optical/auditory neuropathy); (4) Neonatal Cushing syndrome: autonomous bilateral adrenal hyperplasia presenting in infancy with severe failure to thrive, frequently resolving spontaneously.

pillars.label: Therapeutic Approaches
pillars.text: Treatment is tailored to organ-specific manifestations. Precocious puberty in girls is managed with third-generation aromatase inhibitors (letrozole 2.5 mg daily) or selective estrogen receptor modulators (tamoxifen, fulvestrant); GnRH agonists are ineffective unless secondary central precocity develops. Bone pain from FD is treated with intravenous bisphosphonates (pamidronate or zoledronic acid); hypophosphatemic rickets requires oral phosphate salts and calcitriol. Denosumab (anti-RANKL) is an emerging option for rapidly expanding lesions. Growth hormone excess is treated with long-acting somatostatin receptor ligands and pegvisomant (GH receptor antagonist). Surgery is reserved for mechanical stabilization, optic canal decompression, and thyroidectomy.

cards.q: Why is McCune-Albright syndrome never inherited or transmitted vertically from parent to child?
cards.a: It is caused by postzygotic somatic mosaic mutations in GNAS; a germline activating GNAS mutation would cause generalized adenylyl cyclase activation that is embryonic lethal.

cards.q: What specific biochemical defect results from the GNAS R201 codon mutation in McCune-Albright syndrome?
cards.a: Loss of intrinsic GTPase activity in Gs-alpha, trapping the protein in an active GTP-bound conformation that constitutively drives adenylyl cyclase and cAMP production.

cards.q: How do the café-au-lait macules of McCune-Albright syndrome differ morphologically from those of Neurofibromatosis type 1?
cards.a: MAS macules are large, unilateral, respect the midline, and feature jagged, irregular 'coast of Maine' borders, unlike the smooth 'coast of California' borders of NF1.

cards.q: Why are standard GnRH agonists ineffective as initial therapy for precocious puberty in young girls with McCune-Albright syndrome?
cards.a: The precocious puberty is peripheral (gonadotropin-independent), driven by autonomous ovarian follicular cysts secreting estrogen independent of pituitary LH and FSH.

cards.q: What metabolic electrolyte complication can severe, extensive polyostotic fibrous dysplasia cause via paracrine tumor secretion?
cards.a: Renal phosphate wasting and hypophosphatemic rickets/osteomalacia, caused by excessive secretion of intact FGF23 by dysplastic bone stromal cells.

cards.q: What pathognomonic femoral deformity frequently develops in children with severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia?
cards.a: 'Shepherd's crook' deformity (severe coxa vara with bowing of the proximal femoral shaft under weight-bearing stress).

cards.q: What pharmacological class is the first-line medical treatment for peripheral precocious puberty in girls with McCune-Albright syndrome?
cards.a: Aromatase inhibitors, such as oral letrozole (2.5 mg daily), which block estrogen biosynthesis by autonomous ovarian cysts.

mcqs.q: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for an acute episode of painless vaginal bleeding. Physical examination reveals unilateral Tanner stage 3 breast development, no pubic hair, and a large, jagged light-brown macule on the right buttock with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders that terminates abruptly at the sacral midline. Pelvic ultrasound reveals a solitary 4-cm cystic lesion in the right ovary with an endometrial stripe; the left ovary is normal. Serum estradiol is 165 pg/mL, and baseline and stimulated LH are <0.1 IU/L. What is the diagnosis?
options: McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
Granulosa cell ovarian tumor
Idiopathic central precocious puberty
mcqs.explanation: This patient exhibits classic features of McCune-Albright syndrome (MAS): peripheral precocious puberty (recurrent autonomous estrogen-secreting ovarian cysts with vaginal bleeding, suppressed LH), paired with a pathognomonic large café-au-lait macule displaying jagged 'coast of Maine' borders that respects the midline. MAS is caused by a somatic activating GNAS mutation.
option_notes: Correct. Autonomous unilateral ovarian cyst, suppressed LH, and jagged midline-respecting macule establish McCune-Albright syndrome.
Incorrect. NF1 features smooth-bordered 'coast of California' macules and axillary freckling, not autonomous ovarian cysts.
Incorrect. Granulosa cell tumors present with precocious puberty but do not have jagged café-au-lait macules or mosaic GNAS mutations.
Incorrect. Central precocity features bilateral ovarian follicular activity and elevated, pubertal stimulated LH levels.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old girl with mosaic activating GNAS mutation and polyostotic fibrous dysplasia presents with chronic bone pain and lower-extremity fatigue. Plain radiographs reveal expansile ground-glass lesions involving the skull, pelvis, and both femurs. Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum calcium 9.2 mg/dL, serum phosphate 1.9 mg/dL (low; reference: 4.0-5.8 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 890 U/L, and TmP/GFR 1.6 mg/dL (severely reduced). Serum intact FGF23 is elevated at 95 pg/mL. What is the mechanism of her hypophosphatemia?
options: Direct oversecretion of intact FGF23 by dysplastic osteogenic cells within the fibrous dysplasia bone lesions
Parathyroid adenoma secreting excess parathyroid hormone
Proximal renal tubular necrosis caused by hypercalciuria
Defective intestinal phosphate absorption
mcqs.explanation: In patients with extensive polyostotic fibrous dysplasia in McCune-Albright syndrome, the dysplastic osteogenic stromal cells oversecrete intact fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Circulating FGF23 acts on the renal proximal tubule to downregulate sodium-phosphate cotransporters, producing profound renal phosphate wasting, severe hypophosphatemia, and secondary osteomalacia that exacerbates bone pain and fractures.
option_notes: Correct. Dysplastic fibrous bone tissue oversecretes intact FGF23, driving renal phosphate wasting and osteomalacia.
Incorrect. PTH is typically normal; hypophosphatemia is driven by FGF23, not hyperparathyroidism.
Incorrect. Tubular necrosis is not the mechanism; the defect is specific hormonal down-regulation of NaPi cotransporters.
Incorrect. FGF23 suppresses renal phosphate reabsorption, which is the primary driver of hypophosphatemia.

mcqs.q: A 5-year-old girl with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and coast-of-Maine café-au-lait pigmentation suffers from recurrent autonomous ovarian cysts and multiple episodes of vaginal bleeding. Treatment with depot leuprolide (GnRH agonist) for 6 months produced no reduction in bleeding or cyst frequency. What is the recommended pharmacological therapy to prevent recurrent estrogenic bleeding?
options: Oral letrozole (third-generation aromatase inhibitor) 2.5 mg daily
Doubling the dose of depot leuprolide
Intravenous bisphosphonate therapy
Bilateral total oophorectomy
mcqs.explanation: In young girls with McCune-Albright syndrome, precocious puberty is peripheral (gonadotropin-independent), driven by autonomous Gs-alpha activation in ovarian follicular cells. GnRH agonists are ineffective because pituitary gonadotropins are already suppressed. First-line medical therapy is oral letrozole (2.5 mg daily), a potent aromatase inhibitor that blocks the conversion of androgens to estrogens in the cysts, halting vaginal bleeding and slowing skeletal maturation.
option_notes: Correct. Aromatase inhibitors (letrozole) block autonomous ovarian estrogen synthesis and are first-line for MAS precocity.
Incorrect. Increasing GnRH agonists is completely futile because the ovaries are functioning independently of LH/FSH.
Incorrect. Bisphosphonates treat fibrous dysplasia bone pain, but have no effect on ovarian steroidogenesis.
Incorrect. Oophorectomy is mutilating and destroys future fertility; cysts fluctuate and respond to medical aromatase inhibition.

mcqs.q: A 14-year-old male with mosaic GNAS activation and craniofacial fibrous dysplasia is noted to have accelerating head circumference, coarse facial features, and expanding jaw lesions. Laboratory testing reveals elevated IGF-1 and unsuppressed growth hormone on oral glucose loading. Why is growth hormone excess particularly dangerous in children with mosaic GNAS activation and fibrous dysplasia?
options: Excess GH and IGF-1 directly stimulate rapid expansion of craniofacial fibrous dysplasia lesions, causing visual loss and hearing impairment
GH excess leads to spontaneous malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia into osteosarcoma in >80% of patients
GH excess causes acute rupture of hepatic adenomas
GH excess triggers immediate renal failure
mcqs.explanation: Growth hormone excess occurs in 20-30% of MAS patients due to somatotrope hyperplasia. GH and IGF-1 are potent mitogenic and osteotropic factors that accelerate the rapid growth and expansion of fibrous dysplasia lesions, particularly in the craniofacial bones. This expansile growth can compress the optic canals and auditory canals, leading to permanent optic nerve compression, irreversible blindness, and severe deafness. Aggressive medical management of GH excess is imperative.
option_notes: Correct. GH/IGF-1 stimulates craniofacial FD expansion, causing optic nerve compression and blindness.
Incorrect. Malignant transformation is rare (<1%) and not primarily driven by GH excess.
Incorrect. MAS is not associated with hepatic adenoma rupture.
Incorrect. GH excess does not cause immediate acute renal failure.

mcqs.q: A pregnant woman who was diagnosed in childhood with mosaic GNAS activating syndrome (MAS) asks her genetic counselor about the risk of transmitting the condition to her unborn child. What is the accurate recurrence risk?
options: Essentially 0% risk of transmission, because McCune-Albright syndrome is caused exclusively by somatic postzygotic mutations
50% risk, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance
25% risk, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
100% risk if the fetus is female
mcqs.explanation: McCune-Albright syndrome is caused exclusively by postzygotic somatic mosaic mutations in GNAS that arise spontaneously during embryonic development. Because the mutation is postzygotic and somatic, it is not present in the germline of all cells, and germline transmission to offspring has never been documented. The recurrence risk for the offspring of an affected patient is virtually zero.
option_notes: Correct. MAS is caused exclusively by somatic postzygotic mutations and cannot be transmitted to offspring (risk ~0%).
Incorrect. MAS is not inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.
Incorrect. MAS is not an autosomal recessive disorder.
Incorrect. There is no sex-linked transmission of postzygotic somatic mutations.

atlas.etiology: Postzygotic somatic mosaic activating missense mutations in GNAS (20q13.3; R201H or R201C); constitutively active Gs-alpha and continuous adenylyl cyclase/cAMP activation. Non-inherited.
atlas.epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated at 1:100,000 to 1:1,000,000; equal gender distribution, but peripheral precocious puberty is much more clinically apparent in females.
atlas.diagnostics: Skeletal plain radiographs (ground-glass lesions) and 99mTc bone scan; pelvic ultrasound (unilateral follicular cysts); serum estradiol, LH, FSH, TSH, free T4, IGF-1, GH, phosphate, FGF23; GNAS mutant-specific PCR on affected tissue.

therapies.section: Endocrine and Skeletal Therapies for MAS
therapies.text: Precocious puberty in girls: Letrozole 2.5 mg orally once daily (or tamoxifen/fulvestrant). Fibrous dysplasia bone pain: Intravenous pamidronate 1 mg/kg/day for 3 days every 4-6 months or zoledronic acid 0.025-0.05 mg/kg every 6 months. FGF23 hypophosphatemia: Oral phosphate salts 20-40 mg/kg/day plus calcitriol 20-30 ng/kg/day. GH excess: Octreotide LAR or Pegvisomant.

pillars.label: Radiation Sensitivity of Hypothalamic-Pituitary Axis
pillars.text: The hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) axis is highly vulnerable to cranial radiation therapy (CRT) used for brain tumors, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and leukemia prophylaxis. Radiation damage progresses in a dose- and time-dependent hierarchical vulnerability: Growth Hormone (GH) deficiency is the earliest and most sensitive defect, occurring at low-to-moderate doses (>=18-24 Gy) in >80-90% of exposed children within 2-5 years. Gonadotropin (LH/FSH) deficiency occurs at >=30-40 Gy; notably, low-dose cranial radiation (18-24 Gy) can paradoxically trigger central precocious puberty by damaging inhibitory cortical pathways. TSH deficiency and ACTH deficiency occur at higher doses (>=40-50 Gy), often presenting insidiously 5 to 15+ years after completion of cancer therapy.

pillars.label: Thyroid Late Effects and Secondary Neoplasia
pillars.text: Direct radiation to the neck or spine (cranial-spinal irradiation, Hodgkin lymphoma mantle fields, total body irradiation [TBI] for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; >=10-20 Gy) causes high rates of thyroid late effects. Primary hypothyroidism develops in 20-50% of exposed survivors (rising with radiation dose and time, compounded by alkylating agents). Furthermore, radiation is the most potent environmental risk factor for secondary thyroid neoplasms: differentiated thyroid cancer (predominantly papillary thyroid carcinoma [PTC]) exhibits an increased incidence beginning 5-10 years post-radiation and peaking 15-25 years later. Lifelong annual thyroid palpation and clinical surveillance are mandatory.

pillars.label: Gonadal Toxicity and Alkylating Chemotherapy
pillars.text: Gonadal damage varies sharply by cell type and sex. In males, testicular germ cells (spermatogonia, Sertoli cells) are exquisitely sensitive to both radiation (oligospermia/azoospermia at >=0.1-1.2 Gy) and alkylating chemotherapy. Cumulative alkylating agent exposure is quantified by the Cyclophosphamide Equivalent Dose (CED); a CED >=4000-8000 mg/m2 confers high risk of permanent azoospermia with elevated FSH and normal testosterone (isolated germ cell failure). Leydig cells are more radioresistant, tolerating up to 20-24 Gy before testosterone deficiency develops. In females, oocytes cannot regenerate; pelvic/spinal radiation (>=10-15 Gy) or high-dose alkylating agents cause premature ovarian insufficiency (POI; elevated FSH/LH, low AMH, early menopause).

pillars.label: Growth Hormone Safety in Cancer Survivors
pillars.text: Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) is the standard treatment for childhood cancer survivors with documented radiation-induced GH deficiency. Multiple large international survivor cohort studies (including the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study [CCSS]) have confirmed that rhGH replacement does NOT increase the risk of primary pediatric cancer recurrence or leukemia relapse. However, survivors must have at least 1 year of documented disease-free remission prior to initiating rhGH, and vigilant surveillance must be maintained for radiation-induced secondary solid neoplasms (such as meningiomas and thyroid nodules).

pillars.label: Metabolic Syndrome and Bone Health Surveillance
pillars.text: Childhood cancer survivors face significantly elevated risks of adult cardiometabolic morbidity. Survivors of cranial irradiation, total body irradiation (TBI), and abdominal radiation display high rates of metabolic syndrome: visceral adiposity, severe insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and early-onset type 2 diabetes (occurring even in non-obese individuals due to defective subcutaneous adipocyte expansion). Chronic glucocorticoids, methotrexate, and hypogonadism also induce early osteoporosis. Long-term survivor protocols (Children's Oncology Group [COG] Long-Term Follow-Up Guidelines) mandate annual screening for fasting glucose, lipids, blood pressure, and DXA densitometry.

cards.q: What is the most radio-sensitive anterior pituitary hormone axis, exhibiting deficiency at the lowest cranial radiation doses (>=18-24 Gy)?
cards.a: Growth hormone (GH) axis, resulting in radiation-induced GH deficiency in >80-90% of exposed children within 2-5 years.

cards.q: What pubertal disorder can paradoxically occur in young girls following low-to-moderate doses (18-24 Gy) of cranial irradiation?
cards.a: Central precocious puberty, caused by radiation-induced disruption of cortical and hypothalamic inhibitory pathways that normally suppress the GnRH pulse generator.

cards.q: What metric is used to calculate cumulative alkylating chemotherapy exposure, and what threshold confers high risk of permanent azoospermia?
cards.a: Cyclophosphamide Equivalent Dose (CED); a cumulative CED >=4000 to 8000 mg/m2 is associated with high risk of permanent germ cell failure and azoospermia.

cards.q: What is the most common secondary solid endocrine malignancy occurring in survivors of childhood cancer exposed to neck radiation?
cards.a: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), which has an increased incidence beginning 5-10 years post-radiation and peaking 15-25 years later.

cards.q: Does recombinant human growth hormone replacement increase the risk of primary disease recurrence in childhood cancer survivors in remission?
cards.a: No. Large-scale international cohort studies show no increased risk of primary cancer recurrence or leukemia relapse in survivors treated with rhGH.

cards.q: How does radiation sensitivity differ between testicular germ cells (spermatogenesis) and Leydig cells (testosterone production)?
cards.a: Germ cells are extraordinarily sensitive (damaged by >=0.1-1.2 Gy), whereas Leydig cells are much more radioresistant (tolerating up to 20-24 Gy before primary hypogonadism develops).

cards.q: Why is lifelong surveillance of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis required in survivors exposed to high-dose cranial radiation (>=40-50 Gy)?
cards.a: Central ACTH deficiency can develop insidiously 10 to 15+ years after radiotherapy, predisposing survivors to fatal adrenal crisis during intercurrent illness.

mcqs.q: A 10-year-old boy who completed treatment for a standard-risk medulloblastoma 3 years ago (including surgical resection and 23.4 Gy craniospinal irradiation with posterior fossa boost) is evaluated for severe growth deceleration. His height velocity has dropped from the 50th percentile to 1.8 cm/year (<3rd percentile). He is in complete oncologic remission. Bone age is delayed by 2.5 years. Two provocative growth hormone stimulation tests show peak GH levels of 2.1 ng/mL and 1.8 ng/mL, with low serum IGF-1. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Initiate recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) therapy at 0.16-0.24 mg/kg/week with regular clinical and oncologic monitoring
Withhold growth hormone therapy permanently due to an unacceptably high risk of medulloblastoma recurrence
Initiate high-dose depot testosterone enanthate 200 mg monthly to promote linear growth
Perform immediate emergent craniotomy and repeat posterior fossa resection
mcqs.explanation: Growth hormone deficiency is the most common and earliest endocrine complication of cranial irradiation (occurring at doses >=18 Gy). Landmark data from the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS) have conclusively proven that rhGH replacement does NOT increase the risk of primary central nervous system tumor recurrence or leukemia relapse in disease-free survivors. Because he has been in remission for >1 year, initiating rhGH therapy is standard care to restore linear growth.
option_notes: Correct. rhGH replacement is safe, does not increase medulloblastoma recurrence, and restores normal growth velocity.
Incorrect. Permanently withholding rhGH based on unproven fears of tumor recurrence severely compromises adult height and metabolic health.
Incorrect. High-dose testosterone causes rapid epiphyseal fusion and arrests remaining growth potential.
Incorrect. Neurosurgical re-exploration is completely inappropriate in an asymptomatic patient in complete remission.

mcqs.q: A 6-year-old girl who received 24 Gy cranial irradiation for acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) 2 years ago presents with rapid linear growth acceleration and bilateral breast enlargement (Tanner stage 3). Bone age is advanced by 2 years. A GnRH stimulation test reveals a peak stimulated LH of 8.4 IU/L. Cranial MRI shows no leukemic relapse or mass. What is the mechanism of precocious puberty in this patient?
options: Radiation-induced damage to cortical and hypothalamic inhibitory pathways, disinhibiting the GnRH pulse generator
Ectopic LH secretion by residual leukemic blast cells
Primary ovarian granulosa cell tumor induced by chemotherapy
Peripheral aromatization of adrenal androgens
mcqs.explanation: Low-to-moderate dose cranial irradiation (18-24 Gy), particularly in girls treated at a young age (<8 years), frequently causes central precocious puberty. Radiation damages the higher cortical and hypothalamic neural pathways that normally exert tonic inhibitory restraint over the GnRH pulse generator, resulting in premature disinhibition of GnRH pulsatility, true central precocious puberty, accelerated bone age, and compromised adult height.
option_notes: Correct. Low-dose cranial radiation disrupts inhibitory neural inputs, triggering early central GnRH release.
Incorrect. Leukemic blasts do not secrete bioactive LH.
Incorrect. Granulosa cell tumors cause peripheral precocity with suppressed (not pubertal) stimulated LH levels.
Incorrect. Elevated peak LH >5 IU/L on GnRH testing confirms central gonadotropin-dependent precocity, not peripheral aromatization.

mcqs.q: A 17-year-old male survivor of adolescent Hodgkin lymphoma who received cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and procarbazine (cumulative Cyclophosphamide Equivalent Dose [CED] 9500 mg/m2) presents for late-effects evaluation. Physical examination reveals normal virilization (Tanner stage 5 pubic hair, adult phallus), but bilateral soft, small testes measuring 6 mL each. Laboratory evaluation reveals: serum testosterone 540 ng/dL (normal male), LH 4.8 IU/L (normal), and FSH 32 IU/L (markedly elevated). Semen analysis confirms azoospermia. How should these findings be explained?
options: Selective alkylator-induced germ cell destruction (azoospermia with high FSH) with spared, functioning Leydig cells (normal testosterone and LH)
Secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism due to hypothalamic radiation damage
Complete primary hypogonadism requiring immediate testosterone replacement therapy
Retrograde ejaculation caused by vincristine autonomic neuropathy
mcqs.explanation: High cumulative doses of alkylating chemotherapy (CED >=8000 mg/m2) exert selective cytotoxicity against rapidly dividing testicular germ cells (spermatogonia), causing permanent azoospermia and loss of inhibin B feedback, which leads to markedly elevated FSH. In contrast, non-dividing Leydig cells are highly resistant to alkylating agents, maintaining normal testosterone production, normal LH levels, and normal secondary sexual virilization.
option_notes: Correct. High-dose alkylators selectively destroy germ cells (high FSH, azoospermia) while sparing Leydig cell testosterone production.
Incorrect. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism features low FSH and low LH, whereas FSH is markedly elevated here.
Incorrect. Testosterone is completely normal (540 ng/dL); testosterone replacement is not indicated.
Incorrect. Semen analysis confirms complete azoospermia, not retrograde ejaculation, and FSH elevation confirms testicular germ cell failure.

mcqs.q: A 22-year-old female who was treated at age 7 with 35 Gy mantle field radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma presents for routine survivor surveillance. What is the most critical lifelong annual screening recommendation for her thyroid health?
options: Annual neck palpation and clinical screening for primary hypothyroidism and secondary thyroid carcinoma (papillary thyroid carcinoma)
Prophylactic total thyroidectomy before age 25
Routine annual 131I radioactive iodine diagnostic whole-body scans
Empirical levothyroxine therapy to suppress TSH to undetectable levels
mcqs.explanation: Survivors of childhood cancer exposed to direct neck or mantle radiation (>=10-20 Gy) have a 20-50% lifetime risk of primary hypothyroidism and an exponentially increased risk of radiation-induced differentiated thyroid carcinoma (predominantly papillary thyroid carcinoma), which peaks 15-25 years post-exposure. Children's Oncology Group (COG) guidelines mandate lifelong annual clinical thyroid examination and serum TSH monitoring.
option_notes: Correct. Annual neck palpation and TSH screening detect radiation-induced hypothyroidism and secondary thyroid neoplasms.
Incorrect. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is indicated for hereditary MEN2, not external radiation exposure.
Incorrect. Diagnostic radioiodine whole-body scans carry unnecessary radiation and are not recommended for screening.
Incorrect. Routine levothyroxine suppression in euthyroid survivors without nodules is not standard and carries cardiac/bone risks.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old male who received 54 Gy cranial radiation for a hypothalamic astrocytoma 8 years ago presents to urgent care with severe lethargy, orthostatic dizziness, and nausea during a viral illness. Blood pressure is 82/46 mmHg. Serum sodium is 126 mEq/L and potassium is 4.2 mEq/L. Morning cortisol drawn in the clinic is 1.8 mcg/dL with plasma ACTH 8 pg/mL (low). What is the diagnosis and urgent therapy?
options: Late-onset radiation-induced central adrenal insufficiency; immediate IV normal saline resuscitation and IV hydrocortisone bolus
Autoimmune Addison disease; fludrocortisone monotherapy
Dehydration alone; oral rehydration solution
Radiation-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; desmopressin
mcqs.explanation: High-dose cranial radiation (>=40-50 Gy) causes late-onset central (secondary) adrenal insufficiency that can manifest 5 to 15+ years after radiotherapy. Presenting with low cortisol (1.8 mcg/dL) and inappropriately low ACTH (8 pg/mL) in the setting of infection and hypotension confirms acute adrenal crisis secondary to radiation-induced ACTH deficiency. Immediate management requires IV isotonic saline and an emergency IV hydrocortisone bolus (50-100 mg/m2).
option_notes: Correct. Late-onset central adrenal crisis secondary to high-dose cranial radiation requires immediate IV saline and hydrocortisone.
Incorrect. Primary Addison disease features elevated ACTH (>100-1000 pg/mL) and hyperkalemia; ACTH is low here.
Incorrect. Treating with oral fluids alone ignores life-threatening cortisol deficiency and leads to fatal vascular collapse.
Incorrect. Normal potassium and low sodium with hypotension reflect adrenal crisis, not nephrogenic DI.

atlas.etiology: Radiotherapy late effects: Cranial (GH deficiency >=18 Gy, precocious puberty 18-24 Gy, LH/FSH >=30-40 Gy, TSH/ACTH >=40-50 Gy); Neck (hypothyroidism, thyroid cancer); Pelvic/gonadal (azoospermia >=0.1-1.2 Gy, POI >=10-15 Gy). Chemotherapy: Alkylators (cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, procarbazine; CED >=4000-8000 mg/m2 causes germ cell failure).
atlas.epidemiology: Over 80% of childhood cancer patients survive >=5 years; >50-70% of long-term survivors develop at least one chronic endocrine disorder.
atlas.diagnostics: Annual growth velocity, bone age; fasting IGF-1, TSH, free T4; LH, FSH, estradiol/testosterone; 8 AM cortisol or cosyntropin test for cranial RT >=30 Gy; annual thyroid exam; semen analysis; DXA.

therapies.text: rhGH: 0.16-0.24 mg/kg/week SC divided daily (initiate only after >=1 year disease-free remission). Central adrenal insufficiency: Hydrocortisone 8-10 mg/m2/day orally divided TID with mandatory stress dosing. Hypothyroidism: Levothyroxine 1.6-1.8 mcg/kg/day. Hypogonadism: Testosterone or Estradiol pubertal induction protocols.

pillars.label: Clinical Foundations and Care Guidelines
pillars.text: Medical care for transgender and gender diverse (TGD) youth is guided by evidence-based consensus guidelines from the Endocrine Society and the World Professional Association for Transgender Health (WPATH Standards of Care, Version 8). TGD identities are recognized as healthy expressions of human diversity. For prepubertal children (Tanner stage 1), care is strictly non-medical, focusing on social transition (clothing, name, hair, pronouns) and family counseling; medical or endocrine interventions are strictly contraindicated prior to the biological onset of puberty.

pillars.label: Pubertal Suppression with GnRH Agonists
pillars.text: Pubertal suppression represents Phase 1 of medical intervention, initiated once biological puberty has commenced (confirmed Tanner stage 2: breast budding in assigned female at birth [AFAB]; testicular volume >=4 mL in assigned male at birth [AMAB]) with established, persistent gender dysphoria and comprehensive multidisciplinary mental health assessment. First-line therapy consists of long-acting GnRH agonists (GnRHa: depot leuprolide acetate 11.25 mg or 30 mg IM every 12 weeks, or histrelin 50 mg subcutaneous implant). GnRHa therapy is fully reversible; it prevents the development of irreversible, distressing secondary sex characteristics, alleviates dysphoria, and allows time for emotional and cognitive maturity.

pillars.label: Masculinizing Hormone Therapy in Transgender Males
pillars.text: Gender-affirming hormone therapy (GAHT / Phase 2) involves partially irreversible sex steroid administration, typically considered in mid-adolescence (generally >=14-16 years with mature patient assent and parental consent). In transgender males (AFAB), masculinization is achieved with intramuscular or subcutaneous testosterone (cypionate or enanthate) initiated at low doses (25-50 mg every 2 weeks or 12.5-25 mg weekly) and titrated gradually over 2-3 years to adult male maintenance (50-100 mg weekly or 100-200 mg every 2 weeks). Clinical effects include voice deepening, clitoromegaly, facial/body hair growth, cessation of menses, and increased muscle mass. Serum total testosterone is targeted in the adult male physiological range (300-1000 ng/dL).

pillars.label: Feminizing Hormone Therapy in Transgender Females
pillars.text: In transgender females (AMAB), feminization is achieved with 17-beta estradiol (oral micronized 1-2 mg daily titrated to 4-8 mg daily; or transdermal matrix patch 25-50 mcg/day titrated to 100-200 mcg/day) combined with an antiandrogen (spironolactone 50-100 mg twice daily, or continuation of GnRHa). Clinical effects include breast bud development, female fat redistribution, softening of skin, and reduced testicular volume and body hair. Serum estradiol is targeted in the normal adult female follicular/luteal range (100-200 pg/mL) with serum testosterone suppressed into the female range (<50 ng/dL).

pillars.label: Safety Monitoring and Fertility Preservation
pillars.text: Long-term monitoring mandates regular surveillance: (1) Transgender males on testosterone: monitor hemoglobin/hematocrit every 3-6 months (erythrocytosis / polycythemia risk; withhold/reduce dose if hematocrit >50-52%), liver function, lipid profiles, and blood pressure; (2) Transgender females on estradiol/spironolactone: monitor serum potassium (hyperkalemia risk with spironolactone), renal function, prolactin, and venous thromboembolism symptoms; (3) Bone health: pubertal blockers pause bone mineral accrual; optimize calcium (1000-1300 mg/day), vitamin D (>30 ng/mL), and weight-bearing exercise, monitoring with DXA. Crucially, counseling regarding options for fertility preservation (oocyte or sperm cryopreservation) must occur BEFORE starting blockers or hormones.

cards.q: At what pubertal stage is pubertal suppression with GnRH agonists officially recommended in transgender youth?
cards.a: At the confirmed onset of biological puberty, defined as Tanner stage 2 (breast budding in AFAB; testicular volume >=4 mL in AMAB); it is not initiated in prepubertal children (Tanner 1).

cards.q: How does the reversibility of GnRH agonist pubertal suppression compare with gender-affirming sex steroid therapy?
cards.a: GnRH agonist pubertal suppression is fully reversible (endogenous puberty resumes if stopped), whereas gender-affirming sex steroid therapy induces partially irreversible changes (e.g., voice deepening, breast tissue).

cards.q: What hematologic parameter must be monitored regularly in transgender males receiving testosterone therapy to prevent polycythemia?
cards.a: Hemoglobin and hematocrit; testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis, and doses should be reduced if hematocrit exceeds 50-52%.

cards.q: What are the therapeutic serum hormone targets for transgender females undergoing feminizing hormone therapy?
cards.a: Serum 17-beta estradiol maintained between 100 and 200 pg/mL, with serum total testosterone suppressed to <50 ng/dL.

cards.q: What electrolyte abnormality requires routine monitoring in transgender females taking spironolactone as an antiandrogen?
cards.a: Hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium), due to spironolactone's aldosterone-antagonist effect on the distal renal tubule.

cards.q: When must counseling regarding fertility preservation options be conducted with transgender youth and their families?
cards.a: Prior to initiating pubertal suppression (GnRHa) or gender-affirming hormone therapy (estrogen/testosterone), while gametogenesis is still intact.

cards.q: Why is DXA bone mineral density monitoring indicated during prolonged GnRH agonist pubertal suppression?
cards.a: Sex steroids are required for normal pubertal bone mineral accretion; prolonged gonadotropin suppression can delay peak bone mass acquisition, requiring calcium/vitamin D optimization.

mcqs.q: An 8-year-old child assigned female at birth (AFAB) identifies as a boy and experiences distress regarding his gender. On physical examination, he has no breast budding (Tanner stage 1) and no pubic hair. His parents ask whether he should start medications to block puberty. According to Endocrine Society and WPATH consensus guidelines, what is the most appropriate management at this time?
options: Support social transition and psychological counseling, but withhold all medical or hormonal interventions until physical onset of puberty (Tanner 2)
Initiate subcutaneous depot leuprolide immediately to prevent future breast development
Initiate low-dose oral testosterone enanthate 25 mg every 2 weeks
Obtain bone mineral density DXA and pelvic ultrasound
mcqs.explanation: Consensus clinical guidelines from the Endocrine Society and WPATH explicitly state that no medical or hormonal interventions (neither pubertal blockers nor sex steroids) are indicated in prepubertal children (Tanner stage 1). Care for prepubertal youth is entirely social, supportive, and psychological. Pubertal suppression with GnRH agonists is considered only after the physical onset of biological puberty is documented (Tanner stage 2).
option_notes: Correct. Guidelines recommend supporting social transition and deferring medical therapies until Tanner stage 2.
Incorrect. GnRH agonists are not indicated before biological puberty has begun (Tanner 1).
Incorrect. Testosterone is contraindicated in prepubertal children.
Incorrect. Densitometry and pelvic imaging are not indicated for prepubertal supportive care.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old transgender male (assigned female at birth) has been taking intramuscular testosterone cypionate 100 mg every 2 weeks for 12 months. He reports excellent voice deepening, increased muscle mass, and amenorrhea. Routine laboratory monitoring reveals: total testosterone 680 ng/dL (normal male range: 300-1000 ng/dL), AST 24 U/L, ALT 22 U/L, hemoglobin 18.2 g/dL (reference: 12-16 g/dL), and hematocrit 54% (reference: 36-46%). What is the most appropriate clinical action?
options: Reduce the testosterone dosage or increase injection interval and recheck hematocrit in 2-3 months to mitigate erythrocytosis risk
Increase testosterone to 150 mg every 2 weeks to maintain amenorrhea
Perform emergency phlebotomy and start hydroxyurea
Reassure the patient that hematocrit >54% is completely normal for adult males
mcqs.explanation: Testosterone stimulates renal erythropoietin production and bone marrow erythropoiesis. Polycythemia / erythrocytosis (hematocrit >50-52%) is a recognized dose-dependent complication of testosterone therapy that increases blood viscosity and thrombotic risk. When hematocrit exceeds 50-52%, guidelines recommend lowering the testosterone dose, lengthening the interval between injections, or switching from intramuscular injections to transdermal gel to avoid peak levels, rechecking CBC in 2-3 months.
option_notes: Correct. Reducing the testosterone dose or interval lowers erythrocytosis and decreases thrombotic risk.
Incorrect. Increasing the testosterone dose will further elevate hematocrit and increase stroke/thromboembolism risk.
Incorrect. Hydroxyurea is a myelosuppressive chemotherapeutic agent used for polycythemia vera, not drug-induced erythrocytosis.
Incorrect. A hematocrit of 54% is abnormally elevated even in adult males and exceeds safe clinical safety thresholds.

mcqs.q: A 15-year-old transgender female (assigned male at birth) who has been on pubertal suppression with depot leuprolide acetate is initiating gender-affirming feminizing hormone therapy. What is the recommended first-line estrogen agent and route?
options: 17-beta estradiol administered orally (micronized) or transdermally via matrix patch
Oral ethinyl estradiol (synthetic estrogen found in oral contraceptives)
Oral conjugated equine estrogens (Premarin)
Intravenous diethylstilbestrol
mcqs.explanation: Endocrine Society guidelines recommend bioidentical 17-beta estradiol (administered orally as micronized estradiol or transdermally via patch) as the first-line estrogen for gender-affirming feminization. Synthetic estrogens (such as ethinyl estradiol) and conjugated equine estrogens are strictly contraindicated because they carry significantly higher risks of venous thromboembolism, cannot be accurately monitored in serum immunoassays, and promote hepatic coagulopathy.
option_notes: Correct. Bioidentical 17-beta estradiol (oral micronized or transdermal) is the recommended first-line therapy.
Incorrect. Ethinyl estradiol is contraindicated due to unacceptable risks of venous thromboembolism and stroke.
Incorrect. Conjugated equine estrogens carry high thrombotic risk and cannot be accurately monitored by estradiol assays.
Incorrect. Diethylstilbestrol is an obsolete synthetic nonsteroidal estrogen linked to clear cell adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.q: A 16-year-old transgender female taking oral 17-beta estradiol 4 mg daily and spironolactone 100 mg twice daily presents for routine 6-month laboratory surveillance. Which laboratory test is most critical to evaluate for spironolactone-related toxicity?
options: Serum potassium and renal function (BUN/creatinine)
Serum alkaline phosphatase
Total serum bilirubin
Serum ionized magnesium
mcqs.explanation: Spironolactone functions as an androgen receptor antagonist and competitive aldosterone receptor antagonist. By blocking aldosterone in the cortical collecting tubule, it impairs renal potassium excretion. Routine monitoring of serum potassium and electrolytes is essential, especially when titrating doses, to detect hyperkalemia and acute renal insufficiency.
option_notes: Correct. Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing aldosterone antagonist; monitoring potassium and creatinine is mandatory.
Incorrect. Alkaline phosphatase is not the primary biomarker of spironolactone toxicity.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not typically cause acute cholestatic jaundice.
Incorrect. Magnesium is not the primary ion altered by aldosterone antagonism.

mcqs.q: What is the primary rationale for recommending discussion of fertility preservation with transgender adolescents prior to initiating GnRH agonist pubertal suppression or gender-affirming hormone therapy?
mcqs.a: Prolonged pubertal suppression followed directly by gender-affirming hormones can halt or impair gametogenesis (spermatogenesis or oocyte maturation), potentially compromising future biological parenthood
options: Prolonged pubertal suppression followed directly by gender-affirming hormones can halt or impair gametogenesis (spermatogenesis or oocyte maturation), potentially compromising future biological parenthood
Cryopreservation is legally required in all jurisdictions before starting hormones
Sex steroids cause permanent genetic mutations in germ cell DNA
GnRH agonists induce irreversible atrophy of pelvic bones
mcqs.explanation: If pubertal suppression is initiated at Tanner stage 2 and followed seamlessly by gender-affirming sex steroids, gonadal tissue never undergoes the full gametogenic maturation required to produce mature sperm or fertilizable oocytes. Although gametogenesis may recover upon prolonged discontinuation of hormones in some individuals, it is not guaranteed. Comprehensive counseling regarding options for cryopreservation of sperm or oocytes prior to medical interventions is mandatory.
option_notes: Correct. Early suppression and cross-sex hormones arrest gametogenesis; pre-treatment counseling protects future parenthood options.
Incorrect. Cryopreservation is a voluntary clinical decision, not a legal mandate.
Incorrect. Sex steroids do not cause mutagenic alterations in germline DNA.
Incorrect. GnRH agonists do not cause irreversible atrophy of pelvic bones.

atlas.etiology: Gender diversity is a normal aspect of human variation. Gender dysphoria involves clinically significant distress from incongruence between gender identity and assigned sex.
atlas.epidemiology: Approximately 1.4-2.0% of adolescents identify as transgender or gender diverse.
atlas.diagnostics: Multidisciplinary psychological assessment; Tanner staging (stage 2 required for medical pubertal suppression); baseline CBC, CMP, lipid profile, LH, FSH, estradiol/testosterone; DXA bone density.

therapies.text: Depot leuprolide acetate 11.25 mg or 30 mg IM every 12 weeks, or histrelin acetate 50 mg subcutaneous implant annually. Reversible; suppresses LH/FSH to prepubertal levels.

Transgender Males (AFAB): Testosterone cypionate or enanthate 25-50 mg IM/SC every 2 weeks, titrating every 6 months to adult dose of 50-100 mg weekly (or 100-200 mg every 2 weeks); target testosterone 300-1000 ng/dL. Transgender Females (AMAB): Oral micronized 17-beta estradiol 1-2 mg daily titrating to 4-8 mg daily (or transdermal patch 50-200 mcg/day) plus spironolactone 50-100 mg BID; target estradiol 100-200 pg/mL, testosterone <50 ng/dL.

pillars.label: Spectrum and Urgency of Endocrine Emergencies
pillars.text: Pediatric endocrine emergencies are acute, life-threatening derangements of hormone excess, hormone deficiency, or metabolic fuel dysregulation requiring rapid clinical recognition and physiological stabilization. The major entities encompass: (1) Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS); (2) Acute adrenal crisis; (3) Thyroid storm and severe thyrotoxicosis; (4) Severe acute hypocalcemia and hypercalcemic crisis; and (5) Severe symptomatic neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

pillars.label: Acute Adrenal Crisis Resuscitation
pillars.text: Adrenal crisis is a critical medical emergency presenting with refractory hypotension, shock unresponsive to inotropes/vasopressors, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia, and vomiting. Immediate management requires: (1) Rapid intravascular expansion with IV 0.9% normal saline at 20 mL/kg bolus over 20-30 minutes (repeated up to 60 mL/kg if in shock) with 5-10% dextrose to treat hypoglycemia; (2) Immediate intravenous hydrocortisone bolus: 50-100 mg/m2 (or age-based: <3 years: 25 mg; 3-12 years: 50 mg; >12 years: 100 mg). Therapy must NEVER be delayed for confirmatory diagnostic testing; continue hydrocortisone at 50-100 mg/m2/day continuous IV or divided Q6H until hemodynamic stabilization.

pillars.label: Multimodal Management of Thyroid Storm
pillars.text: Thyroid storm is a hypermetabolic emergency characterized by hyperpyrexia (fever >38.5-40°C), tachycardia out of proportion to fever, delirium, cardiac arrhythmias, high-output heart failure, and vomiting/diarrhea. Multimodal treatment must be instituted in an exact sequence: (1) Beta-blocker: IV or oral propranolol (0.01-0.1 mg/kg slow IV or 1-2 mg/kg/day orally) to block adrenergic overdrive; (2) Antithyroid synthesis blocker: Methimazole (0.5-1.0 mg/kg orally or per rectum); (3) Thyroid hormone release blocker: Lugol's strong iodine solution (5-10 drops TID) or potassium iodide (SSKI), administered AT LEAST 1 HOUR AFTER methimazole (to avoid providing substrate for new hormone synthesis); (4) Peripheral conversion blocker: IV hydrocortisone (100 mg/m2/day), which inhibits 5'-deiodinase conversion of T4 to T3; (5) Cooling blankets and acetaminophen (avoid aspirin which displaces thyroid hormone from TBG).

pillars.label: Acute Electrolyte Emergencies: Calcium Disturbances
pillars.text: Severe acute hypocalcemia (tetany, laryngospasm, prolonged QTc, seizures) requires immediate intravenous 10% calcium gluconate at 1-2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg; maximum 1-2 g or 10-20 mL) infused slowly over 10-20 minutes under continuous ECG monitoring (stop if bradycardia occurs).
